And thus, monks, should the Kathina be lifted. A competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha: 'Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me... thus do I take it.'"

Etena [M 2.0146][V 2.0107] ca kathinubbhārena pubbe kataṃ kathinadussadānañattidutiyakammavācaṃ ubbhatanti vadanti, na pana kathinadussadānañattidutiyakammaṃ ubbhataṃ, atha kho atthārakammamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi hi kathinadussadānañattidutiyakammaṃ ubbhataṃ bhaveyya, tāya kammavācāya kathinadussadānassa sijjhanato imāya kathinubbhārakammavācāya taṃ pubbe dinnadussaṃ puna āharāpetabbaṃ siyā, na pañcānisaṃsavigamanaṃ. Yasmā pana imāya kathinubbhārakammavācāya pañcānisaṃsavigamanameva hoti, na pubbe dinnakathinadussassa puna āharāpanaṃ. Tena viññāyati “pañcānisaṃsalābhakāraṇaṃ attharaṇakammameva imāya kathinabbhārakammavācāya uddharīyati, na kathinadussadānañattidutiyakammavācāti, tasmā kathinubbhārakammavācākaraṇato pacchā saṅghassa uppannaṃ cīvaraṃ akālacīvaraṃ hoti, saṅgho pañcānisaṃse na labhati, cīvaraṃ sabbasaṅghikaṃ hutvā āgatāgatassa saṅghassa bhājanīyaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayamattho kathinadussadānañattidutiyakammavācāya ca kathinubbhārakammavācāya ca atthañca adhippāyañca suṭṭhu vinicchinitvā pubbāparaṃ saṃsanditvā paccetabboti.

By this kathina removal, they say that the previously performed formal act of giving the kathina cloth with a motion and one proclamation is removed. However, it is not the formal act of giving the kathina cloth with a motion and one proclamation that is removed; rather, it should be understood that only the act of spreading is removed. For if the formal act of giving the kathina cloth with a motion and one proclamation were removed, then, due to the accomplishment of the giving of the kathina cloth by that formal act, this formal act of kathina removal would have to cause the previously given cloth to be brought back again, and there would not be the cessation of the five benefits. But since by this formal act of kathina removal only the cessation of the five benefits occurs, and not the bringing back of the previously given kathina cloth, it is understood that only the act of spreading—which is the cause for the acquisition of the five benefits—is removed by this formal act of kathina removal, not the formal act of giving the kathina cloth with a motion and one proclamation. Therefore, after performing the formal act of kathina removal, any robe that arises for the Sangha becomes an untimely robe. The Sangha does not obtain the five benefits, and the robe, being common to the entire Sangha, becomes available for distribution to the members of the Sangha as they arrive; this should be understood. This meaning, concerning both the formal act of giving the kathina cloth with a motion and one proclamation and the formal act of kathina removal, should be understood after having carefully determined their meaning and intent and having connected the preceding and subsequent context.

Ettha siyā – kathinubbhāraṃ yācantānaṃ sabbesaṃ kathinubbhāro dātabbo, udāhu ekaccānanti, kiñcettha – yadi tāva sabbesaṃ dātabbo, kathinubbhārakammena pañcānisaṃsavigamanato saṅghassa lābhantarāyo bhaveyya, atha ekaccānaṃ mukholokanaṃ viya siyāti? Yadi kathinatthāramūlakalābhato kathinubbhāramūlakalābho mahanto bhaveyya, tesaṃ yācantānaṃ kathinubbhāro dātabbo. Yadi appako, na dātabbo. Yadi samo, kulappasādatthāya dātabboti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 927) “kīdiso kathinuddhāro dātabbo, kīdiso na dātabboti? Yassa [M 2.0147] atthāramūlako ānisaṃso mahā, ubbhāramūlako appo, evarūpo na dātabbo. Yassa pana atthāramūlako ānisaṃso appo, ubbhāramūlako mahā, evarūpo dātabbo. Samānisaṃsopi saddhāparipālanatthaṃ dātabbovā”ti. Imināpi viññāyati “pañcānisaṃsānaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ atthārakammameva uddharīyati, na kathinadussadānabhūtaṃ ñattidutiyakamma”nti.

Here the question might arise: Should the kathina removal be granted to all who request it, or only to some? And what is the issue here? If it is to be given to all, then due to the cessation of the five benefits by the act of kathina removal, there might be an impediment to the Sangha's gain. But if to some, it might be like showing favoritism. If the gain rooted in the removal of the kathina is greater than the gain rooted in the spreading of the kathina, then the kathina removal should be granted to those who request it. If it is small, it should not be granted. If it is equal, it should be granted for the sake of inspiring faith in families. For so it is stated in the commentary (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 927): "What kind of kathina removal should be given, and what kind should not? If the benefit rooted in the spreading is great and the benefit rooted in the removal is small, such should not be given. But if the benefit rooted in the spreading is small and the benefit rooted in the removal is great, such should be given. Even if the benefits are equal, it should be given to nurture faith." From this, too, it is understood that it is the act of spreading, which is the cause of the five benefits, that is removed—not the formal act with a motion and one proclamation which constitutes the giving of the kathina cloth.

Ānisaṃsakathāyaṃ pañcāti idāni vuccamānā anāmantacārādayo pañca kiriyā. Kappissantīti kappā bhavissanti, anāpattikāraṇā bhavissantīti attho. Anāmantacāroti anāmantetvā caraṇaṃ. Yo hi dāyakehi bhattena nimantito hutvā sabhatto samāno vihāre santaṃ [V 2.0108] bhikkhuṃ anāmantetvā kulesu cārittaṃ āpajjati, tassa bhikkhuno cārittasikkhāpadena pācittiyāpatti hoti, sā āpatti atthatakathinassa na hotīti attho. Tattha cārittasikkhāpadaṃ nāma “yo pana bhikkhu nimantito sabhatto samāno santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā kulesu cārittaṃ āpajjeyya aññatra samayā, pācittiyaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ samayo cīvaradānasamayo cīvarakārasamayo, ayaṃ tattha samayo”ti acelakavagge pañcamasikkhāpadaṃ (pāci. 299-300). Cīvaravippavāsoti tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññatarena vā sabbena vā vinā hatthapāse akatvā aruṇuṭṭhāpanaṃ, evaṃ karotopi dutiyakathinasikkhāpadena āpatti na hotīti adhippāyo. Tattha ca dutiyakathinasikkhāpadaṃ nāma “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ pana bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine ekarattampi ce bhikkhu ticīvarena vippavaseyya aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti āgataṃ nissaggiyesu dutiyasikkhāpadaṃ (pārā. 472).

In the discussion of benefits, 'five' refers to the five actions, such as going without informing, which are now being mentioned. 'Will be permissible' means they will be allowable, that is, they will be causes for non-offense. 'Going without informing' means going without announcing. For if a monk, having been invited by donors for a meal and having eaten, goes on a round among families without informing a monk present in the monastery, that monk incurs a pācittiya offense under the training rule on conduct; that offense does not occur for one for whom the kathina has been spread, this is the meaning. Therein, the training rule on conduct is the fifth training rule in the Acelaka Vagga: "If a monk, having been invited and having eaten, should go on a round among families before or after the meal without asking a monk who is present, except on an appropriate occasion, it is a pācittiya offense. Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the time of giving robes, the time of making robes—this is the appropriate occasion in that case." 'Being apart from a robe' means allowing dawn to break without one of the three robes, or all of them, being within arm's reach. Even when doing so, there is no offense under the second kathina training rule; this is the intent. Therein, the second kathina training rule is the second rule among the rules entailing relinquishment: "When the kathina has been removed for a monk whose robes are completed, if a monk is apart from the set of three robes even for a single night, except with the Sangha's consent, it is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense."

Gaṇabhojananti [M 2.0148] etena gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadena anāpatti vuttāti sambandho. Tattha gaṇabhojanaṃ nāma “amhākaṃ bhattaṃ dethā”ti bhikkhūnaṃ viññattiyā vā “amhākaṃ bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti dāyakānaṃ nimantanena vā akappiyavohārena cattāro vā atirekā vā bhikkhū ekato paṭiggaṇhitvā ekato bhuñjanaṃ. Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ nāma “gaṇabhojane aññatra samayā pācittiyaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ samayo gilānasamayo cīvaradānasamayo cīvarakārasamayo addhānagamanasamayo nāvābhiruhanasamayo mahāsamayo samaṇabhattasamayo, ayaṃ tattha samayo”ti āgataṃ bhojanavagge dutiyasikkhāpadaṃ (pāci. 215). Anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappitaṃ vaṭṭatīti paṭhamakathinasikkhāpadena āpatti na hotīti adhippāyo. Tattha paṭhamakathinasikkhāpadaṃ nāma “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ pana bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabbaṃ, taṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti āgataṃ nissaggiyesu paṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ (pārā. 472). Kathinatthatasīmāyāti upacārasīmaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Matakacīvaranti matassa cīvaraṃ. Tatruppādenāti saṅghasantakena ārāmuyyānakhettavatthuādinā. Yaṃ saṅghikaṃ cīvaraṃ uppajjati, taṃ tesaṃ bhavissatīti iminā cīvarameva kathinatthārakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santakaṃ hoti, tato aññaṃ piṇḍapātabhesajjādikaṃ āgatāgatassa saṅghassa santakaṃ hotīti dasseti.

By 'group meal,' it is stated that there is no offense under the training rule on group meals; this is the connection. Therein, a group meal means four or more monks receiving and eating together, either by the monks' request, 'Give us a meal,' by the donors' invitation, 'Take our meal,' or by an improper transaction. The training rule on group meals is the second training rule in the Bhojana Vagga: "In the case of a group meal, except on an appropriate occasion, it is a pācittiya offense. Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: a time of sickness, a time of giving robes, a time of making robes, a time of traveling, a time of embarking on a boat, a time of a great assembly, a time of a meal for ascetics; this is the appropriate occasion in that case." The intent is that it is permissible to use a robe that has not been determined or shared, and there is no offense under the first kathina training rule. Therein, the first kathina training rule is the first rule among the rules entailing relinquishment: "When the kathina has been removed for a monk whose robes are completed, an extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days. One who exceeds that commits a nissaggiya pācittiya offense." By 'within the boundary where the kathina has been spread,' it is said with reference to the precinct boundary. 'Robe of a deceased monk' means the robe of one who has died. By 'its arising there' means by means of Sangha property such as a monastery, park, field, or land. By 'whatever Sangha robe arises, that will belong to them,' it shows that only the robe becomes the property of the monks who have spread the kathina, while other things like almsfood and medicines become the property of the Sangha as they arrive.

Evaṃ [V 2.0109] aṭṭhaṅgasampanno, lajjī bhikkhu supesalo;

Kareyya kathinatthāraṃ, ubbhārañcāpi sādhukanti.

Thus endowed with eight qualities, a conscientious, amiable monk should spread the kathina and also properly remove it.

Iti vinayasaṅgahasaṃvaṇṇanābhūte vinayālaṅkāre

Thus, in the Vinayālaṅkāra, which is a commentary on the Vinayasaṅgaha.

Kathinatthāravinicchayakathālaṅkāro nāma

The Adornment of the Discourse on the Determination of the Spreading of the Kathina.

Ekūnatiṃsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Ninth Chapter.

30. Garubhaṇḍavinicchayakathā

30. The Discourse on the Determination of Heavy Requisites

227. Evaṃ [M 2.0149] kathinavinicchayaṃ kathetvā idāni garubhaṇḍādivinicchayaṃ dassetuṃ “garubhaṇḍānīti etthā”tiādimāha. Tattha garūti –

227. Having thus spoken on the determination of the Kathina, now, in order to show the determination of heavy requisites and so forth, he begins with the words, “Here, ‘heavy requisites’…”. Therein, ‘garu’—

“Pume ācariyādimhi, garu mātāpitūsupi;

Garu tīsu mahante ca, dujjarālahukesu cā”ti. –

“In the masculine, ‘garu’ refers to teachers and so forth, and also to parents; in all three genders, it refers to what is great, and to things that are hard to digest and not light.”

Vuttesu anekatthesu alahukavācako. Bhaṇḍa-saddo “bhājanādiparikkhāre, bhaṇḍaṃ mūladhanepi cā”ti ettha bhājanādiparikkhārattho hoti. Vacanattho pana garanti uggacchanti uggatā pākaṭā hontīti garūni, bhaḍitabbāni icchitabbānīti bhaṇḍāni, garūni ca tāni bhaṇḍāni cāti garubhaṇḍāni, ārāmādīni vatthūni. Iti ādinā nayena senāsanakkhandhake bhagavatā dassitāni imāni pañca vatthūni garubhaṇḍāni nāmāti yojetabbaṃ.

Among the many meanings stated, it is a term signifying 'not light,' that is, heavy. The word 'bhaṇḍa' is used here in the sense of 'utensils and other requisites,' as in the saying, 'bhaṇḍa means utensils and other requisites, and also capital.' However, the etymological meaning is: 'garūni' are things that are weighty, that are prominent, that become manifest; 'bhaṇḍāni' are things to be desired, to be sought after. Thus, 'garubhaṇḍāni' are those things that are heavy and also requisites, such as monasteries and other objects. In this way, by this method, these five objects shown by the Blessed One in the section on lodgings are to be construed as 'heavy requisites'.

Mañcesu masārakoti mañcapāde vijjhitvā tattha aṭaniyo pavesetvā kato. Bundikābaddhoti aṭanīhi mañcapāde ḍaṃsāpetvā pallaṅkasaṅkhepena kato. Kuḷīrapādakoti assameṇḍakādīnaṃ pādasadisehi pādehi kato. Yo vā pana koci vaṅkapādako, ayaṃ vuccati “kuḷīrapādako”ti. Āhaccapādakoti ayaṃ pana “āhaccapādako nāma mañco aṅge vijjhitvā kato hotī”ti evaṃ parato pāḷiyaṃyeva (pāci. 131) vutto, tasmā aṭaniyo vijjhitvā [V 2.0110] tattha pādasikhaṃ pavesetvā upari āṇiṃ datvā katamañco āhaccapādakoti veditabbo. Pīṭhepi eseva nayo.

Among beds, 'masāraka' refers to a bed made by piercing the bed legs and inserting the rails there. 'Bundikābaddha' refers to a bed made by clamping the bed legs with rails, thus making it in the manner of a couch. 'Kuḷīrapādaka' refers to a bed made with legs resembling those of crabs, rams, and so forth. Or any bed with curved legs is called 'kuḷīrapādaka'. 'Āhaccapādaka' refers to a bed. This, however, is stated in the Pāli text itself later (Pāc. 131) as: “A bed called 'āhaccapādaka' is made by piercing the frame.” Therefore, a bed made by piercing the rails, inserting the leg tips there, and securing them with a nail above, should be understood as an 'āhaccapādaka' bed. The same method applies to stools.

Uṇṇabhisiādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ aññatarāti uṇṇabhisi coḷabhisi vākabhisi tiṇabhisi paṇṇabhisīti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ bhisīnaṃ aññatarā[M 2.0150]. Pañca bhisiyoti pañcahi uṇṇādīhi pūritabhisiyo. Tūlagaṇanāya hi etāsaṃ gaṇanā. Tattha uṇṇaggahaṇena na kevalaṃ eḷakalomameva gahitaṃ, ṭhapetvā pana manussalomaṃ yaṃ kiñci kappiyākappiyamaṃsajātīnaṃ pakkhicatuppadānaṃ lomaṃ, sabbaṃ idha uṇṇaggahaṇeneva gahitaṃ, tasmā channaṃ cīvarānaṃ, channaṃ anulomacīvarānañca aññatarena bhisicchaviṃ katvā taṃ sabbaṃ pakkhipitvā bhisiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Eḷakalomāni pana apakkhipitvā kambalameva catugguṇaṃ vā pañcaguṇaṃ vā pakkhipitvā katāpi uṇṇabhisisaṅkhameva gacchati. Coḷabhisiādīsu yaṃ kiñci navacoḷaṃ vā purāṇacoḷaṃ vā saṃharitvā vā anto pakkhipitvā vā katā coḷabhisi, yaṃ kiñci vākaṃ pakkhipitvā katā vākabhisi, yaṃ kiñci tiṇaṃ pakkhipitvā katā tiṇabhisi, aññatra suddhatamālapattaṃ yaṃ kiñci paṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā katā paṇṇabhisīti veditabbā. Tamālapattaṃ pana aññena missameva vaṭṭati, suddhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Bhisiyā pamāṇaniyamo natthi, mañcabhisi pīṭhabhisi bhūmattharaṇabhisi caṅkamanabhisi pādapuñchanabhisīti etāsaṃ anurūpato sallakkhetvā attano rucivasena pamāṇaṃ kātabbaṃ. Yaṃ panetaṃ uṇṇādipañcavidhatūlampi bhisiyaṃ vaṭṭati, taṃ masūrakepi vaṭṭatīti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha masūraketi cammamayabhisiyaṃ. Etena masūrakaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ hoti.

Among the five types of cushions beginning with wool cushions, it means any one of these five cushions: a wool cushion, a cloth cushion, a bark cushion, a grass cushion, or a leaf cushion. The 'five cushions' are cushions filled with the five materials beginning with wool. Indeed, their classification is by the type of stuffing. Here, by the inclusion of 'wool,' not only sheep's wool is taken, but excluding human hair, any hair of birds and quadrupeds, whether from permissible or impermissible animal species, is all included here by the inclusion of 'wool.' Therefore, it is permissible to make a cushion by using any of the six robes or six supplementary robes as the outer covering and stuffing it entirely with such material. However, even if sheep's wool is not stuffed in, but a blanket folded four or five times is stuffed in, it still falls under the designation of a wool cushion. Among the cloth cushions and so forth, a cloth cushion is made by gathering any new or old cloth and stuffing it inside; a bark cushion is made by stuffing any bark inside; a grass cushion is made by stuffing any grass inside; and a leaf cushion is made by stuffing any leaves, except for pure tamāla leaves—this should be understood. However, tamāla leaves are permissible only when mixed with other materials; they are not permissible alone. There is no fixed size for a cushion. One should determine the appropriate size according to one's preference, considering its suitability for these uses: a bed cushion, a chair cushion, a floor-covering cushion, a cushion for a walkway, or a foot-wiping cushion. However, it is stated in the Kurundī that whatever of these five kinds of stuffing beginning with wool is permissible for a cushion, that is also permissible for a leather cushion. Here, 'masūraka' means a cushion made of hide. By this, it is established that it is permissible to use a leather cushion.

Bimbohane tīṇi tūlāni rukkhatūlaṃ latātūlaṃ poṭakītūlanti. Tattha rukkhatūlanti simbalirukkhādīnaṃ yesaṃ kesañci rukkhānaṃ tūlaṃ. Latātūlanti khīravalliādīnaṃ yāsaṃ kāsañci latānaṃ tūlaṃ. Poṭakītūlanti poṭakītiṇādīnaṃ yesaṃ kesañci tiṇajātikānaṃ antamaso ucchunaḷādīnampi tūlaṃ. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.297) pana “poṭakītūlanti erakatiṇatūla”nti vuttaṃ, etehi tīhi sabbabhūtagāmā saṅgahitā honti. Rukkhavallitiṇajātiyo [M 2.0151] hi muñcitvā añño bhūtagāmo nāma natthi, tasmā yassa kassaci bhūtagāmassa tūlaṃ bimbohane vaṭṭati, bhisiṃ pana pāpuṇitvā sabbampetaṃ “akappiyatūla”nti vuccati na kevalañca bimbohane etaṃ tūlameva, haṃsamorādīnaṃ sabbasakuṇānaṃ, sīhādīnaṃ sabbacatuppadānañca [V 2.0111] lomampi vaṭṭati. Piyaṅgupupphabakuḷapupphādi pana yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ na vaṭṭati. Tamālapattaṃ suddhameva na vaṭṭati, missakaṃ pana vaṭṭati, bhisīnaṃ anuññātaṃ pañcavidhaṃ uṇṇāditūlampi vaṭṭati. Addhakāyikāni pana bimbohanāni na vaṭṭanti. Addhakāyikānīti upaḍḍhakāyappamāṇāni, yesu kaṭito paṭṭhāya yāva sīsaṃ upadahanti ṭhapenti. Sīsappamāṇaṃ pana vaṭṭati, sīsappamāṇaṃ nāma yassa vitthārato tīsu kaṇṇesu dvinnaṃ kaṇṇānaṃ antaraṃ miniyamānaṃ vidatthi ceva caturaṅgulañca hoti, majjhaṭṭhānaṃ muṭṭhiratanaṃ hoti, dīghato pana diyaḍḍharatanaṃ vā dviratanaṃ vāti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ, ayaṃ sīsappamāṇassa ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo, ito uddhaṃ na vaṭṭati, heṭṭhā pana vaṭṭatīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 297) vuttaṃ. Tattha “tīsu kaṇṇesu dvinnaṃ kaṇṇāna”nti pāṭhaṃ upanidhāya bimbohanassa ubhosu antesu ṭhapetabbacoḷakaṃ tikoṇameva karonti ekacce. “Idañca ṭhānaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhāna”nti vadanti.

For pillows, there are three kinds of stuffing: tree stuffing, creeper stuffing, and grass stuffing. Here, 'tree stuffing' means the stuffing from any trees whatsoever, such as the silk-cotton tree and so forth. 'Creeper stuffing' means the stuffing from any creepers whatsoever, such as the milk creeper and so forth. 'Grass stuffing' means the stuffing from any kinds of grass whatsoever, such as poṭakī grass and so forth, even the stuffing from sugarcane stalks and so forth. However, in the Sāratthadīpanī, it is stated: “'Grass stuffing' means eraka grass stuffing.” By these three, all plant life is included, for there is no other plant life apart from trees, creepers, and grasses. Therefore, the stuffing from any plant life whatsoever is permissible for a pillow. However, when it comes to a mattress, all of this is called 'unsuitable stuffing.' Not only this stuffing is permissible for pillows, but also the feathers of all birds, such as swans and peacocks, and the fur of all quadrupeds, such as lions. However, any flowers whatsoever, such as piyaṅgu flowers, bakuḷa flowers, and so forth, are not permissible. Tamāla leaves are not permissible alone, but are permissible when mixed. The five kinds of stuffing beginning with wool, which are permitted for cushions, are also permissible. However, half-body pillows are not permissible. 'Half-body' means those approximately half the body in size, on which one places the body from the waist up to the head. But a head-sized pillow is permissible. A 'head-sized' pillow is one whose width, when measuring the distance between two of the three corners, is a span and four finger-widths, and whose middle part is a fist-measure. In length, it is one and a half cubits or two cubits, as stated in the Kurundī. This is the maximum limit for a head-sized pillow; anything beyond this is not permissible, but anything less is permissible, as stated in the commentary. Here, based on the phrase “between two of the three corners,” some make the cloth to be placed at both ends of the pillow triangular. They say, “This place is the knotting point.”

Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.297) pana “sīsappamāṇaṃ nāma yattha gīvāya saha sakalaṃ sīsaṃ ṭhapetuṃ sakkā, tassa ca muṭṭhiratanaṃ vitthārappamāṇanti dassento ‘vitthārato’tiādimāha. Idañca bimbohanassa ubhosu antesu ṭhapetabbacoḷappamāṇadassanaṃ, tassa vasena bimbohanassa vitthārappamāṇaṃ paricchijjati, taṃ vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā katvā sibbitaṃ yathā koṭito koṭi vitthārato puthulaṭṭhānaṃ muṭṭhiratanappamāṇaṃ hoti, evaṃ sibbitabbaṃ, ito adhikaṃ na vaṭṭati. Taṃ pana antesu ṭhapitacoḷaṃ koṭiyā koṭiṃ āhacca diguṇaṃ kataṃ [M 2.0152] tikaṇṇaṃ hoti, tesu tīsu kaṇṇesu dvinnaṃ kaṇṇānaṃ antaraṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ hoti, majjhaṭṭhānaṃ koṭito koṭiṃ āhacca muṭṭhiratanaṃ hoti, idamassa ukkaṭṭhappamāṇa”nti vuttattā bimbohanassa ubhosu antesu ṭhapetabbacoḷakaṃ pakatiyāyeva tikaṇṇaṃ na hoti, atha kho koṭiyā koṭiṃ āhacca diguṇakatakāleyeva hoti, tasmā taṃ coḷakaṃ vaṭṭaṃ vā hotu caturassaṃ vā, diguṇaṃ katvā miniyamānaṃ tikaṇṇameva hoti, dvinnañca kaṇṇānaṃ antaraṃ caturaṅgulādhikavidatthimattaṃ hoti, tassa ca coḷakassa majjhaṭṭhānaṃ muṭṭhiratanaṃ hoti, tasseva coḷakassa pamāṇena bimbohanassa majjhaṭṭhānampi muṭṭhiratanaṃ hotīti viññāyatīti.

However, in the Vimativinodanī, it is stated: “'Head-sized' means where the entire head, including the neck, can be placed. And showing that its width measurement is a fist-measure, he begins with 'in width' and so forth.” This is a demonstration of the measurement of the cloth to be placed at both ends of the pillow, by which the width measurement of the pillow is determined. It should be made round or square and stitched so that from corner to corner, the widest part in width is the size of a fist-measure. It should be stitched in this way; anything more than this is not permissible. However, that cloth placed at the ends, when folded in half from corner to corner, becomes triangular. Among those three corners, the distance between two corners is a span and four finger-widths. The middle part, from corner to corner, is a fist-measure. Since it is stated, “This is its maximum measurement,” the cloth to be placed at both ends of the pillow is not naturally triangular, but becomes so only when folded in half from corner to corner. Therefore, whether that cloth is round or square, when folded in half and measured, it becomes triangular, and the distance between two corners is a span and four finger-widths. The middle part of that cloth is a fist-measure. By the measurement of that very cloth, it is to be understood that the middle part of the pillow is also a fist-measure.

“Kambalameva…pe… uṇṇabhisisaṅkhameva gacchatīti sāmaññato vuttattā gonakādiakappiyampi uṇṇamayattharaṇaṃ bhisiyaṃ pakkhipitvā sayituṃ vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Masūraketi cammamayabhisiyaṃ, cammamayaṃ pana bimbohanaṃ tūlapuṇṇampi na vaṭṭatī”ti ca vimativinodaniyaṃ [V 2.0112] (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.297) vuttaṃ. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.297) pana “sīsappamāṇanti yattha galavāṭakato paṭṭhāya sabbasīsaṃ upadahanti, taṃ sīsappamāṇaṃ hoti, tañca ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato tiriyaṃ muṭṭhiratanaṃ hotīti dassetuṃ ‘yattha vitthārato tīsu kaṇṇesū’tiādimāha. Majjhaṭṭhānaṃ muṭṭhiratanaṃ hotīti bimbohanassa majjhaṭṭhānaṃ tiriyato muṭṭhiratanappamāṇaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Arañjaroti bahuudakagaṇhanakā mahācāṭi. Jalaṃ gaṇhituṃ alanti arañjaro, vaṭṭacāṭi viya hutvā thokaṃ dīghamukho majjhe paricchedaṃ dassetvā katoti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyanti ajjhāhārasambandho.

Since it is generally stated, 'Just a blanket... or it is counted as a woolen mattress,' it should be understood that it is permissible to sleep on even an unallowable woolen covering, such as one made of goat hair, by placing it in a cushion. And in the Vimativinodanī it is stated: 'Masūraka means a leather cushion; but a leather bolster, even if filled with cotton, is not permissible.' In the Sāratthadīpanī, however, it is stated: '‘The size of the head’ means where one places the entire head, starting from the base of the neck; that is the measure of the head. And to show that its maximum transverse measurement is a fist’s breadth, it is said, ‘where the width is in three corners,’ and so on. ‘The middle part of the bolster is a fist’s breadth’ means the middle section of the bolster is a fist’s breadth across.’ An arañjara is a large pot that holds much water. It is called an arañjara because it is capable of holding water. It is stated in the glosses that it is made like a round pot, with a slightly elongated mouth, showing a division in the middle. The connection 'This has been stated in the commentary' is by supplying the ellipsis.

Dvisaṅgahāni [M 2.0153] dve hontīti dve paṭhamadutiyaavissajjiyāni “ārāmo ārāmavatthū”ti ca “vihāro vihāravatthū”ti ca vuttadvedvevatthusaṅgahāni honti. Tatiyaṃ avissajjiyaṃ “mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bimbohana”nti vuttacatuvatthusaṅgahaṃ hoti. Catutthaṃ avissajjiyaṃ “lohakumbhī lohabhāṇakaṃ lohavārako lohakaṭāhaṃ vāsi pharasu kuṭhārī kudālo nikhādana”nti vuttanavakoṭṭhāsavantaṃ hoti. Pañcamaṃ avissajjiyaṃ “valli veḷu muñjaṃ pabbajaṃ tiṇaṃ mattikā dārubhaṇḍaṃ mattikābhaṇḍa”nti vuttaaṭṭhabhedanaṃ aṭṭhapabhedavantaṃ hotīti yojanā. Pañcanimmalalocanoti maṃsacakkhudibbacakkhudhammacakkhubuddhacakkhusamantacakkhūnaṃ vasena nimmalapañcalocano.

‘There are two with a twofold inclusion’ means that the first and second unalienable items are inclusions of two items each, as stated: ‘a monastery and monastery land’ and ‘a dwelling and dwelling land.’ The third unalienable item is an inclusion of four things, as stated: ‘a bed, a chair, a mattress, a bolster.’ The fourth unalienable item has nine parts, as stated: ‘an iron pot, an iron vessel, an iron pan, an iron cauldron, an adze, an axe, a hatchet, a spade, and a digging tool.’ The fifth unalienable item has eight divisions, as stated: ‘creepers, bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, grass, clay, wooden goods, and earthenware goods’—this is the construction. ‘One with five stainless eyes’ means one with five stainless eyes by way of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the Dhamma eye, the Buddha eye, and the universal eye.

Senāsanakkhandhake avissajjiyaṃ kīṭāgirivatthusmiṃ avebhaṅgiyanti ettha “senāsanakkhandhake gāmakāvāsavatthusmiṃ avissajjiyaṃ kīṭāgirivatthusmiṃ avebhaṅgiya”nti vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Dvinnampi vatthūnaṃ senāsanakkhandhake āgatattā. Senāsanakkhandhaketi ayaṃ sāmaññādhāro. Gāmakāvāsavatthusmiṃ kīṭāgirivatthusminti visesādhāro. Ayamattho pāḷiṃ oloketvā paccetabbo. Teneva hi samantapāsādikāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 321) “senāsanakkhandhake”ti avatvā “idha”icceva vuttaṃ, idhāti iminā gāmakāvāsavatthuṃ dasseti, kīṭāgirivatthu pana sarūpato dassitameva. Sāmaññādhāro pana taṃsaṃvaṇṇanābhāvato avuttopi sijjhatīti na vuttoti viññāyati.

Regarding 'the unalienable property in the chapter on lodgings, and the non-divisible property in the Kīṭāgiri matter,' here it should be stated: 'the unalienable property in the chapter on lodgings concerning the village residence matter, and the non-divisible property in the Kīṭāgiri matter.' Why? Because both matters are included in the chapter on lodgings. 'The chapter on lodgings' is the general basis. 'Regarding the village residence matter and the Kīṭāgiri matter' are the specific bases. This meaning should be understood by examining the Pāli text. Indeed, in the Samantapāsādikā (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 321), instead of saying 'in the chapter on lodgings,' it simply states 'here.' 'Here' refers to the village residence matter, while the Kīṭāgiri matter is shown by its own form. The general basis, however, is understood to be established even though unstated, due to the absence of its detailed explanation.

228. Thāvarena ca thāvaraṃ, garubhaṇḍena ca garubhaṇḍanti ettha pañcasu koṭṭhāsesu purimadvayaṃ thāvaraṃ, pacchimattayaṃ garubhaṇḍanti veditabbaṃ. Samakameva detīti ettha ūnakaṃ dentampi vihāravatthusāmantaṃ [V 2.0113] gahetvā dūrataraṃ dukkhagopaṃ vissajjetuṃ vaṭṭatīti [M 2.0154] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vakkhati hi “bhikkhūnañce mahagghataraṃ…pe… sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Jānāpetvāti bhikkhusaṅghassa jānāpetvā, apaloketvāti attho. Nanu tumhākaṃ bahutaraṃ rukkhāti vattabbanti idaṃ sāmikesu attano bhaṇḍassa mahagghataṃ ajānitvā dentesu taṃ ñatvā theyyacittena gaṇhato avahāro hotīti vuttaṃ. Vihārena vihāro parivattetabboti savatthukena aññesaṃ bhūmiyaṃ katapāsādādinā, avatthukena vā savatthukaṃ parivattetabbaṃ, avatthukaṃ pana avatthukeneva parivattetabbaṃ kevalaṃ pāsādassa bhūmito athāvarattā. Evaṃ thāvaresupi thāvaravibhāgaṃ ñatvāva parivattetabbaṃ.

228. Regarding 'what is stationary with what is stationary, and what is heavy with what is heavy,' here, among the five categories, the first two should be understood as stationary, and the last three as heavy goods. Regarding 'one gives equally,' here, it should be understood that even when giving less, it is acceptable to take into account the land near the monastery and give away something far away and difficult to guard. For it will be said: 'If something more valuable is given to the monks... it is permissible to accept.' 'Having informed' means having informed the community of monks; the meaning is 'having obtained consent.' The saying, 'But you have more trees!'—this is said to be misappropriation when owners give their goods without knowing their high value, and one, knowing this, takes them with thieving intent. 'A monastery should be exchanged for a monastery'—this means a monastery with a site, such as a mansion built on another's land, may be exchanged for one without a site, or one without a site for one with a site. However, one without a site should be exchanged only for one without a site, because a mansion, apart from its land, is not an immovable item. Similarly, even with stationary items, one should make an exchange only after understanding the distinctions among stationary items.

“Kappiyamañcā sampaṭicchitabbāti iminā suvaṇṇādivicittaṃ akappiyamañcaṃ ‘saṅghassā’ti vuttepi sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. ‘Vihārassa demā’ti vutte saṅghassa vaṭṭati, na puggalassa khettādi viyāti daṭṭhabba”nti vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.321) vuttaṃ. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷvagga 3.321) pana “kappiyamañcā sampaṭicchitabbāti ‘saṅghassa demā’ti dinnaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sace pana ‘vihārassa demā’ti vadanti, suvaṇṇarajatamayādiakappiyamañcepi sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Na kevalaṃ…pe… parivattetuṃ vaṭṭantīti iminā athāvarena thāvarampi athāvarampi parivattetuṃ vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Thāvarena athāvarameva hi parivattetuṃ na vaṭṭati. “Akappiyaṃ vā mahagghaṃ kappiyaṃ vāti ettha akappiyaṃ nāma suvaṇṇamayamañcādi akappiyabhisibimbohanāni ca. Mahagghaṃ kappiyaṃ nāma dantamayamañcādi, pāvārādikappiyaattharaṇādīni cā”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ vuttaṃ, vimativinodaniyaṃ pana “akappiyaṃ vāti āsandiādi, pamāṇātikkantaṃ bimbohanādi ca. Mahagghaṃ kappiyaṃ vāti suvaṇṇādivicittaṃ kappiyavohārena dinna”nti vuttaṃ.

By 'allowable couches should be accepted,' it shows that even if an unallowable couch adorned with gold, etc., is offered with the words 'for the Sangha,' it is not proper to accept it. However, if it is said, 'We give this to the monastery,' it is permissible for the Sangha, but not for an individual, as in the case of fields and the like. This is explained in the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.321). The Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.321), however, states: 'The phrase 'It is proper to accept allowable couches' refers to what is given with the words 'we give to the Sangha'. But if they say, 'We give this to the monastery,' even unallowable couches like those made of gold or silver may be accepted.' Not only that… but also… 'It is permissible to exchange' indicates that with what is movable, both what is immovable and what is movable may be exchanged. Indeed, it is not permissible to exchange an immovable item for a movable item. In the Sāratthadīpanī, it is said: 'Here, 'unallowable' refers to items like couches made of gold and unallowable cushions and bolsters. 'Expensive but allowable' refers to items like couches decorated with ivory and allowable coverings such as those made of silk.' The Vimativinodanī, however, states: ''Unallowable' refers to high seats and oversized bolsters, and the like. 'Expensive but allowable' refers to items adorned with gold, etc., given under the guise of being allowable.'

229. “Kāḷaloha [M 2.0155] …pe… bhājetabbo”ti vuttattā vaṭṭakaṃsalohamayampi bhājanaṃ puggalikampi sampaṭicchitumpi pariharitumpi vaṭṭati puggalānaṃ pariharitabbasseva bhājetabbattāti vadanti, taṃ upari “kaṃsalohavaṭṭalohabhājanavikati saṅghikaparibhogena vā gihivikaṭā vā vaṭṭatī”tiādikena mahāpaccarivacanena virujjhati. Imassa hi “vaṭṭalohakaṃsalohānaṃ yena kenaci kato sīhaḷadīpe pādaggaṇhanako bhājetabbo”ti vuttassa mahāaṭṭhakathāvacanassa paṭikkhepāya taṃ mahāpaccarivacanaṃ pacchā dassitaṃ, tasmā vaṭṭalohakaṃsalohamayaṃ yaṃ kiñci pādaggaṇhanakavārakampi upādāya abhājanīyameva, gihīhi dīyamānampi puggalassa sampaṭicchitumpi [V 2.0114] na vaṭṭati. Pārihāriyaṃ na vaṭṭatīti pattādiparikkhāraṃ viya sayameva paṭisāmetvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Gihisantakaṃ viya ārāmikādayo ce sayameva gopetvā viniyogakāle ānetvā paṭidenti, paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, “paṭisāmetvā bhikkhūnaṃ dethā”ti vattumpi vaṭṭatīti.

229. Because it is said, 'Black iron... should be broken up,' some say that even a vessel made of bronze or round metal, even if it is personal, is permissible to accept and to use, on the grounds that what is for the use of individuals is itself to be broken up. This is contradicted by the great counter-statement above, which states: 'A modified vessel of bronze or round metal is permissible either for the Sangha’s use or as fashioned by laypeople.' For this great counter-statement was later shown in order to refute this statement of the Great Commentary, which says: 'Any foot-scraper made of round metal or bronze in the island of Sri Lanka should be broken up.' Therefore, any object made of round metal or bronze, up to and including a foot-scraper or bowl-stand, is indeed not to be broken up; even if given by laypeople, it is not permissible for an individual to accept it. 'It is not permissible as personal property' means that, like a bowl and other requisites, it is not permissible to put it away oneself and use it. If monastery attendants and others guard it themselves as if it were laypeople’s property, and bring it and give it back at the time of use, it is permissible to use it. It is also permissible to say, 'Having put it away, give it to the monks.'

Paṇṇasūci nāma lekhanīti vadanti. Attanā laddhānipītiādinā paṭiggahaṇe doso natthi, pariharitvā paribhogova āpattikaroti dasseti. Yathā cettha, evaṃ upari bhājanīyavāsiādīsu attano santakesupi.

A paṇṇasūci, they say, is a writing instrument. By the phrase beginning with 'even if obtained by oneself,' it shows that there is no fault in accepting it, but that using it after carrying it about incurs an offense. Just as here, so too in the case of divisible items such as an axe and others mentioned above, even if they are one's own.

Anāmāsampīti suvaṇṇādimayampi, sabbaṃ taṃ āmasitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

Even if it is something not to be touched, such as an item made of gold and the like, it is permissible to touch and use all of it.

Upakkhareti upakaraṇe. Sikharaṃ nāma yena paribbhamantā chindanti. Pattabandhako nāma pattassa gaṇṭhiādikārako. “Paṭimānaṃ suvaṇṇādipattakārako”tipi vadanti.

Upakkhara means an implement. A sikhara is that by which they cut while it revolves. A pattabandhaka is one who makes knots and the like for a bowl. Some also say, 'A paṭimāna is a maker of bowls of gold and the like.'

“Aḍḍhabāhūti kapparato paṭṭhāya yāva aṃsakūṭa”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. “Aḍḍhabāhu nāma vidatthicaturaṅgulantipi vadantī”ti [M 2.0156] sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.321) vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyampi (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 321) “aḍḍhabāhūti kapparato paṭṭhāya yāva aṃsakūṭanti likhita”nti vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.321) pana “aḍḍhabāhuppamāṇā nāma aḍḍhabāhumattā, aḍḍhabyāmamattātipi vadantī”ti vuttaṃ. Yottānīti cammarajjukā. Tatthajātakāti saṅghikabhūmiyaṃ jātā.

'A half-arm' means from the elbow up to the shoulder-peak,' it is said in the commentaries on the points of knots. 'A half-arm is also said to be a span and four finger-breadths,' it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.321). In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 321) too it is said, ''A half-arm' means from the elbow up to the shoulder-peak,' as it is written.' In the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.321), however, it is said, ''Of the measure of a half-arm' means the size of a half-arm; some also say the size of half a fathom.' Yottāni means leather straps. Tatthajātaka means grown on that land, that is, on Sangha land.

“Aṭṭhaṅgulasūcidaṇḍamattoti dīghaso aṭṭhaṅgulamatto pariṇāhato paṇṇasūcidaṇḍamatto”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī.. Cūḷavagga 3.321) vimativinodaniyaṃ pana (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.321) “aṭṭhaṅgulasūcidaṇḍamattoti saradaṇḍādisūciākāratanudaṇḍakamattopī”ti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇoti dīghato aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇo. Rittapotthakopīti alikhitapotthakopi, idañca paṇṇappasaṅgena vuttaṃ.

“'The size of an eight-aṅgula needle-handle' means 'eight aṅgulas in length, and in thickness the size of a leaf-stylus handle,'” as stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.321). However, the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.321) says, “'The size of an eight-aṅgula needle-handle' means 'the measure of a thin handle in the shape of a needle, like an arrow shaft, etc.'” “'Of the measure of eight aṅgulas'” means “eight aṅgulas in length.” “'Also a blank book'” means “also an unwritten book,” and this is said in connection with leaves.

Āsandikoti caturassapīṭhaṃ vuccati “uccakampi āsandika”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato[V 2.0115]. Ekatobhāgena dīghapīṭhameva hi aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ vaṭṭati, caturassāsandiko pana pamāṇātikkantopi vaṭṭatīti veditabbo. Sattaṅgo nāma tīsu disāsu apassayaṃ katvā katamañco, ayampi pamāṇātikkantopi vaṭṭati. Bhaddapīṭhanti vettamayaṃ pīṭhaṃ vuccati. Pīṭhikāti pilotikabandhaṃ pīṭhameva. Eḷakapādapīṭhaṃ nāma dārupaṭikāya uparipāde ṭhapetvā bhojanaphalakaṃ viya katapīṭhaṃ vuccati. Āmaṇḍakavaṇṭakapīṭhaṃ nāma āmalakākārena yojitabahaupādapīṭhaṃ. Imāni tāva pāḷiyaṃ āgatapīṭhāni. Dārumayaṃ pana sabbampi pīṭhaṃ vaṭṭati.

An āsandika is called a square seat. From the statement 'even a high āsandika' (Cūḷavagga 297), it is to be understood that while a long seat is only permissible with eight-aṅgula legs, a square āsandika, on the other hand, is permissible even if it exceeds the measure. A sattaṅga is a couch made with backrests on three sides; this too is permissible even if it exceeds the measure. A bhaddapīṭha is called a seat made of cane. A pīṭhikā is a seat bound with cloth strips. An eḷakapādapīṭha is called a seat made like a dining board, with its legs placed on top of a wooden plank. An āmaṇḍakavaṇṭakapīṭha is a seat with many legs fitted in the shape of myrobalan fruit stalks. These are the seats that appear in the Pāli Canon. However, any seat made of wood is permissible.

“Ghaṭṭanaphalakaṃ nāma yattha ṭhapetvā rajitacīvaraṃ hatthena ghaṭṭenti. Ghaṭṭanamuggaro nāma anuvātādighaṭṭanatthaṃ katoti vadantī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.321) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.321) “ghaṭṭanaphalakaṃ ghaṭṭanamuggaroti idaṃ rajitacīvaraṃ ekasmiṃ maṭṭhe daṇḍamuggare [M 2.0157] veṭhetvā ekassa maṭṭhaphalakassa upari ṭhapetvā upari aparena maṭṭhaphalakena nikkujjitvā eko upari akkamitvā tiṭṭhati, dve janā upariphalakaṃ dvīsu koṭīsu gahetvā aparāparaṃ ākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanaṃ karonti, etaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Hatthe ṭhapāpetvā hatthena paharaṇaṃ pana niṭṭhitarajanassa cīvarassa allakāle kātabbaṃ, idaṃ pana phalakamuggarehi ghaṭṭanaṃ sukkhakāle thaddhabhāvavimocanatthanti daṭṭhabba”nti vuttaṃ. “Ambaṇanti phalakehi pokkharaṇīsadisakatapānīyabhājanaṃ. Rajanadoṇīti yattha pakkarajanaṃ ākiritvā ṭhapentī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ pana “ambaṇanti ekadoṇikanāvāphalakehi pokkharaṇīsadisaṃ kataṃ. Pānīyabhājanantipi vadanti. Rajanadoṇīti ekadārunāva kataṃ rajanabhājanaṃ. Udakadoṇīti ekadārunāva kataṃ udakabhājana”nti vuttaṃ.

'A rubbing-board' is a board on which they place a dyed robe and rub it with the hand. 'A rubbing-mallet,' they say, is made for the purpose of rubbing away wrinkles and the like.' This is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.321). In the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.321) it is said: 'Regarding the rubbing-board and rubbing-mallet: this refers to when they wrap a dyed robe around a smooth wooden mallet, place it on a smooth board, cover it with another smooth board placed upside down, and one person stands on top treading on it, while two people, holding the upper board at its two ends, pull it back and forth. This is what is meant. Beating it with the hand after placing it on the hand, however, should be done to a completely dyed robe while it is still wet. But this rubbing with boards and mallets, it should be understood, is for the purpose of releasing its stiffness when it is dry.' 'An ambaṇa is a water vessel made with planks to resemble a lotus pond. A rajanadoṇī is a trough where they pour the boiled dye and keep it,' it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī. In the Vimativinodanī, however, it is said: 'An ambaṇa is made with planks from a single-trough boat to resemble a lotus pond. They also call it a water vessel. A rajanadoṇī is a dye vessel made from a single-log boat. An udakadoṇī is a water vessel made from a single-log boat.'

“Bhūmattharaṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti akappiyacammaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paccattharaṇagatikanti iminā mañcapīṭhepi attharituṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Pāvārādipaccattharaṇampi garubhaṇḍanti eke. Noti apare, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabba”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.321) vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 321) pana “daṇḍamuggaro nāma ‘yena rajitacīvaraṃ pothenti, tampi garubhaṇḍamevā’ti vuttattā, ‘paccattharaṇagatika’nti vuttattā ca api-saddena pāvārādipaccattharaṇaṃ sabbaṃ garubhaṇḍamevāti vadanti. Eteneva suttena aññathā atthaṃ vatvā pāvārādipaccattharaṇaṃ na garubhaṇḍaṃ, bhājanīyameva, senāsanatthāya dinnapaccattharaṇameva garubhaṇḍanti vadanti. Upaparikkhitabba”nti vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.321) pana [V 2.0116] “bhūmattharaṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti akappiyacammaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha bhūmattharaṇasaṅkhepena sayitumpi vaṭṭatiyeva. Paccattharaṇagatikanti iminā mañcādīsu [M 2.0158] attharitabbaṃ mahācammaṃ eḷakacammaṃ nāmāti dassetī”ti vuttaṃ. Chattamuṭṭhipaṇṇanti tālapaṇṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pattakaṭāhanti pattapacanakaṭāhaṃ. Gaṇṭhikāti cīvaragaṇṭhikā. Vidhoti kāyabandhanavidho.

'It is permissible to make a ground covering' is said with reference to an unallowable hide. By the phrase 'of the nature of a coverlet,' it indicates that it is also permissible to spread it on a couch or a seat. Some say that coverlets such as cloaks are also heavy items. Others say they are not; this should be accepted after investigation,' it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.321). In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 321), however, it is said: 'Because it is stated, 'A staff or club, that with which they beat a dyed robe, that too is indeed a heavy item,' and because it is stated to be 'of the nature of a coverlet,' some say that by the word 'api' (also), all coverlets such as cloaks are indeed heavy items. By this very rule, others, stating the meaning differently, say that coverlets such as cloaks are not heavy items, but are indeed divisible; only a coverlet given for the sake of lodging is a heavy item. This should be examined.' In the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.321), however, it is said: ''It is permissible to make a ground covering' is said with reference to an unallowable hide. In that case, it is indeed permissible even to sleep on it in its capacity as a ground covering. By the phrase 'of the nature of a coverlet,' it shows that what is meant is a large hide, namely a sheep's hide, to be spread on couches and so on.' 'Leaf for an umbrella handle' is said with reference to a palm leaf. 'Bowl-pan' means a pan for preparing a bowl. 'Gaṇṭhikā' is a robe-tie. 'Vidho' is a type of body-band.

Idāni vinayatthamañjūsāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. abhi. ṭī. dubbalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) āgatanayo vuccate – ārāmo nāma pupphārāmo vā phalārāmo vā. Ārāmavatthu nāma tesaṃyeva ārāmānaṃ atthāya paricchinditvā ṭhapitokāso. Tesu vā ārāmesu vinaṭṭhesu tesaṃ porāṇakabhūmibhāgo. Vihāro nāma yaṃ kiñci pāsādādisenāsanaṃ. Vihāravatthu nāma tassa patiṭṭhānokāso. Mañco nāma masārako bundikābaddho kuḷīrapādako āhaccapādakoti imesaṃ pubbe vuttānaṃ catunnaṃ mañcānaṃ aññataro. Pīṭhaṃ nāma masārakādīnaṃyeva catunnaṃ pīṭhānaṃ aññataraṃ. Bhisi nāma uṇṇabhisiādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ bhisīnaṃ aññataraṃ. Bimbohanaṃ nāma rukkhatūlalatātūlapoṭakītūlānaṃ aññatarena puṇṇaṃ. Lohakumbhī nāma kāḷalohena vā tambalohena vā yena kenaci katakumbhī. Lohabhāṇakādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha pana bhāṇakanti arañjaro vuccati. Vārakoti ghaṭo. Kaṭāhaṃ kaṭāhameva. Vāsiādīsu valliādīsu ca duviññeyyaṃ nāma natthi…pe….

Now, the method found in the Vinayatthamañjūsā (the new subcommentary to the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, in the explanation of the weak training rules) is stated: An ārāma is a flower park or a fruit park. An ārāmavatthu is the site demarcated and set aside for the purpose of those very parks; or, if those parks are ruined, it is their former portion of land. A vihāra is any lodging, such as a mansion. A vihāravatthu is the site for its foundation. A mañca (couch) is any one of the four types of couches previously mentioned: a masāraka, a bundikābaddha, a kuḷīrapādaka, or an āhaccapādaka. A pīṭha (seat) is any one of the four types of seats, such as the masāraka, etc. A bhisi (mattress) is any one of the five types of mattresses, such as one of wool, etc. A bimbohana (pillow) is one filled with either tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, or cloth-cotton. A lohakumbhī (metal pot) is a pot made of any metal, whether black metal (iron) or red metal (copper). The same method applies to a metal vessel (lohabhāṇaka), etc. Here, however, a bhāṇaka is called an arañjara (a large water jar). A vāraka is a pot. A kaṭāha is just a kaṭāha (a pan). Regarding items such as an adze (vāsi) or a creeper (valli), there is nothing difficult to understand... and so on.

Tattha thāvarena thāvaranti vihāravihāravatthunā ārāmaārāmavatthuṃ vihāravihāravatthuṃ. Itarenāti athāvarena, pacchimarāsittayenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Akappiyenāti suvaṇṇamayamañcādinā ceva akappiyabhisibimbohanehi ca. Mahagghakappiyenāti dantamayamañcādinā ceva pāvārādinā ca. Itaranti athāvaraṃ. Kappiyaparivattanena parivattetunti yathā akappiyaṃ na hoti, evaṃ parivattetuṃ…pe… evaṃ [M 2.0159] tāva thāvarena thāvaraparivattanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Itarena itaraparivattane pana mañcapīṭhaṃ mahantaṃ vā hotu, khuddakaṃ vā, antamaso caturaṅgulapādakaṃ gāmadārakehi paṃsvāgārakesu kīḷantehi katampi saṅghassa dinnakālato paṭṭhāya garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti…pe… satagghanakena vā sahassagghanakena vā mañcena aññaṃ mañcasatampi labhati, parivattetvā gahetabbaṃ. Na kevalaṃ mañcena mañcoyeva, ārāmaārāmavatthuvihāravihāravatthupīṭhabhisibimbohanānipi parivattetuṃ vaṭṭanti. Esa nayo pīṭhabhisibimbohanesupi.

Therein, “with the immovable for the immovable” (thāvarena thāvaraṃ) means exchanging a monastery or monastery site for a park or park site, or a monastery or monastery site for another monastery or monastery site. “By the other” (itarena) means by what is not immovable; it is said to be by the latter three groups. “With what is improper” (akappiyena) means with a golden couch, etc., and with improper cushions and pillows. “With what is highly valuable and proper” (mahagghakappiyena) means with an ivory couch, etc., and with fine cloths, etc. “The other” (itaraṃ) means what is not immovable. “By exchanging with what is allowable, one should exchange it” (kappiyaparivattanena parivattetuṃ) means to exchange it so that what is improper ceases to be so… Thus, firstly, the exchange of the immovable for the immovable should be understood. Now, as for the exchange of the other for the other, whether a bed or a bench is large or small—even one with four-aṅgula legs made by village boys playing in dust-houses—from the moment it is given to the Saṅgha, it becomes valuable property… Even if one obtains a hundred beds with a bed worth a hundred or a thousand, it should be taken after exchanging. Not only a bed for a bed, but a park or park site, a monastery or monastery site, benches, cushions, and pillows may also be exchanged. This same method applies to benches, cushions, and pillows as well.

Kāḷalohatambalohakaṃsalohavaṭṭalohānanti ettha kaṃsalohaṃ vaṭṭalohañca kittimalohaṃ. Tīṇi hi [V 2.0117] kittimalohāni kaṃsalohaṃ vaṭṭalohaṃ hārakūṭanti. Tattha tiputambe missetvā kataṃ kaṃsalohaṃ. Sīsatambe missetvā kataṃ vaṭṭalohaṃ. Rasatambe missetvā kataṃ hārakūṭaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “kaṃsalohaṃ vaṭṭalohañca kittimaloha”nti. Tato atirekanti tato atirekagaṇhanako. Sārakoti majjhe makuḷaṃ dassetvā mukhavaṭṭivitthataṃ katvā piṭṭhito nāmetvā kātabbaṃ ekaṃ bhājanaṃ. Sarāvantipi vadanti. Ādi-saddena kañcanakādīnaṃ gihiupakaraṇānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tāni hi khuddakānipi garubhaṇḍāneva gihiupakaraṇattā. Pi-saddena pageva mahantānīti dasseti, imāni pana bhājanīyāni bhikkhupakaraṇattāti adhippāyo. Yathā ca etāni, evaṃ kuṇḍikāpi bhājanīyā. Vakkhati hi “yathā ca mattikābhaṇḍe, evaṃ lohabhaṇḍepi kuṇḍikā bhājanīyakoṭṭhāsameva bhajatī”ti. Saṅghikaparibhogenāti āgantukānaṃ vuḍḍhatarānaṃ datvā paribhogena. Gihivikaṭāti gihīhi vikatā paññattā, attano vā santakakaraṇena virūpaṃ katā. Puggalikaparibhogena na vaṭṭatīti āgantukānaṃ adatvā attano santakaṃ viya gahetvā [M 2.0160] paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Pipphalikoti kattari. Ārakaṇṭakaṃ sūcivedhakaṃ. Tāḷaṃ yantaṃ. Kattarayaṭṭhivedhako kattarayaṭṭhivalayaṃ. Yathā tathā ghanakataṃ lohanti lohavaṭṭi lohaguḷo lohapiṇḍi lohacakkalikanti evaṃ ghanakataṃ lohaṃ. Khīrapāsāṇamayānīti mudukakhīravaṇṇapāsāṇamayāni.

Black iron, copper, bronze, and round iron—here, bronze and round iron are known as kittimaloha. Indeed, there are three kinds of kittimaloha: bronze, round iron, and hārakūṭa. Among these, bronze is made by mixing tin and copper. Round iron is made by mixing lead and copper. Hārakūṭa is made by mixing mercury and copper. Hence, it is said, "bronze and round iron are kittimaloha." Beyond that: meaning one who takes excessively. Sāraka: a vessel that should be made by showing a bud-like shape in the middle, widening the mouth, and bending it from the back. Some also call it sarāva. By the term 'etc.' (ādi-saddena) are included household utensils such as golden bowls. Indeed, even small ones are heavy goods because they are household utensils. The word 'also' (pi-saddena) indicates that this is all the more so for large items; however, the intention here is that these are vessels to be distributed as requisites for monks. Just as these, so too is the kuṇḍikā (water pot) to be distributed. For it will be said: "Just as in the case of earthenware, so too in the case of metalware, the kuṇḍikā belongs to the category of things to be distributed." By communal use: by giving to senior visiting monks for their use. Rejected by householders: made unsuitable or designated as such by householders, or made unsightly by making them one's own property. Not permissible for personal use: it is not permissible to take and use them as if they were one's own property without offering them to visiting monks. Pipphalikā: a knife. Ārakaṇṭaka: a needle for piercing. Tāḷa: a lock. Kattarayaṭṭhivedhako: a ring for a knife handle. Hardened iron: iron rods, iron balls, iron lumps, iron discs—thus, any iron that has been hardened. Made of milk-stone: made of soft, milk-colored stone.

Gihivikaṭānipi na vaṭṭanti anāmāsattā. Pi-saddena pageva saṅghikaparibhogena vā puggalikaparibhogena vāti dasseti. Senāsanaparibhogo pana sabbakappiyo, tasmā jātarūpādimayā sabbāpi senāsanaparikkhārā āmāsā. Tenāha “senāsanaparibhoge panā”tiādi.

Even things made unsuitable by householders are not allowable, because they are not to be touched. The word 'also' indicates that this is all the more so for things for communal or personal use. However, the use of dwelling places is always allowable. Therefore, all dwelling requisites made of gold and so forth are to be touched. Hence it is said, 'But in the case of the use of dwelling requisites,' and so on.

Sesāti tato mahattarī vāsi. Yā panāti yā kuṭhārī pana. Kudālo antamaso caturaṅgulamattopi garubhaṇḍameva. Nikhādanaṃ caturassamukhaṃ vā hotu doṇimukhaṃ vā vaṅkaṃ vā ujukaṃ vā, antamaso sammuñjanīdaṇḍavedhanampi, daṇḍabandhañce, garubhaṇḍameva. Tenāha “kudālo daṇḍabandhanikhādanaṃ vā agarubhaṇḍaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Sipāṭikā nāma khurakoso, sikharaṃ pana daṇḍabandhanikhādanaṃ anulometīti āha “sikharampi nikhādaneneva saṅgahita”nti. Sace pana vāsi adaṇḍakaṃ phalamattaṃ, bhājanīyaṃ. Upakkhareti vāsiādibhaṇḍe.

The rest: a larger adze than that. And what is 'the axe'? It is the hatchet. A pickaxe, even if only four finger-breadths in size, is still heavy goods. The digging tool, whether it has a four-sided mouth, a trough-shaped mouth, a curved one, or a straight one—even if it is just for piercing a broom handle, and if it has a handle attachment, it is still heavy goods. Therefore, it is said: 'There is no such thing as a pickaxe, a digging tool with a handle attachment, that is not heavy goods.' Sipāṭikā: a razor case. But the point (sikharaṃ) is included with the digging tool; hence it is said: 'Even the point is included with the digging tool.' However, if an adze has no handle and is just the blade, it is to be distributed. Upakkhareti: refers to tools like adzes and others.

Pattabandhako nāma pattassa gaṇṭhikādikārako. “Paṭimānaṃ suvaṇṇādipattakārako”tipi vadanti. Tipucchedanakasatthaṃ suvaṇṇacchedanakasatthaṃ kataparikammacammacchindanakakhuddakasatthanti imāni [V 2.0118] cettha tīṇi pipphalikaṃ anulomantīti āha “ayaṃ pana viseso”tiādi. Itarānīti mahākattariādīni.

Pattabandhaka: one who makes knots, etc., for the bowl. Some also say: 'He is the maker of bowls of gold, etc., for measuring.' The knife for cutting tin, the knife for cutting gold, and the small knife for cutting prepared leather—these three here are in accordance with the pipphalikā (knife); hence it is said: 'But this is the distinction,' and so on. The others: large knives, etc.

Aḍḍhabāhuppamāṇāti [M 2.0161] kapparato paṭṭhāya yāva aṃsakūṭappamāṇā, vidatthicaturaṅgulappamāṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatthajātakāti saṅghikabhūmiyaṃ jātā, ārakkhasaṃvidhānena rakkhitattā rakkhitā ca sā mañjūsādīsu pakkhittaṃ viya yathā taṃ na nassati, evaṃ gopanato gopitā cāti rakkhitagopitā. Tatthajātakāpi pana arakkhitā garubhaṇḍameva na hoti. Saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca kateti iminā saṅghasantakena cetiyasantakaṃ rakkhituṃ parivattituñca vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Suttaṃ panāti vaṭṭitañceva avaṭṭitañca suttaṃ.

Half an arm's length: from the elbow up to the shoulder joint, which is said to be a span and four finger-breadths in size. Those born there: born on land belonging to the Saṅgha, and protected by security arrangements, they are guarded and preserved, just as something placed in a casket, etc., is protected so that it does not perish. But even those born there, if unprotected, are not heavy goods. By stating 'in Saṅgha matters and shrine matters it has been done,' it is indicated that it is permissible to protect and exchange property belonging to the Saṅgha for property belonging to a shrine. As for the thread: it refers to both twisted and untwisted thread.

Aṭṭhaṅgulasūcidaṇḍamattoti antamaso dīghaso aṭṭhaṅgulamatto pariṇāhato sīhaḷa-paṇṇasūcidaṇḍamatto. Etthāti veḷubhaṇḍe. Daḍḍhaṃ gehaṃ yesaṃ teti daḍḍhagehā. Na vāretabbāti “mā gaṇhitvā gacchathā”ti na nisedhetabbā. Desantaragatena sampattavihāre saṅghikāvāse ṭhapetabbā.

A needle-stick of eight finger-breadths: meaning at least eight finger-breadths in length, and in circumference, like a Sinhalese palm-leaf needle-stick. Here: in a bamboo vessel. Those whose house is burnt: they are called 'those with a burnt house.' They should not be prevented: meaning they should not be forbidden by saying, 'Do not take it and go.' Having gone to another region, it should be placed in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha in the monastery one has arrived at.

Avasesañca chadanatiṇanti muñjapabbajehi avasesaṃ yaṃ kiñci chadanatiṇaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇopīti vitthārato aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇo. Likhitapotthako pana garubhaṇḍaṃ na hoti. Kappiyacammānīti migādīnaṃ cammāni. Sabbaṃ cakkayuttayānanti rathasakaṭādikaṃ sabbaṃ cakkayuttayānaṃ. Visaṅkhatacakkaṃ pana yānaṃ bhājanīyaṃ. Anuññātavāsi nāma yā sipāṭikāya pakkhipitvā pariharituṃ sakkāti vuttā. Muṭṭhipaṇṇaṃ tālapattaṃ. Tañhi muṭṭhinā gahetvā pariharantīti “muṭṭhipaṇṇa”nti vuccati. “Muṭṭhipaṇṇanti chattacchadapaṇṇamevā”ti keci. Araṇīsahitanti araṇīyugaḷaṃ, uttarāraṇī adharāraṇīti araṇīdvayanti attho. Phātikammaṃ katvāti antamaso taṃagghanakavālikāyapi thāvaraṃ vaḍḍhikammaṃ katvā. Kuṇḍikāti ayakuṇḍikā ceva tambalohakuṇḍikā ca. Bhājanīyakoṭṭhāsameva bhajatīti bhājanīyapakkhameva sevati[M 2.0162], na tu garubhaṇḍanti attho. Kañcanako pana garubhaṇḍamevāti adhippāyo.

And the remaining thatching grass: any leftover thatching grass apart from muñja and pabbaja. Even eight finger-breadths in size: meaning eight finger-breadths in width. However, a written book is not considered heavy goods. Permitted hides: the hides of deer, etc. All wheeled vehicles: all wheeled vehicles such as chariots and carts. But a vehicle with a disassembled wheel is to be distributed. An allowed adze: one that is said can be carried by placing it in a sheath. Muṭṭhipaṇṇa: a palm leaf. It is called 'muṭṭhipaṇṇa' because it is carried by holding it in the fist. Some say: 'Muṭṭhipaṇṇa means only umbrella-covering leaves.' With fire-sticks: a pair of fire-sticks, meaning two fire-sticks, the upper fire-stick and the lower fire-stick. Having made an improvement: having made a permanent improvement, even if just with sand of that value. Kuṇḍikā: refers to both an iron kuṇḍikā and a copper kuṇḍikā. It belongs to the category of things to be distributed: meaning it belongs to the side of things to be distributed, not to heavy goods. However, a golden one is indeed considered heavy goods—this is the intention.

Iti vinayasaṅgahasaṃvaṇṇanābhūte vinayālaṅkāre

Thus, in the Vinayālaṅkāra, which is the commentary on the Vinayasaṅgaha,

Garubhaṇḍavinicchayakathālaṅkāro nāma

The Ornament of the Elucidation of Heavy Goods.

Tiṃsatimo paricchedo.

The Thirtieth Chapter.

31. Codanādivinicchayakathā

31. Discussion on the Determination of Accusations and so forth.

230. Evaṃ [V 2.0119] garubhaṇḍavinicchayaṃ kathetvā idāni codanādivinicchayaṃ kathetuṃ “codanādivinicchayoti ettha panā”tiādimāha. Tattha codīyate codanā, dosāropananti attho. Ādi-saddena sāraṇādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Vuttañhetaṃ kammakkhandhake (cūḷava. 4, 5) “codetvā kataṃ hoti, sāretvā kataṃ hoti, āpattiṃ ropetvā kataṃ hotī”ti. “Codetuṃ pana ko labhati, ko na labhatī”ti idaṃ anuddhaṃsanādhippāyaṃ vināpi codanālakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlasampannoti idaṃ dussīlassa vacanaṃ appamāṇanti adhippāyena vuttaṃ. Bhikkhunīnaṃ pana bhikkhuṃ codetuṃ anissarattā ‘bhikkhunimevā’ti vuttaṃ. Satipi bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūsu anissarabhāve tāhi katacodanāpi codanārahattā codanāyevāti adhippāyena “pañcapi sahadhammikā labhantī”ti vuttaṃ. Bhikkhussa sutvā codetītiādinā codako yesaṃ sutvā codeti, tesampi vacanaṃ pamāṇamevāti sampaṭicchitattā tesaṃ codanāpi ruhatevāti dassetuṃ “thero suttaṃ nidassesī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.385-386) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.386) pana “amūlakacodanāpasaṅgena samūlakacodanālakkhaṇādiṃ dassetuṃ ‘codetuṃ pana ko [M 2.0163] labhati, ko na labhatī’tiādi āraddhaṃ. ‘Bhikkhussa sutvā codetī’tiādisuttaṃ yasmā ye codakassa aññesaṃ vipattiṃ pakāsenti, tepi tasmiṃ khaṇe codakabhāve ṭhatvāva pakāsenti, tesañca vacanaṃ gahetvā itaropi yasmā codetuñca asampaṭicchantaṃ tehi titthiyasāvakapariyosānehi paṭhamacodakehi sampaṭicchāpetuñca labhati, tasmā idha sādhakabhāvena uddhaṭanti veditabba”nti vuttaṃ.

230. Having thus explained the determination of grave items, now, to explain the determination of accusations and so forth, it begins with, “Now, as to the determination of accusations and so forth, here…” Herein, 'codanā' is an accusation; the meaning is the imputation of a fault. The word 'ādi' includes reminders and the like. For this is said in the Kammakkhandhaka (Cūḷavagga 4, 5): “It is done by accusing, it is done by reminding, it is done by charging with an offense.” “But who is entitled to accuse, and who is not?” This is said to show the characteristic of an accusation even without the intention of disparagement. The phrase 'endowed with virtue' is stated with the intention that the words of an immoral person are not authoritative. However, since nuns have no authority to accuse a monk, it is said, 'a nun only'. Even though nuns lack authority over monks, an accusation made by them is still an accusation because it has the nature of an accusation. With this intention, it is said, “five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma are also entitled.” By the phrase 'having heard from a monk, one accuses,' it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha Ṭīkā 2.385-386) that 'the elder set forth the sutta' to show that because the accuser, having heard from others, then makes an accusation, and their words are accepted as authoritative, their accusation also takes root. However, in the Vimativinodanī (Vinaya Ṭīkā 1.386), it is said: “To show the characteristics of a well-founded accusation and so forth, so as to avoid the contingency of a baseless accusation, the passage beginning ‘But who is entitled to accuse, and who is not?’ is introduced. The sutta passage ‘Having heard from a monk, one accuses’ should be understood as being cited here as supporting evidence, because those who reveal the faults of others to an accuser are also, at that moment, standing in the position of accusers when they reveal it; and because, by accepting their words, another person is entitled both to accuse and to make someone who does not accept it—by means of those first accusers, up to and including the disciples of heretics—accept it.”

Garukānaṃ dvinnanti pārājikasaṅghādisesānaṃ. Avasesānanti thullaccayādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ āpattīnaṃ. Micchādiṭṭhi nāma “natthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattā dasavatthukā diṭṭhi. “Antavā loko anantavā loko”tiādikā antaṃ gaṇhāpakadiṭṭhi antaggāhikā nāma. Ājīvahetu paññattānaṃ channanti ājīvahetupi āpajjitabbānaṃ uttarimanussadhamme pārājikaṃ, sañcaritte saṅghādiseso, “yo te vihāre vasati, so arahā”ti pariyāyena thullaccayaṃ, bhikkhussa paṇītabhojanaviññattiyā pācittiyaṃ, bhikkhuniyā paṇītabhojanaviññattiyā pāṭidesanīyaṃ, sūpodanaviññattiyā dukkaṭanti imesaṃ parivāre (pari. 287) vuttānaṃ channaṃ. Na hetā āpattiyo ājīvahetu eva paññattā sañcarittādīnaṃ aññathāpi āpajjitabbato. Ājīvahetupi [V 2.0120] etāsaṃ āpajjanaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ, ājīvahetupi paññattānanti attho. Diṭṭhivipattiājīvavipattīhi codentopi tammūlikāya āpattiyā eva codeti.

“Of the two grave offenses” refers to pārājika and saṅghādisesa. “Of the remaining” refers to the five kinds of offenses beginning with thullaccaya. “Wrong view” is the ten-fold view that proceeds in the manner of “There is nothing given,” and so on. Views that grasp at extremes, such as “The world is finite” or “The world is infinite,” are called “views that grasp at extremes.” “Of the six prescribed for the sake of livelihood” refers to the six mentioned in the Parivāra (Pari. 287) that can also be incurred for the sake of livelihood: a pārājika for a claim to superhuman states; a saṅghādisesa for acting as a go-between; a thullaccaya for saying indirectly, “He who lives in your monastery is an arahant”; a pācittiya for a monk who asks for fine foods; a pāṭidesanīya for a nun who asks for fine foods; and a dukkaṭa for asking for soup or rice. These offenses are not prescribed solely for the sake of livelihood, since offenses such as acting as a go-between can also be incurred in other ways. This was said with reference to incurring these offenses for the sake of livelihood as well; the meaning is “prescribed for the sake of livelihood as well.” Even when one accuses another of a failure in view or a failure in livelihood, one accuses based on the offense that is its root.

“Kasmā maṃ na vandasī”ti pucchite “assamaṇosi, asakyaputtiyosī”ti avandanakāraṇassa vuttattā antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpanno na vanditabboti vadanti. Codetukāmatāya eva avanditvā attanā vattabbassa vuttamatthaṃ ṭhapetvā [M 2.0164] avandiyabhāve taṃ kāraṇaṃ na hotīti cūḷagaṇṭhipade majjhimagaṇṭhipade ca vuttaṃ. Antimavatthuajjhāpannassa avandiyesu avuttattā tena saddhiṃ sayantassa sahaseyyāpattiyā abhāvato, tassa ca paṭiggahaṇassa ruhanato tadeva yuttataranti viññāyati. Kiñcāpi yāva so bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānāti, tāva vanditabbo, yadā pana “assamaṇomhī”ti paṭijānāti, tadā na vanditabboti ayamettha viseso veditabbo. Antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannassa hi bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānantasseva bhikkhubhāvo, na tato paraṃ. Bhikkhubhāvaṃ appaṭijānanto hi anupasampannapakkhaṃ bhajati. Yasmā āmisaṃ dento attano icchitaṭṭhāneyeva deti, tasmā paṭipāṭiyā nisinnānaṃ yāgubhattādīni dentena ekassa codetukāmatāya adinnepi codanā nāma na hotīti āha “na tāva tā codanā hotī”ti.

When asked, “Why do you not pay homage to me?” and the reason for not paying homage is stated as, “You are not a recluse, you are not a son of the Sakyan,” they say one who has committed a final offense should not be paid homage. It is stated in the Cūḷagaṇṭhipada and the Majjhimagaṇṭhipada that if one, solely out of a desire to accuse, does not pay homage, setting aside the matter to be stated by oneself, this is not a valid reason for the other being unworthy of homage. Because it is not stated among those unworthy of homage that one who has committed a final offense is such, and because there is no offense of sharing a sleeping place for one who sleeps with him, and because his acceptance of offerings is valid, this alone appears more appropriate. Although he should be paid homage as long as he claims the status of a monk, when he admits, “I am not a recluse,” then he should not be paid homage—this distinction should be understood here. For one who has committed a final offense, his status as a monk exists only as long as he claims to be a monk, and not beyond that. One who does not claim the status of a monk sides with the unordained. Since one who gives material things gives only where he wishes, therefore, when one is giving rice porridge, meals, and so on to those seated in order, even if one does not give to someone out of a desire to accuse, this is not an accusation. Thus it is said, “That is not yet an accusation.”

231. Codetabboti cudito, cudito eva cuditako, aparādhavanto puggalo. Codetīti codako, aparādhapakāsako. Cuditako ca codako ca cuditakacodakā. Ubbāhikāyāti ubbahanti viyojenti etāya alajjīnaṃ tajjaniṃ vā kalahaṃ vāti ubbāhikā, saṅghasammuti, tāya. Vinicchinanaṃ nāma tāya sammatabhikkhūhi vinicchinanameva. Alajjussannāya hi parisāya samathakkhandhake āgatehi dasahaṅgehi samannāgatā dve tayo bhikkhū tattheva vuttāya ñattidutiyakammavācāya sammannitabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ samathakkhandhake (cūḷava. 231-232) –

231. ‘Codetabbo’ means one who is to be accused; ‘cudito’ means one who has been accused; ‘cuditako’ is the one who has been accused, a person who has committed an offense. ‘Codeti’ means one who accuses; ‘codako’ is one who reveals an offense. The accused and the accuser are the ‘accused-and-accuser.’ ‘Ubbāhikāya’ means by an ‘ubbāhikā.’ By this they remove or separate the shameless, or a rebuke, or a dispute; hence it is called ‘ubbāhikā,’ a resolution of the Saṅgha; by this. ‘Vinicchinanaṃ’ means the investigation itself by the monks appointed by that resolution. For in an assembly abounding in shameless monks, two or three monks endowed with the ten qualities mentioned in the Samathakkhandhaka should be appointed right there by an act consisting of a motion and one announcement, as stated therein. For this is said in the Samathakkhandhaka (Cūḷavagga 231-232):

“Tehi ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhūhi tasmiṃ adhikaraṇe vinicchiyamāne anantāni ceva bhassāni jāyanti, na cekassa bhāsitassa attho viññāyati[M 2.0165]. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, evarūpaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ ubbāhikāya vūpasametuṃ. Dasahaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu ubbāhikāya sammannitabbo, sīlavā hoti, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu[V 2.0121], bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo, ye te dhammā ādikalyāṇā majjhekalyāṇā pariyosānakalyāṇā sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ abhivadanti, tathārūpassa dhammā bahussutā honti dhātā vacasā paricitā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā, ubhayāni kho panassa pātimokkhāni vitthārena svāgatāni honti suvibhattāni suppavattīni suvinicchitāni suttaso anubyañjanaso, vinaye kho pana cheko hoti asaṃhīro, paṭibalo hoti ubho atthapaccatthike assāsetuṃ saññāpetuṃ nijjhāpetuṃ pekkhetuṃ passituṃ pasādetuṃ, adhikaraṇasamuppādavūpasamakusalo hoti, adhikaraṇaṃ jānāti, adhikaraṇasamudayaṃ jānāti, adhikaraṇanirodhaṃ jānāti, adhikaraṇanirodhagāminipaṭipadaṃ jānāti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, imehi dasahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ bhikkhuṃ ubbāhikāya sammannituṃ.

“Monks, if, while those monks are investigating that legal issue, endless discussions arise and the meaning of not a single statement is understood, I allow, monks, such a legal issue to be settled by an arbitration committee. A monk to be appointed to an arbitration committee should be endowed with ten qualities: he is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the Pāṭimokkha restraint, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, he undertakes and trains in the training rules; he is learned, a preserver of what he has heard, a treasurer of what he has heard; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, that proclaim the spiritual life, utterly complete and pure—such teachings he has heard much, retained, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well with understanding; both Pāṭimokkhas have been well transmitted to him in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, well determined, rule by rule, phrase by phrase; he is skilled in the discipline, not uncertain; he is capable of reassuring, convincing, persuading, making see, making understand, and satisfying both parties, the proponent and the opponent; he is skilled in the arising and settling of legal issues; he knows a legal issue, he knows the origin of a legal issue, he knows the cessation of a legal issue, and he knows the way leading to the cessation of a legal issue. I allow, monks, a monk endowed with these ten qualities to be appointed to an arbitration committee.”

“Evañca pana, bhikkhave, sammannitabbo. Paṭhamaṃ bhikkhu yācitabbo, yācitvā byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo –

“And this, monks, is how he should be appointed. First, the monk should be asked. Having asked him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, amhākaṃ imasmiṃ adhikaraṇe vinicchiyamāne anantāni ceva bhassāni [M 2.0166] jāyanti, na cekassa bhāsitassa attho viññāyati. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmañca itthannāmañca bhikkhuṃ sammanneyya ubbāhikāya imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametuṃ, esā ñatti.

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. While this dispute is being adjudicated among us, endless discussions arise, and the meaning of any single statement is not understood. If it is timely for the Sangha, may the Sangha appoint the monks so-and-so and so-and-so to settle this dispute by means of ubbāhikā. This is the motion."

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, amhākaṃ imasmiṃ adhikaraṇe vinicchiyamāne anantāni ceva bhassāni jāyanti, na cekassa bhāsitassa attho viññāyati. Saṅgho itthannāmañca itthannāmañca bhikkhuṃ sammannati ubbāhikāya imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametuṃ. Yassāyasmato khamati itthannāmassa ca itthannāmassa ca bhikkhuno sammuti ubbāhikāya imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametuṃ, so tuṇhassa. Yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. While this dispute is being adjudicated, endless discussions arise, and the meaning of any single statement is not understood. The Sangha appoints the monks so-and-so and so-and-so to settle this dispute by means of ubbāhikā. To whichever venerable one the appointment of the monks so-and-so and so-and-so to settle this dispute by means of ubbāhikā is agreeable, he should remain silent. Whomever it does not please, he should speak."

“Sammato saṅghena itthannāmo ca itthannāmo ca bhikkhu ubbāhikāya imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametuṃ, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti.

"The monks so-and-so and so-and-so have been appointed by the Sangha to settle this dispute by means of ubbāhikā. This is agreeable to the Sangha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold it."

Tehi [V 2.0122] ca sammatehi visuṃ vā nisīditvā tassā eva vā parisāya “aññehi na kiñci kathetabba”nti sāvetvā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchitabbaṃ. Tumhākanti cuditakacodake sandhāya vuttaṃ.

"By those who have been appointed, having sat apart or in that very assembly, and having announced, 'Nothing should be said by others,' that dispute should be settled. The phrase 'for you' is said with reference to the accused and the accuser."

“Kimhīti kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ. Kimhi nampi na jānāsīti kimhi nanti vacanampi na jānāsi. Nāssa anuyogo dātabboti nāssa pucchā paṭipucchā dātabbā”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.385-386) vuttaṃ, vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.386) pana – kimhīti kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ, kataravipattiyanti attho. Kimhi naṃ nāmāti idaṃ “katarāya vipattiyā [M 2.0167] etaṃ codesī”ti yāya kāyaci viññāyamānāya bhāsāya vuttepi codakassa vinaye apakataññutāya “sīlācāradiṭṭhiājīvavipattīsu katarāyāti maṃ pucchatī”ti viññātuṃ asakkontassa pucchā, na pana “kimhī”tiādipadatthamattaṃ ajānantassa. Na hi anuvijjako codakaṃ bālaṃ aparicitabhāsāya “kimhi na”nti pucchati. Kimhi nampi na jānāsīti idampi vacanamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ na hoti. “Kataravipattiyā”ti vutte “asukāya vipattiyā”ti vattumpi “na jānāsī”ti vacanassa adhippāyameva sandhāya vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Teneva vakkhati “nāssa anuyogo dātabbo”ti.

"'In what?' means 'in what matter?' 'You do not even know 'in what'?' means 'you do not even know the words 'in what'?' 'No investigation should be given to him' means 'no question or counter-question should be given to him.' This is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī. However, in the Vimativinodanī it is said: 'In what?' means 'in what matter?'; the meaning is 'in what kind of transgression?' The phrase 'What is this 'in what'?' refers to the question of one who, even when it is said in some intelligible language, 'In what kind of transgression do you accuse him?', is unable to discern, due to his lack of skill in the discipline, 'Is he asking me which transgression among those of morality, conduct, view, or livelihood?' It is not the question of one who does not know the mere meaning of the words 'in what?' and so forth. For an investigator does not ask a foolish accuser, 'In what?', using unfamiliar language. Nor is the phrase 'You do not even know 'in what'?' spoken merely with reference to the words themselves. Rather, it should be understood that the statement 'you do not know' is said with reference to the intention that he does not even know how to say 'by such-and-such a transgression' when asked 'By which transgression?' Therefore, it will be said, 'No investigation should be given to him.'"

“Tassa nayo dātabbo”ti tassāti bālassa lajjissa. “Tassa nayo dātabbo”ti vatvā ca “kimhi naṃ codesīti sīlavipattiyā”tiādi adhippāyappakāsanameva nayadānaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana kimhi-naṃ-padānaṃpariyāyamattadassanaṃ. Na hi bālo “kataravipattiyaṃ naṃ codesī”ti imassa vacanassa atthe ñātepi vipattippabhedaṃ, attanā codiyamānaṃ vipattisarūpañca jānituṃ sakkoti, tasmā teneva ajānanena alajjī apasādetabbo. Kimhi nanti idampi upalakkhaṇamattaṃ. Aññena vā yena kenaci ākārena aviññutaṃ pakāsetvā vissajjetabbova. “Dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyā”tiādivacanato “alajjīniggahatthāya…pe… paññatta”nti vuttaṃ. Ehitīti eti, hi-kāro ettha āgamo daṭṭhabbo, āgamissatīti attho. Diṭṭhasantānenāti diṭṭhaniyāmena. Alajjissa paṭiññāya eva kātabbanti vacanapaṭivacanakkameneva dose āvibhūtepi alajjissa “asuddho aha”nti dosasampaṭicchanapaṭiññāya eva āpattiyā kātabbanti attho. Keci pana “alajjissa etaṃ natthīti suddhapaṭiññāya eva anāpattiyā kātabbanti ayamettha attho saṅgahito”ti [M 2.0168] vadanti, taṃ [V 2.0123] na yuttaṃ anuvijjakasseva niratthakattāpattito, codakeneva alajjipaṭiññāya ṭhātabbato. Dosopagamapaṭiññā eva hi idha paṭiññāti adhippetā, teneva vakkhati “etampi natthi, etampi natthīti paṭiññaṃ na detī”tiādi.

"'The method should be given to him' refers to that foolish but modest one. And having said, 'The method should be given to him,' the giving of the method is said to be the clarification of the intention, such as 'On what ground do you accuse him? In a breach of virtue,' and so forth, not merely a demonstration of synonyms for the words 'in what?' For a fool, even if the meaning of the words 'In which transgression do you accuse him?' is known, cannot discern the different kinds of transgressions or the nature of the transgression of which he is being accused. Therefore, by that very ignorance, a shameless one should be dismissed. The phrase 'in what?' is also merely indicative. Alternatively, he should be dismissed by revealing his ignorance in any manner whatsoever. From the statement beginning 'For the restraint of wicked persons,' it is said, 'It was prescribed for restraining the shameless...' 'Ehi' means 'he comes'; the particle 'hi' here should be seen as an augment, meaning 'he will come.' 'By the seen sequence' means 'by the observed procedure.' 'It should be done only by the shameless one's acknowledgment' means that even when the fault is evident through the exchange of words, the procedure regarding the offense should be conducted only by the shameless one's acknowledgment of accepting the fault, saying, 'I am impure.' Some, however, say, 'For the shameless, this does not exist; thus, the meaning included here is that it should be made a non-offense only by a confession of purity.' That is not proper, for it would render the investigator pointless, and because the accuser must stand by the shameless one's confession.
