Indeed, here, the acknowledgment intended is only the admission of fault. Therefore, it will be said, 'He does not give acknowledgment, saying, 'This too is not, that too is not,' and so forth.'"

Tadatthadīpanatthanti alajjissa dose āvibhūtepi tassa dosopagamapaṭiññāya eva kātabbatādīpanatthaṃ. Vivādavatthusaṅkhāte atthe paccatthikā atthapaccatthikā. Saññaṃ datvāti tesaṃ kathāpacchedatthaṃ abhimukhakaraṇatthañca saddaṃ katvā. Vinicchinituṃ ananucchavikoti asuddhoti saññāya codakapakkhe paviṭṭhattā anuvijjakabhāvato bahibhūtattā anuvijjituṃ asakkuṇeyyattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sandehe eva hi sati anuvijjituṃ sakkā, asuddhaladdhiyā pana sati cuditakena vuttaṃ sabbaṃ asaccatopi paṭibhāti, kathaṃ tattha anuvijjanā siyāti.

"'For the purpose of clarifying that matter' means for the purpose of clarifying that, even when the faults of a shameless one are evident, it should be done only by his acknowledgment of accepting the fault. In a matter classified as a ground for dispute, 'opponents' (paccatthikā) are opponents in the matter (atthapaccatthikā). 'Having given a sign' means having made a sound for the purpose of cutting off their speech and making them face forward. 'Unsuitable to discern' means 'impure'; it is said with reference to the inability to investigate because, having entered the side of the accuser with this perception, he is excluded from the role of an investigator. For investigation is possible only when there is doubt; but when there is an impure view, everything said by the accused appears as untrue—how then could there be an investigation?"

Tathā nāsitakova bhavissatīti iminā vinicchayampi adatvā saṅghato viyojanaṃ nāma liṅganāsanā viya ayampi eko nāsanappakāroti dasseti. Ekasambhogaparibhogāti idaṃ attano santikā tesaṃ vimocanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana tesaṃ aññamaññasambhoge yojanatthaṃ.

"By 'Thus, he will be like one who has been destroyed,' it is shown that this separation from the Sangha, without even giving a judgment, is also a type of destruction, like the destruction of the characteristic marks. 'Of common communion and use'—this is said for the purpose of freeing them from one's own presence, not for the purpose of joining them in mutual communion."

Viraddhaṃ hotīti sañcicca āpattiṃ āpanno hoti. Ādito paṭṭhāya alajjī nāma natthīti idaṃ “pakkhānaṃ anurakkhaṇatthāya paṭiññaṃ na detī”ti imassa alajjīlakkhaṇasambhavassa karaṇavacanaṃ. Paṭicchāditakālato paṭṭhāya alajjī nāma eva, purimo lajjibhāvo na rakkhatīti attho. Paṭiññaṃ na detīti “sace mayā katadosaṃ vakkhāmi, mayhaṃ anuvattakā bhijjissantī”ti paṭiññaṃ na deti. Ṭhāne na tiṭṭhatīti lajjiṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhati, kāyavācāsu vītikkamo [M 2.0169] hoti evāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “vinicchayo na dātabbo”ti, pubbe pakkhikānaṃ paṭiññāya vūpasamitassapi adhikaraṇassa duvūpasantatāya ayampi tathā nāsitakova bhavissatīti adhippāyo.

"'He has failed' means he has intentionally committed an offense. The statement 'There is no such thing as a shameless one from the very beginning' is a statement of the reason for the arising of the characteristic of shamelessness, which is, 'he does not give an acknowledgment in order to protect his faction.' From the time of concealment, he is indeed shameless; the meaning is that his previous state of modesty is not preserved. 'He does not give an acknowledgment' means he does not give an acknowledgment, thinking, 'If I declare the fault I have committed, my followers will be broken.' 'He does not stand in his position' means he does not stand in the position of a modest person; the intention is that there is indeed transgression in body and speech. Therefore, it is said, 'No judgment should be given'; the intention is that because a dispute, even one previously settled by the acknowledgment of partisans, was badly settled, this one too will be similarly destroyed."

232. Adinnādānavatthuṃ vinicchinantena pañcavīsati avahārā sādhukaṃ sallakkhetabbāti ettha pañcavīsati avahārā nāma pañca pañcakāni, tattha pañca pañcakāni nāma nānābhaṇḍapañcakaṃ ekabhaṇḍapañcakaṃ sāhatthikapañcakaṃ pubbapayogapañcakaṃ theyyāvahārapañcakanti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā) “te pana avahārā pañca [V 2.0124] pañcakāni samodhānetvā sādhukaṃ sallakkhetabbā”tiādi. Tattha nānābhaṇḍapañcakaekabhaṇḍapañcakāni padabhājane (pārā. 92) vuttānaṃ “ādiyeyya, hareyya, avahareyya, iriyāpathaṃ vikopeyya, ṭhānā cāveyyā”ti imesaṃ padānaṃ vasena labbhanti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ porāṇehi –

232. When adjudicating a case of taking what is not given, the twenty-five modes of theft should be carefully examined. Here, the twenty-five modes of theft are five sets of five. These five sets of five are: the fivefold classification of diverse goods, the fivefold classification of a single good, the fivefold classification of direct action, the fivefold classification of prior effort, and the fivefold classification of theft. Thus it is stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī (commentary on the second Pārājika), 'Those modes of theft, by combining the five sets of five, should be carefully examined,' and so forth. Among these, the fivefold classification of diverse goods and the fivefold classification of a single good are obtained by means of the terms stated in the word-analysis (Pārā. 92): 'should take, should carry away, should misappropriate, should disturb the posture, should remove from its place.' Thus it is said by the ancients:

“Ādiyanto harantova;

Haranto iriyāpathaṃ;

Vikopento tathā ṭhānā;

Cāventopi parājiko”ti.

“One who takes, or carries away; / One who carries away, disturbs the posture; / And likewise one who removes from its place, / Is defeated.”

Tattha nānābhaṇḍapañcakaṃ saviññāṇakaaviññāṇakavasena daṭṭhabbaṃ, itaraṃ saviññāṇakavaseneva. Kathaṃ? Ādiyeyyāti ārāmaṃ abhiyuñjati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādeti, āpatti thullaccayassa. Sāmiko “na mayhaṃ bhavissatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, āpatti pārājikassa. Hareyyāti aññassa bhaṇḍaṃ haranto sīse bhāraṃ theyyacitto āmasati, dukkaṭaṃ. Phandāpeti, thullaccayaṃ. Khandhaṃ oropeti, pārājikaṃ. Avahareyyāti upanikkhittaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ “dehi [M 2.0170] me bhaṇḍa”nti vuccamāno “nāhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti bhaṇati, dukkaṭaṃ. Sāmikassa vimatiṃ uppādeti, thullaccayaṃ. Sāmiko “na mayhaṃ bhavissatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, pārājikaṃ. Iriyāpathaṃ vikopeyyāti “sahabhaṇḍahārakaṃ nessāmī”ti paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmeti, thullaccayaṃ. Dutiyaṃ pādaṃ atikkāmeti, pārājikaṃ. Ṭhānā cāveyyāti thalaṭṭhaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ theyyacitto āmasati, dukkaṭaṃ. Phandāpeti, thullaccayaṃ. Ṭhānā cāveti, pārājikaṃ. Evaṃ tāva nānābhaṇḍapañcakaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sassāmikassa pana dāsassa vā tiracchānagatassa vā yathāvuttena abhiyogādinā nayena ādiyanaharaṇa avaharaṇa iriyāpathavikopana ṭhānācāvanavasena ekabhaṇḍapañcakaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Here, the fivefold classification of diverse goods should be understood in terms of animate and inanimate objects; the other (the fivefold classification of a single good) should be understood only in terms of animate objects. How? 'Should take' (ādiyeyya): If one lays claim to a monastery, there is an offense of wrong conduct. If one causes doubt in the owner, there is an offense of grave misconduct. If the owner abandons the responsibility, thinking, 'It will not be mine,' there is an offense entailing expulsion. 'Should carry away' (hareyya): If one, carrying another's goods, touches the load on the head with the intention to steal, it is wrong conduct. If one causes it to move, it is grave misconduct. If one lowers the load from the shoulder, it is an offense entailing expulsion. 'Should misappropriate' (avahareyya): If, regarding deposited goods, when told, 'Give me the goods,' one says, 'I did not take them,' it is wrong conduct. If one causes doubt in the owner, it is grave misconduct. If the owner abandons the responsibility, thinking, 'It will not be mine,' there is an offense entailing expulsion. 'Should disturb the posture' (iriyāpathaṃ vikopeyya): If, with the intention, 'I will lead away the carrier of the goods,' one causes them to take the first step, it is grave misconduct. If one causes them to take the second step, it is an offense entailing expulsion. 'Should remove from its place' (ṭhānā cāveyya): If one touches goods on land with the intention to steal, it is wrong conduct. If one causes them to move, it is grave misconduct. If one removes them from their place, it is an offense entailing expulsion. Thus, the fivefold classification of diverse goods should be understood. However, regarding a slave or an animal belonging to an owner, the fivefold classification of a single item should be understood in the same manner, by way of laying claim, taking, carrying away, misappropriating, disturbing posture, and removing from the place, as has been stated. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Tattha nānekabhaṇḍānaṃ, pañcakānaṃ vasā pana;

Ādiyanādipañcakā, duvidhāti udīritā”ti.

“Therein, the fivefold classifications beginning with 'taking' are declared to be twofold, by way of the classifications of various goods.”

Katamaṃ [V 2.0125] sāhatthikapañcakaṃ? Sāhatthiko āṇattiko nissaggiyo atthasādhako dhuranikkhepoti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

What is the fivefold classification of direct action? It is direct action, by command, by relinquishment, by accomplishing the purpose, and by laying down the burden. Thus it is said:

“Sāhatthāṇattiko ceva, nissaggiyotthasādhako;

Dhuranikkhepako cāti, idaṃ sāhatthapañcaka”nti.

“Direct action and by command, / By relinquishment, by accomplishing the purpose, / And by laying down the burden— / This is the fivefold classification of direct action.”

Tattha sāhatthiko nāma parassa bhaṇḍaṃ sahatthā avaharati. Āṇattiko nāma “asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā”ti aññaṃ āṇāpeti. Nissaggiyo nāma suṅkaghātaparikappitokāsānaṃ anto ṭhatvā bahi pātanaṃ. Atthasādhako nāma “asukassa bhaṇḍaṃ yadā sakkosi, tadā taṃ avaharā”ti āṇāpeti. Tattha sace paro anantarāyiko hutvā taṃ avaharati, āṇāpakassa āṇattikkhaṇeyeva pārājikaṃ. Parassa vā pana telakumbhiyā pādagghanakaṃ telaṃ avassaṃ pivanakāni upāhanādīni pakkhipati[M 2.0171], hatthato muttamatteyeva pārājikaṃ. Dhuranikkhepo pana ārāmābhiyogaupanikkhittabhaṇḍavasena veditabbo. Tāvakālikabhaṇḍadeyyāni adentassapi eseva nayoti idaṃ sāhatthikapañcakaṃ.

Here, 'direct action' (sāhatthiko) is when one takes another's goods with one's own hand. 'By command' (āṇattiko) is when one orders another, saying, “Take such and such goods.” 'By relinquishment' (nissaggiyo) is when, standing inside a place designated for evading customs duties, one throws something outside. 'By accomplishing the purpose' (atthasādhako) is when one orders another, saying, “When you are able, then take such and such goods.” Here, if the other person, being without obstruction, takes it, the one who ordered commits an offense entailing expulsion at the very moment of the order. Or if one puts oil worth a quarter-coin, or drinkables, or footwear and the like into another's oil jar, the offense entailing expulsion is incurred as soon as the hand is released. 'By laying down the burden' (dhuranikkhepo) should be understood by way of the cases of laying claim to a monastery and of deposited goods. The same principle applies even for not giving back temporarily borrowed goods. This is the fivefold classification of direct action.

Katamaṃ pubbapayogapañcakaṃ? Pubbapayogo sahapayogo saṃvidāvahāro saṅketakammaṃ nimittakammanti. Tena vuttaṃ –

What is the fivefold classification of prior effort? It is prior effort, simultaneous effort, theft by pre-arrangement, an act of signaling, and an act of making a sign. As it is said:

“Pubbasahapayogo ca, saṃvidāharaṇaṃ tathā;

Saṅketakammaṃ nimittaṃ, idaṃ sāhatthapañcaka”nti.

“Prior and simultaneous effort, and likewise theft by pre-arrangement; an act of signaling, a sign—this is the fivefold classification of direct action.”

Tattha āṇattivasena pubbapayogo veditabbo. Ṭhānācāvanavasena, khilādīni saṅkāmetvā khettādiggahaṇavasena ca sahapayogo veditabbo. Saṃvidāvahāro nāma “asukaṃ nāma bhaṇḍaṃ avaharissāmā”ti saṃvidahitvā sammantayitvā avaharaṇaṃ. Evaṃ saṃvidahitvā gatesu hi ekenapi tasmiṃ bhaṇḍe ṭhānā cāvite sabbesaṃ avahāro hoti. Saṅketakammaṃ nāma sañjānanakammaṃ. Sace hi purebhattādīsu yaṃ kiñci kālaṃ paricchinditvā “asukasmiṃ kāle itthannāmaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā”ti vutto saṅketato apacchā apure taṃ avaharati, saṅketakārakassa saṅketakaraṇakkhaṇeyeva avahāro. Nimittakammaṃ nāma saññuppādanatthaṃ akkhinikhaṇanādinimittakaraṇaṃ[V 2.0126]. Sace hi evaṃ katanimittato apacchā apure “yaṃ avaharā”ti vutto, taṃ avaharati, nimittakārakassa nimittakkhaṇeyeva avahāroti idaṃ pubbapayogapañcakaṃ.

Here, prior effort (pubbapayoga) should be understood by way of giving an order. Simultaneous effort (sahapayoga) should be understood by way of displacing from its place, or by removing boundary posts and seizing fields and the like. Theft by pre-arrangement (saṃvidāvahāro) is stealing after having planned and agreed, saying, “We will steal such and such a thing.” For if, having gone after planning thus, the thing is moved from its place by even one of them, the theft is complete for all. An act of signaling (saṅketakammaṃ) means an act of signifying. For if, having specified some time such as before the meal, and having been told “At such a time steal such and such a thing,” one steals it exactly at the appointed time, the theft is complete for the one who made the signal at the very moment of making it. An act of making a sign (nimittakammaṃ) means making a sign, such as winking, for the purpose of producing understanding. For if, having been told 'Steal that,' one steals it exactly in accordance with the sign thus made, the theft is complete for the one who made the sign at the very moment of making it. This is the fivefold classification of prior effort.

Katamaṃ theyyāvahārapañcakaṃ? Theyyāvahāro pasayhāvahāro parikappāvahāro paṭicchannāvahāro kusāvahāroti. Tena vuttaṃ –

What is the fivefold classification of theft? It is theft by stealth, theft by force, theft by planning, theft by concealment, and theft by trickery. As it is said:

“Theyyā [M 2.0172] pasayhā parikappā, paṭicchannā kusā tathā;

Avahārā ime pañca, theyyāvahārapañcaka”nti.

“By stealth, by force, by planning, by concealment, and by trickery—these five are the modes of theft, the fivefold classification of theft.”

Tattha yo sandhicchedādīni katvā adissamāno avaharati, kūṭatulākūṭamānakūṭakahāpaṇādīhi vā vañcetvā gaṇhāti, tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro theyyāvahāroti veditabbo. Yo pana pasayha balakkārena paresaṃ santakaṃ gaṇhāti gāmaghātakādayo viya, attano pattabalito vā vuttanayeneva adhikaṃ gaṇhāti rājabhaṭādayo viya, tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro pasayhāvahāroti veditabbo. Parikappetvā gahaṇaṃ pana parikappāvahāro nāma.

Therein, one who, having made breaches in walls and so forth, takes unseen, or deceives with false scales, false measures, false coins, and so forth, and takes—such taking is to be understood as theft by stealth. But one who forcibly and violently takes the belongings of others, like village raiders and so forth, or who, by virtue of their acquired power, takes more than is due, like royal officers and so forth—such taking is to be understood as theft by force. Taking after planning, however, is called theft by planning.

So bhaṇḍokāsassa vasena duvidho. Tatrāyaṃ bhaṇḍaparikappo – sāṭakatthiko antogabbhaṃ pavisitvā “sace sāṭako bhavissati, gaṇhissāmi. Sace suttaṃ, na gaṇhissāmī”ti parikappetvā andhakāre pasibbakaṃ gaṇhāti. Tatra ce sāṭako hoti, uddhāreyeva pārājikaṃ. Suttañce hoti, rakkhati. Bahi nīharitvā muñcitvā “sutta”nti ñatvā puna āharitvā ṭhapeti, rakkhatiyeva. “Sutta”nti ñatvāpi yaṃ laddhaṃ, taṃ gahetabbanti gacchati, padavārena kāretabbo. Bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā gaṇhāti, uddhāre pārājikaṃ. “Coro coro”ti anubandho chaḍḍetvā palāyati, rakkhati. Sāmikā disvā gaṇhanti, rakkhatiyeva. Añño ce gaṇhāti, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Sāmikesu nivattantesu sayaṃ disvā paṃsukūlasaññāya “pagevetaṃ mayā gahitaṃ, mama dāni santaka”nti gaṇhantassapi bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Tattha yvāyaṃ “sace sāṭako bhavissati, gaṇhissāmī”tiādinā nayena pavatto parikappo, ayaṃ bhaṇḍaparikappo nāma. Okāsaparikappo pana evaṃ veditabbo – ekacco pana parapariveṇādīni paviṭṭho kiñci lobhaneyyabhaṇḍaṃ disvā gabbhadvārapamukhaheṭṭhā [M 2.0173] pāsādadvārakoṭṭhakarukkhamūlādivasena paricchedaṃ katvā “sace maṃ etthantare passissanti, daṭṭhukāmatāya gahetvā vicaranto viya dassāmi. No ce passissanti[V 2.0127], harissāmī”ti parikappeti, tassa taṃ ādāya parikappitaparicchedaṃ atikkantamatte avahāro hoti. Iti yvāyaṃ vuttanayeneva pavatto parikappo, ayaṃ okāsaparikappo nāma. Evamimesaṃ dvinnaṃ parikappānaṃ vasena parikappetvā gaṇhato avahāro parikappāvahāroti veditabbo.

It is twofold, based on the object and the place. Herein is the planning regarding the object: a person desiring a cloth enters an inner chamber and plans, “If there is a cloth, I will take it. If there is thread, I will not take it.” Then, in the darkness, he grabs a bag. If it is a cloth, he commits a pārājika offense as soon as he lifts it. If it is thread, he is safe. Taking it outside, opening it, and realizing it is thread, he brings it back and sets it down—he remains safe. Even knowing it is thread, if he proceeds thinking, “I will take whatever I have obtained,” he is to be made to pay its value. If he sets it on the ground and then takes it, it is pārājika upon lifting. If he is pursued with shouts of “Thief! Thief!” and he drops it and flees, he is safe. If the owners see it and take it back, he remains safe. If someone else takes it, the goods must be compensated. If the owners turn back and he sees it again, thinking it is discarded cloth, and takes it with the thought, “I took this before, now it is mine,” the goods must still be compensated. Herein, the planning that proceeds with the thought, “If it is a cloth, I will take it,” etc., is called planning regarding the object. Planning regarding the place, however, should be understood as follows: someone enters another’s monastic cell, etc., and seeing some desirable goods, marks a boundary—such as below the entrance of an inner chamber, a palace gatehouse, or the foot of a tree—and plans, “If they see me within this space, I will act as if I am walking around having taken it out of a desire to look at it. If they do not see me, I will carry it away.” For him, as soon as he takes it beyond the planned boundary, the theft occurs. Thus, the planning that proceeds in this manner is called planning regarding the place. In this way, theft committed after planning in these two ways is to be understood as theft by planning.

Paṭicchādetvā pana avaharaṇaṃ paṭicchannāvahāro. So evaṃ veditabbo – yo bhikkhu uyyānādīsu paresaṃ omuñcitvā ṭhapitaṃ aṅgulimuddikādiṃ disvā “pacchā gaṇhissāmī”ti paṃsunā vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādeti, tassa ettāvatā uddhāro natthīti na tāva avahāro hoti. Yadā pana sāmikā vicinantā apassitvā “sve jānissāmā”ti sālayāva gatā honti, athassa taṃ uddharato uddhāre avahāro. “Paṭicchannakāleyeva etaṃ mama santaka”nti sakasaññāya vā “gatādāni te, chaḍḍitabhaṇḍaṃ ida”nti paṃsukūlasaññāya vā gaṇhantassa pana bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Tesu dutiyatatiyadivase āgantvā vicinitvā adisvā dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā gatesupi gahitaṃ bhaṇḍadeyyameva. Pacchā ñatvā codiyamānassa adadato sāmikānaṃ dhuranikkhepe avahāro hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā tassa payogena tehi na diṭṭhaṃ. Yo pana tathārūpaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ yathāṭhāne ṭhitaṃyeva appaṭicchādetvā theyyacitto pādena akkamitvā kaddame vā vālikāya vā paveseti, tassa pavesitamatteyeva avahāro.

Theft by concealing and then taking is called theft by concealment. It should be understood thus: when a monk sees a signet ring or the like, which others have taken off and left in a park or similar place, and thinking, “I will take it later,” covers it with dust or leaves, at that point there is no lifting, so theft has not yet occurred. However, when the owners search for it, do not find it, and depart, saying, “We will find out tomorrow,” then for him, the theft occurs upon lifting it. But if he takes it with the perception that it is his own, thinking, “This became my property at the very time of concealment,” or with the perception that it is discarded, thinking, “They have gone now, this is abandoned property,” then the goods must be compensated. Even if on the second or third day the owners come, search, do not find it, and leave, having abandoned their responsibility, the goods taken must still be compensated. If, having later learned the truth, he is accused but does not give it back, the theft occurs when the owners abandon their responsibility. Why? Because it was not seen by them due to his action. But as for one who, with a thieving mind, does not conceal such an item that is in its proper place, but steps on it with his foot and presses it into mud or sand, for him the theft occurs at the very moment of pressing it in.

Kusaṃ saṅkāmetvā pana avaharaṇaṃ kusāvahāro nāma. Sopi evaṃ veditabbo – yo bhikkhu vilīvamayaṃ vā tālapaṇṇamayaṃ vā katasaññāṇaṃ yaṃ kiñci kusaṃ pātetvā cīvare [M 2.0174] bhājiyamāne attano koṭṭhāsassa samīpe ṭhitaṃ samagghataraṃ vā mahagghataraṃ vā samasamaṃ vā agghena parassa koṭṭhāsaṃ haritukāmo attano koṭṭhāse patitaṃ kusaṃ parassa koṭṭhāse pātetukāmatāya uddharati, rakkhati tāva. Parassa koṭṭhāse pātite rakkhateva. Yadā pana tasmiṃ patite parassa koṭṭhāsato parassa kusaṃ uddharati, uddhaṭamatte avahāro. Sace paṭhamataraṃ parassa koṭṭhāsato kusaṃ uddharati, attano koṭṭhāse pātetukāmatāya uddhāre rakkhati, pātanepi rakkhati. Attano koṭṭhāsato pana attano kusaṃ uddharato uddhāreyeva rakkhati, taṃ uddharitvā parakoṭṭhāse pātentassa hatthato muttamatte avahāro hoti, ayaṃ kusāvahāro. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana samantapāsādikato (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92) gahetabbo.

Theft by moving a lot is called theft by moving a lot. This too should be understood thus: when robes are being distributed by dropping lots—any kind of marked lot, whether made of a bamboo strip or a palm leaf—a monk, desiring to take another’s share that is of better quality, more valuable, or of equal value, which is situated near his own share, lifts the lot that has fallen on his own share with the desire to drop it on the other’s share; for now, he is safe. When it is dropped on the other’s share, he is still safe. But when, after it has been dropped there, he lifts the other’s lot from the other’s share, the theft occurs at the very moment of lifting. If he first lifts the other’s lot from the other’s share with the desire to drop it on his own share, he is safe upon lifting it, and also safe when dropping it. Then, when lifting his own lot from his own share, he is safe upon the very lifting; but when, having lifted it, he drops it on the other’s share, the theft occurs at the very moment it is released from his hand. This is theft by moving a lot. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the Samantapāsādikā (Pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92).

Tulayitvāti [V 2.0128] upaparikkhitvā.

“Tulayitvā” means “having examined.”

Sāmīcīti vattaṃ, āpatti pana natthīti adhippāyo.

“Sāmīcī” means proper conduct, but the meaning is that there is no offense.

Mahājanasammaddoti mahājanasaṅkhobho. Bhaṭṭhe janakāyeti apagate janakāye. “Idañca kāsāvaṃ attano santakaṃ katvā etasseva bhikkhuno dehī”ti kiṃ kāraṇā evamāha? Cīvarassāmikena dhuranikkhepo kato, tasmā tassa adinnaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Avahārakopi vippaṭisārassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya cīvarassāmikaṃ pariyesanto vicarati “dassāmī”ti, cīvarassāmikena ca “mameta”nti vutte etenapi avahārakena ālayo pariccatto, tasmā evamāha. Yadi evaṃ cīvarassāmikoyeva “attano santakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti kasmā na vuttoti? Ubhinnaṃ kukkuccavinodanatthaṃ. Kathaṃ? Avahārakassa “mayā sahatthena na dinnaṃ, bhaṇḍadeyyameta”nti kukkuccaṃ uppajjeyya[M 2.0175], itarassa “mayā paṭhamaṃ dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā pacchā adinnaṃ gahita”nti kukkuccaṃ uppajjeyyāti.

‘Mahājanasammadda’ means ‘agitation of the multitude’. ‘Bhaṭṭhe janakāye’ means ‘when the gathering of people has departed’. ‘And having made this robe one’s own property, give it to this monk’—for what reason was this said? Because the responsibility was relinquished by the owner of the robe, therefore it is not permissible to take what was not given. Also, the purloiner, from the moment regret arose, wandered seeking the owner of the robe, thinking, ‘I will give it back.’ And when the owner of the robe said, ‘This is mine,’ even this purloiner’s attachment was abandoned. Therefore, it was said thus. If so, why did not the owner of the robe simply say, ‘Take it as your own property’? It was to dispel the scruples of both. How? The purloiner might feel scruples, thinking, ‘I did not give it with my own hand; this is something to be returned.’ The other might feel scruples, thinking, ‘First, I relinquished responsibility, and then took what was not given.’

Samagghanti appagghaṃ.

‘Samaggha’ means ‘of little value’.

Dāruatthaṃ pharatīti dārūhi kattabbakiccaṃ sādheti. Mayi santetiādi sabbaṃ raññā pasādena vuttaṃ, therena pana “ananucchavikaṃ kata”nti na maññitabbaṃ.

‘Dāruatthaṃ pharati’ means ‘it accomplishes the task to be done with wood’. The phrase beginning ‘While I am here,’ and so on—all this was said by the king out of faith. However, it should not be thought by the elder, ‘This was done inappropriately.’

Ekadivasaṃ dantakaṭṭhacchedanādinā yā ayaṃ agghahāni vuttā, sā bhaṇḍassāminā kiṇitvā gahitameva sandhāya vuttā. Sabbaṃ panetaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇena gahetabbaṃ. Pāsāṇañca sakkharañca pāsāṇasakkharaṃ.

The loss of value for one day that was mentioned, due to cutting tooth-sticks and so on, was said in reference to that which was bought and taken by the owner of the goods. All this, however, should be taken according to the authority of the commentary teachers. `Pāsāṇasakkharaṃ` is a compound of `pāsāṇa` (stone) and `sakkhara` (gravel).

“Dhāreyya atthaṃ vicakkhaṇo”ti imasseva vivaraṇaṃ “āpattiṃ vā anāpattiṃ vā”tiādi. “Sikkhāpadaṃ samaṃ tenā”ti ito pubbe ekā gāthā –

‘The wise one should bear in mind the meaning’—this is the explanation of ‘whether it is an offense or not,’ and so on. Before ‘The training rule is the same as that,’ there is one verse:

“Dutiyaṃ adutiyena, yaṃ jinena pakāsitaṃ;

Parājitakilesena, pārājikapadaṃ idhā”ti.

‘The second, by the unsurpassed one, which the Conqueror declared; by him whose defilements are conquered, here is the Pārājika rule.’

Tāya [V 2.0129] saddhiṃ ghaṭetvā adutiyena parājitakilesena jinena dutiyaṃ yaṃ idaṃ pārājikapadaṃ pakāsitaṃ, idha tena samaṃ anekanayavokiṇṇaṃ gambhīratthavinicchayaṃ aññaṃ kiñci sikkhāpadaṃ na vijjatīti yojanā. Tattha parājitakilesenāti santāne puna anuppattidhammatāpādane catūhi maggañāṇehi saha vāsanāya samucchinnasabbakilesena. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.159) pana “parājitakilesenāti vijitakilesena, nikilesenāti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane.

Combining with that, the explanation is: ‘By the unsurpassed Victor, who has conquered the defilements, this second Pārājika rule was declared. Herein, equal to it, no other training rule exists that is interspersed with various methods and profound in meaning and analysis.’ Herein, ‘by one who has conquered the defilements’ means by one who has eradicated all defilements together with their latent tendencies through the four path-knowledges, bringing them to a state where they cannot arise again in the mental continuum. However, in the Vimativinodanī, it is said: ‘“By one who has conquered the defilements” means “by one who has vanquished the defilements”; the meaning is “by one without defilements”.’ ‘Here’ means ‘in this Dispensation’.

Tenāti tena dutiyapārājikasikkhāpadena. Attho nāma pāḷiattho. Vinicchayo nāma pāḷimuttavinicchayo. Attho ca vinicchayo ca atthavinicchayā, te gambhīrā yasminti gambhīratthavinicchayaṃ [M 2.0176] . Vatthumhi otiṇṇeti codanāvasena vā attanāva attano vītikkamārocanavasena vā saṅghamajjhe adinnādānavatthusmiṃ otiṇṇe. Etthāti otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ. Vinicchayoti āpattānāpattiniyamanaṃ. Avatvāvāti “tvaṃ pārājikaṃ āpanno”ti avatvāva. Kappiyepi ca vatthusminti attanā gahetuṃ kappiye mātupituādisantakepi vatthusmiṃ. Lahuvattinoti theyyacittuppādena lahuparivattino. Āsīvisanti sīghameva sakalasarīre pharaṇasamatthavisaṃ.

‘By that’ means ‘by that second Pārājika training rule’. ‘Meaning’ means ‘the meaning of the Pāli text’. ‘Analysis’ means ‘the analysis beyond the Pāli text’. ‘Meaning and analysis’ are ‘atthavinicchayā’; because they are profound, it is called ‘gambhīratthavinicchaya’ (profound in meaning and analysis). ‘When involved in the matter’ means ‘when involved in a matter of taking what is not given in the midst of the Saṅgha, either by way of an accusation or by way of declaring one’s own transgression’. ‘Herein’ means ‘in the matter in which one is involved’. ‘Analysis’ means ‘the determination of an offense or non-offense’. ‘Without speaking’ means ‘without even saying, “You have committed a Pārājika offense”’. ‘Even in a permissible matter’ means ‘even in a matter that is permissible for oneself to take, such as what belongs to one’s mother, father, and so on’. ‘Of one who is quick to change’ means ‘of one who is quick to change due to the arising of a thievish thought’. ‘Like a viper’ means ‘like venom that is capable of quickly spreading throughout the entire body’.

233. Pakatimanussehi uttaritarānaṃ buddhādiuttamapurisānaṃ adhigamadhammoti uttarimanussadhammo, tassa paresaṃ ārocanaṃ uttarimanussadhammārocanaṃ. Taṃ vinicchinantena cha ṭhānāni sodhetabbānīti yojanā. Tattha kiṃ te adhigatanti adhigamapucchā. Kinti te adhigatanti upāyapucchā. Kadā te adhigatanti kālapucchā. Kattha te adhigatanti okāsapucchā. Katame te kilesā pahīnāti pahīnakilesapucchā. Katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhīti paṭiladdhadhammapucchā. Idāni tameva chaṭṭhānavisodhanaṃ vitthāretumāha “sace hī”tiādi. Tattha ettāvatāti ettakena byākaraṇavacanamattena na sakkāro kātabbo. Byākaraṇañhi ekassa ayāthāvatopi hotīti. Imesu chasu ṭhānesu sodhanatthaṃ evaṃ vattabboti yathā nāma jātarūpapatirūpakampi jātarūpaṃ viya khāyatīti jātarūpaṃ nighaṃsanatāpanachedanehi sodhetabbaṃ, evameva idāneva vuttesu chasu ṭhānesu pakkhipitvā sodhanatthaṃ vattabbo. Vimokkhādīsūti ādi-saddena samāpattiñāṇadassanamaggabhāvanāphalasacchikiriyādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Pākaṭo hoti adhigatavisesassa satisammosābhāvato. Sesapucchāsupi “pākaṭo hotī”ti pade eseva nayo.

233. The attainment-state of supreme persons such as the Buddha, who are superior to ordinary humans, is called the superior human state. The declaration of that state to others is called the declaration of the superior human state. To discern this, six points should be clarified—thus is the connection. Herein, ‘What have you attained?’ is the question about attainment. ‘How have you attained it?’ is the question about the means. ‘When did you attain it?’ is the question about time. ‘Where did you attain it?’ is the question about the place. ‘Which defilements have you abandoned?’ is the question about abandoned defilements. ‘Which qualities have you gained?’ is the question about acquired qualities. Now, to elaborate on the clarification of these six points, it is said: ‘If indeed…’ and so on. Herein, ‘to this extent’ means that honor should not be paid based on a mere verbal declaration, for a declaration may be made by one who is not in accordance with reality. To clarify these six points, one should be questioned thus: Just as counterfeit gold that appears like genuine gold must be tested by rubbing, heating, and cutting, even so, one should be questioned for the purpose of clarification by applying these six points. Regarding liberation, and so on—the word ‘and so on’ includes attainments, knowledge-and-vision, path-development, fruition-realization, and so on. ‘It becomes evident’ because there is no loss of mindfulness regarding the distinctive attainment. This same principle applies to the phrase ‘it becomes evident’ in the remaining questions.

Sabbesañhi [M 2.0177][V 2.0130] attanā adhigatamaggena pahīnā kilesā pākaṭā hontīti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ. Kassaci hi attanā adhigatamaggavajjhakilesesu sandeho uppajjatiyeva mahānāmassa sakkassa viya. So hi sakadāgāmī samānopi “tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, evaṃ hoti – ko su nāma me dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno, yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, dosadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, mohadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.175) bhagavantaṃ pucchi. Ayaṃ kira rājā sakadāgāmimaggena lobhadosamohā niravasesā pahīyantīti saññī ahosīti.

For it is generally said that all defilements abandoned by oneself through the attained path become evident. Indeed, doubt may arise regarding the defilements that should be abandoned by the path one has attained, as in the case of Mahānāma the Sakyan. For though he was a once-returner, he asked the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, this occurs to me—what quality remains unabandoned within me, due to which lustful states sometimes overwhelm my mind, hateful states sometimes overwhelm my mind, and deluded states sometimes overwhelm my mind?’ It is said that this king had the perception that greed, hatred, and delusion were abandoned without remainder by the path of the once-returner.

Yāya paṭipadāya yassa ariyamaggo āgacchati, sā pubbabhāgapaṭipatti āgamanapaṭipadā. Sodhetabbāti suddhā, udāhu na suddhāti vicāraṇavasena sodhetabbā. “Na sujjhatīti tattha tattha pamādapaṭipattisambhavato. Apanetabboti attano paṭiññāya apanetabbo”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.197-198). Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.197) pana “na sujjhatīti pucchiyamāno paṭipattikkamaṃ ullaṅghitvā kathesi. Apanetabboti tayā vuttakkamenāyaṃ dhammo na sakkā adhigantunti adhigatamānato apanetabbo”ti vuttaṃ. “Sujjhatī”ti vatvā sujjhanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “dīgharatta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Paññāyatīti etthāpi “yadī”ti padaṃ ānetvā yadi so bhikkhu tāya paṭipadāya paññāyatīti sambandho. Catūsu paccayesu alaggattā “ākāse pāṇisamena cetasā”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttasadisaṃ byākaraṇaṃ hotīti yojanā. Tattha vuttasadisanti tassa bhikkhuno byākaraṇaṃ imasmiṃ sutte vuttena sadisaṃ, samanti attho. Khīṇāsavassa paṭipattisadisā paṭipatti hotīti dīgharattaṃ [M 2.0178] suvikkhambhitakilesattā, idañca arahattaṃ paṭijānantassa vasena vuttaṃ. Tenāha “khīṇāsavassa nāmā”tiādi. Khīṇāsavassa nāma…pe… na hotīti pahīnavipallāsattā, jīvitanikantiyā ca abhāvato na hoti, puthujjanassa pana appahīnavipallāsattā jīvitanikantisabbhāvato ca appamattakenapi hoti, evaṃ suvikkhambhitakilesassa vattanasekkhadhammapaṭijānanaṃ iminā bhayuppādanena, ambilādidassane kheḷuppādādinā ca na sakkā vīmaṃsituṃ, tasmā tassa vacaneneva taṃ saddhātabbaṃ.

The preliminary practice by which one’s noble path arises is called the ‘path of approach’. ‘It should be purified’ means ‘it should be investigated as to whether it is pure or not’. ‘“It is not purified” because negligence in the practice may occur here and there. “It should be removed” means “one should retract one’s claim,”’ as explained in the Sāratthadīpanī. However, the Vimativinodanī states: ‘“It is not purified” means “when questioned, he spoke while bypassing the proper sequence of practice.” “It should be removed” means “this Dhamma cannot be attained in the manner you described; one should retract it from the conceit of having attained.”’ Having said ‘it is purified,’ the manner of purification is then explained with ‘for a long time,’ and so on. ‘It is discerned’—here too, the word ‘if’ is supplied, meaning: ‘If that bhikkhu is discerned by that practice,’ thus establishing the connection. Because of non-attachment to the four requisites, it is said: ‘with a mind like a hand in space’. The explanation is: ‘The declaration is similar to what has been stated.’ Here, ‘similar to what has been stated’ means that the bhikkhu’s declaration is similar to what is said in this sutta—such is the meaning. His practice is like the practice of one whose taints are destroyed—because his defilements have long been suppressed, and this is stated with reference to one who claims arahantship. Hence it is said: ‘For one whose taints are destroyed,’ and so on. For one whose taints are destroyed… it does not occur—because his distortions are abandoned, and there is no desire for life. But for an ordinary person, because his distortions are not abandoned and desire for life is present, it occurs even with a slight thing. Thus, for one whose defilements are well-suppressed, a claim to the ongoing state of a trainee cannot be investigated by this production of fear, nor by things like the production of saliva upon seeing something sour. Therefore, it should be believed on his word alone.

Ayaṃ bhikkhu sampannaveyyākaraṇoti idaṃ na kevalaṃ abhāyanakameva sandhāya vuttaṃ ekaccassa sūrajātikassa puthujjanassapi abhāyanato, rajjanīyārammaṇānaṃ badarasāḷavādiambilamaddanādīnaṃ [V 2.0131] upayojanepi kheḷuppādāditaṇhuppattirahitaṃ sabbathā suvisodhitameva sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

‘This monk is accomplished in expression’—this is not said merely with regard to fearlessness, for even some ordinary individuals of a courageous nature are fearless. It should be understood that this is said with reference to being entirely purified, without any arising of saliva or craving even when using desirable objects such as jujubes, sālava fruits, sour wood apples, and so on.

234. “Nīharitvāti sāsanato nīharitvā”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) vuttaṃ, vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45) pana “nīharitvāti pāḷito uddharitvā”ti. Tathā hi “pañcahupāli, aṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā nānuyuñjitabbaṃ. Katamehi pañcahi? Suttaṃ na jānāti, suttānulomaṃ na jānātī”tiādipāḷito (pari. 442) suttaṃ suttānulomañca nīhariṃsu, “anāpatti evaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyānaṃ uggaho paripucchāti bhaṇatī”ti evamādito ācariyavādaṃ, “āyasmā upāli evamāha ‘anāpatti āvuso supinantenā”ti (pārā. 78) evamādito attanomatiṃ nīhariṃsu. Sā ca therassa attanomati suttena saṅgahitattā suttaṃ jātaṃ, evamaññāpi suttādīhi saṅgahitāva gahetabbā, netarāti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā nīharitvāti [M 2.0179] vibhajitvā, sāṭṭhakathaṃ sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ suttādīsu catūsu padesesu pakkhipitvā catudhā vibhajitvā vinayaṃ pakāsesuṃ tabbinimuttassa abhāvāti adhippāyo. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyampi (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 45) “nīharitvāti ettha sāsanato nīharitvāti attho…pe… tāya hi attanomatiyā thero etadaggaṭṭhapanaṃ labhati. Apica vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā ‘anupasampannena paññattena vā apaññattena vā vuccamāno…pe… anādariyaṃ karoti, āpatti dukkaṭassā’ti. Tattha hi paññattaṃ nāma suttaṃ, sesattayaṃ apaññattaṃ nāma. Tenāyaṃ ‘catubbidhañhi vinayaṃ, mahātherā’ti gāthā suvuttā”ti vuttaṃ.

234. “‘Having extracted’ (nīharitvā) means having extracted from the Teaching,” is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. ṭī. 2.45). However, in the Vimativinodanī (Vimativinodanī. ṭī. 1.45) it is stated, “‘Having extracted’ means having drawn out from the Pāḷi.” For instance, from the Pāḷi passage: “O Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should not be questioned. Which five? He does not know the Sutta, he does not know what accords with the Sutta,” etc. (Parivāra 442), they extracted the Sutta and what accords with the Sutta. From statements like, “Thus our teachers say: ‘There is no offense in learning and questioning,’” they extracted the teachers’ opinions. From statements like, “Venerable Upāli said thus: ‘There is no offense, friend, in a dream,’” etc. (Pārājika 78), they extracted their own opinions. And that personal view of the Elder, being included in the Sutta, became a Sutta. Similarly, other views included in the Suttas, etc., should be understood as accepted, and not otherwise. Alternatively, ‘having extracted’ means having analyzed; having placed the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, together with its commentaries, into the four categories of Suttas etc., they expounded the Vinaya by dividing it into four parts, the intention being that nothing is excluded from these. In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. ṭī. Pārājika 45) it is also stated: “Here, ‘having extracted’ means having extracted from the Teaching... Indeed, through that personal view, the Elder attained the foremost position. Moreover, this was said by the Blessed One: ‘When spoken to by one who is not fully ordained concerning what is laid down or not laid down... if one shows disrespect, there is an offense of wrong-doing.’ There, what is laid down is called the Sutta; the remaining three are called what is not laid down. Therefore, this verse, ‘Indeed, the Vinaya is fourfold, O great elders,’ is well-stated.”

Vuttanti milindapañhe nāgasenattherena vuttaṃ. Pajjate anena atthoti padaṃ, bhagavatā kaṇṭhādivaṇṇuppattiṭṭhānaṃ āhacca visesetvā bhāsitaṃ padaṃ āhaccapadaṃ, bhagavatoyeva vacanaṃ. Tenāha “āhaccapadanti suttaṃ adhippeta”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45) pana “kaṇṭhādivaṇṇuppattiṭṭhānakaraṇādīhi nīharitvā attano vacīviññattiyāva bhāsitaṃ vacanaṃ āhaccapada”nti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 45) pana “aṭṭha vaṇṇaṭṭhānāni āhacca vuttena padanikāyenāti attho, udāhaṭena kaṇṭhokkantena padasamūhenāti adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ. “Idaṃ kappati, idaṃ na kappatī”ti evaṃ avisesetvā “yaṃ bhikkhave mayā ‘idaṃ na kappatī’ti appaṭikkhittaṃ[V 2.0132], tañce akappiyaṃ anulometi, kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo na kappatī”tiādinā (mahāva. 305) vuttasāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ idha rasoti adhippetanti āha “rasoti suttānuloma”nti. Rasoti sāro “pattaraso”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 628-630) viya, paṭikkhittānuññātasuttasāroti attho. Rasoti vā [M 2.0180] lakkhaṇaṃ paṭivatthukaṃ anuddharitvā lakkhaṇānulomena vuttattā. Rasenāti tassa āhaccabhāsitassa rasena, tato uddhaṭena vinicchayenāti attho. Suttachāyā viya hi suttānulomanti. Dhammasaṅgāhakapabhutiācariyaparamparato ānītā aṭṭhakathātanti idha “ācariyavaṃso”ti adhippetāti āha “ācariyavaṃsoti ācariyavādo”ti, ācariyavādo “ācariyavaṃso”ti vutto pāḷiyaṃ vuttānaṃ ācariyānaṃ paramparāya ābhatova pamāṇanti dassanatthaṃ. Adhippāyoti kāraṇopapattisiddho uhāpohanayapavatto paccakkhādipamāṇapatirūpako. Adhippāyoti ettha “attanomatī”ti keci atthaṃ vadanti.

It is said (vuttaṃ) by the Elder Nāgasena in the Milindapañha. Pada (word) means that by which meaning is understood. Āhaccapada is a word spoken by the Blessed One, specifically addressing the places where sounds originate, such as the throat; it is indeed the Blessed One's own utterance. Therefore, it is said: “Āhaccapada means the intended Sutta.” This is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. ṭī. 2.45). However, in the Vimativinodanī (Vimativinodanī. ṭī. 1.45), it is said: “Āhaccapada refers to speech spoken by drawing out sounds from the places of sound production, such as the throat, through one's own vocal expression.” In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. ṭī. Pārājika 45), it is said: “The meaning is that it is a body of words spoken by addressing the eight places of articulation; the intention is that it is a collection of words uttered with the throat fully engaged.” Without making distinctions like “this is allowable, this is not allowable,” the general characteristic stated in such passages as (Mahāvagga 305): “Monks, what I have not rejected as ‘this is not allowable,’ if it conforms to what is unallowable and obstructs what is allowable, that is not allowable for you,” is here intended as the essence (rasa). Therefore, it is said: “Rasa means what accords with the Sutta.” Rasa means the essence, as in ‘the essence of the bowl’ (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 628-630), etc. The meaning is the essence of the Suttas that reject or permit. Or, rasa means the characteristic, because it is spoken in accordance with the characteristic without extracting the individual object. By the rasa means by the essence of that directly spoken (āhacca) teaching; hence, it means the discernment drawn from it. For what accords with the Sutta is like the shadow of the Sutta. The commentary tradition (aṭṭhakathātanti) brought down through the lineage of teachers, starting from the Reciters of the Dhamma, is here intended as the ‘lineage of teachers.’ Therefore, it is said: “Ācariyavaṃsa means the tradition of the teachers.” The tradition of the teachers, called ‘ācariyavaṃsa,’ is stated to show that it is authoritative, having been brought down by the succession of teachers mentioned in the Pāḷi. Adhippāya means the intention established through reasoning, proceeding by the method of inference and deduction, comparable to direct perception and other standards of proof. Here, some explain adhippāya as ‘one's own opinion.’”

Vinayapiṭake pāḷīti idha adhikāravasena vuttaṃ, sesapiṭakesupi suttādicatunayā yathānurūpaṃ labbhanteva.

Here, the phrase ‘in the Vinaya Piṭaka’ is stated in accordance with the topic under discussion; in the remaining Piṭakas too, the four methods such as Suttas are indeed found appropriately.

“Mahāpadesāti mahāokāsā. Mahantāni vinayassa patiṭṭhāpanaṭṭhānāni, yesu patiṭṭhāpito vinayo vinicchinīyati asandehato, mahantāni vā kāraṇāni mahāpadesā, mahantāni vinayavinicchayakāraṇānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthato pana ‘yaṃ bhikkhave’tiādinā vuttāsādhippāyā pāḷiyeva mahāpadesāti vadanti. Tenevāha ‘ye bhagavatā evaṃ vuttā’tiādi. Ime ca mahāpadesā khandhake āgatā, tasmā tesaṃ vinicchayakathā tattheva āvi bhavissatīti idha na vuccatī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45) pana “mahāpadesāti mahāokāsā mahāvisayā, te atthato ‘yaṃ bhikkhavetiādipāḷivasena akappiyānulomato kappiyānulomato ca puggalehi nayato tathā tathā gayhamānā atthanayā eva. Te hi bhagavatā sarūpato avuttesupi paṭikkhittānulomesu anuññātānulomesu [M 2.0181] ca sesesu kiccesu nivattipavattihetutāya mahāgocarāti ‘mahāpadesā’ti vuttā, na pana ‘yaṃ bhikkhave mayā idaṃ na kappatī’tiādinā vuttā sādhippāyā pāḷiyeva tassā sutte paviṭṭhattā. ‘Suttānulomampi sutte otāretabbaṃ…pe… suttameva balavatara’nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.45) hi vuttaṃ. Na hesā sādhippāyā pāḷi sutte otāretabbā, na gahetabbā [V 2.0133] vā hoti. Yenāyaṃ suttānulomaṃ siyā, tasmā imaṃ pāḷiadhippāyaṃ nissāya puggalehi gahitā yathāvuttaatthāva suttānulomaṃ, taṃpakāsakattā pana ayaṃ pāḷipi suttānulomanti gahetabbaṃ. Tenāha ‘ye bhagavatā evaṃ vuttā’tiādi. ‘Yaṃ bhikkhave’tiādipāḷinayena hi puggalehi gahitabbā ye akappiyānulomādayo atthā vuttā, te mahāpadesāti attho”ti vuttaṃ.

“‘Mahāpadesā’ (great authorities) means great opportunities. They are the great foundations for establishing the Vinaya, in which the established Vinaya is decisively settled without doubt. Or, the great reasons are the great authorities; it is said that they are the great reasons for deciding the Vinaya. In meaning, however, they say that the Pāḷi itself, beginning ‘Whatever, O monks,’ etc., with its intended significance, is the great authority. Therefore, it is said, ‘Those spoken thus by the Blessed One,’ etc. These great authorities are found in the Khandhaka; hence, the discussion of their decisions will be clearly presented there and so is not mentioned here.” This is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. ṭī. 2.45). However, the Vimativinodanī (Vimativinodanī. ṭī. 1.45) states: “‘Great authorities’ are the great opportunities, the vast scopes. In meaning, these are indeed the principles of meaning which, in accordance with the Pāḷi beginning ‘Whatever, O monks,’ etc., are taken by individuals in various ways, whether aligning with what is unallowable or aligning with what is allowable. For though not explicitly stated by the Blessed One, in other matters concerning what is rejected or permitted, they are called ‘great authorities’ because they are great scopes serving as causes for refraining or proceeding. But the Pāḷi, ‘Whatever, O monks, that I have said is not allowable,’ etc., with its intended significance, is not itself the great authority, because it is already included in the Sutta. For it is said, ‘What accords with the Sutta should be compared with the Sutta... the Sutta itself is the strongest’ (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.45). This Pāḷi with its intended meaning is not to be compared with the Sutta, nor is it to be taken in such a way that it would be what accords with the Sutta. Therefore, the meanings that are taken by individuals based on this intended meaning of the Pāḷi, as stated, are what accord with the Sutta; and because this Pāḷi reveals them, this Pāḷi too should be taken as what accords with the Sutta. Hence, it is said, ‘Those spoken thus by the Blessed One,’ etc. For the meanings—such as what aligns with the unallowable, and so on—which are to be taken by individuals in accordance with the Pāḷi method beginning ‘Whatever, O monks,’ etc., are the great authorities—this is the meaning.”

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyampi (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 45) “parivāraṭṭhakathāyaṃ idha ca kiñcāpi ‘suttānulomaṃ nāma cattāro mahāpadesā’ti vuttaṃ, atha kho mahāpadesanayasiddhaṃ paṭikkhittāpaṭikkhittaṃ anuññātānanuññātaṃ kappiyākappiyanti atthato vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha yasmā ‘ṭhānaṃ okāso padesoti kāraṇavevacanāni ‘aṭṭhānametaṃ, ānanda, anavakāso’tiādi sāsanato, ‘niggahaṭṭhāna’nti ca ‘asandiṭṭhiṭṭhāna’nti ca ‘asandiṭṭhi ca pana padeso’ti ca lokato, tasmā mahāpadesāti mahākāraṇānīti attho. Kāraṇaṃ nāma ñāpako hetu idhādhippetaṃ, mahantabhāvo pana tesaṃ mahāvisayattā mahābhūtānaṃ viya. Te duvidhā vinayamahāpadesā suttantikamahāpadesā cāti. Tattha vinayamahāpadesā vinaye yogaṃ gacchanti, itare ubhayatthāpi, teneva parivāre (pari. 442) anuyogavatte [M 2.0182] ‘dhammaṃ na jānāti, dhammānulomaṃ na jānātī’ti” vuttaṃ. Tattha dhammanti ṭhapetvā vinayapiṭakaṃ avasesaṃ piṭakadvayaṃ, dhammānulomanti suttantike cattāro mahāpadesetiādi.

In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajirabuddhiṭīkā, Pārājika 45), it is stated: "Although in the Parivāra Aṭṭhakathā and here it is said that 'What accords with the Sutta is called the four great authorities,' nevertheless, what is established by the method of the great authorities—what is rejected or not rejected, permitted or not permitted, allowable or unallowable—is stated in terms of meaning. Herein, because 'ṭhāna' (place), 'okāsa' (opportunity), and 'padesa' (region) are synonyms for 'kāraṇa' (reason) from the Teaching, as in 'This is impossible, Ānanda, there is no opportunity,' etc., and from common usage, as in 'a place of censure,' 'a place of wrong view,' and 'a wrong view is also a place,' therefore, 'great authorities' means 'great reasons.' Reason here refers to the cause that makes known, the motive intended here; and their greatness is due to their vast scope, like the great elements. They are of two kinds: the Vinaya great authorities and the Suttanta great authorities. Among them, the Vinaya great authorities apply to the Vinaya, while the others apply to both. Hence, in the Parivāra (Parivāra 442), in the section on investigation, it is said, 'He does not know the Dhamma, he does not know what accords with the Dhamma.' Here, 'Dhamma' refers to the remaining two Piṭakas excluding the Vinaya Piṭaka, and 'what accords with the Dhamma' refers to the four great authorities in the Suttanta, and so forth."

Yadi sāpi tattha tattha bhagavatā pavattitā pakiṇṇakadesanāva aṭṭhakathā, sā pana dhammasaṅgāhakehi paṭhamaṃ tīṇi piṭakāni saṅgāyitvā tassa atthavaṇṇanānurūpeneva vācanāmaggaṃ āropitattā “ācariyavādo”ti vuccati “ācariyā vadanti saṃvaṇṇenti pāḷiṃ etenā”ti katvā. Tenāha “ācariyavādo nāma…pe… aṭṭhakathātantī”ti. Tisso hi saṅgītiyo āruḷhoyeva buddhavacanassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanābhūto kathāmaggo mahāmahindattherena tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ ābhato, pacchā tambapaṇṇiyehi mahātherehi sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapito nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkarapariharaṇatthaṃ. Bhagavato pakiṇṇakadesanābhūtā ca suttānulomabhūtā ca aṭṭhakathā yasmā dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi pāḷivaṇṇanākkamena saṅgahetvā vuttā, tasmā ācariyavādoti vuttā. Etena ca aṭṭhakathā suttasuttānulomesu atthato saṅgayhatīti veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca esā, evaṃ attanomatipi pamāṇabhūtā. Na hi bhagavato vacanaṃ vacanānulomañca anissāya [V 2.0134] aggasāvakādayopi attano ñāṇabalena suttābhidhammavinayesu kiñci sammutiparamatthabhūtaṃ atthaṃ vattuṃ sakkonti, tasmā sabbampi vacanaṃ sutte suttānulome ca saṅgayhati. Visuṃ pana aṭṭhakathādīnaṃ saṅgahitattā tadavasesaṃ suttasuttānulomato gahetvā catudhā vinayo niddiṭṭho.

If even the miscellaneous teachings expounded by the Blessed One here and there are the commentary, then since the Dhamma compilers first recited the three Piṭakas and established the path of recitation in accordance with the explanation of its meaning, it is called 'ācariyavāda' (the teachers' doctrine), because 'the teachers speak, they explain the Pāli by means of this.' Therefore, it is said: 'Ācariyavāda means... etc.... the commentary tradition.' Indeed, the path of discourse, which is the explanation of the meaning of the Buddha's word and which ascended the three Councils, was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the great elder Mahinda. Later, it was established in the Sinhalese language by the great elders of Tambapaṇṇi to avoid confusion with the tenets of other schools. Because the commentaries, which consist of the Blessed One’s miscellaneous teachings and are in accordance with the suttas, were compiled by the elder Dhamma compilers following the sequence of Pāli explanations, they are called ācariyavāda. And it should be understood that through this, the commentary is comprehended in the suttas and what is in accordance with them, in terms of meaning. Just as this is so, one’s own opinion is also authoritative. For even the foremost disciples and others cannot declare any meaning—whether conventional or ultimate—in the Suttas, Abhidhamma, or Vinaya based on the power of their own knowledge, without relying on the word of the Buddha and what is in accordance with his word. Therefore, all speech is comprehended in the suttas and what is in accordance with them. However, because the commentaries and so forth were compiled separately, the remaining portion of the Vinaya was set forth in four ways, having been taken from the suttas and what is in accordance with them.

Kiñcāpi attanomati suttādīhi saṃsanditvāva parikappīyati, tathāpi sā na suttādīsu visesato niddiṭṭhāti āha “suttasuttānulomaācariyavāde muñcitvā”ti. Anubuddhiyāti suttādīniyeva anugatabuddhiyā. Nayaggāhenāti suttādito [M 2.0183] labbhamānanayaggahaṇena. Attanomatiṃ sāmaññato paṭhamaṃ dassetvā idāni tameva visesetvā dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha “suttantābhidhammavinayaṭṭhakathāsū”ti vacanato piṭakattayassapi sādhāraṇā esā kathāti veditabbā. Theravādoti mahāsumattherādīnaṃ gāho. Idāni tattha paṭipajjitabbākāraṃ dassento āha “taṃ panā”tiādi. Tattha atthenāti attanā nayato gahitena atthena. Pāḷinti attano gāhassa nissayabhūtaṃ sāṭṭhakathaṃ pāḷiṃ. Pāḷiyāti tappaṭikkhepatthaṃ parenābhatāya sāṭṭhakathāya pāḷiyā, attanā gahitaṃ atthaṃ nissāya, pāḷiñca saṃsanditvāti attho. Ācariyavādeti attanā parena ca samuddhaṭaaṭṭhakathāya. Otāretabbāti ñāṇena anuppavesetabbā. Otarati ceva sameti cāti attanā uddhaṭehi saṃsandanavasena otarati, parena uddhaṭena sameti. Sabbadubbalāti asabbaññupuggalassa dosavāsanāya yāthāvato atthasampaṭipattiabhāvato vuttaṃ.

Although one's own opinion is formulated by aligning with the suttas and so forth, still, as it is not specifically stated in the suttas and other texts, it is said, 'excluding the suttas, what is in accordance with the suttas, and the teachers’ doctrines.' 'By subsequent understanding' means by an understanding that follows from the suttas and other texts. 'By grasping the method' means by grasping the method obtained from the suttas and other sources. Having first shown one's own opinion in a general way, now, showing that very point specifically, it is said, 'but also,' etc. Herein, from the phrase 'in the suttas, Abhidhamma, Vinaya, and commentaries,' it should be understood that this discussion is common to all three Piṭakas. 'Theravāda' refers to the view of the great elders like Mahāsuma Thera. Now, explaining the manner in which one should proceed in that matter, it is said, 'but that,' etc. Herein, 'by meaning' means by the meaning grasped by oneself according to a method. 'The Pāli' refers to the Pāli text along with its commentary, which serves as the basis for one's own view. 'By the Pāli' means by the Pāli text along with its commentary brought forward by another for refutation, relying on the meaning grasped by oneself, and comparing it with the Pāli. 'By the teachers’ doctrine' refers to the commentary cited by oneself and by others. 'Should be examined' means should be penetrated by knowledge. 'It descends and concurs' means it descends by way of comparison with what one has cited oneself, and concurs with what another has cited. 'All weak' is said because an individual who is not all-knowing lacks the attainment of the meaning as it truly is, due to the latent tendencies of defilements.

Pamādapāṭhavasena ācariyavādassa suttānulomena asaṃsandanāpi siyāti āha “itaro na gahetabbo”ti. Samentameva gahetabbanti ye suttena saṃsandanti, evarūpāva atthā mahāpadesato uddharitabbāti dasseti tathā tathā uddhaṭaatthānaṃyeva suttānulomattā. Tenāha “suttānulomato hi suttameva balavatara”nti. Atha vā suttānulomassa suttekadesattepi sutte viya “idaṃ kappati, idaṃ na kappatī”ti paricchinditvā āhaccabhāsitaṃ kiñci natthīti āha “suttā…pe… balavatara”nti. Appaṭivattiyanti appaṭibāhiyaṃ. Kārakasaṅghasadisanti pamāṇattā saṅgītikārakasaṅghasadisaṃ. “Buddhānaṃ ṭhitakālasadisa”nti iminā buddhānaṃyeva kathitadhammabhāvaṃ dasseti, dharamānabuddhasadisanti vuttaṃ [M 2.0184] hoti. Sutte hi paṭibāhite buddhova paṭibāhito hoti. “Sakavādī suttaṃ gahetvā kathetīti sakavādī attano suttaṃ gahetvā voharati. Paravādī suttānulomanti [V 2.0135] aññanikāyavādī attano nikāye suttānulomaṃ gahetvā kathetī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) vuttaṃ.

Through negligence and error, the teachers’ doctrines may not align with what is in accordance with the suttas; hence it is said, 'the other should not be taken.' 'Only what concurs should be taken' means that meanings that align with the suttas should be extracted from the great authorities, showing that only meanings extracted in such a way are in accordance with the suttas. Therefore, it is said, 'for the sutta itself is stronger than what conforms to the suttas.' Alternatively, even if what is in accordance with the sutta is a part of the sutta, there is nothing spoken directly and definitively in it, as in the sutta, saying 'this is allowable, this is not allowable'; hence it is said, 'the sutta... is stronger.' 'Irreversible' means unrejectable. 'Like the council of compilers' means it is comparable in authority to the council that compiled the texts. By 'like the time when the Buddhas were present,' the very nature of the Dhamma as spoken by the Buddhas is shown; it is said to be like a living Buddha. For if the sutta is rejected, the Buddha himself is rejected. It is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.45): '“A proponent of his own view takes the sutta and speaks” means a proponent of his own view takes his own sutta and makes his case. “A proponent of another view, what is in accordance with the suttas” means a follower of another school takes what is in accordance with the suttas in his own school and speaks.'

Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45) pana “sakavādī suttaṃ gahetvā kathetītiādīsu yo yathābhūtamatthaṃ gahetvā kathanasīlo, so sakavādī. Suttanti saṅgītittayāruḷhaṃ pāḷivacanaṃ. Paravādīti mahāvihāravāsī vā hotu aññanikāyavāsī vā, yo viparītato atthaṃ gahetvā kathanasīlo, sova idha ‘paravādī’ti vutto. Suttānulomanti saṅgītittayāruḷhaṃ vā anāruḷhaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci vipallāsato vā vañcanāya vā ‘saṅgītittayāgatamida’nti dassiyamānaṃ suttānulomaṃ. Keci ‘aññanikāye suttānuloma’nti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ sakavādīparavādīnaṃ ubhinnampi saṅgītittayāruḷhasuttādīnameva gahetabbato. Tathā hi vakkhati ‘tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhaṃ pāḷiāgataṃ paññāyati, gahetabba’ntiādi (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.45). Na hi sakavādī aññanikāyasuttādiṃ pamāṇato gaṇhāti. Yena tesu suttādīsu dassitesu tattha ṭhātabbaṃ bhaveyya, vakkhati ca ‘paro tassa akappiyabhāvasādhakaṃ suttato bahuṃ kāraṇañca vinicchayañca dasseti…pe… sādhūti sampaṭicchitvā akappiyeyeva ṭhātabba’nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.45), tasmā paravādināpi saṅgītittaye anāruḷhampi anāruḷhamicceva dassīyati, kevalaṃ tassa tassa suttādino saṅgītittaye anāgatassa kūṭatā, āgatassa ca byañjanacchāyāya aññathā adhippāyayojanā ca visesā, tattha ca yaṃ kūṭaṃ, taṃ apanīyati. Yaṃ aññathā yojitaṃ, taṃ tassa viparītatādassanatthaṃ tadaññena suttādinā [M 2.0185] saṃsandanā karīyati. Yo pana paravādinā gahito adhippāyo suttantādinā saṃsandati, so sakavādināpi attano gāhaṃ vissajjetvā gahetabboti ubhinnampi saṅgītittayāgatameva suttaṃ pamāṇanti veditabbaṃ. Teneva kathāvatthupakaraṇe ‘sakavāde pañca suttasatāni paravāde pañcā’ti, suttasahassampi adhippāyaggahaṇanānattena saṅgītittayāgatameva gahitaṃ, na nikāyantare”ti vuttaṃ.

However, in the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.45), it is stated: "One who, in contexts such as 'taking up a sutta and explaining it,' takes up the true meaning and is accustomed to speaking accordingly, is called a 'sakavādī' (one who adheres to his own doctrine). 'Sutta' refers to the Pali texts established in the three Councils. 'Paravādī' (one who follows another doctrine) refers to anyone, whether a resident of the Mahāvihāra or a resident of another school, who takes up a distorted meaning and is accustomed to speaking accordingly—here, such a person is called 'paravādī.' 'Suttānuloma' means anything, whether established in the three Councils or not, that is presented as though it comes from the three Councils, either through distortion or deceit. Some say, 'Suttānuloma refers to the texts of another school,' but this is incorrect, because both 'sakavādī' and 'paravādī' should only take what is established in the three Councils. As it will be said: 'The Pali texts that have come down established in the three Councils are recognized, and should be taken.' For the 'sakavādī' does not take the texts etc. of another school as authoritative, so that when such texts etc. are presented, one should have to stand by them. And it will be said: 'The opponent presents from the sutta much reason and judgment proving its unsuitability... and having accepted it as valid, one would have to stand by what is indeed unsuitable.' Therefore, even the 'paravādī' presents what is not established in the three Councils as precisely not established; merely the falsity of that particular text etc. that has not come down in the three Councils, and the misinterpretation of the wording and intention of that which has come down, are the differences. And there, what is false is rejected, and what is misinterpreted is compared with another text etc. to show its distortion. However, if the meaning taken up by the 'paravādī' accords with the suttas etc., then the 'sakavādī' should abandon his own position and accept it. Thus, it should be understood that for both, only the sutta included in the three Councils is authoritative. Hence, in the Kathāvatthu treatise, it is said: 'In the sakavāda, there are five hundred suttas; in the paravāda, five hundred.' Even a thousand suttas are taken, due to the variety of grasping intentions, only from those included in the three Councils, not from another school."

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 45) pana “paravādīti amhākaṃ samayavijānanako aññanikāyikoti vuttaṃ. Paravādī suttānulomanti kathaṃ? ‘Aññatra udakadantaponā’ti suttaṃ sakavādissa, tadanulomato nāḷikeraphalassa udakampi udakameva hotīti paravādī ca.

However, in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 45), it is stated: "'Paravādī' means one who understands our conventions, said to be a follower of another sect. How is the 'paravādī's view' in accordance with the sutta? The sutta, ‘except for water and tooth-cleaners,’ is for the ‘sakavādī’; and in accordance with that, the ‘paravādī’ says that the water of a coconut fruit is also simply water.

‘Nāḷikerassa [V 2.0136] yaṃ toyaṃ, purāṇaṃ pittavaḍḍhanaṃ;

Tameva taruṇaṃ toyaṃ, pittaghaṃ balavaḍḍhana’nti. –

'Coconut water, when old, increases bile; but that same water, when young, destroys bile and increases strength.'

Evaṃ paravādinā vutte sakavādī dhaññaphalassa gatikattā, āhāratthassa ca pharaṇato ‘yāvakālikameva ta’nti vadanto paṭikkhipatī”ti. Khepaṃ vā garahaṃ vā akatvāti “kiṃ iminā”ti khepaṃ paṭikkhepaṃ chaḍḍanaṃ vā “kimesa bālo vadati, kimesa bālo jānātī”ti garahaṃ nindaṃ vā akatvā. Suttānulomanti attanā avuttaṃ aññanikāye suttānulomaṃ. “Sutte otāretabbanti sakavādinā sutte otāretabba”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45). Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45) pana “sutte otāretabbanti yassa suttassa anulomanato idaṃ suttānulomaṃ akāsi, tasmiṃ, tadanurūpe vā aññatarasmiṃ sutte attanā gahitaṃ suttānulomaṃ atthato saṃsandanavasena otāretabbaṃ. ‘Iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇena imasmiṃ sutte saṃsandatī’ti saṃsandetvā dassetabbanti attho”ti [M 2.0186] vuttaṃ. Suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbanti attano sutteyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Ayanti sakavādī. Paroti paravādī. Ācariyavādo sutte otāretabboti yassa suttassa saṃvaṇṇanāvasena ayaṃ ācariyavādo pavatto, tasmiṃ, tādise ca aññasmiṃ sutte pubbāparaatthasaṃsandanavasena otāretabbaṃ. Gārayhācariyavādoti pamādalikhito, bhinnaladdhikehi ca ṭhapito, esa nayo sabbattha.

When the opponent has spoken thus, the proponent rejects it, saying, “It is only for a limited time,” because it falls into the category of grain-fruit and serves as sustenance. Without making a disparagement or a censure—that is, without saying, “What is this?” as a disparagement, rejection, or abandonment, or without saying, “What does this fool say? What does this fool know?” as a censure or blame. ‘In accordance with the Sutta’ means what was not stated by oneself but is in line with the Suttas of another school. ‘It should be brought into the Sutta’ means that the proponent should bring it into the Sutta. This is explained in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.45). However, the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.45) states: “‘It should be brought into the Sutta’—that is, the suttānuloma taken up by oneself should be brought into that Sutta in accordance with which one made this suttānuloma, or into another suitable Sutta, by way of connecting the meaning. The meaning is that one should show the connection by saying, “For this and this reason, it aligns with this Sutta.” ‘One should stand only in the Sutta’ means one should stand by one’s own Sutta. ‘This one’ refers to the proponent. ‘The other’ refers to the opponent. ‘The teacher’s doctrine should be brought into the Sutta’ means that the teacher’s doctrine, which has been presented through the explanation of a certain Sutta, should be brought into that Sutta or another similar Sutta by way of connecting the earlier and later meanings. ‘A blameworthy teacher’s doctrine’ refers to one written carelessly or established by those of schismatic views. This method applies everywhere.

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 45) pana – paro ācariyavādanti “suṅkaṃ pariharatīti ettha upacāraṃ okkamitvā kiñcāpi pariharati, avahāro evā”ti aṭṭhakathāvacanato “tathā karonto pārājikamāpajjatī”ti paravādinā vutte sakavādī “suṅkaṃ pariharati, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti suttaṃ tattheva āgatamahāaṭṭhakathāvacanena saddhiṃ dassetvā paṭisedheti. Tathā karontassa dukkaṭamevāti. Paro attanomatinti ettha “purebhattaṃ parasantakaṃ avaharāti purebhattameva harissāmīti vāyamantassa pacchābhattaṃ hoti, purebhattapayogova so, tasmā mūlaṭṭho na muccatīti tumhākaṃ theravādattā mūlaṭṭhassa pārājikamevā”ti paravādinā vutte sakavādī “taṃ saṅketaṃ pure vā pacchā vā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, mūlaṭṭhassa anāpattī”ti suttaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipati.

In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 45), however, it is stated: ‘The opponent’s teacher’s doctrine’—when the opponent, citing the commentary’s statement that “Regarding ‘He avoids the tax’—here, even though he avoids it by entering the vicinity, it is still theft,” argues that “Thus doing, he incurs a pārājika offense,” the proponent responds, “He avoids the tax; the offense is a dukkaṭa,” and presenting the sutta along with the statement from the Great Commentary that appears there, he refutes it. Thus, for one who does so, only a dukkaṭa offense applies. ‘The opponent’s own opinion’—here, when the opponent says, “Regarding ‘He steals another’s property before the meal’—for one who endeavors to steal it before the meal, it becomes after the meal. That is still an effort made before the meal. Therefore, the original offender is not absolved. Thus, according to your Theravāda view, the original offender incurs a pārājika,” the proponent counters, “Whether before or after that appointed time, if he steals that item, the original offender incurs no offense,” and presents the sutta to reject the claim.

Paro suttanti “aniyatahetudhammo sammattaniyatahetudhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti suttaṃ [V 2.0137] paṭṭhāne likhitaṃ dassetvā “ariyamaggassa na nibbānamevārammaṇa”nti paravādinā vutte sakavādī ārammaṇattikādisuttānulomena otaratīti paṭikkhipati. Suttānulome otarantaṃyeva hi suttaṃ nāma, netaraṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “pāḷiāgataṃ paññāyatī”ti ettakenapi [M 2.0187] siddhe “tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhaṃ pāḷiāgataṃ paññāyatī”tiādi. Tādisañhi pamādalekhanti ācariyo. “Appamādo amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno pada”nti (dha. pa. 21) vacanato dinnabhojane bhuñjitvā parissayāni parivajjitvā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā viharanto nicco hotīti. Evarūpassa atthassa āruḷhampi suttaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “no ce tathā paññāyatī”ti siddhepi “no ce tathā paññāyati, na otarati na sametīti. Bāhirakasuttaṃ vā”ti vuttattā attano suttampi atthena asamentaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Paro ācariyavādantiādīsu dvīsu nayesu pamādalekhavasena tattha tattha āgataṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ theravādehi saddhiṃ yojetvā veditabbaṃ.

‘The opponent’s Sutta’—having shown this sutta written in the Paṭṭhāna: “The indeterminate-cause Dhamma is a condition for the determinate-cause Dhamma by way of the object condition,” when the opponent says, “For the noble path, Nibbāna is not the sole object,” the proponent refutes by bringing it into conformity with suttas like the Ārammaṇattika, etc. For indeed, only what is brought into conformity with the Sutta is called a sutta, not anything else. Therefore, it is said, “What has come down in the Pāli is understood.” Even if this much is established, it is said, “What has come down in the Pāli, having been established in the three councils, is understood,” and so on. For such is careless writing, say the teachers. According to “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path to death” (Dhammapada 21), one who, having eaten the given meal, avoiding dangers, and establishing mindfulness, dwells, becomes eternal. Even a sutta that has been established with such a meaning should not be accepted. Therefore, it is said, “If it is not understood thus,” even when established, “If it is not understood thus, it does not come into conformity, it does not agree. Or it is an extraneous sutta.” Thus, even one’s own sutta, if it does not agree with the meaning, should not be accepted. In the two methods, such as ‘the opponent’s teacher’s doctrine,’ etc., the commentarial statements found here and there due to careless writing should be understood by reconciling them with the Theravāda.

Athāyaṃ ācariyavādaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttanti paravādinā “mūlabījaṃ nāma haliddi siṅgiveraṃ vacā…pe… bīje bījasaññī chindati vā chedāpeti vā bhindati vā…pe… āpatti pācittiyassā”ti (pāci. 91) tumhākaṃ pāṭhattā “haliddigaṇṭhiṃ chindantassa pācittiya”nti vutte sakavādī “yāni vā panaññāni atthi mūle jāyanti, mūle sañjāyantī”tiādiṃ dassetvā tassa aṭṭhakathāsaṅkhātena ācariyavādena paṭikkhipati. Na hi gaṇṭhimhi gaṇṭhi jāyatīti. Paro suttānulomanti paravādinā “anāpatti evaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyānaṃ uggaho”ti vacanassānulomato “amhākaṃ porāṇabhikkhū ekapāsāde gabbhaṃ thaketvā anupasampannena sayituṃ vaṭṭatīti tathā katvā āgatā, tasmā amhākaṃ vaṭṭatīti tumhesu eva ekaccesu vadantesu “tumhākaṃ na kiñci vattuṃ sakkā”ti vutte sakavādī “suttaṃ suttānulomañca uggahitakānaṃyeva ācariyānaṃ uggaho pamāṇa”ntiādiaṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ dassetvā paṭisedheti. Paro attanomatinti “dvāraṃ [M 2.0188] vivaritvā anāpucchā sayitesu ke muccantī”ti ettha pana dvepi janā muccanti – yo ca yakkhagahitako, yo ca bandhitvā nipajjāpitoti tumhākaṃ theravādattā aññe sabbepi yathā tathā vā nipannādayopi muccantīti paṭisedheti.

Then, taking up the teacher’s doctrine, he speaks. ‘The opponent’s Sutta’—when the opponent says, “The root seed, namely, turmeric, ginger, orris root… if one cuts, causes to be cut, or breaks a seed while perceiving it as a seed… the offense is a pācittiya” (Pac. 91), and when you recite, “For one who cuts a turmeric rhizome, it is a pācittiya,” one’s own proponent, citing “whatever else grows from the root, originates in the root,” and so on, refutes it by means of the teacher’s doctrine, which is considered a commentary. For indeed, a rhizome does not grow on a rhizome. ‘The opponent’s conformity with the Sutta’—when the opponent says, in accordance with the statement, “There is no offense, thus was the instruction of our teachers,” and when some among you say, “Our ancient monks, having sealed a room in a single-storied building and deemed it allowable for one who is not fully ordained to sleep inside, and having done so, they came to this opinion, therefore it is allowable for us,” and when told, “You have nothing to say,” one’s own proponent, citing the commentary statement, “For those who have learned the sutta and what accords with the sutta, the instruction of the teachers is the standard,” and so on, refutes it. ‘The opponent’s own opinion’—here, when the opponent says, “When the door has been opened and some sleep without asking permission, who are absolved?” and then says, “Here, indeed, two kinds of people are absolved—one possessed by a spirit and one who is bound and made to lie down. According to your Theravāda position, all others, lying down in whatever way, are also absolved,” one’s own proponent refutes this.

Atha panāyaṃ attanomatiṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttanti “āpattiṃ āpajjantī”ti paravādinā vutte sakavādī “divā kilantarūpo mañce nisinno pāde bhūmito amocetvāva niddāvasena [V 2.0138] nipajjati, tassa anāpattī”tiādiaṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ dassetvā ekabhaṅgena nipannādayopi muccantīti paṭisedheti.

Then, taking up his own opinion, he speaks. ‘The opponent’s Sutta’—when the opponent says, “They incur an offense,” one’s own proponent, citing the commentary passage, “Being weary during the day, sitting on a couch, without removing his feet from the ground, he falls down due to sleep—for him there is no offense,” and so on, refutes it, saying that even those who lie down in a single posture are exempt.

Athāyaṃ attanomatiṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttānulomanti “domanassampāhaṃ devānaminda duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi asevitabbampītiādivacanehi (dī. ni. 2.360) saṃsandanato sadārapose doso tumhākaṃ natthi, tena vuttaṃ ‘puttadārassa saṅgaho”ti (khu. pā. 5.6; su. ni. 265) paravādinā vutte “kiñcāpi sakavādī bahussuto na hoti, atha kho rāgasahiteneva akusalena bhavitabba”nti paṭikkhipati. Sesesupi iminā nayena aññathāpi anurūpato yojetabbaṃ, idaṃ sabbaṃ upatissattherādayo āhu. Dhammasiritthero pana “ettha paroti vutto aññanikāyiko, so pana attano suttādīniyeva āharati, tāni sakavādī attano suttādimhi otāretvā sace sameti, gaṇhāti. No ce, paṭikkhipatī”ti vadatīti āgataṃ.

Then, taking up his own opinion, he speaks. ‘The opponent’s conformity with the Sutta’—when the opponent says, “Sorrow, O Lord of the Devas, I declare to be of two kinds—to be cultivated and not to be cultivated,” and so on (Dī. Ni. 2.360), and from this connection, “there is no fault in cherishing one’s wife and children for you. Therefore, it is said, ‘cherishing wife and children’” (Khu. Pā. 5.6; Su. Ni. 265), one’s own proponent rejects it, saying, “Even though one’s own proponent is not very learned, still, he must be associated with unwholesome states tainted by lust.” In the remaining cases too, this method should be applied, either differently or suitably. All this is said by elders like Upatissa. However, the elder Dhammasiri says, “Here, ‘the other’ refers to one of another sect; he brings forth only his own suttas, etc. One’s own proponent examines them by bringing them into his own suttas, etc. If they agree, he accepts them; if not, he rejects them.” Thus it is handed down.

Nanu ca “suttānulomato suttameva balavatara”nti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ, idha pana “suttaṃ suttānulome otāretabba”ntiādi kasmā vuttanti? Nāyaṃ virodho, “suttānulomato suttameva balavatara”nti idañhi sakamateyeva suttaṃ [M 2.0189] sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha hi sakamatipariyāpannameva suttādiṃ sandhāya “attanomati sabbadubbalā, attanomatito ācariyavādo balavataro, ācariyavādato suttānulomaṃ balavataraṃ, suttānulomato suttameva balavatara”nti ca vuttaṃ. Idha pana paravādinā ānītaṃ aññanikāye suttaṃ sandhāya “suttānulome suttaṃ otāretabba”ntiādi vuttaṃ, tasmā paravādinā ānītaṃ suttādi attano suttānulomaācariyavādaattanomatīsu otāretvā samentaṃyeva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ na gahetabbanti ayaṃ nayo idha vuccatīti na koci pubbāparavirodhoti ayaṃ sāratthadīpaniyāgato (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) nayo. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45) pana “yaṃ kiñci kūṭasuttaṃ bāhirakasuttādivacanaṃ na gahetabbanti dassetuṃ suttaṃ suttānulome otāretabbantiādi vutta”nti vuttaṃ.

But wasn’t it stated earlier that “the sutta itself is stronger than conformity with the sutta”? Then why is it said here that “a sutta should be tested against conformity with the sutta,” and so on? There is no contradiction here. For the statement “the sutta itself is stronger than conformity with the sutta” refers specifically to a sutta within one’s own school. There, concerning a sutta and other texts that fall within one’s own school, it is said: “One’s own opinion is the weakest of all; the teacher’s doctrine is stronger than one’s own opinion; conformity with the sutta is stronger than the teacher’s doctrine; and the sutta itself is stronger than conformity with the sutta.” Here, however, it is said with reference to a sutta brought by an opponent from another school: “A sutta should be tested against conformity with the sutta,” and so on. Therefore, a sutta or other text brought by an opponent should be accepted only if it agrees when tested against one’s own conformity with the sutta, teacher’s doctrine, and own opinion. What does not agree should not be accepted. This is the principle being explained here, and there is no contradiction between the earlier and later statements. This is the approach given in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.45). However, the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.45) states: “To show that any false sutta, such as a statement from an external school, should not be accepted, it is said that ‘a sutta should be tested against conformity with the sutta,’ and so on.”

Bāhirakasuttanti tisso saṅgītiyo anāruḷhaguḷhavessantarādīni ca mahāsaṅghikanikāyavāsīnaṃ suttāni. Vedallādīnanti ādi-saddena guḷhaummaggādiggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ[V 2.0139]. Itaraṃ gārayhasuttaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. “Attanomatiyameva ṭhātabba”nti iminā aññanikāyato ānītasuttatopi sakanikāye attanomatiyeva balavatarāti dasseti. “Sakavādī suttaṃ gahetvā katheti, paravādī suttamevā”ti evamādinā samānajātikānaṃ vasena vāro na vutto. Suttassa sutteyeva otāraṇaṃ bhinnaṃ viya hutvā na paññāyati, vuttanayeneva ca sakkā yojetunti.

By 'external suttas' are meant those not included in the three councils, such as the Guḷhavessantara, and the suttas of those belonging to the Mahāsaṅghika school. Regarding 'Vedalla and others,' by the word 'ādi' (etc.), the inclusion of texts like the Guḷha-ummagga should be understood. Other blameworthy suttas should not be accepted. By the statement, 'One should stand by one's own opinion,' it is shown that within one's own school, one's own opinion is stronger even than a sutta brought from another school. A turn based on categories of the same kind, such as 'the proponent of one's own doctrine takes a sutta and speaks, the opponent a sutta as well,' is not stated.
