The testing of a sutta against a sutta is not presented as a separate category, but it can be done according to the method stated.

Idāni sakavādīparavādīnaṃ kappiyākappiyādibhāvaṃ sandhāya vivāde uppanne tattha paṭipajjitabbavidhiṃ dassento āha “atha panāyaṃ kappiyanti gahetvā kathetī”tiādi. Atha vā evaṃ suttasuttānulomādimukhena sāmaññato vivādaṃ [M 2.0190] dassetvā idāni visesato vivādavatthuṃ tabbinicchayamukhena suttādiñca dassetuṃ “atha panāyaṃ kappiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sutte ca suttānulome ca otāretabbanti sakavādinā attanoyeva sutte ca suttānulome ca otāretabbaṃ. Paro kāraṇaṃ na vindatīti paravādī kāraṇaṃ na labhati. Suttato bahuṃ kāraṇañca vinicchayañca dassetīti paravādī attano suttato bahuṃ kāraṇañca vinicchayañca āharitvā dasseti, “sādhūti sampaṭicchitvā akappiyeyeva ṭhātabba”nti iminā attano nikāye suttādīni alabhantena sakavādinā paravādīvacaneyeva ṭhātabbanti vadati. Sutte ca suttānulome cāti ettha ca-kāro vikappanattho, tena ācariyavādādīnampi saṅgaho. Tenāha “kāraṇañca vinicchayañca dassetī”ti. Tattha kāraṇanti suttādinayaṃ nissāya attanomatiyā uddhaṭaṃ hetuṃ. Vinicchayanti aṭṭhakathāvinicchayaṃ.

Now, regarding the disputes that arise among proponents of one's own doctrine and others' doctrines concerning what is allowable or unallowable, the method to be followed is explained by saying, 'But if one takes this as allowable and speaks thus,' and so on. Alternatively, having first shown the dispute in a general way through the discourse, conformity with the discourse, and so on, now the specific grounds of dispute are to be explained through the means of decision, along with the discourses and other sources, hence the statement, 'But if one takes this as allowable,' etc. There, in the discourse and in conformity with the discourse, one should apply it—this means that the proponent of one's own doctrine should themselves apply it to their own discourse and its conformity. 'The other party does not find a reason'—this means the opponent does not obtain a valid argument. 'From the discourse, much reasoning and decision are shown'—this means the opponent brings forth much reasoning and decision based on their own discourse and presents it. By this statement, 'Having accepted it with “Good,” one should stand by what is unallowable,' it is stated that when the proponent of one's own doctrine cannot find support in the discourses and other sources of their own school, they should stand by the opponent's statement. In 'Sutte ca suttānulome ca' (And in the discourse and in conformity with the discourse), here the word 'ca' (and) serves to indicate alternatives, thus including the views of the teachers and others as well. Hence it is said, 'One shows reasoning and decision.' There, 'reasoning' refers to the argument drawn from one's own opinion based on the method of the discourses and other sources. 'Decision' refers to the commentary's decision.

Dvinnampi kāraṇacchāyā dissatīti sakavādīparavādīnaṃ ubhinnampi kappiyākappiyabhāvasādhakaṃ kāraṇapatirūpakacchāyā dissati. Tattha kāraṇacchāyāti suttādīsu “kappiya”nti gāhassa, “akappiya”nti gāhassa ca nimittabhūtena kicchena paṭipādanīyaṃ avibhūtakāraṇaṃ kāraṇacchāyā, kāraṇapatirūpakanti attho. Yadi dvinnampi kāraṇacchāyā dissati, kasmā akappiyeyeva ṭhātabbanti āha “vinayañhi patvā”tiādi. “Vinayaṃ patvā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassento āha “kappiyākappiyavicāraṇaṃ āgammā”ti. Rundhitabbantiādīsu dubbiññeyyavinicchaye kappiyākappiyabhāve sati “kappiya”nti gahaṇaṃ rundhitabbaṃ, “akappiya”nti gahaṇaṃ gāḷhaṃ kātabbaṃ, aparāparappavattaṃ kappiyaggahaṇaṃ sotaṃ pacchinditabbaṃ, garukabhāvasaṅkhate [M 2.0191] akappiyeyeva ṭhātabbanti attho. Atha vā rundhitabbanti kappiyasaññāya [V 2.0140] vītikkamakāraṇaṃ rundhitabbaṃ, taṃnivāraṇacittaṃ daḷhataraṃ kātabbaṃ. Sotaṃ pacchinditabbanti tattha vītikkamappavatti pacchinditabbā. Garukabhāveti akappiyabhāveti attho.

The shadow of a reason is seen in both means that for both proponents of one's own view and proponents of others' views, a shadow resembling a reason, which establishes what is allowable and unallowable, is seen. Herein, 'the shadow of a reason' is the indistinct reason that must be established with difficulty, serving as the basis for grasping either 'allowable' or 'unallowable' in the discourses and other texts; the meaning is that it is a semblance of a reason. If a shadow of a reason is seen in both, why should one stand firm only on the unallowable? To this, he says, 'for having come to the Vinaya,' and so on. Showing the meaning of 'having come to the Vinaya' more clearly, he says, 'having come to the examination of what is allowable and unallowable.' In cases such as 'should be restrained,' when there is a state of allowability and unallowability in a decision that is difficult to discern, the grasping of 'allowable' should be restrained, while the grasping of 'unallowable' should be made firm. The stream of repeatedly occurring grasping of what is allowable should be cut off. The meaning is that one should stand firm only on the unallowable, which is considered a grave matter. Alternatively, 'should be restrained' means that the cause of transgression due to the perception of allowability should be restrained, and the mind preventing that should be made firmer. 'The stream should be cut off' means that the occurrence of transgression there should be severed. 'In a grave matter' means in the case of what is unallowable.

Bahūhi suttavinicchayakāraṇehīti bahūhi suttehi ceva tato ānītavinicchayakāraṇehi ca. Atha vā suttena aṭṭhakathāvinicchayena ca laddhakāraṇehi. Attano gahaṇaṃ na vissajjetabbanti sakavādinā attano “akappiya”nti gahaṇaṃ na vissajjetabbanti attho.

By many reasons for deciding from the discourses means by many discourses and also by reasons for deciding derived from them. Or else, by reasons obtained from the discourse and from the decision of the commentary. 'One should not relinquish one's own position' means that the proponent of his own doctrine should not relinquish his own holding of 'unallowable'.

Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ nigamento “eva”ntiādimāha. Tattha yoti sakavādīparavādīsu yo koci. Keci pana “sakavādīsuyeva yo koci idhādhippeto”ti vadanti, evaṃ sante “atha panāyaṃ kappiyanti gahetvā kathetī”tiādīsu sabbattha ubhopi sakavādinoyeva siyuṃ heṭṭhā vuttasseva nigamanavasena “eva”ntiādinā vuttattā, tasmā taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Atirekakāraṇaṃ labhatīti ettha suttādīsu purimaṃ purimaṃ atirekakāraṇaṃ nāma, yo vā suttādīsu catūsu bahutaraṃ kāraṇaṃ labhati, so atirekakāraṇaṃ labhati nāma.

Now, summarizing the meaning just stated, he says, 'thus,' and so on. Herein, 'whoever' refers to anyone among proponents of one's own view and proponents of others' views. Some, however, say, 'Here, "whoever" is intended to mean only someone among the proponents of one's own view.' If that were so, then in statements such as, 'But if this one, taking it as allowable, speaks thus,' and so on, in all cases both parties would be proponents of one's own view, because it is stated with 'thus,' and so on, by way of summarizing what was said previously. Therefore, that view should not be accepted. Regarding 'obtains a superior reason,' herein, among the discourses and so on, the preceding one is called the superior reason. Or, whoever obtains more numerous reasons among the four—the discourses and so on—is said to obtain a superior reason.

Suṭṭhu pavatti etassāti, suṭṭhu pavattati sīlenāti vā suppavatti. Tenāha “suppavattīti suṭṭhu pavatta”nti. Vācāya uggataṃ vācuggataṃ, vacasā suggahitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā vācuggatanti vācāya uggataṃ, tattha nirantaraṃ ṭhitanti attho. Suttatoti imassa vivaraṇaṃ “pāḷito”ti. Ettha ca “suttaṃ nāma sakalaṃ vinayapiṭaka”nti vuttattā puna suttatoti tadatthapaṭipādakaṃ suttābhidhammapāḷivacanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Anubyañjanasoti imassa vivaraṇaṃ “paripucchato ca aṭṭhakathāto cā”ti. Pāḷiṃ anugantvā atthassa byañjanato pakāsanato [M 2.0192] “anubyañjana”nti hi paripucchā aṭṭhakathā ca vuccati. Ettha ca aṭṭhakathāya visuṃ gahitattā “paripucchā”ti theravādo vutto. Atha vā paripucchāti ācariyassa santikā pāḷiyā atthasavanaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāti pāḷimuttakavinicchayo. Tadubhayampi pāḷiṃ anugantvā atthassa byañjanato “anubyañjana”nti vuttaṃ.

One whose practice is good, or one who practices well in virtue, is 'suppavatti' (of good practice). Therefore, he said, 'Suppavatti means well-practiced.' 'Vācuggataṃ' means learned by heart through speech; it means well-grasped by word. Alternatively, 'vācuggataṃ' means risen up in speech; the meaning is that it is constantly established therein. The explanation of 'suttato' is 'from the Pāli.' And here, since it has been said, 'Sutta means the entire Vinaya Piṭaka,' 'suttato' is again intended to mean the word of the Pāli from the Sutta and Abhidhamma which conveys that meaning. The explanation of 'anubyañjanaso' is 'from inquiry and from the commentary.' For inquiry and the commentary are called 'anubyañjana' because they follow the Pāli and clarify the meaning by way of the letter. And here, since the commentary is taken separately, 'inquiry' refers to the tradition of the elders (Theravāda). Alternatively, 'inquiry' is the hearing of the meaning of the Pāli from a teacher. 'Commentary' is a decision independent of the Pāli. Both of these are called 'anubyañjana' because they follow the Pāli and clarify the meaning by way of the letter.

Vinayeti vinayācāre. Teneva vakkhati “vinayaṃ ajahanto avokkamanto”tiādi. Tattha patiṭṭhānaṃ nāma sañcicca āpattiyā anāpajjanādinā hotīti āha “lajjibhāvena patiṭṭhito”ti, tena lajjī hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Vinayadharassa lakkhaṇe vattabbe kiṃ iminā lajjibhāvenāti [V 2.0141] āha “alajjī hī”tiādi. Tattha bahussutopīti iminā paṭhamalakkhaṇasamannāgamaṃ dasseti. Lābhagarukatāyāti iminā vinaye ṭhitatāya abhāve paṭhamalakkhaṇayogā kiccakaro na hoti, atha kho akiccakaro anatthakaro evāti dasseti. Saṅghabhedassa pubbabhāge pavattakalahassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ saṅgharājīti. Kukkuccakoti aṇumattesupi vajjesu bhayadassanavasena kukkuccaṃ uppādento. Tantiṃ avisaṃvādetvāti pāḷiṃ aññathā akatvā. Avokkamantoti anatikkamanto.

`Vinaye` means in the conduct of the Vinaya. For that reason, he will say, 'not abandoning the Vinaya, not departing from it,' and so on. Therein, establishment occurs through not intentionally committing an offense, and so on; thus he says, 'established through conscientiousness,' which means he is conscientious. When the characteristics of a Vinaya-holder are to be discussed, what is the purpose of this conscientiousness? To this, he says, 'For one who is shameless,' and so on. Therein, 'though very learned' shows the possession of the first characteristic. By 'due to being intent on gain,' he shows that, in the absence of being established in the Vinaya, even with the possession of the first characteristic, one does not do what ought to be done; rather, one does what ought not to be done and what is harmful. 'Saṅgharājī' (a rift in the Saṅgha) is a term for a quarrel that occurs in the preliminary stage of a schism in the Saṅgha. 'Scrupulous' means one who arouses scrupulousness by seeing danger even in minute faults. 'Without corrupting the textual tradition' means without altering the Pāli. 'Not departing from it' means not transgressing.

Vitthunatīti atthaṃ adisvā nitthunati, vitthambhati vā. Vipphandatīti kampati. Santiṭṭhituṃ na sakkotīti ekasmiṃyeva atthe patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Tenāha “yaṃ yaṃ parena vuccati, taṃ taṃ anujānātī”ti. Sakavādaṃ chaḍḍetvā paravādaṃ gaṇhātīti “ucchumhi kasaṭaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ, raso sattāhakāliko, tadubhayavinimutto ca ucchu nāma visuṃ natthi, tasmā ucchupi vikāle vaṭṭatī”ti paravādinā vutte tampi gaṇhāti. Ekekalomanti palitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yamhīti yasmiṃ puggale. Parikkhayaṃ pariyādānanti atthato ekaṃ.

He grumbles without seeing the meaning, or he boasts. He trembles. He is unable to settle, unable to stand firm on a single point. Hence it is said, 'Whatever is said by another, he approves of it.' Abandoning his own view, he takes up the view of another—as when another says, 'In sugarcane, the dregs are for a lifetime, the juice is for seven days, and apart from these two, there is no separate thing called sugarcane; therefore, even sugarcane is allowable out of season,' he accepts even that. 'One by one hair' is said with reference to gray hair. 'In whom' means in which person. 'Exhaustion' and 'depletion' are one in meaning.

Ācariyaparamparāti [M 2.0193] ācariyānaṃ vinicchayaparamparā. Teneva vakkhati “attanomatiṃ pahāya…pe… yathā ācariyo ca ācariyācariyo ca pāḷiñca paripucchañca vadanti, tathā ñātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Na hi ācariyānaṃ nāmamattato paramparajānane payojanaṃ atthi. Pubbāparānusandhitoti pubbavacanassa aparavacanena saha atthasambandhajānanato. Atthatoti saddatthapiṇḍatthaadhippetatthādito. Kāraṇatoti tadatthupapattito. Ācariyaparamparanti imasseva vevacanaṃ “theravādaṅga”nti, therapaṭipāṭinti attho. Dve tayo parivaṭṭāti dve tayo paramparā.

'The succession of teachers' means the succession of the teachers' decisions. For that reason, it will be said, 'Having abandoned one's own opinion... it is proper to understand in accordance with what the teacher, the teacher's teacher, the Pāli, and the inquiry declare.' For there is no benefit in knowing the succession merely from the names of the teachers. 'From connecting the preceding and subsequent' means from knowing the connection in meaning of a preceding statement with a subsequent statement. 'From the meaning' means from the literal meaning, the condensed meaning, the intended meaning, and so on. 'From the reason' means from the cogency of that meaning. 'A component of the Theravāda' is a synonym for this 'succession of teachers'; the meaning is the lineage of the elders. 'Two or three rounds' means two or three successions.

Imehi ca pana tīhi lakkhaṇehīti ettha paṭhamena lakkhaṇena vinayassa suṭṭhu uggahitabhāvo vutto, dutiyena tattha lajjibhāvena ceva acalatāya ca suppatiṭṭhitatā, tatiyena pāḷiaṭṭhakathāsu sarūpena anāgatānampi tadanulomato ācariyehi dinnanayato vinicchinituṃ samatthatā. Otiṇṇe vatthusminti codanāvasena vītikkamavatthusmiṃ saṅghamajjhe otiṇṇe. Codakena ca cuditakena ca vutte vattabbeti evaṃ otiṇṇavatthuṃ nissāya codakena “diṭṭhaṃ suta”ntiādinā, cuditakena “atthī”tiādinā ca yaṃ vattabbaṃ, tasmiṃ vattabbe vutteti attho. Vatthu oloketabbanti tassa tassa sikkhāpadassa vatthu oloketabbaṃ. “Tiṇena vā paṇṇena [V 2.0142] vā…pe… yo āgaccheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti hidaṃ nissaggiye aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadassa (pārā. 517) vatthusmiṃ paññattaṃ.

By these three characteristics—here, the first characteristic indicates thorough grasping of the discipline; the second, steadfastness in it due to conscientiousness and immovability; and the third, the ability to decide even cases not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi or commentaries, in accordance with the method given by the teachers, following their principles. 'When a matter has arisen' (otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ) means when a matter of transgression has arisen in the Saṅgha on account of an accusation. 'What should be said by the accuser and the accused' means that, based on the arisen matter, what should be said by the accuser, such as 'I have seen, I have heard,' and by the accused, such as 'It is so,' etc.; when that which is to be said has been said, this is the meaning. 'The matter should be examined' means the basis of each training rule should be examined. For instance, this is prescribed in the basis of the Nissaggiya training rule concerning requesting from an unrelated person (Pārā. 517): 'If one asks for grass or leaves… whoever comes, there is an offense of wrong-doing.'

Thullaccayadubbhāsitāpattīnaṃ mātikāya anāgatattā “pañcannaṃ āpattīnaṃ aññatara”nti vuttaṃ. Tikadukkaṭanti “anupasampanne upasampannasaññī ujjhāyati khīyati, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādinā (pāci. 106) āgataṃ tikadukkaṭaṃ. Aññataraṃ vā āpattinti [M 2.0194] “kāle vikālasaññī, āpatti dukkaṭassa, kāle vematiko, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādikaṃ (pāci. 250) dukadukkaṭaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Since thullaccaya and dubbhāsita offenses are not included in the mātikā (summary), it is said, 'one of the five offenses.' The term 'tikadukkaṭa' refers to the threefold dukkaṭa offense, as stated in the phrase: 'If one who is not fully ordained is perceived as fully ordained and is disparaged or resented, there is an offense of wrong-doing'—and so on (Pāci. 106). The phrase 'or any other offense' refers to the twofold dukkaṭa offense, as in the case where: 'One perceives the proper time as an improper time, there is an offense of wrong-doing; one is doubtful about the proper time, there is an offense of wrong-doing'—and so on (Pāc. 250).

Antarāpattinti ettha tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sikkhāpade āgatavatthuvītikkamaṃ vinā aññasmiṃ vatthuvītikkame nidānato pabhuti vinītavatthupariyosānā antarantarā vuttā āpatti. Idha pana “vatthuṃ oloketī”ti visuṃ gahitattā tadavasesā antarāpattīti gahitā. Paṭilātaṃ ukkhipatīti idampi visibbanasikkhāpade (pāci. 350) āgataṃ, tattha ḍayhamānaṃ alātaṃ aggikapālādito bahi patitaṃ avijjhātameva paṭiukkhipati, puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetīti attho. Vijjhātaṃ pana paṭikkhipantassa pācittiyameva.

Here, 'antarāpatti' refers to an offense that occurs intermittently from the origin up to the conclusion of the matter, due to a transgression of a case other than the one specified in each training rule. But in this context, because 'examines the matter' is taken separately, the remaining offenses are considered 'antarāpatti.' The phrase 'lifts up a firebrand again' is also found in the training rule concerning a firebrand (Pāci. 350). There, a burning firebrand that has fallen outside from a fire pot or similar is picked up again without being extinguished, meaning it is placed back in its original position. However, for one who puts back an extinguished brand, it is a pācittiya offense.

Anāpattinti ettha antarantarā vuttā anāpattipi atthi, “anāpatti, bhikkhave, iddhimassa iddhivisaye”tiādi viya sāpi saṅgayhati. Sikkhāpadantaresūti vinītavatthuṃ antokatvā ekekasmiṃ sikkhāpadantare.

Here, the term 'no offense' includes those instances of no offense mentioned incidentally, such as 'Monks, there is no offense for one with psychic power in the sphere of psychic power,' and so on—these are also included. 'Among the training rules' means, including the vinīta matter, in each individual training rule.

Pārājikāpattīti na vattabbanti idaṃ āpannapuggalena lajjidhamme ṭhatvā yathābhūtaṃ āvikaraṇepi dubbinicchayaṃ adinnādānādiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana methunādīsu vijānanaṃ, taṃ vattabbameva. Tenāha “methunadhammavītikkamo hī”tiādi. Yo pana alajjitāya paṭiññaṃ adatvā vikkhepaṃ karoti, tassa āpatti na sakkā oḷārikāpi vinicchinituṃ. Yāva so yathābhūtaṃ nāvikaroti, saṅghassa ca āpattisandeho na vigacchati, tāva nāsitakova bhavissati. Sukhumāti attanopi duviññeyyasabhāvassa lahuparivattino cittassa sīghaparivattitāya vuttaṃ. Sukhumāti vā cittaparivattiyā sukhumatāya sukhumā. Tenāha “cittalahukā”ti, cittaṃ viya [M 2.0195] lahukāti attho. Atha vā cittaṃ lahu sīghaparivatti etesanti [V 2.0143] cittalahukā. Teti te vītikkame. Taṃvatthukanti te adinnādānamanaussaviggahavītikkamā vatthu adhiṭṭhānaṃ kāraṇametassāti taṃvatthukaṃ.

'It should not be called a pārājika offense'—this is said regarding a person who has committed an offense but, while possessing shame, truthfully confesses, yet still faces uncertainty concerning matters like theft, etc. However, regarding knowledge in cases of sexual misconduct, it must indeed be stated. Hence it is said, 'The transgression of sexual misconduct...' etc. But if someone, due to shamelessness, does not admit the offense but instead equivocates, even a gross offense cannot be clearly determined in their case. As long as they do not truthfully disclose it, and the Saṅgha’s doubt about the offense does not cease, they will remain as one who is ruined. 'Subtle'—this is said because even one’s own nature, being difficult to discern, is of a mind that is swiftly changing and undergoes rapid transformations. 'Subtle' may also refer to the subtlety of the mind's changing. Hence it is said, 'light-minded'—meaning, light like the mind. Alternatively, 'light-minded' means those whose minds are light and swiftly changing. 'Those' refers to those transgressions. 'Having that as their basis'—meaning those transgressions of theft and human killing have that as their basis, foundation, or cause. Thus, it is 'having that as their basis.'

Yaṃ ācariyo bhaṇati, taṃ karohītiādi sabbaṃ lajjīpesalaṃ kukkuccakameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yo yāthāvato pakāsetvā suddhimeva gavesati, tenapi. Pārājikosīti na vattabboti anāpattikoṭiyāpi saṅkiyamānattā vuttaṃ. Teneva “pārājikacchāyā”ti vuttaṃ. “Sīlāni sodhetvāti yaṃvatthukaṃ kukkuccaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃ amanasikaritvā avasesasīlāni sodhetvā”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) vuttaṃ, vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45) pana “sīlāni sodhetvāti yasmiṃ vītikkame pārājikāsaṅkā vattati, tattha pārājikābhāvapakkhaṃ gahetvā desanāvuṭṭhānagāminīnaṃ āpattīnaṃ sodhanavasena sīlāni sodhetvā”ti. Pākaṭabhāvato sukhavalañjatāya ca “dvattiṃsākāraṃ tāva manasi karohī”ti vuttaṃ, upalakkhaṇavasena vā. Aññasmiṃ kammaṭṭhāne kataparicayena tameva manasi kātabbaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci vā abhirucitaṃ manasi kātuṃ vaṭṭateva. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ ghaṭayatīti antarantarā khaṇḍaṃ adassetvā cittena saddhiṃ ārammaṇabhāvena cirakālaṃ ghaṭayati. Saṅkhārā pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahantīti vipassanākammaṭṭhāniko ce, tassa saṅkhārā pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti.

What the teacher says, 'Do that,' and so on—all this is said with reference to one who is modest, amiable, and scrupulous; one who explains things as they truly are and seeks only purity. It should not be said, 'You have committed a pārājika offense'—this is said because it is suspected of also falling into the category of non-offenses. Therefore, it is called 'the shadow of a pārājika.' 'Purifying the precepts'—the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.45) states: 'Purifying the precepts means disregarding the object about which scruples have arisen, and purifying the remaining precepts.' However, the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.45) states: 'Purifying the precepts' means, concerning a transgression where there is doubt about a pārājika, taking the side of non-pārājika, and purifying the precepts by way of clearing offenses that are removed by confession and reinstatement. Because of its obvious nature and ease of practice, it is said, 'First, focus on the thirty-two parts'—or as a way of illustration. In the case of someone who has past experience with another meditation subject, that same subject should be focused on. Or, whatever is pleasing, it is indeed fitting to focus on. 'The meditation subject takes hold' means one engages with it as the mind's object for a long time, without showing any intermittent breaks. 'Formations become evident and appear'—if he is one who practices insight meditation, then for him formations become evident and appear.

Sace katapārājikavītikkamo bhaveyya, tassa satipi asaritukāmatāya vippaṭisāravatthuvasena punappunaṃ taṃ upaṭṭhahatīti cittekaggataṃ na vindati. Tena vuttaṃ “kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ghaṭayatī”tiādi. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ghaṭayatīti cittakkhobhādibahulassa suddhasīlassapi cittaṃ na samādhiyati, taṃ idha [M 2.0196] pārājikamūlanti na gahetabbaṃ. Katapāpamūlakena vippaṭisārenevettha cittassa asamādhiyanaṃ sandhāya “kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ghaṭayatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāha “vippaṭisāragginā”tiādi. Attanāti cittena karaṇabhūtena puggalo kattā jānāti, paccatte vā karaṇavacanaṃ, attā sayaṃ jānātīti attho. Aññā ca devatā jānantīti ārakkhadevatāhi aññā paracittaviduniyo devatā jānanti.

If one has committed a pārājika transgression, then for him, even with a desire not to remember, it repeatedly arises as a basis for remorse; thus, he does not attain one-pointedness of mind. Therefore, it is said, 'The meditation subject does not take hold,' and so on. 'The meditation subject does not take hold'—even for one of pure virtue whose mind is frequently disturbed and agitated, the mind does not become concentrated; this should not be taken here as being rooted in a pārājika. It is with reference to the non-concentration of the mind due to remorse rooted in an evil deed that it is said, 'The meditation subject does not take hold,' and so on. Hence, it is stated, 'By the fire of remorse,' and so on. 'By oneself'—the individual, the agent, knows through the mind as the instrument; or it is an instrumental expression for the self, meaning one knows by oneself. 'And other deities know'—deities other than guardian deities, those who know the minds of others, know.

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne paṇḍitehi vicāretabbaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthi. Kathaṃ? Idāni ekacce vinayadharā paṭhamapārājikavisaye vatthumhi otiṇṇe itthiyā vā purisena vā gahaṭṭhena vā pabbajitena vā codiyamāne cuditakaṃ bhikkhuṃ pucchitvā paṭiññāya adīyamānāya taṃ bhikkhuṃ susāne ekakameva [V 2.0144] sayāpenti, evaṃ sayāpiyamāno so bhikkhu sace bhayasantāsavirahito sabbarattiṃ tasmiṃ susāne sayituṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā sakkoti, taṃ “parisuddho eso”ti vinicchinanti. Sace pana bhayasantāsappatto sabbarattiṃ sayituṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā na sakkoti, taṃ “asuddho”ti vinicchinanti, taṃ ayuttaṃ viya dissati. Kasmāti ce? Aṭṭhakathāya viruddhoti, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dutiyatatiyapārājikavisaye eva tathārūpo vicāro vutto, na paṭhamacatautthapārājikavisaye. Vuttañhi tattha “methunadhammavītikkamo hi uttarimanussadhammavītikkamo ca oḷāriko, adinnādānamanussaviggahavītikkamā pana sukhumā cittalahukā, te sukhumeneva āpajjati, sukhumena rakkhati, tasmā visesena taṃvatthukaṃ kukkuccaṃ pucchiyamāno”ti. Ṭīkāyañca (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) vuttaṃ “taṃvatthukanti te adinnādānamanussaviggahavītikkamā vatthu adhiṭṭhānaṃ kāraṇametassāti taṃvatthuka”nti, idampi ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ.

On this point, there is a matter to be considered by the wise. How? At present, some masters of the Vinaya, when a case concerning the first pārājika has arisen and a monk is accused by a woman or a man, by a householder or one gone forth, after questioning the accused monk, if a confession is not forthcoming, they make that monk lie down alone in a charnel ground. If that monk, being made to lie down thus, is free from fear and terror and is able to lie down or sit for the entire night in that charnel ground, they determine, 'He is pure.' But if, being afflicted by fear and terror, he is not able to lie down or sit for the entire night, they determine, 'He is impure.' This appears to be improper. Why so? Because it contradicts the commentary. In the commentary, such an investigation is spoken of only in relation to the second and third pārājika offenses, not in relation to the first and fourth. For it is stated therein: 'The transgression of sexual intercourse and the transgression of claiming superhuman attainments are gross, whereas the transgressions of theft and taking a human life are subtle and light of mind; one falls into them subtly and guards against them subtly. Therefore, when being questioned about a scruple specifically concerning these matters…' And in the sub-commentary it is said: '“Taṃvatthuka” means: those transgressions of theft and taking a human life are the object, the basis, the cause of this scruple, thus it is “taṃvatthuka”.' This is one reason.

Tatthāpi [M 2.0197] aññe paṇḍitepi vinicchināpetvā tesampi pārājikacchāyādissaneyeva tathā vinicchayo kātabbo, na suddhabhāvadissane. Vuttañhi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “āpattīti avatvā ‘sacassa ācariyo dharati…pe… atha daharassapi pārājikacchāyāva upaṭṭhāti, tenapi ‘pārājikosī’ti na vattabbo. Dullabho hi buddhuppādo, tato dullabhatarā pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca, evaṃ pana vattabba”nti, idamekaṃ. Nisīdāpiyamānopi vivittokāseyeva nisīdāpetabbo, na susāne. Vuttañhi tattha “vivittaṃ okāsaṃ sammajjitvā divāvihāraṃ nisīditvā”tiādi, idamekaṃ. Vivittokāse nisīdāpiyamānopi divāyeva nisīdāpetabbo, na rattiṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “divasaṃ atikkantampi na jānāti, so divasātikkame upaṭṭhānaṃ āgato evaṃ vattabbo”ti, idamekaṃ.

Moreover, even having had other wise ones investigate, the determination should be made in that way only when the shadow of a pārājika appears, not when a state of purity appears. For it is stated in the commentary: "Without saying 'It is an offense,' if his teacher is alive… even for a young monk, only the shadow of a pārājika arises. Therefore, he should not be told, ‘You are a pārājika offender.’ For the arising of a Buddha is rare, and rarer still are going forth and higher ordination. Thus, one should speak in this way." This is one point. Even when being made to sit down, one should be seated in a secluded place, not in a charnel ground. For it is said there: "Having swept a secluded spot, having sat for the daytime abiding," and so on. This is one point. Even when being seated in a secluded place, it should be done during the day, not at night. For thus it is stated: "He does not know that the day has passed; when he has come to attend after the day has passed, he should be told thus." This is one point.

Īdisaṃ vidhānaṃ sayaṃ ārocite eva vidhātabbaṃ, na parehi codiyamāne. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “evaṃ katavītikkamena bhikkhunā sayameva āgantvā ārocite paṭipajjitabba”nti. Atha kasmā idāni evaṃ karontīti? Gihīnaṃ asakkhikaaṭṭakaraṇe udake nimujjāpanaṃ viya maññamānā evaṃ karonti. Tampi māyākusalā manussā vividhehi upāyehi vitathaṃ karonti, tasmā saccampi hoti, asaccampi hoti. Teneva ca kāraṇena mahosadhapaṇḍitādayo bodhisattā asakkhikampi aṭṭaṃ udakanimujjāpanādinā na vinicchinanti, ubhinnaṃ vacanaṃ parisaṃ gāhāpetvā tesaṃ vacanañca kiriyañca pariggahetvā saccañca vitathañca ñatvāva vinicchinanti. Sāsane [V 2.0145] pana bhikkhū sūrajātikāpi santi, bhīrukajātikāpi santi. Susānañca nāma pakatimanussānampi bhayasantāsakaraṃ hoti, rattikāle pana ativiya bhayānakaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti[M 2.0198], evaṃbhūte susāne rattiyaṃ eko asahāyo hutvā nipajjāpiyamāno bhīrukajātiko bhikkhu parisuddhasīlopi samāno kiṃ na bhāyeyya, kathaṃ sabbarattiṃ sayituṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā sakkuṇeyya, tathārūpaṃ bhikkhuṃ “aparisuddho”ti vadanto kathaṃ kiccakaro bhavissati.

Such a procedure should be carried out only when reported by oneself, not when one is accused by others. For thus it is said: "When a monk has committed such a transgression, he should come forward and report it himself, and then the procedure should be undertaken." Why then do they act this way now? They act thus, thinking it is like the submersion of laypeople in water in a case without witnesses. Even that, people skilled in deceit can falsify through various means; therefore, it can be both true and false. For this very reason, Bodhisattas such as the wise Mahosadha do not judge even a case without witnesses by means of submersion in water and so forth. Instead, having had both parties address the assembly, and having considered their words and actions, they make a decision only after discerning truth from falsehood. In the Dispensation, however, there are monks of both courageous and timid natures. A charnel ground is indeed terrifying even to ordinary people, and at night it presents itself as especially dreadful. In such a charnel ground, a timid monk made to lie down alone at night without a companion—even being one of pure virtue—why should he not be afraid? How could he manage to lie down or sit for the entire night? One who calls such a monk "impure"—how will he be one who has done his duty?

Alajjī pana sūrajātiko attano vajjaṃ paṭicchādetukāmo bhāyantopi abhāyanto viya hutvā “sace vikāraṃ dassessāmi, anatthaṃ me karissantī”ti anatthabhayena adhivāsetvā sayituṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā sakkuṇeyya, evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ “parisuddho”ti vadanto kathaṃ suvinicchito bhavissatīti. Idampi ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ.

On the other hand, a shameless person of a bold nature, wishing to conceal his own fault, though afraid, might act as if unafraid, and thinking, "If I show any sign of agitation, they will bring about my ruin," he might endure it out of fear of ruin and be able to lie down or sit. As for one who calls such a person "pure"—how can the judgment be considered a good one? This, too, is a reason.

Athāpi vadeyyuṃ – yathā udake nimujjāpitamanussānaṃ asaccavādīnaṃ devatānubhāvena kumbhīlādayo āgantvā gaṇhantā viya upaṭṭhahanti, tasmā asaccavādino sīghaṃ plavanti, saccavādīnaṃ pana na upaṭṭhahanti, tasmā te sukhena nisīdituṃ sakkonti, evaṃ tesampi bhikkhūnaṃ aparisuddhasīlānaṃ devatānubhāvena sīhabyagghādayo āgatā viya paññāyanti, tasmā te sabbarattiṃ sayituṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā na sakkonti. Parisuddhasīlānaṃ pana tathā na paññāyanti, tasmā te sabbarattiṃ devatāhi rakkhitā hutvā bhayasantāsarahitā susāne sayituṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā sakkonti, evaṃ devatā sakkhiṃ katvā vinicchitattā suvinicchitameva hotīti, tampi tathā na sakkā vattuṃ. Kasmā? Aṭṭhakathāṭīkādīsu tathā avuttattā. Aṭṭhakathāyañhi “vivittaṃ okāsaṃ sammajjitvā divāvihāraṃ nisīditvā sīlāni sodhetvā ‘dvattiṃsākāraṃ tāva manasikarohī’ti vattabbo. Sace tassa arogaṃ sīlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ghaṭayati, saṅkhārā pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, upacārappanāppattaṃ viya cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, divasaṃ atikkantampi na jānāti…pe… yassa pana sīlaṃ bhinnaṃ hoti, tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ na [M 2.0199] ghaṭayati, patodābhitunnaṃ viya cittaṃ kampati, vippaṭisāragginā ḍayhati, tattapāsāṇe nisinno viya taṅkhaṇaññeva vuṭṭhātī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ.

They might also say: Just as for untruthful humans who have been made to submerge in water, crocodiles and other creatures appear by the power of the deities as if coming to seize them, and therefore the untruthful float up quickly; but for the truthful, they do not appear thus, and therefore they are able to remain submerged at ease—so too, for those monks of impure virtue, lions, tigers, and the like appear as if by the power of the deities, and thus they cannot lie down or sit all night. But for those of pure virtue, they do not appear in that way, so they, protected by deities all night and free from fear and terror, can lie down or sit in the charnel ground. Thus, since the determination is made with the deities as witness, it is indeed well-determined. But even that cannot be said to be so. Why? Because it is not stated thus in the commentaries, sub-commentaries, and so on. For in the commentary, only this much is said: “Having swept a secluded spot and sat for the daytime abiding, one should purify one's virtues and then be told, ‘For now, direct your mind to the thirty-two parts of the body.’ If his virtue is sound, the meditation subject connects, the formations become manifest and appear to him, the mind becomes one-pointed as if having reached access or absorption, and he does not even notice the passing of the day… But for one whose virtue is broken, the meditation subject does not connect; his mind trembles as if pierced by a goad, burns with the fire of remorse, and he rises up at that very moment as if sitting on a hot stone.”

Ṭīkāyampi (sārattha. ṭī. 2.45) “kammaṭṭhānaṃ ghaṭayatīti antarantarā khaṇḍaṃ adassetvā cittena saddhiṃ ārammaṇabhāvena cirakālaṃ ghaṭayati. Saṅkhārā pākaṭā upaṭṭhahantīti vipassanākammaṭṭhāniko [V 2.0146] ce, tassa saṅkhārā pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Sace katapārājikavītikkamo bhaveyya, tassa satipi asaritukāmatāya vippaṭisāravatthuvasena punappunaṃ taṃ upaṭṭhahatīti cittekaggataṃ na vindatī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ.

In the sub-commentary (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.45) also, only this much is said: "'The meditation subject connects' means it connects with the mind as its object for a long time without showing any break in between. 'The formations become manifest and appear' means: if one is a practitioner of insight meditation, for him the formations become manifest and appear. If he has committed a pārājika transgression, even when there is a desire not to remember it, that transgression presents itself to him again and again as a basis for remorse, and thus he does not find one-pointedness of mind."

Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45) “kammaṭṭhānaṃ ghaṭayatīti vippaṭisāramūlakena vikkhepena antarantarā khaṇḍaṃ adassetvā pabandhavasena cittena saṅghaṭayati. Saṅkhārāti vipassanākammaṭṭhānavasena vuttaṃ. Sāpattikassa hi paguṇampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ na suṭṭhu upaṭṭhāti. Pageva pārājikassa. Tassa hi vippaṭisāraninnatāya cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na hoti. Ekassa pana vitakkavikkhepādibahulassa suddhasīlassapi cittaṃ na samādhiyati, taṃ idha pārājikamūlanti na gahetabbaṃ. Katapāpamūlakena vippaṭisārenevettha cittassa asamādhiyanaṃ sandhāya ‘kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ghaṭayatī’tiādi vutta”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “devatānubhāvenā”tiādi, tasmā yadi buddhasāsane sagāravo sikkhākāmo bhikkhu dutiyatatiyapārājikavisaye attano kañci vītikkamaṃ disvā “pārājikaṃ āpanno nu kho ahaṃ, na nu kho”ti saṃsayapakkhando vinayadharaṃ upasaṅkamitvā taṃ vītikkamaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ācikkhitvā puccheyya, tato vinayadharena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva “sabbaṃ pubbavidhānaṃ katvā vivittaṃ okāsaṃ sammajjitvā divāvihāraṃ nisīditvā sīlāni sodhetvā dvattiṃsākāre tāva manasikarohī”ti ettakameva vattabbo[M 2.0200], na vattabbo “susāne seyyaṃ kappehī”tiādi. Āgatakālepi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatanayeneva pucchitvā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatanayenevassa suddhāsuddhabhāvo vattabboti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In the Vimativinodanī (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.45), it is said: “'He connects the meditation subject' means he connects it with the mind continuously, without showing a break in between caused by distraction rooted in remorse. 'Formations' is said in the sense of the meditation subject of insight. For one who has committed an offense, even a familiar meditation subject does not properly present itself. How much more so for one who has committed a pārājika offense. For him, the mind, being inclined toward remorse, does not become one-pointed. However, when the mind of even a virtuous person—one with many initial thoughts, distractions, and so on—does not become concentrated, this should not be taken here as being rooted in a pārājika offense. The statement 'the meditation subject does not connect,' etc., is said with reference to the non-concentration of the mind due to remorse rooted in a past misdeed.” Only this much is said, not “by the power of deities,” etc. Therefore, if a monk who is respectful toward the Buddha’s teaching and desirous of training sees some transgression of his concerning the second or third pārājika and, becoming doubtful, thinks, “Have I committed a pārājika offense or not?” he should approach a Vinaya expert, truthfully disclose that transgression, and ask. Then, the Vinaya expert should instruct him only according to the method stated in the commentary: “Having performed all the preliminary duties, sweep a secluded place, sit for the day's abiding, purify your precepts, and then direct your mind to the thirty-two parts of the body.” Only this much should be said, not “prepare a bed in the charnel ground,” etc. When he comes also, the question should be asked according to the method given in the commentary, and his purity or impurity should be declared according to the method given in the commentary. This should be understood.

Evaṃ hotu, evaṃ sante idāni paṭhamapārājikavisaye codentānaṃ kathaṃ vinicchayo kātabboti? Codakena vatthusmiṃ ārocite cuditako pucchitabbo “santametaṃ, no”ti evaṃ vatthuṃ upaparikkhitvā bhūtena vatthunā codetvā sāretvā ñattisampadāya anussāvanasampadāya taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ. Evampi alajjī nāma “etampi natthi, etampi natthī”ti vadeyya, paṭiññaṃ na dadeyya, atha kiṃ kātabbanti? Evampi alajjissa paṭiññāya eva āpattiyā kāretabbaṃ yathā taṃ tipiṭakacūḷābhayattherenāti. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.385-386) “evaṃ lajjinā codiyamāno alajjī bahūsupi vatthūsu uppannesu paṭiññaṃ na deti, so ‘neva suddho’ti vattabbo, na ‘asuddho’ti, jīvamatako nāma āmakapūtiko nāma [V 2.0147] cesa. Sace panassa aññampi tādisaṃ vatthu uppajjati, na vinicchitabbaṃ, tathā nāsitakova bhavissatī”tiādi.

So be it. This being the case, how should a decision now be made concerning the first pārājika when one is being accused? When the accuser has stated the matter, the accused should be questioned: “Is this true, or not?” Having thus examined the matter, and having accused with a factual basis and reminded him, the legal issue should be settled by means of a proper motion and proclamation. But if, even then, a shameless person says, “This too is not so, and that too is not so,” and does not make an admission, what should be done? Even for such a shameless person, the offense must be dealt with only by his admission, as in the case of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. For it is said in the commentary (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.385-386): “When accused by a conscientious person, if a shameless person does not make an admission even when many grounds have arisen, he should be told, ‘You are not pure,’ but not, ‘You are impure.’ He is called ‘one who is living-dead’ or ‘one who is raw and rotten.’ And if another such matter concerning him arises, it should not be decided; he will remain just as ruined.” And so on.

235. Evaṃ vinayadharalakkhaṇañca chaṭṭhānaolokanañca viditvā idāni…pe… vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Kimatthanti āha “yā sā…pe… jānanattha”nti. Yā sā pubbe vuttappabhedā codanā atthi, tassāyeva sampattivipattijānanatthaṃ ādimajjhapaayosānādīnaṃ vasena vinicchayo veditabbo, na avuttacodanāpabhedajānanatthanti attho. Seyyathidanti pucchanatthe nipāto, so vinicchayo katamoti attho.

235. Having understood the characteristics of a Vinaya-holder and the sixfold examination, now…the decision should be known; this is the connection. For what purpose? It is said, "for the sake of knowing." That previously stated classification of accusations exists—for the sake of knowing its success or failure, the decision should be understood through the beginning, middle, and end, etc.; it is not for the sake of knowing an unstated classification of accusations—this is the meaning. "Seyyathidaṃ" is a particle used for the purpose of questioning, meaning "what is that decision?"

Codanāya [M 2.0201] kati mūlāni, kati vatthūni, kati bhūmiyoti ettha “katihākārehī”tipi vattabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ parivāre (pari. 362) codanākaṇḍe “codanāya kati mūlāni, kati vatthūni, kati bhūmiyo, katihākārehi codetī”ti. Mettacitto vakkhāmi, no dosantaroti etassapi parato “codanāya imā pañca bhūmiyo. Katamehi dvīhākārehi codeti, kāyena vā codeti, vācāya vā codeti, imehi dvīhākārehi codetī”ti vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Codanākaṇḍe (pari. 362) tathā vijjamānatoti. Pannarasasu dhammesu patiṭṭhātabbanti parisuddhakāyasamācāratā, parisuddhavacīsamācāratā, mettacitte paccupaṭṭhitatā, bahussutatā, ubhayapātimokkhasvāgatatā, kālena vacanatā, bhūtena vacanatā, saṇhena vacanatā, atthasañhitena vacanatā, mettacitto hutvā vacanatā, kāruññatā, hitesitā, anukampatā, āpattivuṭṭhānatā, vinayapurekkhāratāti. Vuttañhetaṃ upālipañcake (pari. 436) “codakenupāli bhikkhunā paraṃ codetukāmena evaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ – parisuddhakāyasamācāro nu khomhi…pe… parisuddhavacīsamācāro nu khomhi…pe… mettaṃ nu kho me cittaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ sabrahmacārīsu…pe… bahussuto nu khomhi sutadharo sutasannicayo…pe… ubhayāni kho me pātimokkhāni vitthārena svāgatāni…pe… kālena vakkhāmi, no akālena, bhūtena vakkhāmi, no abhūtena, saṇhena vakkhāmi, no pharusena, atthasañhitena vakkhāmi, no anatthasañhitena, mettacitto vakkhāmi, no dosantaro…pe… kāruññatā, hitesitā, anukampatā, āpattivuṭṭhānatā, vinayapurekkhāratā”ti.

How many roots are there for an accusation, how many grounds, how many bases? Here, it should also be said, "In how many ways?" For it is stated in the Parivāra (Pari. 362) in the section on accusations: "How many roots are there for an accusation, how many grounds, how many bases, in how many ways does one accuse?" With a mind of loving-kindness I will speak, not with inner aversion. Regarding this too, further on, it should be said: "There are these five bases for an accusation. In how many ways does one accuse? One accuses in two ways: either by body or by speech. One accuses in these two ways." Why? Because it is found thus in the section on accusations (Pari. 362). One should be established in fifteen qualities: purity of bodily conduct, purity of verbal conduct, being established in a mind of loving-kindness, being very learned, being well-versed in both Pātimokkhas, speaking at the right time, speaking truthfully, speaking gently, speaking meaningfully, speaking with a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, wishing for welfare, sympathy, rising from offenses, and prioritizing the Vinaya. For it is stated in the Upāli Pañcaka (Pari. 436): "Upāli, when a monk wishes to accuse another, he should reflect thus: 'Am I of pure bodily conduct?... Am I of pure verbal conduct?... Is my mind established in loving-kindness toward my fellow monastics?... Am I very learned, a bearer of what I have heard, a storer-up of what I have heard?... Have I thoroughly mastered both Pātimokkhas in detail?... Do I speak at the right time, not at the wrong time? Do I speak truthfully, not falsely? Do I speak gently, not harshly? Do I speak meaningfully, not meaninglessly? Do I speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner aversion?... With compassion, wishing for welfare, sympathy, rising from offenses, and prioritizing the Vinaya.'"

Tattha kāruññatāti kāruṇikabhāvo. Iminā karuṇā ca karuṇāpubbabhāgo ca dassito[V 2.0148]. Hitesitāti hitagavesanatā[M 2.0202]. Anukampatāti tena hitena saṃyojanatā. Āpattivuṭṭhānatāti āpattito vuṭṭhāpetvā suddhante patiṭṭhāpanatā. Vatthuṃ codetvā sāretvā paṭiññaṃ āropetvā yathāpaṭiññāya kammakaraṇaṃ vinayapurekkhāratā nāma. Amūlakampi samūlakampi “mūla”nti gahetvā vadantīti āha “dve mūlānī”ti. Kālena vakkhāmītiādīsu eko ekaṃ okāsaṃ kāretvā codento kālena vadati nāma. Saṅghamajjhe gaṇamajjhe salākaggayāguaggavitakkamāḷakabhikkhācāramaggaāsanasālādīsu, upaṭṭhākehi parivāritakkhaṇe vā codento akālena vadati nāma. Tacchena vatthunā codento bhūtena vadati nāma. Tucchena codento abhūtena vadati nāma. “Ambho mahallaka parisāvacara paṃsukūlika dhammakathika patirūpaṃ tava ida”nti vadanto pharusena vadati nāma. “Bhante, mahallakā parisāvacarā paṃsukūlikā dhammakathikā patirūpaṃ tumhākaṃ ida”nti vadanto saṇhena vadati nāma. Kāraṇanissitaṃ katvā vadanto atthasañhitena vadati nāma. Mettacitto vakkhāmi, no dosantaroti mettacittaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā vakkhāmi, na duṭṭhacitto hutvā. Sacce ca akuppe cāti vacīsacce ca akuppatāya ca. Cuditakena hi saccañca vattabbaṃ, kopo ca na kātabbo, attanā ca na kucchitabbaṃ, paro ca na ghaṭṭetabboti attho.

Herein, compassion (kāruññatā) means the state of being compassionate. Through this, both compassion (karuṇā) and its preliminary aspect (karuṇāpubbabhāgo) are shown. Desiring welfare (hitesitā) means seeking what is beneficial. Sympathy (anukampatā) means connecting one with that benefit. Restoration from an offense (āpattivuṭṭhānatā) means establishing someone in purity after raising them up from an offense. To point out the matter, remind, secure an admission, and then perform the formal act according to that admission is what is called prioritizing the Vinaya (vinayapurekkhāratā). They speak taking both the baseless and the well-founded as a 'basis'—thus it is said, 'two bases.' In the phrase 'I will speak at the proper time,' one who reproves after securing a private opportunity is said to speak at the proper time. One who reproves in the midst of the Sangha, in the midst of a group, at the distribution of voting tickets, at the distribution of gruel, in the pavilion for deliberation, on the alms-round path, in the assembly hall, or when surrounded by attendants, is said to speak at an improper time. One who reproves with a true matter is said to speak truthfully. One who reproves with an empty matter is said to speak falsely. One who speaks saying, 'Hey, old man, frequenter of the assembly, rag-robe wearer, Dhamma speaker—this is fitting for you!' is said to speak harshly. One who speaks saying, 'Venerable sirs, elders, frequenters of the assembly, wearers of rag-robes, speakers of the Dhamma—this is fitting for you,' is said to speak gently. One who speaks based on a reason is said to speak meaningfully. 'I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred' means: having established a mind of loving-kindness, I will speak, not with a hostile mind. And 'in truth and steadfastness' (sacce ca akuppe ca) means in truthful speech and in unshakeability. For the one being reproved should speak the truth, should not become angry, should not disparage himself, and should not provoke the other; this is the meaning.

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne “saṅghena otiṇṇānotiṇṇaṃ jānitabbaṃ – anuvijjakena yena dhammena yena vinayena yena satthusāsanena taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasammati, tathā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabba”nti vattabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ codanākaṇḍe (pari. 363) “codakena kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ? Cuditakena kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ? Saṅghena kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ? Anuvijjakena kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ? Codakena [M 2.0203] kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? Codakena pañcasu dhammesu patiṭṭhāya paro codetabbo. Kālena vakkhāmi no akālena, bhūtena vakkhāmi no abhūtena, saṇhena vakkhāmi no pharusena, atthasañhitena vakkhāmi no anatthasañhitena, mettacitto vakkhāmi no dosantaroti. Codakena evaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Cuditakena kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? Cuditakena dvīsu dhammesu patiṭṭhātabbaṃ sacce ca akuppe ca. Cuditakena evaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Saṅghena kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? Saṅghena otiṇṇānotiṇṇaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Saṅghena evaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Anuvijjakena kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? Anuvijjakena yena dhammena yena vinayena yena satthusāsanena taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasammati, tathā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ. Anuvijjakena evaṃ paṭipajjitabba”nti.

In this case, it should be stated: "The Sangha should know whether the matter has been taken up or not. The legal issue should be settled by the investigator in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction by which that legal issue is settled; so should that legal issue be settled." For it has been said in the Codanākaṇḍa (Pari. 363): "How should the accuser proceed? How should the accused proceed? How should the Sangha proceed? How should the investigator proceed? How should the accuser proceed? The accuser should accuse another after being established in five qualities: ‘I will speak at the proper time, not at the wrong time; I will speak truthfully, not falsely; I will speak gently, not harshly; I will speak what is beneficial, not what is unbeneficial; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hate.’ Thus should the accuser proceed. How should the accused proceed? The accused should be established in two qualities: truth and steadfastness. Thus should the accused proceed. How should the Sangha proceed? The Sangha should know whether the matter has been taken up or not. Thus should the Sangha proceed. How should the investigator proceed? The investigator should settle the legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction by which that legal issue is settled; so should that legal issue be settled. Thus should the investigator proceed."

Aṭṭhakathāyampi [V 2.0149] (pari. aṭṭha. 362-363) “codanāya ko ādītiādipucchānaṃ vissajjane sacce akuppe cāti ettha sacce patiṭṭhātabbaṃ akuppe ca, yaṃ kataṃ vā akataṃ vā, tadeva vattabbaṃ, na codake vā anuvijjake vā saṅghe vā kopo uppādetabbo. Otiṇṇānotiṇṇaṃ jānitabbanti otiṇṇañca anotiṇṇañca vacanaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ jānanavidhi – ettakā codakassa pubbakathā, ettakā pacchimakathā, ettakā cuditakassa pubbakathā, ettakā pacchimakathāti jānitabbā. Codakassa pamāṇaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ, cuditakassa pamāṇaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ, anuvijjakassa pamāṇaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ. Anuvijjako appamattakampi ahāpento ‘āvuso, samannāharitvā ujuṃ katvā āharā’ti vattabbo, saṅghena evaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Yena dhammena yena vinayena yena satthusāsanena taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasammatīti ettha dhammoti bhūtaṃ vatthu. Vinayoti codanā ceva sāraṇā ca. Satthusāsananti ñattisampadā ceva anussāvanasampadā [M 2.0204] ca. Etena hi dhammena ca vinayena ca satthusāsanena ca adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasammati, tasmā anuvijjakena bhūtena vatthunā codetvā āpattiṃ sāretvā ñattisampadāya ceva anussāvanasampadāya ca taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ, anuvijjakena evaṃ paṭipajjitabba”nti āgataṃ, tasmā vattabbamettakaṃ dvayanti.

Also in the commentary (Pari. Aṭṭha. 362-363), in the explanation of the questions beginning with 'What is the origin of the accusation?', it is said: 'Regarding "in truth and steadfastness," one should be established in truth and in steadfastness; whatever was done or not done, that alone should be stated; anger should not be aroused toward the accuser, the investigator, or the Sangha. "One should know what has been taken up and what has not been taken up" means that the statement that has been taken up and the one that has not been taken up should be known. Herein, this is the method of knowing: this much is the accuser’s prior statement, this much is his later statement; this much is the accused’s prior statement, this much is his later statement—this should be known. The measure of the accuser should be taken, the measure of the accused should be taken, the measure of the investigator should be taken. The investigator, not omitting even a little, should be told, "Friend, having reflected and made it straight, present it." Thus should the Sangha proceed. Regarding "by whatever Dhamma, by whatever Vinaya, by whatever teaching of the Teacher that legal issue is settled," herein, "Dhamma" means the true matter. "Vinaya" means the accusation and the reminding. "Teaching of the Teacher" means the accomplishment of the motion and the accomplishment of the proclamation. For by this Dhamma, Vinaya, and teaching of the Teacher a legal issue is settled. Therefore, the investigator, having accused based on the true matter and having reminded of the offense, should settle that legal issue through the accomplishment of the motion and the accomplishment of the proclamation. Thus should the investigator proceed.' Since this is what is found there, this much is the pair of things to be said.

Evaṃ ekadesena codanākaṇḍanayaṃ dassetvā idāni ekadeseneva mahāsaṅgāmanayaṃ dassento “anuvijjakena codako pucchitabbo”tiādimāha. Tattha yaṃ kho tvaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ bhikkhuṃ codesi, kimhi naṃ codesīti codanāsāmaññato vuttaṃ, pāḷiyaṃ (mahāva. 237) pana pavāraṇaṭṭhapanavasena codanaṃ sandhāya “yaṃ kho tvaṃ, āvuso, imassa bhikkhuno pavāraṇaṃ ṭhapesī”ti vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Having thus shown in part the method of the chapter on accusation, now, showing in part the method of the Mahāsaṅgāma, he says, 'The investigator should question the accuser,' and so on. Therein, the phrase, 'Friend, on what grounds do you accuse this monk whom you are accusing?' is stated in a general way about accusation. But in the Pāli text (Mahāva. 237), referring to an accusation by way of suspending the Pavāraṇā ceremony, it is said: 'Friend, you who have suspended this monk's Pavāraṇā.' The rest is very easy to understand.

Evaṃ ekadesena mahāsaṅgāmanayaṃ dassetvā idāni ekadeseneva cūḷasaṅgāmanayaṃ dassetuṃ “saṅgāmāvacarena bhikkhunā”tiādimāha. Tattha saṅgāmāvacarena bhikkhunāti saṅgāmo vuccati adhikaraṇavinicchayatthāya saṅghasannipāto. Tatra hi attapaccatthikā ceva sāsanapaccatthikā ca uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ dīpentā samosaranti vesālikā vajjiputtakā viya. Yo bhikkhu tesaṃ paccatthikānaṃ laddhiṃ madditvā sakavādadīpanatthāya tattha avacarati, ajjhogāhetvā vinicchayaṃ pavatteti, so saṅgāmāvacaro nāma yasatthero viya, tena saṅgāmāvacarena bhikkhunā saṅghaṃ upasaṅkamantena nīcacittena saṅgho upasaṅkamitabbo. Nīcacittenāti mānaddhajaṃ nipātetvā nihatamānacittena[V 2.0150]. Rajoharaṇasamenāti pādapuñchanasamena, yathā rajoharaṇassa saṃkiliṭṭhe vā asaṃkiliṭṭhe vā pāde puñchiyamāne [M 2.0205] neva rāgo na doso, evaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu arajjantena adussantenāti attho. Yathāpatirūpe āsaneti yathāpatirūpaṃ āsanaṃ ñatvā attano pāpuṇanaṭṭhāne therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ piṭṭhiṃ adassetvā nisīditabbaṃ.

Having thus shown in part the method of the Mahāsaṅgāma, now, to show in part the method of the Cūḷasaṅgāma, he begins by saying, 'by a monk who engages in the assembly.' Herein, 'by a monk who engages in the assembly': an assembly (saṅgāma) is a gathering of the Sangha for the purpose of settling a legal issue. For there, both personal adversaries and adversaries of the Dispensation gather, proclaiming what is not the Dhamma and not the Vinaya as the Teacher's Dispensation, like the Vajjian monks of Vesālī. A monk who, having crushed the views of those adversaries, engages there for the purpose of clarifying his own teaching, and having plunged in, conducts the settlement—he is called one who 'engages in the assembly,' like the Elder Yasa. Such a monk, when approaching the Sangha, should approach with a humble mind. 'With a humble mind' means with a mind whose pride is struck down, having lowered the banner of pride. 'Like a dust-cloth' means like a foot-wiping cloth; just as for a dust-cloth, when soiled or unsoiled feet are being wiped, there is neither attraction nor aversion, so too, one should not be attracted to the agreeable nor averse to the disagreeable; this is the meaning. 'In a suitable seat' means that, having recognized a suitable seat, one should sit in a place that one is entitled to, without showing one's back to the elder monks.

Anānākathikenāti nānāvidhaṃ taṃ taṃ anatthakathaṃ akathentena. Atiracchānakathikenāti diṭṭhasutamutampi rājakathādikaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ akathentena. Sāmaṃ vā dhammo bhāsitabboti saṅghasannipātaṭṭhāne kappiyākappiyasannissitā vā rūpārūpaparicchedasamathacāravipassanācāraṭṭhānanisajjavattādinissitā vā kathā dhammo nāma. Evarūpo dhammo sayaṃ vā bhāsitabbo, paro vā ajjhesitabbo. Yo bhikkhu tathārūpiṃ kathaṃ kathetuṃ pahoti, so vattabbo “āvuso, saṅghamajjhamhi pañhe uppanne tvaṃ katheyyāsī”ti. Ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo nātimaññitabboti ariyā tuṇhī nisīdantā na bālaputhujjanā viya nisīdanti, aññataraṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva nisīdanti. Iti kammaṭṭhānamanasikāravasena tuṇhībhāvo ariyo tuṇhībhāvo nāma, so nātimaññitabbo, “kiṃ kammaṭṭhānānuyogenā”ti nāvajānitabbo, attano patirūpaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva nisīditabbanti attho.

By one who does not engage in various kinds of unbeneficial talk. By one who does not engage in worldly talk, such as talk about kings, whether seen, heard, or cognized. Or the Dhamma should be spoken by oneself: in the place of the Sangha’s gathering, talk connected with what is allowable or unallowable, or connected with the delineation of form and formlessness, the practice of serenity and insight, or the conduct of sitting and so forth—this is called Dhamma. Such Dhamma should be spoken by oneself, or another should be requested to speak it. If a monk is capable of speaking such talk, he should be told, “Friend, when a question arises in the midst of the Sangha, you should speak.” Or noble silence should not be disparaged: the noble ones, when sitting in silence, do not sit like foolish ordinary people; they sit having taken up some meditation subject. Thus, silence by way of attention to a meditation subject is called noble silence. It should not be disparaged, thinking, “What is the use of applying oneself to a meditation subject?” One should sit having taken up a meditation subject suitable for oneself—this is the meaning.

Na upajjhāyo pucchitabboti “ko nāma tuyhaṃ upajjhāyo”ti na pucchitabbo. Esa nayo sabbattha. Na jātīti “khattiyajātiyo tvaṃ brāhmaṇajātiyo”ti evaṃ jāti na pucchitabbā. Na āgamoti “dīghabhāṇako tvaṃ majjhimabhāṇako”ti evaṃ āgamo na pucchitabbo. Kulapadesopi khattiyakulādivaseneva veditabbo. Atrassa pemaṃ vā doso vāti tatra puggale etesaṃ kāraṇānaṃ aññataravasena pemaṃ vā bhaveyya doso vā.

The preceptor should not be asked about: one should not ask, “What is your preceptor’s name?” This method applies everywhere. Birth should not be asked about: one should not ask about birth thus, “Are you of the warrior caste or the brahmin caste?” Tradition should not be asked about: one should not ask about tradition thus, “Are you a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya or the Majjhima Nikāya?” Family origin too should be understood just as with warrior families and the like. There might be affection or aversion towards that person: towards that person, affection or aversion might arise by way of one or another of these reasons.

No [M 2.0206] parisakappikenāti parisakappakena parisānuvidhāyakena na bhavitabbaṃ, yaṃ parisāya ruccati, tadeva cetetvā kappetvā na kathetabbanti attho. Na hatthamuddā dassetabbāti kathetabbe ca akathetabbe ca saññājananatthaṃ hatthavikāro na kātabbo.

One should not be a schemer for the assembly: one should not be one who plans for the assembly, who follows the assembly. One should not speak having considered and planned only what pleases the assembly—this is the meaning. Hand gestures should not be displayed: no hand movements should be made for the purpose of conveying signals regarding what should or should not be said.

Atthaṃ anuvidhiyantenāti vinicchayapaṭivedhameva sallakkhentena, “idaṃ suttaṃ upalabbhati, imasmiṃ vinicchaye idaṃ vakkhāmī”ti evaṃ paritulayantena nisīditabbanti attho. Na ca āsanā [V 2.0151] vuṭṭhātabbanti na āsanā vuṭṭhāya sannipātamaṇḍale vicaritabbaṃ. Vinayadhare hi uṭṭhite sabbā parisā vuṭṭhahanti, tasmā na vuṭṭhātabbaṃ. Na vītihātabbanti na vinicchayo hāpetabbo. Na kummaggo sevitabboti na āpatti dīpetabbā. Asāhasikena bhavitabbanti na sahasā kārinā bhavitabbaṃ, na sahasā duruttavacanaṃ kathetabbanti attho. Vacanakkhamenāti duruttavācaṃ khamanasīlena. Hitaparisakkināti hitesinā hitagavesinā karuṇā ca karuṇāpubbabhāgo ca upaṭṭhāpetabboti ayaṃ padadvayepi adhippāyo. Anasuruttenāti na asuruttena, asuruttaṃ vuccati viggāhikakathāsaṅkhātaṃ asundaravacanaṃ, taṃ na kathetabbanti attho. Attā pariggahetabboti “vinicchinituṃ vūpasametuṃ sakkhissāmi nu kho, no”ti evaṃ attā pariggahetabbo, attano pamāṇaṃ jānitabbanti attho. Paro pariggahetabboti “lajjiyā nu kho ayaṃ parisā sakkā saññāpetuṃ, udāhu no”ti evaṃ paro pariggahetabbo. Codako pariggahetabboti “dhammacodako nu kho, no”ti evaṃ pariggahetabbo. Cuditako pariggahetabboti “dhammacuditako nu kho, no”ti evaṃ pariggahetabbo. Adhammacodako pariggahetabboti tassa pamāṇaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

By one who follows the meaning: by one who carefully considers the penetration of the decision, thinking, “This Sutta is found; in this decision I will speak thus”—by one who thus weighs it, one should sit down—this is the meaning. And one should not rise from the seat: one should not rise from the seat and wander around the assembly area. For when the Vinaya-holder rises, the entire assembly rises; therefore, one should not rise. It should not be abandoned: the decision should not be abandoned. A wrong path should not be followed: an offense should not be revealed. One should be without rashness: one should not be one who acts rashly, nor should harsh words be spoken rashly—this is the meaning. By one who is forbearing of speech: by one whose nature is to endure harsh words. By one who seeks the good of the assembly: by one who is benevolent, who seeks welfare, and compassion and what precedes compassion should be established—this is the meaning in both these terms. By one who is not surly: not by one who is surly. Surliness is called unlovely speech, reckoned as contentious talk; that should not be spoken—this is the meaning. Oneself should be taken note of: “Will I be able to decide and settle this matter or not?”—thus oneself should be taken note of, one’s own measure should be known—this is the meaning. Another should be taken note of: “Is this assembly deferential and can it be made to understand, or not?”—thus another should be taken note of. The accuser should be taken note of: “Is this a righteous accuser or not?”—thus he should be taken note of. The accused should be taken note of: “Is this one righteously accused or not?”—thus he should be taken note of. An unrighteous accuser should be taken note of: his measure should be known. The same method applies to the rest.

Vuttaṃ [M 2.0207] ahāpentenāti codakacuditakehi vuttavacanaṃ ahāpentena. Avuttaṃ apakāsentenāti anosaṭaṃ vatthuṃ apakāsentena. Mando hāsetabboti mando momūḷho paggaṇhitabbo, “nanu tvaṃ kulaputto”ti uttejetvā anuyogavattaṃ kathāpetvā tassa anuyogo gaṇhitabbo. Bhīru assāsetabboti yassa saṅghamajjhaṃ vā gaṇamajjhaṃ vā anosaṭapubbattā sārajjaṃ uppajjati, tādiso “mā bhāyi, vissattho kathayāhi, mayaṃ te upatthambhā bhavissāmā”ti vatvāpi anuyogavattaṃ kathāpetabbo. Caṇḍo nisedhetabboti apasāretabbo tajjetabbo. Asuci vibhāvetabboti alajjiṃ pakāsetvā āpattiṃ desāpetabbo. Ujumaddavenāti yo bhikkhu uju sīlavā kāyavaṅkādirahito, so maddaveneva upacaritabbo. Dhammesu ca puggalesu cāti ettha yo dhammagaruko hoti, na puggalagaruko, ayameva dhammesu ca puggalesu ca majjhattoti veditabbo. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

By one who does not let what was said be lost: by one who does not let the words spoken by the accuser and the accused be lost. By one who does not reveal what was not said: by one who does not reveal an unestablished matter. A dull-witted one should be encouraged: a dull-witted, deluded person should be taken hold of, and having roused him by saying, “Are you not a clansman?”, and having made him speak the course of questioning, his questioning should be taken up. A timid one should be reassured: one for whom timidity arises due to never having entered the midst of the Sangha or a group, such a one should be made to speak the course of questioning even by saying, “Do not be afraid, speak confidently, we will be your support.” A violent one should be restrained: he should be warded off, he should be rebuked. An impure one should be exposed: having revealed his shamelessness, he should be made to confess his offense. With uprightness and gentleness: a monk who is upright, virtuous, and free from bodily crookedness and the like, he should be treated with gentleness. Regarding both the Dhamma and individuals: here, one who is respectful of the Dhamma, not respectful of individuals, he alone should be understood as being impartial regarding both the Dhamma and individuals. The rest is easily understood.

Iti vinayasaṅgahasaṃvaṇṇanābhūte vinayālaṅkāre

Thus, in the Vinayālaṅkāra, which is a commentary on the Vinayasaṅgaha,

Codanādivinicchayakathālaṅkāro nāma

The Ornament of the Discussion on the Investigation of Accusations and So Forth,

Ekatiṃsatimo paricchedo.

The Thirty-first Chapter.

32. Garukāpattivuṭṭhānavinicchayakathā

32. Discussion on Determining Restoration from Grave Offenses

Paṭicchannaparivāsakathā

The Discussion on Concealed Probation

236. Evaṃ [V 2.0152] codanādivinicchayaṃ kathetvā idāni garukāpattivuṭṭhānavinicchayaṃ kathetuṃ “garukāpattivuṭṭhāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha garu alahukaṃ paṭikaraṇaṃ etissā āpattiyāti garukā, āpajjitabbāti āpatti, garukā ca sā āpatti [M 2.0208] cāti garukāpatti, vuṭṭhahate vuṭṭhānaṃ, garukāpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ garukāpatti vuṭṭhānaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Saṅghādisesāpattito parisuddhabhāvo. Tenāha “parivāsamānattādīhi vinayakammehi garukāpattito vuṭṭhāna”nti. Kiñcāpi catubbidho parivāso, appaṭicchannaparivāso pana idha nādhippetoti āha “tividho parivāso”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ samantapāsādikāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 75) “tattha catubbidho parivāso – appaṭicchannaparivāso paṭicchannaparivāso suddhantaparivāso samodhānaparivāsoti. Tesu ‘yo so, bhikkhave, aññopi aññatitthiyapubbo imasmiṃ dhammavinaye ākaṅkhati pabbajjaṃ, ākaṅkhati upasampadaṃ, tassa cattāro māse parivāso dātabbo’ti evaṃ mahākhandhake (mahāva. 86) vutto titthiyaparivāso appaṭicchannaparivāso nāma. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vuttameva. Ayaṃ pana idha anadhippeto”ti. Ito paraṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva suviññeyyoti tasmā dubbiññeyyaṭṭhāneyeva vaṇṇayissāma.

236. Having thus explained the judgment of accusations and so forth, now he proceeds to explain the judgment of rising from grave offenses, beginning with “rising from grave offenses.” Herein, the atonement for this offense is heavy, not light; thus it is called a grave offense. ‘Āpajjitabbā’ means what one falls into—thus ‘āpatti’ (offense). ‘Garukā ca sā āpatti cāti’ means that which is a grave offense—thus ‘garukāpatti’ (grave offense). ‘Vuṭṭhahate’ means rising—thus ‘vuṭṭhānaṃ’ (rising). ‘Garukāpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ’ means rising from a grave offense—thus ‘garukāpattivuṭṭhānaṃ’ (rising from a grave offense). What is that? It is the state of being purified from a Saṅghādisesa offense. Therefore, it is said: “Rising from a grave offense through disciplinary procedures such as probation and penance.” Although probation is fourfold, unconcealed probation is not intended here—thus it is said: “threefold probation.” For it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Cūḷavagga-aṭṭhakathā 75): “Herein, probation is fourfold: unconcealed probation, concealed probation, probation until purification, and combined probation. Among these, the probation for former adherents of other sects, as mentioned in the Mahākhandhaka (Mahāvagga 86): ‘Bhikkhus, if someone who was formerly a follower of another sect desires to go forth in this Dhamma-Vinaya, desires ordination, he should be given probation for four months’—this is called unconcealed probation. What needs to be said about this has already been said. But this is not intended here.” From here onward, the meaning is easily understood in accordance with the commentary, so we will elaborate only on the difficult points.

237. Evaṃ yo yo āpanno hoti, tassa tassa nāmaṃ gahetvā kammavācā kātabbāti etena pāḷiyaṃ sabbasādhāraṇavasena “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhū”ti ca “yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmassa bhikkhuno”ti ca āgatepi kammavācābhaṇanakāle tathā abhaṇitvā “ayaṃ buddharakkhito bhikkhū”ti ca “imassa buddharakkhitassa bhikkhuno”ti ca evaṃ sakasakanāmaṃ uddharitvāva kammavācā kātabbāti dasseti.

237. Thus, for each one who has committed an offense, the formal act should be performed by taking his name. This Pāli passage shows that, even though the general formula contains “Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me, this bhikkhu named so-and-so…” and “If the Saṅgha is ready, the Saṅgha [should grant the request] for so-and-so bhikkhu…”, at the time of reciting the formal act, instead of reciting it that way, one should say: “This bhikkhu Buddharakkhita…” and “For this bhikkhu Buddharakkhita…” – thus, the formal act must be performed by specifically stating each individual’s name.

Māḷakasīmāyameva vattaṃ samādātabbaṃ, na tato bahi. Kasmā? “Aññattha kammavācā aññattha samādāna”nti vattabbadosappasaṅgato. Asamādinnavattassa ārocanāsambhavato, māḷakasīmāya [M 2.0209] sannipatitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ekassapi anārocane sati ratticchedasambhavato ca. Parivāsaṃ samādiyāmi, vattaṃ samādiyāmīti imesu dvīsu padesu ekekena vā ubhohi padehi vā [V 2.0153] samādātabbaṃ. Kathaṃ viññāyatīti ce? “Ekapadenapi cettha nikkhitto hoti parivāso, dvīhi pana sunikkhittoyeva, samādānepi eseva nayo”ti vakkhamānattā. Samādiyitvā tattheva saṅghassa ārocetabbaṃ, na tattha anārocetvā aññattha gantabbaṃ. Kasmā? Vuṭṭhitāya parisāya puna sannipātetuṃ dukkarattā, ekassapi bhikkhuno anārocetvā aruṇuṭṭhāpane sati ratticchedakarattā.

The observance should be undertaken within the boundary of the māḷaka, not outside it. Why? Because of the possible fault of saying, “The kammavācā is in one place, the undertaking in another.” Because it is impossible to announce without having undertaken the observance; and because if even one bhikkhu assembled within the boundary of the māḷaka fails to announce, it can result in the breaking of the night. One should undertake the period of probation or the observance using one or both of these phrases: “I undertake the period of probation,” or “I undertake the observance.” How is this understood? “Even with one phrase, the period of probation is established; with two, it is even more firmly established. The same applies to the undertaking,” as will be explained. After undertaking it, one should announce it to the Saṅgha right there; one should not leave and go elsewhere without announcing it there. Why? Because once the assembly has dispersed, it is difficult to reassemble; and because if one bhikkhu fails to announce it, it can lead to the breaking of the night when dawn breaks.

Ārocentena evaṃ ārocetabbanti sambandho. “Ahaṃ bhante…pe… saṅgho dhāretū”ti ettakameva vatvā yācane viya “dutiyampi tatiyampī”ti avuttattā accāyikakaraṇe sati ekavāraṃ ārocitepi upapannamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vediyāmahaṃ bhante, vediyatīti maṃ saṅgho dhāretūti ettha “vediyāmīti cittena sampaṭicchitvā sukhaṃ anubhavāmi, na tappaccayā ahaṃ dukkhitoti adhippāyo”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.97) vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “sukhaṃ vedemi vedana”ntiādīsu viya pi-saddo anubhavanattho hoti. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 97) pana “vediyāmīti jānemi, cittena sampaṭicchitvā sukhaṃ anubhavāmi, na tappaccayā ahaṃ dukkhitoti adhippāyoti likhita”nti vuttaṃ. Ettha pana “dīpaṅkaro lokavidū”tiādīsu viya ñāṇattho anubhavanattho ca. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.97) pana “vediyāmahanti jānāpemahaṃ, ārocemīti attho, anubhavāmītipissa atthaṃ vadanti. Purimaṃ pana pasaṃsanti ārocanavacanattā”ti. Ettha tu –

The connection is that it should be announced thus by the announcer. “I, venerable sirs… may the Saṅgha remember me”—having said only this much, since it is not stated to repeat “a second time, a third time” as in a request, it should be understood that even if announced once in urgent matters, it is still valid. Here, “I experience, venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha remember me as one who experiences,” the meaning is: “I accept with the mind and experience happiness, but it is not the case that I am suffering because of that”—this is explained in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.97). Here, as in phrases like “sukhaṃ vedemi vedanaṃ” (I experience a pleasant feeling), the word has the meaning of experiencing. However, in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 97), it is written: “‘I experience’ means ‘I know,’ that is, having accepted with the mind, I experience happiness, but it is not the case that I am suffering because of that—this is the meaning.” Here, as in phrases like “Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World,” the sense is both of knowing and experiencing. But in the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.97), it is said: “‘I experience’ means ‘I make known,’ that is, ‘I announce.’ Some say it also means ‘I experience.’ However, the former is praised because it is a word of announcement.” Here, however—

“Sampannaṃ [M 2.0210] sālikedāraṃ, suvā khādanti brāhmaṇa;

Paṭivedemi te brahme, na naṃ vāretumussahe”ti. –

“The field of rice is bountiful, the parrots eat it, O Brahmin; I declare this to you, O Brahmin, I am not able to prevent them.”

Ādīsu viya ārocanatthoti daṭṭhabbo.

It should be understood as being for the purpose of announcement, like in the aforementioned instances.

Ārocetvā…pe… nikkhipitabbanti dukkaṭaparimocanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Keci pana “tadaheva puna vattaṃ samādiyitvā aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetukāmassa ratticchedaparihāratthampī”ti vadanti. Yassa māḷake nārocitaṃ, tassa ārocetvā nikkhipitabbaṃ. Yassa ārocitaṃ, tassa puna ārocanakiccaṃ natthi, kevalaṃ nikkhipitabbameva. “Sabhāgā bhikkhū vasantī”ti vuttattā visabhāgānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne vattaṃ asamādiyitvā bahi eva kātumpi vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dve leḍḍupāte [V 2.0154] atikkamitvāti idaṃ vihāre bhikkhūnaṃ sajjhāyādisaddasavanūpacāravijahanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, mahāmaggato okkammāti idaṃ maggapaṭipannānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ savanūpacārātikkamanatthaṃ, gumbena vātiādi dassanūpacāravijahanatthaṃ. Sopi kenaci kammena purearuṇe eva gacchatīti iminā ārocanāya katāya sabbesu bhikkhūsu bahivihāraṃ gatesupi ūnegaṇecaraṇadoso vā vippavāsadoso vā na hoti ārocanatthattā sahavāsassāti dasseti. Tenāha “ayañcā”tiādi. Anikkhittavattena antoupacāragatānaṃ sabbesampi ārocetabbā. “Ayaṃ nikkhittavattassa parihāro”ti vuttaṃ, tattha nikkhittavattassāti vattaṃ nikkhipitvā parivasantassāti attho. Ayaṃ panettha therassa adhippāyo – vattaṃ nikkhipitvā parivasantassa upacāragatānaṃ sabbesaṃ ārocanakiccaṃ natthi, diṭṭharūpānaṃ sutasaddānaṃ ārocetabbaṃ, adiṭṭhaasutānampi antodvādasahatthagatānaṃ ārocetabbaṃ. Idaṃ vattaṃ nikkhipitvā parivasantassa lakkhaṇanti. Therassāti mahāpadumattherassa.

Having informed… and so on… it should be put down—this was stated for the purpose of releasing from the minor offense. Some, however, say, “On that very day, having undertaken the duty again, it is also for the purpose of safeguarding against the breaking of the night for one who wishes to rise at dawn.” He who has not made the announcement in the māḷaka should announce it and then relinquish the observance. For him who has made the announcement, there is no further duty of announcement; he should simply relinquish it. Because it is said, “The bhikkhus who share the same residence,” it should be understood that for those not sharing the same residence, the duty need not be undertaken, and it is permissible to perform it outside. “Having passed two stone-throws”—this was stated for the purpose of bhikkhus in the monastery avoiding the disturbance of sounds such as recitation. “Turning away from the great road”—this was for the purpose of bhikkhus on the path avoiding the disturbance of hearing. “Or by a clump,” etc.—this was for the purpose of avoiding the disturbance of sight. Even if he goes before dawn by some duty—by this, it is shown that even if all the bhikkhus have gone outside the monastery after the announcement was made, there is no fault of incomplete group conduct or of separation, because the purpose of the announcement is co-residence. Therefore, it is said, “And this,” etc. For one who has not put down the duty, all those who have come within the boundary must be informed. “This is the safeguard for one who has put down the duty”—this was stated. Here, “one who has put down the duty” means one who has put aside the duty and is dwelling on probation. Moreover, this is the intention of the elder here—for one who has put down the duty and is dwelling on probation, there is no duty of announcement for all those within the boundary. Those who are seen or whose sounds are heard should be announced, and even those unseen and unheard who come within twelve arm-lengths should be announced. This is the characteristic for one who has put down the duty and is dwelling on probation. “Of the elder”—this refers to the great elder Mahāpaduma.

238. Kukkuccavinodanatthāyāti imesu paṭicchannadivasappamāṇena parivasitadivasesu “siyuṃ nu kho tividharatticchedakāraṇayuttāni [M 2.0211] kānici divasāni, evaṃ sati aparipuṇṇaparivāsadivasattā na mānattāraho bhaveyya, asati ca mānattārahabhāve mānattaṃ dinnampi adinnaṃyeva bhaveyya, evañca sati āpannāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ na bhaveyyā”ti imassa vinayakukkuccassa vinodanatthāya. Ekena vā dvīhi vā tīhi vā divasehi adhikatarāni divasāni parivasitvā nanu cāyaṃ parivutthaparivāso, tasmānena mānattameva yācitabbaṃ, atha kasmā vattaṃ samādiyitvā mānattaṃ yācitabbanti āhāti codanaṃ manasi karontena vuttaṃ “ayañhi vatte samādinne”tiādi. Hi yasmā ayaṃ bhikkhu vatte samādinne eva mānattāraho hoti, na asamādinne, iti tasmā vattaṃ samādiyitvā mānattaṃ yācitabbanti sambandho. Nanu ca kammavācāyaṃ “so parivutthaparivāso saṅghaṃ mānattaṃ yācati”icceva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “samādinnavatto”ti, atha kasmā “vatte samādinne eva mānattāraho hotī”ti vuttanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “nikkhittavattena parivutthattā”ti. Yasmā ayaṃ bhikkhu nikkhittavattena hutvā parivuttho hoti, no anikkhittavattena, tasmā nikkhittavattena hutvā parivutthattā ayaṃ bhikkhu vatte samādinne eva mānattāraho hoti, no asamādinneti yojanā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “anikkhittavattassa pana puna samādānakiccaṃ natthi. So hi paṭicchannadivasātikkameneva mānattāraho hoti, tasmā tassa mānattaṃ dātabbamevā”ti.

238. To dispel scruples—this is to dispel the Vinaya scruples that arise during the days of probation, which are equal in number to the days of concealment, thinking: "Might there be some days connected with the three kinds of causes for the breaking of the night? If so, due to the days of probation being incomplete, he would not be worthy of mānatta. And if he is not worthy of mānatta, even if mānatta is given, it would be as if not given.
