Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. pācittiya 2.217-218) pana “yena kenaci vevacanenāti vuttattā ‘bhojanaṃ gaṇhathā’tiādisāmaññanāmenapi gaṇabhojanaṃ hoti. Yaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ addhānagamanādivatthūsu ‘idheva bhuñjathā’ti vuttavacanassa kukkuccāyanaṃ, tampi odanādināmaṃ gahetvā vuttattā eva katanti veditabba”nti vuttaṃ.

Regarding “having taken the name of the five kinds of food”: here some say that it is indeed a group meal even when it is said, “Take food.” In the three commentaries it is said: “Below, in the case of going on a journey and in the case of embarking on a boat, because they felt scrupulous and did not accept when it was said, ‘Venerable sirs, eat right here,’ therefore it is indeed a group meal even when it is said, ‘Eat.’” However, since it is said, “one invites having taken the name of the five kinds of food,” it is a group meal only when one speaks having taken the name of a food—such as by saying, “Eat rice,” or “Eat a meal”—and not otherwise. Even here, regarding the phrase “Venerable sirs, eat right here,” it should be understood that they invited them only after saying “rice” or “a meal.” Or, because those bhikkhus were invited as a group, they felt scrupulous about being ungrateful and so did not accept—this is our preference. Having investigated, the more suitable view should be adopted. In the Vimativinodanī, however, it is said: “Since it is stated ‘by any expression whatsoever,’ it becomes a group meal even by a general name such as ‘Take food,’ etc. As for the scrupulousness mentioned in the Pāli in the cases of going on a journey, etc., regarding the statement ‘Eat right here,’ that too should be understood as having been done only after taking the name of rice, etc.”

Kurundīvacane [M 2.0299] vicāretīti pañcakhaṇḍādivasena saṃvidahati. Ghaṭṭetīti anuvātaṃ chinditvā hatthena, daṇḍakena vā ghaṭṭeti. Suttaṃ karotīti suttaṃ vaṭṭeti. Valetīti daṇḍake vā hatthe vā āvaṭṭeti. “Abhinavasseva cīvarassa karaṇaṃ idha cīvarakammaṃ nāma, purāṇacīvare sūcikammaṃ cīvarakammaṃ nāma na hotī”ti vadanti. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. pācittiya 2.217-218) pana “āgantukapaṭṭanti acchinditvā anvādhiṃ āropetvā karaṇacīvaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ṭhapetīti ekaṃ antaṃ cīvare bandhanavasena ṭhapeti. Paccāgataṃ sibbatīti tasseva dutiyaantaṃ parivattitvā āhataṃ sibbati. Āgantukapaṭṭaṃ bandhatīti cīvarena laggaṃ karonto punappunaṃ tattha tattha suttena bandhati. Ghaṭṭetīti pamāṇena gahetvā daṇḍādīhi ghaṭṭeti. Suttaṃ karotīti suttaṃ tiguṇādibhāvena vaṭṭeti. Valetīti anekaguṇasuttaṃ hatthena [V 2.0219] vā cakkadaṇḍena vā vaṭṭeti ekattaṃ karoti. Parivattanaṃ karotīti parivattanadaṇḍayantakaṃ karoti. Yasmiṃ suttaguḷaṃ pavesetvā veḷunāḷikādīsu ṭhapetvā paribbhamāpetvā suttakoṭito paṭṭhāya ākaḍḍhantī”ti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pācittiya 209-218) na “āgantukapaṭṭaṃ moghasuttena sibbitvā ṭhapenti. Tattha anuvāte yathā ekatalaṃ hoti, tathā hatthehi ghaṭṭeti. Valetīti āvaṭṭeti. Parivattananti suttaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ suttaparivattanaṃ karoti, paṭṭaṃ sibbantānaṃ sukhasibbanatthaṃ paṭṭaparivattanañca, navacīvarakārako idhādhippeto, na itaro”ti vuttaṃ.

Considering the statement in the Kurundī, he arranges it on the basis of the five sections and so on. `Ghaṭṭeti` means one cuts the weft and then strikes it with the hand or a stick. `Suttaṃ karoti` means one twists the thread. `Valeti` means one turns it on a stick or in the hand. Some say: 'Here, `cīvarakamma` refers to the making of a new robe; needlework on an old robe is not called `cīvarakamma`.' But in the Vimativinodanī it is said: 'The term `āgantukapaṭṭa` is said with reference to a robe being made, which is done by not cutting off the inserted patch but attaching it by overlapping. `Ṭhapeti` means one secures one end to the robe by tying it. `Paccāgataṃ sibbati` means one turns the other end and sews it back. `Āgantukapaṭṭaṃ bandhati` means, making it adhere to the robe, one repeatedly ties it with thread in various places. `Ghaṭṭeti` means, after taking the measurement, one strikes it with a stick or the like. `Suttaṃ karoti` means one twists the thread into three or more strands. `Valeti` means one twists multiple strands of thread by hand or with a spinning rod to make them one. `Parivattanaṃ karoti` means one makes a turning device. It is said: “Having inserted a ball of thread into it, placed it in a bamboo tube or the like, and made it revolve, one draws out the thread from its end.”' In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is said: 'They sew the `āgantukapaṭṭa` with a temporary thread and secure it. There, so that the weft becomes a single layer, it is beaten with the hands. `Valeti` means to twist. `Parivattana` means the turning of the thread for ease of handling for those taking the thread, and the turning of the patch for ease of sewing for those sewing the patch. Here, the maker of a new robe is intended, not another.'

Animantitacatutthanti animantito catuttho yassa bhikkhucatukkassa, taṃ animantitacatutthaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Tenāha “pañcannaṃ catukkāna”nti, “catutthe āgate na yāpentīti [M 2.0300] vacanato sace añño koci āgacchanto natthi, cattāroyeva ca tattha nisinnā yāpetuṃ na sakkonti, na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Gaṇabhojanāpattijanakanimantanabhāvato “akappiyanimantana”nti vuttaṃ. Sampavesetvāti nisīdāpetvā. Gaṇo bhijjatīti gaṇo āpattiṃ na āpajjatīti adhippāyo. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. pācittiya 2.220) pana “sampavesetvāti tehi yojetvā. Gaṇo bhijjatīti nimantitasaṅgho na hotīti attho”ti vuttaṃ.

`The fourth uninvited` means a group of four bhikkhus of which the fourth is uninvited; that is `the fourth uninvited`. So too for the rest. Therefore he said, 'of the five groups of four.' Some say: 'In accordance with the statement, “When a fourth arrives, they do not continue,” if no one else is coming and only four are seated there, they cannot continue; it is not allowable.' Because it is an invitation that generates an offense of eating in a group, it is called an 'improper invitation.' `Having admitted him` means having had him sit down. `The group is broken` means the group does not incur an offense; this is the intention. But in the Vimativinodanī it is said: '`Having admitted him` means having joined him with them. `The group is broken` means the invited group no longer exists; this is the meaning.'

“Yattha cattāro bhikkhū…pe… bhuñjantī”ti imāya pāḷiyā saṃsandanato “itaresaṃ pana gaṇapūrako hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Avisesenāti “gilāno vā cīvarakārako vā”ti avisesetvā sabbasādhāraṇavacanena. Tasmāti avisesitattā.

In connection with this Pāli passage, 'Where four bhikkhus... eat,' it is said, 'but for the others, he becomes one who completes the group.' `Without distinction` means without making a distinction such as 'a sick person or a robe-maker,' by a statement common to all. `Therefore` means because it has not been specified.

Adhivāsetvā gatesūti ettha akappiyanimantanādhivāsanakkhaṇe pubbapayoge dukkaṭampi natthi, viññattito pasavane pana viññattikkhaṇe itarasikkhāpadehi dukkaṭaṃ hotīti gahetabbaṃ. Bhutvā gatesūti ettha āgatesupi bhojanakicce niṭṭhite gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Tāni ca tehi ekato na gahitānīti yehi bhojanehi visaṅketo natthi, tāni bhojanāni tehi bhikkhūhi ekato na gahitāni ekena pacchā gahitattā. Mahāthereti bhikkhū sandhāya vuttaṃ. Nimantanaṃ sādiyathāti nimantanabhattaṃ paṭiggaṇhatha. Yānīti kummāsādīni tehi bhikkhūhi ekena pacchā gahitattā ekato na gahitāni. Bhattuddesakena paṇḍitena bhavitabbaṃ…pe… mocetabbāti etena bhattuddesakena [V 2.0220] akappiyanimantane sādite sabbesampi sāditaṃ hoti, ekato gaṇhantānaṃ gaṇabhojanāpatti ca hotīti dasseti. Dūtassa dvāre āgantvā puna “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti [M 2.0301] vacanabhayena “gāmadvāre aṭṭhatvā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha tattha gantvāti antaravīthiādīsu tattha tattha ṭhitānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā. Bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya gharadvāre ṭhapetvā dīyamānepi eseva nayo. Nivattathāti vutte pana nivattituṃ vaṭṭatīti “nivattathā”ti vicchinditvā pacchā “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttattā vaṭṭati.

`When they have consented and gone`: Here, at the moment of consenting to an improper invitation, there is not even an offense of wrong-doing in the preliminary effort. But when it results from an intimation, at the moment of the intimation an offense of wrong-doing occurs in accordance with the other training rules; this should be understood. `When they have eaten and gone`: Here, even when they have come, once the business of the meal is finished, it is allowable to take more. `And those were not taken together by them`: This means those foods for which there was no prior arrangement were not taken together by those bhikkhus because they were taken later by one of them. `The great elder`: This is said with reference to the bhikkhus. `Accept the invitation`: This means accept the invited meal. `Which`: This refers to things like gruel, etc., which were not taken together because they were taken later by one of those bhikkhus. `The meal-apportioner should be wise... should be released`: By this it is shown that when an improper invitation is accepted by the meal-apportioner, it is accepted by all, and for those taking the food together, there is an offense of eating in a group. Fearing that if he came to the messenger's door he would again say, 'Take the meal,' it was said, 'having stood at the village gate.' `Going here and there`: This means going to those standing here and there in the inner streets and so on. Even when food is placed at a house door and given for the benefit of the bhikkhus, this same method applies. But when it is said, 'Turn back,' it is allowable to turn back, because after interrupting with 'Turn back,' it was later said, 'Take the meal.'

Paramparabhojanakathā

The Talk on Successive Meals

2. Paramparabhojanakathāyaṃ pana parassa parassa bhojanaṃ paramparabhojanaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Paṭhamaṃ nimantitabhattaṃ ṭhapetvā aññassa bhojanakiriyā. Paramparabhojanaṃ gaṇabhojanaṃ viya viññattito ca nimantanato ca na pasavatīti āha “paramparabhojanaṃ panā”tiādi. Pana-saddo visesatthajotako. Vikappanāvaseneva taṃ bhattaṃ asantaṃ nāma hotīti anupaññattivasena vikappanaṃ aṭṭhapetvā yathāpaññattasikkhāpadameva ṭhapitaṃ. Parivāre (pari. 86) pana vikappanāyaṃ anujānanampi anupaññattisadisanti katvā “catasso anupaññattiyo”ti vuttaṃ, mahāpaccariyādīsu vuttanayaṃ pacchā vadanto pāḷiyā saṃsandanato parammukhāvikappanameva patiṭṭhāpeti. Keci pana “tadā attano santike ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ aññassa abhāvato thero sammukhāvikappanaṃ nākāsi, bhagavatā ca visuṃ sammukhāvikappanā na vuttā, tathāpi sammukhāvikappanāpi vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “yo bhikkhu pañcasu sahadhammikesu aññatarassa ‘mayhaṃ bhattapaccāsaṃ tuyhaṃ dammī’ti vā ‘vikappemī’ti vā evaṃ sammukhā vā ‘itthannāmassa dammī’ti vā ‘vikappemī’ti vā evaṃ parammukhā vā paṭhamanimantanaṃ avikappetvā pacchā nimantitakule laddhabhikkhato ekasitthampi ajjhoharati, pācittiya”nti vuttaṃ.

2. In the talk on successive meals, eating one after another is a successive meal. What is that? It is the act of eating another meal after having set aside the first invited meal. It is said, “Regarding successive meals…,” etc., because a successive meal, unlike a group meal, is not contingent on a request or an invitation. The word 'pana' indicates a specific point. It is solely by means of making-over that that meal is considered non-existent; thus, without establishing the making-over by way of a supplementary regulation, only the training rule as originally laid down is maintained. In the Parivāra, however, since the permission for making-over is similar to a supplementary regulation, it is said, “There are four supplementary regulations.” Explaining later, by comparing with the Pāḷi, he establishes only making-over to someone not present, following the method stated in the Mahāpaccariya and other texts. Some, however, say: “At that time, since there was no one else present besides the Blessed One, the elder did not perform the making-over in his presence, and the Blessed One did not separately speak of making-over in someone's presence; nevertheless, making-over in someone's presence is also allowable.” For this reason, it is also said in the Mātikā Commentary (in the explanation of the training rule on successive meals in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī): “Whatever bhikkhu, without first making over the initial invitation, should later consume even a single mouthful of almsfood received from the invited family—whether in person to one of five co-religionists, saying, ‘I give my expectation of a meal to you,’ or ‘I make it over,’ or not in person, saying, ‘I give it to so-and-so,’ or ‘I make it over’—it is a Pācittiya offense.”

Pañcahi [M 2.0302] bhojanehi nimantitassa yena yena paṭhamaṃ nimantito, tassa tassa bhojanato uppaṭipāṭiyā avikappetvā vā parassa parassa bhojanaṃ paramparabhojananti āha “sace pana mūlanimantanaṃ heṭṭhā hoti, pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ upari, taṃ uparito paṭṭhāya bhuñjantassa āpattī”ti. Hatthaṃ anto pavesetvā sabbaheṭṭhimaṃ gaṇhantassa majjhe ṭhitampi antohatthagataṃ hotīti āha “hatthaṃ [V 2.0221] pana…pe… yathā yathā vā bhuñjantassa anāpattī”ti. Khīrassa rasassa ca bhattena amissaṃ hutvā upari ṭhitattā “khīraṃ vā rasaṃ vā pivato anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ.

He said that for one invited with the five kinds of staple foods, eating the meal of one after another out of order from the meal of the one by whom one was first invited, or without having made it over, is a successive meal: “But if the original invitation is at the bottom and the later ones are on top, there is an offense for one who starts eating from the top.” He said: “But for one who inserts his hand… (etc.) … or there is no offense for one eating in whatever way,” meaning that for one who inserts his hand and takes the very bottom portion, what is situated in the middle is also considered to have come into the hand. Because milk and broth, being unmixed with the rice, are situated on top, it is said: “There is no offense in drinking milk or broth.”

“Mahāupāsakoti gehassāmiko. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘āpattī’ti vacanena kurundiyaṃ ‘vaṭṭatī’ti vacanaṃ viruddhaṃ viya dissati. Dvinnampi adhippāyo mahāpaccariyaṃ vibhāvito”ti mahāgaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

“‘Great lay follower’ means the master of the house. The statement ‘there is an offense’ in the Great Commentary seems to contradict the statement ‘it is allowable’ in the Kurundī. The intention of both is made clear in the Mahāpaccariya.” So it is said in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada.

Sabbe nimantentīti akappiyanimantanavasena nimantenti. “Paramparabhojanaṃ nāma pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena bhojanena nimantito, taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjati, etaṃ paramparabhojanaṃ nāmā”ti vuttattā satipi bhikkhācariyāya paṭhamaṃ laddhabhāve “piṇḍāya caritvā laddhaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjati, āpattī”ti vuttaṃ.

“All invite” means they invite by way of an improper invitation. Because it is said: “A successive meal is this: having been invited with one of the five kinds of staple foods, one sets that aside and eats another of the five kinds of staple foods; this is called a successive meal,” it is therefore said, even when almsfood has been obtained first: “If he eats food obtained by wandering for alms, there is an offense.”

Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. pācittiya 2.229) pana “khīraṃ vā rasaṃ vāti pañcabhojanāmissaṃ bhattato upari ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi abhojanattā uppaṭipāṭiyā pivatopi anāpatti. Tenāha ‘bhuñjantenā’tiādī”ti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pācittiya 229) pana “ettha ‘mahāupāsako bhikkhū nimanteti…pe… pacchā laddhaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjantassa āpatti. Piṇḍāya caritvā laddhabhattaṃ bhuñjati, āpattī’ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vacanato, ‘kālasseva piṇḍāya caritvā [M 2.0303] bhuñjimhā’ti pāḷito, khandhake ‘na ca, bhikkhave, aññatra nimantane aññassa bhojjayāgu paribhuñjitabbā, yo bhuñjeyya, yathādhammo kāretabbo’ti vacanato ca nimantetvā vā pavedetu animantetvā vā, paṭhamagahitanimantitassa bhikkhuno paṭhamanimantanabhojanato aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci parasantakaṃ bhojanaṃ paramparabhojanāpattiṃ karoti. Attano santakaṃ, saṅghagaṇato laddhaṃ vā agahaṭṭhasantakaṃ vaṭṭati, nimantanato paṭhamaṃ nibaddhattā pana niccabhattādiparasantakampi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

But in the Vimativinodanī it is said: “The words ‘milk or broth’ are said with reference to what is placed on top of the meal, unmixed with the five staple foods. For since that is not a staple food, there is no offense even for one who drinks it out of order. For that reason he said: ‘by one who is eating,’ etc.” But in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is said: “Here, according to the commentary: ‘A great lay follower invites bhikkhus… (etc.) … for one who eats a meal obtained later, there is an offense. If he eats food obtained by wandering for alms, there is an offense’; and according to the Pāḷi: ‘We wandered for alms early and ate’; and according to the Khandhaka: ‘And, bhikkhus, apart from an invitation, another’s food or gruel should not be consumed. Whoever should consume it should be dealt with according to the Dhamma.’ Thus, whether one is invited, informed, or not invited, for a bhikkhu who has first accepted an invitation, any food whatsoever belonging to another, apart from the meal of the first invitation, incurs the offense of a successive meal. What belongs to oneself, or what is received from the Saṅgha or a group, or what does not belong to a householder is allowable. However, because it was established before the invitation, even what belongs to another, such as a permanent meal, etc., is also allowable.”

Anāpucchākathā

The Discourse on Not Taking Leave

3. Anāpucchākathāyaṃ “pakativacanenāti ettha yaṃ dvādasahatthabbhantare ṭhitena sotuṃ sakkā bhaveyya, taṃ pakativacanaṃ nāma. Āpucchitabboti ‘ahaṃ itthannāmassa gharaṃ gacchāmī’ti vā ‘cārittakaṃ [V 2.0222] āpajjāmī’ti vā īdisena vacanena āpucchitabbo. Sesamettha uttānameva. Pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena nimantanasādiyanaṃ, santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā, bhattiyagharato aññagharappavesanaṃ, majjhanhikānatikkamo, samayassa vā āpadānaṃ vā abhāvoti imāni panettha pañca aṅgānī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.298) ettakameva vuttaṃ, vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. pacittiya 2.298) pana “pariyesitvā ārocanakiccaṃ natthīti vuttattā yo apariyesitabbo upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṭṭhāne dissati, so sacepi pakativacanassa savanūpacāraṃ atikkamma ṭhito, upasaṅkamitvā āpucchitabbo. Tenāha ‘apica…pe… yaṃ passati, so āpucchitabbo’tiādi. Anāpattivāre cettha antarārāmādīnaññeva vuttattā vihārato gāmavīthiṃ anuññātakāraṇaṃ vinā atikkamantassāpi āpatti hoti, na pana gharūpacāraṃ [M 2.0304] atikkamantasseva. Yaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ ‘aññassa gharūpacāraṃ okkamantassa…pe… paṭhamapādaṃ ummāraṃ atikkāmetī’tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ gāme paviṭṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tathāpi aññassa gharūpacāraṃ anokkamitvā vīthimajjheneva gantvā icchiticchitagharadvārābhimukhe ṭhatvā manusse oloketvā gacchantassapi pācittiyameva. Tattha keci ‘vīthiyaṃ atikkamantassa gharūpacāragaṇanāya āpattiyo’ti vadanti. Aññe pana ‘yāni kulāni uddissa gato, tesaṃ gaṇanāyā’ti. Pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena nimantanasādiyanaṃ, santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchanā, bhattiyagharato aññagharūpasaṅkamanaṃ, majjhanhikānatikkamo, samayāpadānaṃ abhāvoti imānettha pañca aṅgānī”ti. Vikālagāmappavesanepi “aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāro adinnādāne vuttanayeneva veditabbo”ti iminā dutiyaleḍḍupāto idha upacāroti dasseti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchanā, anuññātakāraṇābhāvo, vikāle gāmappavesananti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

3. In the discussion on not taking leave: Herein, “by ordinary speech” means that which can be heard by someone standing within a distance of twelve cubits; this is called ordinary speech. “One should take leave” means one should take leave with a statement such as, “I am going to the house of so-and-so,” or “I am going on an almsround.” The rest here is clear. The five factors here are: (1) accepting an invitation for any of the five kinds of meals; (2) not taking leave from a bhikkhu who is present; (3) entering another house from the house where one is to have a meal; (4) exceeding midday; and (5) the absence of a suitable occasion or an emergency. This much is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī. However, in the Vimativinodanī it is stated: “Since it is said that there is no need to announce after having searched, if one who does not need to be sought out is seen in a suitable place to be approached, leave should be taken from him after approaching him, even if he is standing beyond the range of hearing ordinary speech. Therefore, it is said, ‘Moreover... whomever one sees, leave should be taken from him,’ etc. In the section on non-offenses here, since only what is within the monastery, etc., is mentioned, for one who crosses from the monastery into a village street without a permitted reason there is also an offense, not just for one who passes beyond the vicinity of a house. What is stated in the Pāli—‘When entering the vicinity of another’s house... when one makes the first foot cross the threshold,’ etc.—is said with reference to one who has entered the village. Nevertheless, for one who does not enter the vicinity of another’s house but goes right down the middle of the street, stands facing the door of whatever house one wishes, and goes after looking for people, there is still an offense of pācittiya. Here, some say: ‘For one crossing in the street, the offenses are according to the count of house-vicinities.’ But others say: ‘It is according to the count of the families one went intending to visit.’ The five factors here are: (1) accepting an invitation for any of the five kinds of meals; (2) not taking leave from a bhikkhu who is present; (3) approaching another house from the house where one is to have a meal; (4) exceeding midday; and (5) the absence of a suitable occasion or an emergency.” Even in the case of entering a village at the wrong time, by the statement, “The vicinity of an unenclosed village should be understood in the way stated in the section on what is not given,” it is shown that here the vicinity is the second throw of a clod. The rest here is clear. The three factors here are: (1) not taking leave from a bhikkhu who is present; (2) the absence of a permitted reason; and (3) entering a village at the wrong time.

Paṃsukūlakathā

The Discourse on Rag-Robes

4. Paṃsukūlakathāyaṃ abhinne sarīreti abbhuṇhe allasarīre. “Abbhuṇhe”ti imināpi vuttameva pariyāyabhedamantarena vibhāvetuṃ “allasarīre”ti vuttaṃ.

4. In the discussion on rag-robes: ‘on an unbroken body’ means on a warm, fresh body. The term ‘on a fresh body’ is stated in order to clarify, by way of a synonymous expression, what was already said by ‘on a warm body’.

Visabhāgasarīreti itthisarīre. Visabhāgasarīrattā accāsannena na bhavitabbanti āha “sīse vā”tiādi. Vaṭṭatīti visabhāgasarīrepi attanāva vuttavidhiṃ kātuṃ sāṭakañca gahetuṃ vaṭṭati[V 2.0223]. Keci pana “kiñcāpi iminā sikkhāpadena anāpatti, itthirūpaṃ pana āmasantassa dukkaṭa”nti vadanti. “Yathākammaṃ gatoti tato petattabhāvato matabhāvaṃ dasseti. Abbhuṇheti āsannamaraṇatāya sarīrassa uṇhasamaṅgitaṃ dasseti, tenevāha ‘allasarīre’ti. Kuṇapasabhāvaṃ [M 2.0305] upagatampi bhinnameva allabhāvato bhinnattā. Visabhāgasarīreti itthisarīre. ‘Sīse vā’tiādi adhakkhake ubbhajāṇumaṇḍale padese cittavikārappattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, yattha katthaci anāmasantena kataṃ sukatameva. Matasarīrampi hi yena kenaci ākārena sañcicca phusantassa anāmāsadukkaṭamevāti vadanti, taṃ yuttameva. Na hi apārājikavatthukepi cittādiitthirūpe bhavantaṃ dukkaṭaṃ pārājikavatthubhūte matitthisarīre nivattatī”ti vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.135) vutta.

A body of a different kind, that is, a woman's body. Because it is a body of a different kind, one should not be too close, hence it is said, “on the head,” etc. It is allowable to follow the prescribed method oneself, even with a body of a different kind, and to take the robe. However, some say, “Although there is no offense under this training rule, touching a woman's form incurs an offense of dukkaṭa.” It is stated in the Vimativinodanī: “‘Gone according to one's kamma’ indicates the state of being dead, from the state of being a departed one. ‘Warm’ suggests the warmth of the body due to nearness to death, hence it is said ‘a fresh body.’ Even though it has reached the nature of a corpse, it is indeed decayed, being distinct from the state of freshness. ‘A body of a different kind,’ that is, a woman's body. ‘On the head,’ etc., refers to the regions under the armpit and above the knee, where mental disturbance may arise. Whatever is done without intentionally touching in any of those places is perfectly acceptable. Even with a dead body, they say, intentionally touching it in any way incurs an offense of dukkaṭa for inappropriate touching, and that is indeed reasonable. For the dukkaṭa offense that arises in a case not involving a pārājika offense with regard to a woman's form in the mind, etc., does not cease in the case of a dead woman's body, which has become a basis for a pārājika offense.”

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne ācariyena avuttāpi paṃsukūlakathā paṃsukūlasāmaññena veditabbā. Sā hi cīvarakkhandhake (mahāva. 340) evaṃ āgatā “tena kho pana samayena ye te bhikkhū gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyanti, te kukkuccāyantā paṃsukūlaṃ na sādiyanti ‘ekaṃyeva bhagavatā cīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ, na dve’ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyantena paṃsukūlampi sādiyituṃ, tadubhayenapāhaṃ, bhikkhave, santuṭṭhiṃ vaṇṇemī”ti. Tattha “ekaṃyeva bhagavatā cīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ, na dveti te ‘kira itarītarena cīvarenā’ti etassa ‘gahapatikena vā paṃsukūlena vā’ti evaṃ atthaṃ sallakkhiṃsu. Tattha pana itarītarenapīti appagghenapi mahagghenapi yena kenacīti attho”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto, tasmā dhutaṅgaṃ asamādiyitvā vinayapaṃsukūlamattasādiyakena bhikkhunā gahapaticīvarampi sāditabbaṃ hoti, paṃsukūladhutaṅgadharassa pana gahapaticīvaraṃ na vaṭṭati “gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipāmi, paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti samādānatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In this context, even if the Teacher has not spoken about rag-robes, the matter should be understood in terms of the general principle regarding rag-robes. For it is stated in the Cīvarakkhandhaka (Mahāvagga 340) as follows: “At that time, those bhikkhus who accepted a householder's robe, feeling scrupulous, did not accept a rag-robe, thinking, ‘The Blessed One has permitted only one kind of robe, not two.’ They reported this matter to the Blessed One. ‘I allow, bhikkhus, one who accepts a householder's robe to also accept a rag-robe. Indeed, bhikkhus, I praise contentment with both of these.’” There, it is said they understood “The Blessed One has permitted only one kind of robe, not two” to mean “with one or the other robe”—that is, “with either a householder's robe or a rag-robe.” But in the commentary, it is explained: “Here, ‘with one or the other’ means with whatever there is, whether of little value or of great value.” Therefore, a bhikkhu who has not undertaken the ascetic practice and accepts only the rag-robe as per the Vinaya may also accept a householder's robe. However, for one who observes the rag-robe ascetic practice, a householder's robe is not allowable, as should be understood from the undertaking: “I reject the householder's robe; I undertake the rag-robe-wearer's practice.”

Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū kosalesu janapadesu addhānamaggappaṭipannā honti. Ekacce bhikkhū susānaṃ okkamiṃsu [M 2.0306] paṃsukūlāya, ekacce bhikkhū nāgamesuṃ. Ye te bhikkhū susānaṃ okkamiṃsu paṃsukūlāya, te paṃsukūlāni labhiṃsu. Ye te bhikkhū nāgamesuṃ, te evamāhaṃsu “amhākampi, āvuso, bhāgaṃ dethā”ti. Te evamāhaṃsu “na mayaṃ, āvuso, tumhākaṃ bhāgaṃ dassāma, kissa tumhe nāgamitthā”ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, nāgamentānaṃ nākāmā bhāgaṃ dātunti. Tattha nāgamesunti yāva te susānato [V 2.0224] āgacchanti, tāva te na acchiṃsu, pakkamiṃsuyeva. Nākāmā bhāgaṃ dātunti na anicchāya dātuṃ. Yadi pana icchanti, dātabbo.

At that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling on a road in the Kosalan districts. Some bhikkhus entered a charnel ground for rag-robes, while others did not wait. Those bhikkhus who entered the charnel ground obtained rag-robes. Those bhikkhus who did not wait said, “Venerable sirs, give us a share too.” They replied, “We will not give you a share, venerable sirs. Why did you not wait?” They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: “Bhikkhus, I allow that a share need not be given unwillingly to those who did not wait.” Here, “did not wait” means that they did not stay until the others returned from the charnel ground; they simply departed. “A share need not be given unwillingly” means it should not be given against one’s will. But if they wish, it should be given.

Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū kosalesu janapadesu addhānamaggappaṭipannā honti. Ekacce bhikkhū susānaṃ okkamiṃsu paṃsukūlāya, ekacce bhikkhū āgamesuṃ. Ye te bhikkhū susānaṃ okkamiṃsu paṃsukūlāya, te paṃsukūlāni labhiṃsu. Ye te bhikkhū āgamesuṃ, te evamāhaṃsu “amhākampi, āvusā,e bhāgaṃ dethā”ti. Te evamāhaṃsu “na mayaṃ, āvuso, tumhākaṃ bhāgaṃ dassāma, kissa tumhe na okkamitthā”ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āgamentānaṃ akāmā bhāgaṃ dātunti.

At that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling on a road in the Kosalan districts. Some bhikkhus entered a charnel ground for rag-robes, while others waited. Those bhikkhus who entered the charnel ground obtained rag-robes. Those bhikkhus who waited said, “Venerable sirs, give us a share too.” They replied, “We will not give you a share, venerable sirs. Why did you not enter?” They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: “Bhikkhus, I allow a share to be given unwillingly to those who waited.”

Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū kosalesu janapadesu addhānamaggappaṭipannā honti. Ekacce bhikkhū paṭhamaṃ susānaṃ okkamiṃsu paṃsukūlāya, ekacce bhikkhū pacchā okkamiṃsu. Ye te bhikkhū paṭhamaṃ susānaṃ okkamiṃsu paṃsukūlāya, te paṃsukūlāni labhiṃsu. Ye te bhikkhū pacchā okkamiṃsu, te na labhiṃsu. Te evamāhaṃsu “amhākampi, āvuso, bhāgaṃ dethā”ti. Te evamāhaṃsu “na mayaṃ, āvuso, tumhākaṃ bhāgaṃ dassāma, kissa tumhe pacchā okkamitthā”ti. Bhagavato [M 2.0307] etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pacchā okkantānaṃ nākāmā bhāgaṃ dātunti.

At that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling on a road in the Kosalan districts. Some bhikkhus entered a charnel ground first for rag-robes, while others entered later. Those who entered first obtained rag-robes, while those who entered later did not. They said, “Venerable sirs, give us a share too.” They replied, “We will not give you a share, venerable sirs. Why did you enter later?” They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: “Bhikkhus, I allow that a share need not be given unwillingly to those who entered later.”

Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū kosalesu janapadesu addhānamaggappaṭipannā honti. Te sadisā susānaṃ okkamiṃsu paṃsukūlāya. Ekacce bhikkhū paṃsukūlāni labhiṃsu, ekacce bhikkhū na labhiṃsu. Ye te bhikkhū na labhiṃsu, te evamāhaṃsu “amhākampi, āvuso, bhāgaṃ dethā”ti. Te evamāhaṃsu “na mayaṃ, āvuso, tumhākaṃ bhāgaṃ dassāma, kissa tumhe na labhitthā”ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sadisānaṃ okkantānaṃ akāmā bhāgaṃ dātunti.

At that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling on a road in the Kosalan districts. They entered a charnel ground together for rag-robes. Some bhikkhus obtained rag-robes, but others did not. Those bhikkhus who did not obtain any said: “Venerable sirs, give us a share too.” They replied: “Venerable sirs, we will not give you a share. Why did you not obtain any?” They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: “Bhikkhus, I allow a share to be given unwillingly among those who entered together.”

Tattha āgamesunti upacāre acchiṃsu. Tenāha bhagavā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āgamentānaṃ akāmā bhāgaṃ dātu”nti. Upacāreti susānassa āsannappadese. Yadi pana manussā “idhāgatā eva gaṇhantū”ti denti, saññāṇaṃ vā katvā gacchanti “sampattā gaṇhantū”ti[V 2.0225]. Sampattānaṃ sabbesampi pāpuṇāti. Sace chaḍḍetvā gatā, yena gahitaṃ, so eva sāmī. Sadisā susānaṃ okkamiṃsūti sabbe samaṃ okkamiṃsu, ekadisāya vā okkamiṃsūtipi attho.

Herein, “waited” means they remained in the vicinity. Therefore the Blessed One said: “I allow, bhikkhus, a share to be given unwillingly to those who waited.” “In the vicinity” means in the area near the charnel ground. But if people give, saying, “Let only those who have come here take them,” or if they make a sign and leave, saying, “Let those who have arrived take them,” then it belongs to all who have arrived. If items have been simply discarded and left, whoever takes them is the owner. “They entered the charnel ground together” means they all entered at the same time, or it means they entered from the same direction.

Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū kosalesu janapadesu addhānamaggappaṭipannā honti. Te katikaṃ katvā susānaṃ okkamiṃsu paṃsukūlāya. Ekacce bhikkhū paṃsukūlāni labhiṃsu, ekacce bhikkhū na labhiṃsu. Ye te bhikkhū na labhiṃsu, te evamāhaṃsu “amhākampi, āvuso, bhāgaṃ dethā”ti. Te evamāhaṃsu “na mayaṃ, āvuso, tumhākaṃ bhāgaṃ dassāma, kissa tumhe na labhitthā”ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, katikaṃ katvā okkantānaṃ akāmā bhāgaṃ dātunti. Tattha te katikaṃ katvāti “laddhaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ sabbe bhājetvā [M 2.0308] gaṇhissāmā”ti bahimeva katikaṃ katvā. Chaḍḍetvā gatāti kiñci avatvāyeva chaḍḍetvā gatā. Etena “bhikkhū gaṇhantū”ti chaḍḍite eva akāmā bhāgadānaṃ vihitaṃ, kevalaṃ chaḍḍite pana katikāya asati ekato bahūsu paviṭṭhesu yena gahitaṃ, tena akāmā bhāgo na dātabboti dasseti. Samānā disā puratthimādibhedā etesanti sadisāti āha “ekadisāya vā okkamiṃsū”ti.

At that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling on a road in the Kosalan districts. Having made an agreement, they entered a charnel ground for rag-robes. Some bhikkhus obtained rag-robes, but others did not. Those bhikkhus who did not obtain any said: “Venerable sirs, give us a share too.” They replied: “Venerable sirs, we will not give you a share. Why did you not obtain any?” They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: “Bhikkhus, I allow a share to be given unwillingly among those who entered after making an agreement.” Herein, “having made an agreement” means having made an agreement beforehand, saying: “Whatever rag-robe is obtained, we will all divide it and take it.” “Discarded and left” means they discarded and left without saying anything. By this it is shown that the giving of a share unwillingly is prescribed only when items are discarded with the thought, “Let the bhikkhus take them.” But when items are simply discarded, if there is no agreement and many have entered together, it shows that a share need not be given unwillingly by the one who took it. It is said, “or they entered from the same direction,” because sadisā means “they have the same direction,” distinguished as east and so on.

Acchinnacīvarakathā

The Account of the Robbed Robe

5. Acchinnacīvarakathāyaṃ anupubbakathāti anupubbena vinicchayakathā. Sesaparikkhārānaṃ saddhivihārikehi gahitattā nivāsanapārupanameva avasiṭṭhanti āha “nivāsanapārupanamattaṃyeva haritvā”ti. Saddhivihārikānaṃ tāva āgamanassa vā anāgamanassa vā ajānanatāya vuttaṃ “therehi neva tāva…pe… bhuñjitabba”nti. Paresampi atthāya labhantīti attano cīvaraṃ dadamānā sayaṃ sākhābhaṅgena paṭicchādentīti tesaṃ atthāyapi bhañjituṃ labhanti. “Tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā āgantabba”nti vacanato īdisesu bhūtagāmapātabyatāpi anuññātāyeva hotīti āha “neva bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiyaṃ hotī”ti. Na tesaṃ dhāraṇe dukkaṭanti tesaṃ titthiyadhajānaṃ dhāraṇepi dukkaṭaṃ natthi.

5. In the Discourse on the Robbed Robe, a gradual discourse means a discourse with a step-by-step determination. Since the other requisites were taken by the co-residents, only the lower garment and outer robe remained; thus it is said: “taking only the lower garment and outer robe.” Because it was not known whether the co-residents would return or not, it was said: “the elders should not yet … use it.” They also obtain for the sake of others: giving their own robe, they cover themselves with a broken branch; thus they are permitted to break one for the sake of others too. From the statement, “One should return after covering oneself with grass or leaves,” it follows that in such cases even the destruction of plant life is allowed; thus it is said: “there is no pācittiya offense for destroying plant life.” There is no dukkaṭa offense in wearing them means there is no dukkaṭa offense even in wearing the banners of the sectarians.

Yāni ca nesaṃ vatthāni dentīti sambandho. Therānaṃ sayameva dinnattā vuttaṃ “acchinnacīvaraṭṭhāne [V 2.0226] ṭhitattā”ti. Yadi laddhiṃ gaṇhāti, titthiyapakkantako nāma hoti. Tasmā vuttaṃ “laddhiṃ aggahetvā”ti. “No ce hoti, saṅghassa vihāracīvaraṃ vā…pe… āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti iminā antarāmagge paviṭṭhavihārato nikkhamitvā aññattha attano [M 2.0309] abhirucitaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, iminā ca “yaṃ āvāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ upagacchatī”ti vuttaṃ antarāmagge ṭhitavihārampi sace naggo hutvā gacchati, dukkaṭamevāti veditabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ tattha kasmā na vuttanti ce? Anokāsattā. Tattha hi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, acchinnacīvarassa vā…pe… cīvaraṃ viññāpetu”nti iminā sambandhena saṅghikampi cīvaraṃ nivāsetuṃ pārupituñca anujānanto “yaṃ āvāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ…pe… gahetvā pārupitu”nti āha, tasmā tattha anokāsattā dukkaṭaṃ na vuttaṃ.

The connection is: “And what cloths they give them.” Since it was given by the elders themselves, it was said: “because it stands in the place of a robbed robe.” If he accepts their view, he is called one who has gone over to the sectarians. Therefore it was said: “without accepting their view.” By this— “If there is none, a monastery robe of the Sangha or … a dukkaṭa offense”—a dukkaṭa offense is stated for one who, having left a monastery he entered on the way, goes elsewhere to a place of his own liking. And by this—“whatever dwelling he first approaches”—it should be understood that even if he goes naked while staying in a monastery on the way, it is still a dukkaṭa offense. If so, why was it not stated there? Because there was no occasion. For there, in connection with “I allow, monks, for one whose robe has been robbed … to ask for a robe,” while allowing him to wear and put on even a robe belonging to the Sangha, he said: “whatever dwelling he first … having taken it, to put it on.” Therefore, because there was no occasion there, the dukkaṭa offense was not mentioned.

Vihāracīvaranti senāsanacīvaraṃ. Cimilikāhīti paṭapilotikāhi. Tassa uparīti bhūmattharaṇassa upari. Videsagatenāti aññaṃ cīvaraṃ alabhitvā videsagatena. Ekasmiṃ…pe… ṭhapetabbanti ettha sesena gahetvā āgatattā ṭhapentena ca saṅghikaparibhogavaseneva ṭhapitattā aññasmiṃ senāsane niyamitampi aññattha ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Paribhogenevāti aññaṃ cīvaraṃ alabhitvā paribhuñjanena.

A monastery robe means a lodging robe. With canopies means with rags or patches of cloth. On top of it means on top of the ground-covering. Having gone to another region means having gone to another region without obtaining another robe. In one … should be placed: here, because the remainder was taken and brought, and because the one placing it placed it for the Sangha’s use, they say it is allowable to place it elsewhere even if it was designated for another lodging. By use alone means by using it, not having obtained another robe.

Paribhogajiṇṇanti yathā tena cīvarena sarīraṃ paṭicchādetuṃ na sakkā, evaṃ jiṇṇaṃ. Kappiyavohārenāti kayavikkayāpattito mocanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Viññāpentassā”ti imasseva atthaṃ vibhāveti “cetāpentassa parivattāpentassā”ti. Attano dhanena hi viññāpanaṃ nāma parivattanamevāti adhippāyo. Saṅghavasena pavāritānaṃ viññāpane vattaṃ dasseti “pamāṇameva vaṭṭatī”ti. Saṅghavasena hi pavārite sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇattā adhikaṃ viññāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ yaṃ pavāretīti yaṃ yaṃ cīvarādiṃ dassāmīti pavāreti. Viññāpanakiccaṃ natthīti vinā viññattiyā dīyamānattā viññāpetvā kiṃ karissatīti adhippāyo. Aññassatthāyāti etthapi “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti [M 2.0310] idaṃ anuvattatiyevāti āha “attano ñātakapavārite”tiādi. Vikappanupagacīvaratā, samayābhāvo, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

Worn out by use means worn out to such an extent that the body cannot be covered with that robe. By allowable expression is said in order to be free from the offense of buying and selling. For one asking: he clarifies this very meaning with for one causing to be bought, for one causing to be exchanged. The meaning is that asking by means of one’s own wealth is indeed just an exchange. In the case of asking from those invited on behalf of the Sangha, he shows the practice: “Only the proper measure is allowable.” For when an invitation is made on behalf of the Sangha, since it is common to all, it is not allowable to ask for more. Whatever he invites with means he invites saying, “I will give such and such robes, etc.” There is no need for asking: the meaning is, since it is given without a request, what would he do by asking? For the sake of another: here too, “from invited relatives” is carried forward; thus he says: “from one’s own invited relatives,” etc. Here there are four factors: the robe not having undergone determination (vikappana), the absence of a time limit, asking a non-relative, and obtaining it thereby.

Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.515) pana pāḷiyaṃ dhammanimantanāti samaṇesu vattabbācāradhammamattavasena [V 2.0227] nimantanā, dātukāmatāya katanimantanā na hotīti attho. Teneva “viññāpessatī”ti vuttaṃ. Aññātakaappavāritato hi viññatti nāma hoti.

But in the Vimativinodanī, in the Pāli, an invitation by the Dhamma means an invitation merely in terms of the Dhamma of proper conduct to be spoken of among ascetics; the meaning is that it is not an invitation made out of a desire to give. For that reason it was said: “he will ask.” For an asking (viññatti) is made of a non-relative who has not made an invitation.

“Tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā āgantabba”nti iminā bhūtagāmavikopanaṃ anuññātanti āha “nevabhūtagāmapātabyatāyā”tiādi. Paṭhamaṃ suddhacittena liṅgaṃ gahetvā pacchā laddhiṃ gaṇhantopi titthiyapakkantako evāti āha “nivāsetvāpi laddhi na gahetabbā”ti.

Because by “One should cover oneself with grass or leaves and then come” the damaging of plant life is permitted, he said: “there is no offense of destroying plant life,” etc. Even one who first takes their characteristic sign with a pure mind but later accepts their view is still one who has gone over to the sectarians; thus he says: “Even after robing oneself, the view should not be accepted.”

Yaṃ āvāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ upagacchatīti etthapi vihāracīvarādiatthāya pavisantenapi tiṇādīhi paṭicchādetvāva gantabbaṃ, “na tveva naggena āgantabba”nti sāmaññato dukkaṭassa vuttattā. Cimilikāhīti paṭapilotikāhi. Paribhogenevāti aññaṃ cīvaraṃ alabhitvā paribhuñjanena. Paribhogajiṇṇanti yathā taṃ cīvaraṃ paribhuñjiyamānaṃ obhaggavibhaggatāya asāruppaṃ hoti, evaṃ jiṇṇaṃ.

Whatever dwelling one first approaches: here too, one who is entering for the sake of a monastery robe, etc., should go only after covering himself with grass and so on, because a dukkaṭa offense is stated in general by “but one should not come naked.” With canopies means with rags or patches of cloth. By use alone means by using it, not having obtained another robe. Worn out by use means worn out to such an extent that when that robe is being used it is unsuitable on account of being broken and torn.

Aññassatthāyāti etthapi “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti idaṃ anuvattatevāti āha “attano ñātakapavārite”tiādi. Idha pana aññassa acchinnanaṭṭhacīvarassa atthāya aññātakaappavārite viññāpentassa nissaggiyena anāpattīti attho gahetabbo, itarathā “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti iminā viseso na bhaveyya, teneva anantarasikkhāpade [M 2.0311] vakkhati “aṭṭhakathāsu (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.526) pana ñātakapavāritaṭṭhāne…pe… pamāṇameva vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ, taṃ pāḷiyā na sametī”ti ca “yasmā panidaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ aññassatthāya viññāpanavatthusmiṃyeva paññattaṃ, tasmā idha ‘aññassatthāyā’ti na vutta”nti ca. Vikappanupagacīvaratā, samayābhāvo, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

For the sake of another: here too, “from invited relatives” is carried forward; thus he says: “from one’s own invited relatives,” etc. Here, however, the meaning should be taken that there is no offense of forfeiture for one who asks an uninvited non-relative for the sake of another whose robe has been robbed or lost. Otherwise there would be no distinction from “from invited relatives.” For that very reason it will be said in the immediately following training rule: “But in the commentaries, in the case of invited relatives … it is said that only the proper measure is allowable, but that does not agree with the Pāli,” and “Because this training rule was laid down only in the case of asking for the sake of another, therefore ‘for the sake of another’ is not stated here.” Here there are four factors: the robe not having undergone determination (vikappana), the absence of a time limit, asking a non-relative, and obtaining it thereby.

“Tañce aññātako gahapati vā gahapatānī vā bahūhi cīvarehi abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyya, santaruttaraparamaṃ tena bhikkhunā tato cīvaraṃ sāditabbaṃ, tato ce uttari sādiyeyya, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti imasmiṃ taduttarisikkhāpade (pārā. 523) abhihaṭṭhunti ettha abhīti upasaggo, haritunti attho, gaṇhitunti vuttaṃ hoti. Pavāreyyāti icchāpeyya, icchaṃ ruciṃ [V 2.0228] uppādeyya vadeyya nimanteyyāti attho. Abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavārentena pana yathā vattabbaṃ. Taṃ ākāraṃ dassetuṃ “yāvattakaṃ icchasi, tāvattakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti evamassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Atha vā yathā “nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato”ti ettha disvāti attho, evamidhapi abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyāti abhiharitvā pavāreyyāti attho. Tattha kāyābhihāro vācābhihāroti duvidho abhihāro. Kāyena vā hi vatthādīni abhiharitvā pādamūle ṭhapetvā “yattakaṃ icchasi, tattakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadanto pavāreyya, vācāya vā “amhākaṃ dussakoṭṭhāgāraṃ paripuṇṇaṃ, yattakaṃ icchasi, tattakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadanto pavāreyya, tadubhayampi ekajjhaṃ katvā “abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyā”ti vuttaṃ.

“‘If an unrelated householder or a householder's wife should invite a bhikkhu by offering many robes, that bhikkhu may accept from that a robe with an under-robe and an upper-robe as the maximum. If he should accept more than that, it is an offense entailing forfeiture and expiation.’ In this training rule concerning more than that (Pārā. 523), regarding ‘abhihaṭṭhuṃ,’ ‘abhi’ is a prefix; the meaning is ‘to bring,’ which is to say ‘to take.’ ‘Pavāreyya’ means to cause to wish, to arouse a wish or inclination, to say, to invite. But when one invites by offering, it should be stated in a certain way. To show that manner, its word-analysis is given thus: ‘Take as much as you wish.’ Alternatively, just as in ‘having seen renunciation as security,’ where ‘daṭṭhu’ means ‘having seen,’ so too here ‘abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyya’ means ‘having brought, one invites.’ Herein, an offering is twofold: a physical offering and a verbal offering. For one might physically bring cloth and other items, place them at the bhikkhu's feet, and invite him by saying, ‘Take as much as you wish’; or one might verbally invite him by saying, ‘Our storeroom of cloth is full; take as much as you wish.’ Combining both, it is said, ‘abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyya.’”

Santaruttaraparamanti saantaraṃ uttaraṃ paramaṃ assa cīvarassāti santaruttaraparamaṃ, nivāsanena saddhiṃ pārupanaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo assāti [M 2.0312] vuttaṃ hoti. Tato cīvaraṃ sāditabbanti tato abhihaṭacīvarato ettakaṃ cīvaraṃ gahetabbaṃ, na ito paranti attho. Yasmā pana acchinnasabbacīvarena tecīvarikeneva bhikkhunā evaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ, aññena aññathāpi, tasmā taṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “sace tīṇi naṭṭhāni hontī”tiādinā nayenassa padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ.

“‘With an under-robe and an upper-robe as the maximum’ means that for this robe, the under-robe and the upper-robe are its maximum; this is to say that the highest limit for him is an upper robe together with a lower robe. ‘From that, a robe should be accepted’ means that from that offered robe-cloth, this much robe-cloth should be taken, not more than this. But since a bhikkhu who possesses the three robes and whose full set of robes is intact should act in this way, while another may act otherwise, therefore, to show that distinction, its word-analysis is given in the manner beginning: ‘If the three have been lost….’”

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – yassa tīṇi naṭṭhāni, tena dve sāditabbāni, ekaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā aññaṃ sabhāgaṭṭhānato pariyesissati. Yassa dve naṭṭhāni, tena ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ. Sace pakatiyāva santaruttarena carati, dve sāditabbāni, evaṃ ekaṃ sādiyanteneva samo bhavissati. Yassa tīsu ekaṃ naṭṭhaṃ, na sāditabbaṃ. Yassa pana dvīsu ekaṃ naṭṭhaṃ, ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ. Yassa ekaṃyeva hoti, tañca naṭṭhaṃ, dve sāditabbāni. Bhikkhuniyā pana pañcasupi naṭṭhesu dve sāditabbāni, catūsu naṭṭhesu ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ, tīsu naṭṭhesu kiñci na sāditabbaṃ, ko pana vādo dvīsu vā ekasmiṃ vā. Yena kenaci hi santaruttaraparamatāya ṭhātabbaṃ, tato uttari na labbhatīti idamettha lakkhaṇaṃ.

“Herein, this is the ruling: One who has lost the three robes may accept two; having worn one as a lower robe and one as an upper robe, he will seek another from a place of common property. One who has lost two may accept one. If one normally goes about with just an under-robe and an upper-robe, two may be accepted; in this way, he becomes equal to the one who accepts one. One who has lost one of three may not accept any. But one who has lost one of two may accept one. One who has only one, and that is lost, may accept two. For a bhikkhunī, however, if all five are lost, two may be accepted; if four are lost, one may be accepted; if three are lost, nothing may be accepted—what then to say of two or one? For in any case, one must abide by the maximum of an under-robe and an upper-robe; more than that is not allowable. This is the guiding principle here.”

Sesakaṃ āharissāmīti dve cīvarāni katvā sesaṃ puna āharissāmīti attho. Na acchinnakāraṇāti bāhusaccādiguṇavasena denti. Ñātakānantiādīsu ñātakānaṃ dentānaṃ sādiyantassa, pavāritānaṃ dentānaṃ sādiyantassa, attano dhanena sādiyantassa anāpattīti attho. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana “ñātakapavāritaṭṭhāne pakatiyā bahumpi vaṭṭati, acchinnakāraṇā pamāṇameva [V 2.0229] vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pāḷiyā na sameti. Yasmā panidaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ aññassatthāya viññāpanavatthusmiṃyeva paññattaṃ, tasmā idha “aññassatthāyā”ti na vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Samuṭṭhānādīsu idampi chasamuṭṭhānaṃ[M 2.0313], kiriyaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ, acittakaṃ, paṇṇattivajjaṃ, kāyakammavacīkammaṃ, ticittaṃ, tivedananti.

“‘I will bring the rest’ means: having made two robes, I will bring the remainder later. ‘Not for the reason of having been deprived’ means: they give on account of qualities such as great learning, etc. Regarding ‘relatives,’ etc., the meaning is that there is no offense for one who accepts when relatives are giving, for one who accepts when those who have made an invitation are giving, or for one who accepts with his own funds. In the commentaries, however, it is said: ‘In the case of relatives and those who have made an invitation, even much is normally allowable; for the reason of having been deprived, only the specified amount is allowable.’ This does not agree with the Pāḷi. However, since this training rule was laid down regarding a case of requesting for the sake of another, the words ‘for the sake of another’ are not stated here. The rest has an obvious meaning. Regarding the origins, etc.: this offense has six origins; it is an action, not a release through perception, unintentional, an offense by legal enactment, a bodily action and a verbal action, involves three kinds of consciousness, and three kinds of feeling.”

Sattame pāḷiyaṃ paggāhikasālanti dussavāṇijakānaṃ āpaṇaṃ, “paggāhitasāla”ntipi paṭhanti. Abhīti upasaggoti tassa visesatthābhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “haritunti attho”ti. Varasaddassa icchāyaṃ vattamānattā āha “icchāpeyyā”ti. Daṭṭhu khematoti ettha gāthābandhavasena anunāsikalopo daṭṭhabbo. Saantaranti antaravāsakasahitaṃ. Uttaranti uttarāsaṅgaṃ. Assa cīvarassāti sāditabbacīvarassa. Acchinnasabbacīvarenāti acchinnāni sabbāni tīṇi cīvarāni assāti acchinnasabbacīvaro, tenāti attho. Yassa hi acchindanasamaye tīṇi cīvarāni sannihitāni honti, tāni sabbāni acchinnānīti so “acchinnasabbacīvaro”ti vuccati. Teneva “acchinnasabbacīvarena tecīvarikenā”ti vuttaṃ. Tecīvarikenāti hi acchindanasamaye ticīvarassa sannihitabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pana vinaye tecīvarikābhāvaṃ, dhutaṅgatecīvarikabhāvaṃ vā sandhāya. Evaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti “santaruttaraparamaṃ tena bhikkhunā tato cīvaraṃ sāditabba”nti vuttavidhinā paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Aññenāti acchinnaasabbacīvarena. Yassa tīsu cīvaresu ekaṃ vā dve vā cīvarāni acchinnāni honti, tenāti attho. Aññathāpīti “santaruttaraparama”nti vuttavidhānato aññathāpi. Yassa hi tīsu dve cīvarāni acchinnāni honti, ekaṃ sāditabbaṃ, ekasmiṃ acchinne na sāditabbanti na tassa santaruttaraparamasādiyanaṃ sambhavati. Ayameva ca attho padabhājanena vibhāvito. Tenāha “taṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetu”nti.

“In the seventh rule, in the Pāḷi, ‘paggāhikasāla’ is a cloth merchant’s shop; some also read it as ‘paggāhitasāla.’ ‘Abhi’ is a prefix; this shows it has no special meaning. Hence he said: ‘the meaning is “to bring.”’ Since the word ‘vara’ is used in the sense of ‘wish,’ he says ‘icchāpeyya.’ In ‘daṭṭhu khemato,’ the elision of the nasal sound should be noted as due to the meter of the verse. ‘Saantaraṃ’ means together with the under-robe. ‘Uttaraṃ’ means the upper-robe. ‘Assa cīvarassa’ means of the robe to be accepted. ‘Acchinnasabbacīvarena’ means: he is one whose full set of robes is intact (acchinnasabbacīvaro), that is, one who has all three robes not stolen; this is the meaning. For one who has his three robes present at a time when he has not been deprived of robes, all those are considered not-deprived, so he is called ‘one whose full set of robes is intact.’ It is for this reason that it is said ‘by a tecīvarika bhikkhu whose full set of robes is intact.’ For ‘tecīvarikena’ is said with reference to the presence of the three robes at a time when he is not deprived, not with reference to the status of being a three-robe-wearer according to the Vinaya, nor with reference to the ascetic practice of being a three-robe-wearer. ‘Evaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ’ means one should practice according to the method stated: ‘that bhikkhu may accept from that a robe with an under-robe and an upper-robe as the maximum.’ ‘Aññena’ means by one whose full set of robes is not intact. The meaning is: by one who has one or two of his three robes not-deprived. ‘Aññathāpi’ means otherwise than the method stated as ‘the maximum of an under-robe and an upper-robe.’ For one who has two of his three robes not-deprived, one may be accepted; when one is not-deprived, none may be accepted. Thus for him the acceptance of the maximum of an under-robe and an upper-robe is not possible. This very meaning is clarified by the word-analysis. Hence he says: ‘to show that distinction.’”

Keci pana “tecīvarikenāti vuttattā ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷavasena adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjato tasmiṃ naṭṭhe bahūnipi gahetuṃ labhatī”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Padabhājanassa hi [M 2.0314] adhippāyaṃ dassentena yasmā pana “acchinnasabbacīvarena…pe… taṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetu”nti vuttaṃ, padabhājane ca na tādiso attho upalabbhati, tasmā taṃ na gahetabbameva. Yampi mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “yassa adhiṭṭhitaticīvarassa tīṇi naṭṭhānī”ti, tatthapi adhiṭṭhitaggahaṇaṃ sarūpakathanamattanti gahetabbaṃ, na pana ticīvarādhiṭṭhānena adhiṭṭhitacīvarassevāti evamattho gahetabbo pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca tathā atthassāsambhavato[V 2.0230]. Na hi ticīvarādhiṭṭhānena adhiṭṭhitacīvarasseva idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti sakkā viññātuṃ. Purimasikkhāpadena hi acchinnacīvarassa aññātakaviññattiyā anuññātattā pamāṇaṃ ajānitvā viññāpanavatthusmiṃ pamāṇato sādiyanaṃ anujānantena bhagavatā idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tasmā parikkhāracoḷikassa bahumpi sādituṃ vaṭṭatīti ayamattho neva pāḷiyā sameti, na ca bhagavato adhippāyaṃ anulometi.

Some, however, say: ‘Since it is said “by one with three robes,” one who uses a cloth having determined it as an accessory requisite-cloth may, if it is lost, accept many more.’ This should not be accepted. For since, when showing the intention of the word-analysis, it was said: ‘Since by a bhikkhu whose full set of robes has been stolen… to show that distinction,’ and such a meaning is not found in the word-analysis, therefore that view should not be accepted at all. And what is said in the Commentary on the Mātikā (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. on this rule): ‘One whose three determined robes are lost…,’ there too the mention of ‘determined’ should be taken as a mere description of its nature, and the meaning should not be taken as referring only to a robe determined as one of the three robes, since such a meaning is impossible in both the Pāḷi and the commentary. For it cannot be understood that this training rule was laid down only for a robe determined as one of the three robes. For since by the previous training rule a request to a non-relative was allowed for one who has been deprived of his robe, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One to allow acceptance according to a measure in a case of requesting, when one does not know the measure. Therefore, the meaning that it is allowable for one who has an accessory requisite-cloth to accept even a large amount neither agrees with the Pāḷi nor conforms to the Blessed One’s intention.

Yassa tīṇi naṭṭhāni, tena dve sāditabbānīti ettha yassa ticīvarato adhikampi cīvaraṃ aññattha ṭhitaṃ atthi, tadā tassa cīvarassa alabbhanīyabhāvato tenapi sādituṃ vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Pakatiyāva santaruttarena caratīti sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavasena vā avippavāsasammutivasena vā tatiyassa alābhena vā carati. “Dve naṭṭhānī”ti adhikārattā vuttaṃ “dve sāditabbānī”ti. Ekaṃ sādiyanteneva samo bhavissatīti tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ dvīsu naṭṭhesu ekaṃ sādiyantena samo bhavissati ubhinnampi santaruttaraparamatāya avaṭṭhānato. Yassa ekaṃyeva hotīti aññena kenaci kāraṇena vinaṭṭhasesacīvaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Herein, regarding ‘One who has lost the three, by him two may be accepted’: if one has a robe in addition to the three robes stored elsewhere, then because that robe is unobtainable, it should be understood that it is still allowable for him to accept. ‘He normally goes about with an under-robe and an upper-robe’ means: he goes about thus either on account of the training rule concerning what is dubious, or on account of the resolution of non-separation, or from not obtaining a third. Because the topic is ‘two are lost,’ it is said ‘two may be accepted.’ ‘Thus he will be on par with one who accepts just one’ means: he will be on par with one who accepts one when two of the three robes are lost, because of the establishment of both in the state of having the under-robe and upper-robe as the maximum. ‘One who has only one’ is said with reference to one whose other robes have been destroyed for some other reason.

“Sesakaṃ tumheva hotūti dentī”ti vuttattā “pamāṇayuttaṃ gaṇhissāma, sesakaṃ āharissāmā”ti vatvā [M 2.0315] gahetvā gamanasamayepi “sesakampi tumhākaṃyeva hotū”ti vadanti, laddhakappiyameva. Pavāritānanti acchinnakālato pubbeyeva pavāritānaṃ. Pāḷiyā na sametīti santaruttaraparamato uttari sādiyane anāpattidassanatthaṃ “anāpatti ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti vuttattā na sameti. Santaruttaraparamaṃ sādiyantassa hi āpattippasaṅgoyeva natthi, sati ca sikkhāpadena āpattippasaṅge anāpatti yuttā dassetunti adhippāyo. Keci pana “pamāṇameva vaṭṭatīti idaṃ sallekhadassanatthaṃ vutta”nti vadanti.

Since it is said, 'They give it saying, "Let the remainder be yours,"' when, after saying, 'We will take a suitable measure and bring back the remainder,' and having taken it, even at the time of departure they say, 'Let the remainder also be yours,' it is allowable as received. 'For those who have been invited' means for those invited even before the time the robe was stolen. 'It does not accord with the Pāḷi': because it is said, 'No offense for relatives who have been invited,' in order to show there is no offense in accepting more than the maximum of an inner and outer robe, it does not accord. For one who accepts the maximum of an inner and outer robe, there is indeed no occasion for an offense; and when there is an occasion for an offense according to the training rule, it is proper to show there is no offense—this is the intention. Some, however, say: 'This was said—"Only the measure is allowable"—to show effacement.'

Yasmā panidaṃ…pe… na vuttanti etthāyamadhippāyo – “aññassatthāyā”ti vuccamāne aññesaṃ atthāya pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvāpi gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatīti āpajjati, tañca aññassatthāya viññāpanavatthusmiṃ paññattattā vatthunā saṃsandiyamānaṃ na sameti. Na hi yaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tasmiṃyeva anāpattivacanaṃ yuttanti. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana tīsupi “imassa sikkhāpadassa attano sādiyanapaṭibaddhatāvasena pavattattā ‘aññassatthāyā’ti vattuṃ okāsoyeva natthi, tasmā na vutta”nti kathitaṃ. Idha “aññassatthāyā”ti avuttattā aññesaṃ atthāya [V 2.0231] ñātakapavāritesu adhikaṃ viññāpentassa āpattīti ce? Na, tattha purimasikkhāpadeneva anāpattisiddhito. Tatuttaritā, acchinnādikāraṇatā, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

Moreover, since this... was not said, the intention here is this: when 'for the sake of another' is said, it would follow that it is allowable to take even in excess of the measure for the sake of others. And that, because it was laid down in the case of making a request for the sake of another, does not accord when compared with the case. For it is not proper to state an exemption in the very case on account of which a training rule was laid down. But in all three Gaṇṭhipadas it is said: 'Since this training rule proceeds by way of being connected to one's own acceptance, there is no opportunity at all to say "for the sake of another"; therefore it was not said.' If it is asked: 'Here, because "for the sake of another" was not said, is there an offense for one who requests more for the sake of others from invited relatives?' No, because non-offense is established there by the previous training rule itself. Being more than that, the reason such as the robe being stolen, a request to a non-relative, and acquisition thereby—these are the four factors here.

Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.522-524) pana “pāḷiyaṃ paggāhikasālanti dussāpaṇaṃ. Tañhi vāṇijakehi dussāni paggahetvā dassanaṭṭhānatāya ‘paggāhikasālā’ti vuccati. Assa cīvarassāti sāditabbacīvarassa. Tecīvarikenāti iminā acchinnaticīvarato aññassa vihārādīsu nihitassa cīvarassa abhāvaṃ dasseti[M 2.0316]. Yadi bhaveyya, viññāpetuṃ na vaṭṭeyya, tāvakālikaṃ nivāsetvā attano cīvaraṃ gahetabbaṃ. Tāvakālikampi alabhantassa bhūtagāmavikopanaṃ katvā tiṇapaṇṇehi chadanaṃ viya viññāpanampi vaṭṭati eva. Aññenāti acchinnaasabbacīvarena. ‘Dve naṭṭhānī’ti adhikārato vuttaṃ ‘dve sāditabbānī’ti. Pāḷiyā na sametīti ‘anāpatti ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna’nti (pārā. 526) imāya pāḷiyā na sameti tatuttari viññāpanaāpattippasaṅge eva vuttattā. Aññassatthāyāti na vuttanti idaṃ aññassatthāya tatuttari viññāpane nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ hotīti imamatthaṃ dīpeti. Tañca pācittiyaṃ yesaṃ atthāya viññāpeti, tesaṃ vā siyā viññāpakasseva vā, na tāva tesaṃ, tehi aviññāpitattā, nāpi viññāpakassa, attānaṃ uddissa aviññattattā. Tasmā aññassatthāya viññāpentassapi nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ na dissati. Pāḷiyaṃ pana imassa sikkhāpadassa attano sādiyanapaṭibaddhatāvasena pavattattā ‘aññassatthāyā’ti anāpattivāre na vuttanti vadanti, tañca yuttaṃ viya dissati, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Tatuttaricīvaratā, acchinnādikāraṇatā, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti imānettha cattāri aṅgānī”ti.

But in the Vimativinodanī it is said: 'In the Pāḷi, a `paggāhikasālā` means a cloth shop. It is called a `paggāhikasālā` because it is a place for showing cloths held up by merchants. "Of this robe" means of the robe to be accepted. "By one with three robes"—by this it shows the absence of another robe, apart from the stolen three robes, that has been put down in a monastery, etc. If there were one, it would not be allowable to make a request; one should wear a temporary one and take one's own robe. For one who does not obtain even a temporary one, just as it is allowable to cover oneself with grass and leaves after having destroyed plant-life, so too is making a request allowable. "By another" means by a robe that is stolen but is not the full set. "Two are lost"—this is said in connection with the topic as "two are to be accepted." "It does not accord with the Pāḷi": it does not accord with this Pāḷi passage, "No offense for relatives who have been invited," because that was said only when there is an occasion for an offense for requesting more. "That 'for the sake of another' was not said"—this clarifies the meaning that when one requests more for the sake of another, there is an offense of expiation with forfeiture. And that offense of expiation might be for those for whose sake one requests, or for the requester himself; it is not for them, since they did not make the request; nor is it for the requester, since he did not make the request with himself as the object. Therefore, an offense of expiation with forfeiture is not seen even for one who makes a request for the sake of another. But they say that in the Pāḷi, because this training rule proceeds by way of being connected to one's own acceptance, "for the sake of another" is not said in the section on exemptions. And that seems proper; it should be accepted after investigation. Being a robe beyond that, the reason such as the robe being stolen, a request to a non-relative, and acquisition thereby—these are the four factors here.'

Idaṃ tatuttarisikkhāpadavinicchayaṃ ācariyena avuttampi acchinnacīvarādhikāreyeva pavattattā amhehi gahitaṃ, aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadassa samayesu acchinnacīvarakāle aññātakānaṃ viññāpetabbabhāvo bhagavatā vutto, tehi dinnacīvarassa mattaso gahitabhāvo tatuttarisikkhāpadena vutto. Tasmā acchinnacīvaraadhikāroyeva hotīti.

This analysis of the training rule on what is beyond that, though not stated by the Teacher, has been taken by us as proceeding only in connection with the case of a stolen robe. In the occasions of the training rule on requesting from non-relatives, the Blessed One has stated that non-relatives may be requested from at the time a robe is stolen; and the training rule on what is beyond that states that a robe given by them is to be accepted in measure. Therefore, it is only a matter concerning a stolen robe.

Cīvaraacchindanavinicchayakathā

An Exposition of the Ruling Concerning the Taking Away of a Robe

Ito [M 2.0317][V 2.0232] paraṃ acchindanasāmaññena cīvaraacchindanavinicchayaṃ vakkhāma – tattha yampi tyāhanti yampi te ahaṃ. So kira “mama pattacīvaraupāhanapaccattharaṇāni vahanto mayā saddhiṃ cārikaṃ pakkamissatī”ti adāsi. Tenevamāha “mayā saddhiṃ janapadacārikaṃ pakkamissatī”ti. Acchindīti balakkārena aggahesi, sakasaññāya gahitattā panassa pārājikaṃ natthi, kilametvā gahitattā āpatti paññattā.

Henceforth, we will explain the ruling on robe confiscation by way of the general principle of confiscation. Therein, the phrase `yampi tyāhaṃ` means `yaṃ pi te ahaṃ` (that which I [gave] to you). It is said that he gave them thinking: 'Carrying my bowl, robes, sandals, and ground-sheet, he will set out on a journey with me.' Therefore he said: 'He will set out on a journey through the countryside with me.' 'He confiscated' (`acchindi`) means he took by force. However, because he took it with the perception that it was his own, there is no pārājika offense for him. But because he took it after causing vexation, an offense has been laid down.

Sayaṃ acchindati, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti ekaṃ cīvaraṃ ekābaddhāni ca bahūni acchindato ekā āpatti, ekato abaddhāni visuṃ visuṃ ṭhitāni bahūni acchindato, “saṅghāṭiṃ āhara, uttarāsaṅgaṃ āharā”ti evaṃ āharāpayato ca vatthugaṇanāya āpattiyo. “Mayā dinnāni sabbāni āharā”ti vadatopi ekavacaneneva sambahulā āpattiyo.

If he confiscates it himself, it is an offense of expiation entailing forfeiture. For one who confiscates a single robe or many robes bound together as one, there is one offense. For one who confiscates many robes that are not bound together but are separate, or for one who has them brought, saying, 'Bring the outer cloak, bring the upper robe,' there are offenses according to the count of the items. Even for one who says, 'Bring all that was given by me,' many offenses arise from a single utterance.

Aññaṃ āṇāpeti, āpatti dukkaṭassāti “cīvaraṃ gaṇhā”ti āṇāpeti, ekaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Āṇatto bahūni gaṇhāti, ekaṃ pācittiyaṃ. “Saṅghāṭiṃ gaṇha, uttarāsaṅgaṃ gaṇhā”ti vadato vācāya vācāya dukkaṭaṃ. “Mayā dinnāni sabbāni gaṇhā”ti vadato ekavācāya sambahulā āpattiyo.

If he orders another, there is an offense of wrong-doing. If he orders, 'Take the robe,' there is one offense of wrong-doing. If the one who was ordered takes many, there is one offense of expiation. For one who says, 'Take the outer cloak, take the upper robe,' there is an offense of wrong-doing for each utterance. For one who says, 'Take all that was given by me,' many offenses arise from the single utterance.

Aññaṃ parikkhāranti vikappanupagapacchimaṃ cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā yaṃ kiñci antamaso sūcimpi. Veṭhetvā ṭhapitasūcīsupi vatthugaṇanāya dukkaṭāni. Sithilaveṭhitāsu evaṃ. Gāḷhaṃ katvā baddhāsu pana ekameva dukkaṭanti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sūcighare pakkhittāsupi eseva nayo. Thavikāya pakkhipitvā sithilabaddhagāḷhabaddhesu tikaṭukādīsu bhesajjesupi eseva nayo.

'Other requisites' means any requisite whatsoever, down to a needle, excepting a final robe that has been made subject to shared ownership (`vikappana`). Even for needles stored wrapped up, there are offenses of wrong-doing according to the count of the items. This is so for those loosely wrapped. But for those bound tightly together, there is only one offense of wrong-doing; so it is said in the Mahāpaccariya. The same principle applies to those placed in a needle case. This same principle also applies to medicines such as the three pungents placed in a bag, whether loosely bound or tightly bound.

So vā detīti “bhante, tumhākaṃyeva idaṃ sāruppa”nti evaṃ vā deti. Atha vā pana “āvuso, mayaṃ tuyhaṃ ‘vattapaṭipattiṃ [M 2.0318] karissati, amhākaṃ santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhissati, dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇissatī’ti cīvaraṃ adamhā, sodāni tvaṃ na vattaṃ karosi, na upajjhaṃ gaṇhāsi, na dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāsī”ti evamādīhi vutto “bhante, cīvaratthāya maññe bhaṇatha, idaṃ [V 2.0233] vo cīvara”nti deti, evampi so vā deti. Disāpakkantaṃ vā pana daharaṃ “nivattetha na”nti bhaṇati, so na nivattati. “Cīvaraṃ gahetvā rundhathā”ti evaṃ ce nivattati, sādhu. Sace “pattacīvaratthāya maññe tumhe bhaṇatha, gaṇhatha na”nti deti, evampi soyeva deti. Vibbhantaṃ vā disvā “mayaṃ tuyhaṃ ‘vattaṃ karissatī’ti pattacīvaraṃ adamhā, sodāni tvaṃ vibbhamitvā carasī”ti vadati, itaro “gaṇhatha tumhākaṃ pattacīvara”nti deti, evampi so vā deti. “Mama santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhantasseva te demi, aññattha gaṇhantassa na demi. Vattaṃ karontasseva demi, akarontassa na demi. Dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇantasseva demi, apariyāpuṇantassa na demi. Avibbhamantasseva demi, vibbhamantassa na demī”ti evaṃ pana dātuṃ na vaṭṭati, dadato dukkaṭaṃ, āharāpetuṃ pana vaṭṭati. Cajitvā dinnaṃ acchinditvā gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Sesamettha uttānameva. Ayaṃ samantapāsādikato uddhaṭavinicchayo.

'Or he gives it' means he gives it saying, 'Venerable sir, this is indeed suitable for you.' Or else, when he is told things such as: 'Friend, we gave you a robe thinking, "He will fulfill his duties, take us as his preceptor, and master the Dhamma." But now you do not fulfill your duties, you do not take us as your preceptor, you do not master the Dhamma,' he says, 'Venerable sirs, I suppose you are speaking for the sake of the robe. Here is your robe,' and gives it. In this case too, he himself gives it. Or a young monk has gone away to another region. They say, 'Won't you return?' but he does not return. If they say, 'Take his robe and detain him,' and he returns, it is good. If he says, 'I suppose you are speaking for the sake of the bowl and robe; take them,' and gives them, in this case too, he himself gives them. Or, seeing that he has become corrupt, they say, 'We gave you a bowl and robe thinking, "He will fulfill his duties," but now you have become corrupt and are wandering about,' and the other says, 'Take your bowl and robe,' and gives them. In this case too, he himself gives them. But it is not proper to give with conditions, saying: 'I give this to you only if you take me as your preceptor, not if you take another. I give it only if you fulfill your duties, not if you do not. I give it only if you master the Dhamma, not if you do not. I give it only if you do not become corrupt, not if you do.' For one who gives thus, there is an offense of wrong-doing. However, it is proper to have it brought back. One who takes by confiscating what was given after it had been relinquished should be dealt with according to the value of the goods. The rest here is self-evident. This is the ruling extracted from the Samantapāsādikā.

Yampi tyāhanti ettha yanti kāraṇavacanaṃ, tasmā evamettha sambandho veditabbo – “mayā saddhiṃ janapadacārikaṃ pakkamissatīti yaṃ kāraṇaṃ nissāya ahaṃ te, āvuso, cīvaraṃ adāsiṃ, taṃ na karosī”ti kupito anattamano acchindīti. Yanti vā cīvaraṃ parāmasati. Tattha “mayā saddhiṃ janapadacārikaṃ pakkamissatīti yampi te ahaṃ cīvaraṃ adāsiṃ, taṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti kupito anattamano acchindīti sambandhitabbaṃ.

Herein, in the phrase `yampi tyāhaṃ`, the word `yaṃ` indicates a reason. Therefore, the connection here should be understood thus: 'Friend, for the reason that you would set out on a journey through the countryside with me I gave you the robe, but you are not doing that.' Thus angry and displeased, he confiscated it. Alternatively, `yaṃ` refers to the robe. In that case, it should be connected thus: 'That very robe which I gave you, thinking you would set out on a a journey through the countryside with me—that robe I will take.' Thus angry and displeased, he confiscated it.

Āṇatto [M 2.0319] bahūni gaṇhāti, ekaṃ pācittiyanti “cīvaraṃ gaṇhā”ti āṇattiyā ekacīvaravisayattā ekameva pācittiyaṃ. Vācāya vācāya dukkaṭanti ettha acchinnesu vatthugaṇanāya pācittiyāni. Ekavācāya sambahulā āpattiyoti idaṃ acchinnesu vatthugaṇanāya āpajjitabbaṃ pācittiyāpattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, āṇattiyā āpajjitabbaṃ pana dukkaṭaṃ ekameva.

[Regarding the statement:] 'If the one who was ordered takes many, there is one `pācittiya` offense'—this is because the command 'Take the robe' pertains to a single robe, so there is only one `pācittiya` offense. [Regarding the statement:] 'For each utterance, a `dukkaṭa` offense'—here, when the items are confiscated, there are `pācittiya` offenses according to the count of the items. [The statement:] 'Many offenses from a single utterance' is said with reference to the `pācittiya` offenses to be incurred according to the count of the items when they are confiscated. However, the `dukkaṭa` offense to be incurred for the command is only one.

Evanti iminā “vatthugaṇanāya dukkaṭānī”ti idaṃ parāmasati. Eseva nayoti sithilaṃ gāḷhañca pakkhittāsu āpattiyā bahuttaṃ ekattañca atidisati.

By `evaṃ` ('This is so'), it refers to the statement 'there are offenses of wrong-doing according to the count of the items.' By `eseva nayo` ('This same principle applies'), it extends the principle to the multiplicity or singularity of the offense for items placed either loosely or tightly.

Āvuso mayantiādīsu gaṇhitukāmatāya evaṃ vuttepi teneva dinnattā anāpatti. Amhākaṃ [V 2.0234] santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhissatīti idaṃ sāmaṇerassapi dānaṃ dīpeti, tasmā kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ “bhikkhussa sāmaṃ cīvaraṃ datvā”ti vuttaṃ, tathāpi anupasampannakāle datvāpi upasampannakāle acchindantassa pācittiyamevāti veditabbaṃ. Acchindanasamaye upasampannabhāvoyeva hettha pamāṇaṃ. Detīti tuṭṭho vā kupito vā deti. Ruddhathāti nivāretha. Evaṃ pana dātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti ettha evaṃ dinnaṃ na tāva “tassa santaka”nti anadhiṭṭhahitvāva paribhuñjitabbanti veditabbaṃ. Āharāpetuṃ pana vaṭṭatīti evaṃ dinnaṃ bhatisadisattā āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Cajitvā dinnanti vuttanayena adatvā anapekkhena hutvā tasseva dinnaṃ. Bhaṇḍagghena kāretabboti sakasaññāya vinā gaṇhanto bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā āpattiyā kāretabbo. Vikappanupagapacchimacīvaratā, sāmaṃ dinnatā, sakasaññitā, upasampannatā, kodhavasena acchindanaṃ vā acchindāpanaṃ vāti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Ayaṃ sāratthadīpanīpāṭho (sārattha. ṭī. 2.635).

In cases such as [the phrase beginning] 'Friend, we...,' even though this is said with the desire to take, because it is given by that very person, there is no offense. 'He will take a preceptor in our presence'—this shows that a gift can be made even to a novice. Therefore, although it is said in the Pāli text, 'having personally given a robe to a bhikkhu,' it should be understood that even if it was given when he was unordained, for one who confiscates it when he is ordained, there is still a `pācittiya` offense. The state of being ordained at the time of confiscation is the standard here. 'Gives' means he gives whether pleased or angry. `Rundhathā` ('detain') means 'prevent.' Regarding 'But it is not proper to give in this way,' it should be understood that what is given in this way should not be used without first determining it as 'his property.' Regarding 'However, it is proper to have it brought back,' since what is given in this way is like wages, it is proper to have it brought back. 'Given after relinquishing' means it was not given in the aforementioned conditional manner, but was given to that person after one had become indifferent and without expectation. 'He should be dealt with according to the value of the goods' means one who takes without the perception that it is his own should be made to pay the value of the goods and be dealt with for the offense. The five factors here are: (1) being a final robe that has been made subject to shared ownership; (2) being personally given; (3) the perception that it is one's own; (4) the other being ordained; and (5) confiscating or causing to be confiscated out of anger. This is the text from the Sāratthadīpanī.

Vimativinodaniyaṃ [M 2.0320] (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.631) pana “yampi…pe… acchindīti ettha yaṃ te ahaṃ cīvaraṃ adāsiṃ, taṃ ‘mayā saddhiṃ pakkamissatī’ti saññāya adāsiṃ, na aññathāti kupito acchindīti evaṃ ajjhāharitvā yojetabbaṃ. Ekaṃ dukkaṭanti yadi āṇatto avassaṃ acchindati, āṇattikkhaṇe eva pācittiyaṃ. Yadi na acchindati, tadā eva dukkaṭanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekavācāya sambahulāpattiyoti yadi āṇatto anantarāyena acchindati, āṇattikkhaṇeyeva vatthugaṇanāya pācittiyāpattiyo payogakaraṇakkhaṇeyeva āpattiyā āpajjitabbato, cīvaraṃ pana acchinneyeva nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Yadi so na acchindati, āṇattikkhaṇe ekameva dukkaṭanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evamaññatthapi īdisesu nayo ñātabbo. Upajjhaṃ gaṇhissatīti sāmaṇerassa dānaṃ dīpeti, tena ca sāmaṇerakāle datvā upasampannakāle acchindatopi pācittiyaṃ dīpeti. “Bhikkhussa sāmaṃ cīvaraṃ datvā”ti idaṃ ukkaṭṭhavasena vuttaṃ. Āharāpetuṃ pana vaṭṭatīti kamme akate bhatisadisattā vuttaṃ. Vikappanupagapacchimacīvaratā, sāmaṃ dinnatā, sakasaññitā, upasampannatā, kodhavasena acchindanaṃ vā acchindāpanaṃ vāti imānettha pañca aṅgānī”ti vuttaṃ.

In the Vimativinodanī, however, it is said: 'Herein, regarding `yampi...pe...acchindi`, it should be supplied and construed thus: `The robe that I gave you, I gave with the perception that “he will set out with me,” not otherwise.` Angry, he confiscated it. Regarding “one offense of wrong-doing”: if the one ordered necessarily confiscates it, at the very moment of the order there is a `pācittiya` offense. If he does not confiscate it, then it should be seen as just an offense of wrong-doing.
