Regarding “many offenses from a single utterance”: if the one ordered confiscates them without interruption, `pācittiya` offenses are incurred at the very moment of the order according to the count of the items, because the offense is to be incurred at the very moment of making the effort. The robe, however, becomes subject to forfeiture only when it is confiscated. If he does not confiscate it, it should be seen as only one offense of wrong-doing at the moment of the order. The principle should be known in this way in other similar cases too. “He will take a preceptor” shows a gift to a novice, and by this it shows that even if given during the novice period, if one confiscates it after ordination, it is a `pācittiya` offense. “Having personally given a robe to a bhikkhu” is stated by way of the highest case. “However, it is proper to have it brought back” is said because, the work not having been done, it is like wages. The five factors here are: (1) being the final robe not made subject to shared ownership; (2) being personally given; (3) the perception that it is one's own; (4) the other being ordained; and (5) confiscating or causing to be confiscated out of anger.'

Paṭibhānacittakathā

The Discussion on Imaginative Designs

6. Paṭibhānacittakathāyaṃ [V 2.0235] aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva suviññeyyanti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ na kiñci vuttaṃ, vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.299) pana “karohīti vattuṃ na vaṭṭatīti āṇattiyā eva paṭikkhittattā dvārapālaṃ ‘kiṃ na karosī’tiādinā pariyāyena vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Jātakapakaraṇanti jātakapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ itthipurisādi yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ adhippetaṃ. ‘Parehi kārāpetu’nti vuttattā buddharūpampi sayaṃ kātuṃ na labhatī”ti vuttaṃ.

6. In the Discussion on Imaginative Designs, since it is easily understood in the way stated in the commentary, nothing is said in the Sāratthadīpanī. In the Vimativinodanī, however, it is said: “It is not proper to say, ‘Do it,’ since this is rejected on account of being a command. It is proper to speak to the gatekeeper indirectly, with such words as, ‘Why do you not do it?’ and so on. By ‘Jātaka scenes’ is meant any form connected with the Jātakas, such as that of a man or a woman. Because it is said, ‘One may have it made by others,’ it is said that one is not permitted to make even a Buddha image oneself.”

Vippakatabhojanakathā

The Discussion on an Unfinished Meal

7. Vippakatabhojanakathāyampi [M 2.0321] sāratthadīpanī vimativinodanī vajirabuddhiṭīkāsu na kiñci vuttaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ kataṃ pakataṃ, vi aniṭṭhitaṃ pakataṃ vippakataṃ, vippakataṃ bhojanaṃ yena so vippakatabhojano, paṭhamaṃ bhuñjitvā aniṭṭhitabhojanakicco bhikkhu. Vuttena bhikkhunā pavisitabbanti sambandho. Rittahatthampi uṭṭhāpetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti ettha kāraṇamāha “vippakatabhojanoyeva hi so hotī”ti, yāgukhajjakādīsupi pītesu khāditesupi bhattassa abhuttattā aniṭṭhitabhojanakicco hoti. Pavārito hoti, tena vattabboti pavāritena āsanā vuṭṭhitena bhuñjituṃ alabhamānattā attano santike udake asante vattabboti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

7. Also concerning the Discussion on an Unfinished Meal, nothing is said in the Sāratthadīpanī, the Vimativinodanī, or the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā. What is first prepared is pakata; with the prefix vi- meaning 'unfinished,' it becomes vippakata. One who has an unfinished meal (vippakataṃ bhojanaṃ) is a vippakatabhojano, that is, a bhikkhu who has started eating but has not yet completed his meal duty. The connection is that one should enter only after being addressed by that bhikkhu. As to why it is not proper to make him get up even with empty hands, the reason is stated: ‘For he is indeed one with an unfinished meal.’ Even if gruel, snacks, and so on have been drunk and eaten, because the rice-meal has not been eaten, his meal duty is unfinished. He is one who has been formally satisfied. The phrase ‘it should be said by him’ means this: because one who has been formally satisfied and has risen from his seat is unable to eat again, he should speak up if there is no water near him. The rest is easily understood.

Uddisantauddisāpanakathā

The Discussion on Reciting and Causing to Recite

8. Uddisantauddisāpanakathāyaṃ uddisantenāti uddesaṃ dentena, pāḷiṃ vācentenāti attho. Uddisāpentenāti uddesaṃ gaṇhantena, pāḷiṃ vācāpentenāti attho. Uccatarepīti pi-saddena samānāsanaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Nīcatarepīti etthāpi eseva nayo.

8. In the Discussion on Reciting and Causing to Recite: ‘By one reciting’ (uddisantena) means by one giving the recitation, that is, by one who recites the Pāli. ‘By one causing to recite’ (uddisāpentena) means by one receiving the recitation, that is, by one who has the Pāli recited. In the phrase ‘on a higher one too’ (uccatarepi), the particle pi also includes ‘on a seat of the same level.’ The same method applies here also to the phrase ‘on a lower one too’ (nīcatarepi).

Tivassantarikakathā

The Discussion on the Three-Year Interval

9. Tivassantarikakathāyaṃ tīṇi vassāni tivassaṃ, tīṇi vā vassāni tivassāni, tivassānaṃ [V 2.0236] antaraṃ tivassantaraṃ, tivassantare ṭhitoti tivassantaro, tena tivassantarena, antara-saddo majjhatthavācako, ṇa-paccayo ṭhitatthe. Tenāha vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 320) “tivassantarenāti tiṇṇaṃ vassānaṃ [M 2.0322] anto ṭhitenā”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 320) pana sarūpameva dassento “tivassantaro nāmā”tiādimāha. Ime sabbeti sabbe tividhā ime samānāsanikā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

9. In the Discussion on the Three-Year Interval: Tīṇi vassāni (three years) is tivassaṃ; or tīṇi vā vassāni is tivassāni. The interval (antaraṃ) of three years (tivassānaṃ) is tivassantaraṃ. One who is situated (ṭhito) in the three-year interval (tivassantare) is a tivassantaro; hence the instrumental tivassantarena. The word antara signifies ‘in the middle,’ and the suffix -ṇa is in the sense of ‘situated.’ Therefore it is said in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā: “‘By one in the three-year interval’ (tivassantarena) means by one situated within three years.” The Commentary, however, showing its very form, says: “‘One in the three-year interval’ (tivassantaro) is the name,” and so on. ‘All these’ means all these three kinds are of the same seating rank. The rest is easily understood.

Dīghāsanakathā

The Discussion on a Long Seat

10. Dīghāsanakathāyaṃ saṃhārimaṃ vāti saṃharituṃ yuttaṃ kaṭasārakādi. Asaṃhārimaṃ vāti saṃharituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ pāsāṇādi āsanaṃ. Tenāha sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.320) “dīghāsanaṃ nāma mañcapīṭhavinimuttaṃ yaṃ kiñci tiṇṇannaṃ ekato sukhaṃ nisīdituṃ pahotī”ti. Kasmā pana “tiṇṇannaṃ pahotī”ti vuttaṃ, nanu dvinnaṃ pahonakāsanampi dīghamevāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “anujānāmi…pe… ettakaṃ pacchimaṃ dīghāsananti hi vutta”nti. Dvinnaṃ pahonake hi adīghāsane samānāsanikeheva saha nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati, tiṇṇannaṃ pahonakato paṭṭhāya gahite dīghāsane pana asamānāsanikehipi saha nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Yadi evaṃ paṇḍakādīhipi saha nisīdituṃ vaṭṭeyyāti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ṭhapetvā paṇḍaka”ntiādi. Tattha attho suviññeyyova.

10. In the Discussion on a Long Seat: ‘Or a portable one’ means one that is suitable to be moved, such as a rush-mat. ‘Or a non-portable one’ means a seat that cannot be moved, such as one of stone. Therefore, it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī: “A ‘long seat’ is any seat, apart from a bed or a bench, that is sufficient for three to sit on together comfortably.” But why was it said, “sufficient for three”? Is not a seat sufficient for two also long? In reference to this objection, it is said: “For it was stated, ‘I allow … this much is the final long seat.’” On a non-long seat sufficient for two, it is proper to sit only with those of the same seating rank. But on a long seat, taken as one from being sufficient for three onwards, it is proper to sit even with those of unequal seating rank. Having kept in mind the objection, “If so, would it be proper to sit even with paṇḍakas and so on?” he said: “I allow, bhikkhus, excepting a paṇḍaka,” and so on. The meaning there is easily understood.

Gilānupaṭṭhānakathā

The Discussion on Attending to the Sick

11. Gilānupaṭṭhānakathāyaṃ palipannoti nimuggo, makkhitoti attho. Uccāretvāti ukkhipitvā. Samānācariyakoti ettha “sacepi ekassa ācariyassa eko antevāsiko hoti, eko saddhivihāriko, etepi aññamaññaṃ samānācariyakā evā”ti vadanti. Bhesajjaṃ yojetuṃ asamattho hotīti vejjena “idañcidañca bhesajjaṃ [M 2.0323] gahetvā iminā yojetvā dātabba”nti vutte tathā kātuṃ asamatthoti attho. Nīhātunti nīharituṃ, chaḍḍetunti attho. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.365-366) pana “bhūmiyaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ akāsīti gilānena nipannabhūmiyaṃ kiliṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ dhovitvā haritūpalittaṃ kāresīti attho. Bhesajjaṃ yojetuṃ asamatthoti parehi vuttavidhimpi kātuṃ asamattho”ti vuttaṃ.

11. In the Discussion on Attending to the Sick: Palipanno means ‘sunk down,’ that is, ‘smeared.’ Uccāretvā means ‘having lifted up.’ Regarding samānācariyako (of the same teacher), here they say: “Even if one teacher has one resident pupil and one co-resident, these too are mutually of the same teacher.” ‘He is unable to prepare medicine’ means that when a physician says, “Take such and such medicines, combine them in this way, and give them,” he is unable to do so. Nīhātuṃ means ‘to take out,’ that is, ‘to discard.’ In the Vimativinodanī, however, it is said: “‘He made the ground into a utensil’ (bhūmiyaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ akāsi) means he had the soiled spot on the ground where the sick person was lying washed and smeared with fresh cow-dung. ‘He is unable to prepare medicine’ means he is unable to follow even the method told by others.”

Maraṇavaṇṇakathā

The Discussion on Praising Death

12. Maraṇavaṇṇakathāyaṃ [V 2.0237] maraṇatthikāva hutvāti imassa kāyassa bhedena saggapāpanādhippāyattā atthato maraṇatthikāva hutvā. Maraṇatthikabhāvaṃ ajānantāti “evaṃ adhippāyino maraṇatthikā nāma hontī”ti attano maraṇatthikabhāvaṃ ajānantā. Na hi te attano cittappavattiṃ na jānanti. Vohāravasenāti pubbabhāgavohāravasena, maraṇādhippāyassa sanniṭṭhāpakacetanākkhaṇe karuṇāya abhāvato kāruññena pāse baddhasūkaramocanaṃ viya na hotīti adhippāyo. “Yathāyunā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ yathānusandhināti pariyāyantarena vuttaṃ, yathānusandhinā yathāyuparicchedenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yathānusandhināti yathānuppabandhena, yāva tasmiṃ bhave santānassa anuppabandho avicchinnapavatti hoti, tāva ṭhatvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

12. In the discourse on praising death, 'having become desirous of death' means that, in essence, one has become desirous of death due to the intention of reaching heaven through the breakup of this body. 'Not knowing the state of being desirous of death' means not knowing their own state of being desirous of death, [thinking,] 'Those who have such an intention are called desirous of death.' For it is not that they do not know the process of their own mind. 'By way of conventional expression' means by way of the conventional expression of the preliminary stage; the meaning is that at the moment of the decisive intention for death, due to the absence of compassion, it is not like the releasing of a pig bound in a snare out of compassion. 'As long as the lifespan' is said to have the very same meaning as 'according to the connection,' expressed in another way. It is said that 'according to the connection' means 'according to the extent of the lifespan.' Alternatively, 'according to the connection' means 'according to the unbroken continuity'; it is said that this means to remain as long as the unbroken continuity of the mental stream proceeds without interruption in that existence.

Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.180) “vohāravasenāti pubbabhāgavohāravasena maraṇādhippāyassa sanniṭṭhāpakacetanākkhaṇe karuṇāya abhāvato, kāruññena pāse baddhasūkaramocanaṃ viya na hotīti adhippāyo. ‘Yathāyunā’ti vuttamevatthaṃ yathānusandhināti pariyāyantarena vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 180) pana “maraṇatthikāva hutvāti [M 2.0324] imassa kāyassa bhedena saggapāpanādhippāyattā atthato maraṇatthikāva hutvā. “Evaṃadhippāyino maraṇatthikā nāma hontī”ti attano maraṇatthikabhāvaṃ ajānantā āpannā pārājikaṃ. Na hi te attano cittappavattiṃ na jānantīti vuccanti. Vohāravasenāti pubbabhāge vohāravasena, sanniṭṭhāne panetaṃ natthi, pāse baddhasūkaramocane viya na hoti. Yathānusandhināti antarā amaritvāti attho”ti vuttaṃ.

In the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.180), it is said: "'By way of conventional expression' means by way of conventional expression in the preliminary stage; the meaning is that at the moment of the decisive intention for death, due to the absence of compassion, it is not like the releasing of a pig bound in a snare. 'As long as the lifespan' is said to have the very same meaning as 'according to the connection,' expressed in another way." In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 180), however, it is said: "'Having become desirous of death' means that, in essence, one has become desirous of death due to the intention of reaching heaven through the breakup of this body. 'Those who have such an intention are called desirous of death'—not knowing their own state of being desirous of death, they incur the pārājika offense. For it is not said that they do not know the process of their own mind. 'By way of conventional expression' is by way of conventional expression in the preliminary stage, but at the decisive moment this is not so; it is not like the release of a pig bound in a snare. 'According to the connection' means 'without dying in between.'"

Attapātanakathā

The Discourse on Causing Oneself to Fall

13. Attapātanakathāyaṃ vibhattibyattayenāti vibhattivipariṇāmena. Visesādhigamoti samādhi vipassanā ca. Ativiya pākaṭattā “hatthappatto viya dissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Upacchindatīti visesādhigamassa vikkhepo mā hotūti āhāraṃ upacchindati. Visesādhigamanti lokuttaradhammapaṭilābhaṃ. Byākaritvāti ārocetvā. Upacchindati, na vaṭṭatīti yasmā sabhāgānaṃ lajjībhikkhūnaṃyeva ariyā attanā adhigatavisesaṃ tādise kāraṇe sati ārocenti, te ca bhikkhū [V 2.0238] appatirūpāya anesanāya paccayaṃ na pariyesanti, tasmā tehi pariyesitapaccaye kukkuccaṃ uppādetvā āhāraṃ upacchindituṃ na vaṭṭatīti attho. Sabhāgānañhi byākatattā upacchindituṃ na labhati. Te hi kappiyakhettaṃ ārocenti. Teneva “sabhāgānañhi lajjībhikkhūnaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatīti idaṃ ‘upacchindati, na vaṭṭatī’ti imassa kāraṇaṃ dassentena vutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Atha vā visesādhigamaṃ byākaritvāti idaṃ visesassa adhigatabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, adhigamantarāyaṃ āsaṅkanteneva ca āhārupacchedo kātabboti anuññātattā adhigatena na kātabboti dassetuṃ “visesādhigamaṃ byākaritvā āhāraṃ upacchindati, na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kiṃ pana ariyā attanā adhigatavisesaṃ aññesaṃ [M 2.0325] ārocentīti imissā codanāya “sabhāgānañhi lajjībhikkhūnaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, ayamettha yuttataroti amhākaṃ khanti, gaṇṭhipadepi ayamattho dassitoyevāti.

13. In the discourse on causing oneself to fall, 'by change of grammatical case' means by alteration of inflection. 'Attainment of distinction' refers to concentration and insight. Because it is extremely evident, it is said, 'it appears as if placed in the hand.' 'He cuts off' means he cuts off food so that there may be no disturbance to the attainment of distinction. 'Attainment of distinction' refers to the acquisition of supramundane states. 'Having declared' means having announced. 'He cuts off, it is not proper'—the meaning is that because noble ones announce the distinction they have attained only to like-minded, conscientious monks when such a reason exists, and those monks do not seek requisites through improper means, it is therefore not proper to cut off food, thereby causing them to have scruples regarding the requisites they have sought. Indeed, because it has been declared to like-minded ones, he is not able to cut it off. For they inform him of a suitable field. For that reason, it is said in all three knot-points: 'For it is proper to tell like-minded, conscientious monks; this is stated by one showing the reason for "he cuts off, it is not proper."' Alternatively, 'having declared the attainment of distinction' is said to show the state of having attained distinction; and to show that it should not be done by one who has attained—since the cutting off of food is permitted only by one fearing an obstacle to attainment—it is said, 'having declared the attainment of distinction, he cuts off food, it is not proper.' But do noble ones announce the distinction they have attained to others? In response to this objection, it is said, 'For it is proper to tell like-minded, conscientious monks.' This is the more fitting meaning here, in our opinion; this meaning is also shown in the knot-points.

Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.182-183) “vibhattibyattayenāti vibhattivipariṇāmena. Visesādhigamoti samādhi vipassanā ca. Visesādhigamanti lokuttaradhammapaṭilābhaṃ. Byākaritvāti ārocetvā, idañca visesassa adhigatabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Adhigatavisesā hi diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanatthaṃ lajjībhikkhūnaṃ avassaṃ adhigamaṃ byākaronti, adhigatavisesena pana abyākaritvāpi āhāraṃ upacchindituṃ na vaṭṭati, adhigamantarāyavinodanatthameva āhārupacchedassa anuññātattā tadadhigame so na kātabbova. Kiṃ panādhigamaṃ ārocetuṃ vaṭṭatīti āha sabhāgānañhītiādī”ti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 181-183) “hatthappatto viya dissati, ‘tassa vikkhepo mā hotū’ti upacchindati, visesādhigamaṃ byākaritvā tappabhavaṃ sakkāraṃ lajjāyanto āhāraṃ upacchindati sabhāgānaṃ byākatattā. Te hi kappiyakhettaṃ ārocentī”ti vuttaṃ.

In the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.182-183), it is said: "'By change of grammatical case' means by alteration of inflection. 'Attainment of distinction' refers to concentration and insight. 'Attainment of distinction' denotes the attainment of supramundane states. 'Having declared' means announcing; and this is stated to show the state of having attained a distinction. For, those who have attained distinction invariably announce their attainment to conscientious monks so that others may follow their example. But for one who has attained a distinction, it is not proper to cut off food, even without having announced it, since the cutting off of food is permitted only for the purpose of removing obstacles to attainment; upon that attainment, it should certainly not be done. But is it proper to announce the attainment? He said, 'For like-minded ones...' and so on." In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 181-183), it is said: "It appears as if it is in his hand; thinking, 'Let there be no distraction for him,' he cuts off [food]. Having announced the attainment of distinction, being ashamed of the honor arising from that, he cuts off food because it has been announced to like-minded ones. For they inform him of a suitable field."

Appaccavekkhitvānisinnakathā

The Discourse on Sitting Down Without Reflecting

14. Appaccavekkhitvā nisinnakathāyaṃ appaṭivekkhitvāti anupaparikkhitvā. Uddhaṃ vā adho vā saṅkamantīti pacchā āgatānaṃ okāsadānatthaṃ nisinnapāḷiyā uddhaṃ vā adho vā gacchanti. Paṭivekkhaṇakiccaṃ natthīti pacchā āgatehi upaparikkhaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Heṭṭhā kismiñci vijjamāne sāṭakaṃ valiṃ gaṇhātīti āha “yasmiṃ vali na paññāyatī”ti. Paṭivekkhaṇañcetaṃ [V 2.0239] gihīnaṃ santakeyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.180) “heṭṭhā kismiñci vijjamāne sāṭakaṃ valiṃ gaṇhātīti āha [M 2.0326] ‘yasmiṃ vali na paññāyatī’ti. Paṭivekkhaṇañcetaṃ gihīnaṃ santake evāti daṭṭhabba”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ, vajirabuddhiṭīkāyampi (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 180) “appaṭivekkhitvāti avicāretvā. Heṭṭhimabhāge hi kismiñci vijjamāne vali paññāyatī”ti ettakameva.

14. In the discourse on sitting down without reflecting: 'Without reflecting' means without examining. 'They move up or down' means they go up or down from the row of seated ones to make space for those who arrive later. 'There is no duty of reflection' means there is no duty of examination by those who come later. 'If there is something underneath, the cloth gathers a fold'—thus it is said: 'in which a fold is not apparent.' And this reflection, it should be understood, pertains only to the belongings of householders. In the Vimativinodanī too (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.180), only this much is said: '“If there is something underneath, the cloth gathers a fold”—thus it is said, “in which a fold is not apparent.” And this reflection, it should be understood, pertains only to the belongings of householders.' In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā too (Vajira. Ṭī. Pārājika 180), only this much is said: '“Without reflecting” means without considering. For if there is something in the lower part, a fold is apparent.'

Davāyasilāvijjhanakathā

The Discourse on Striking a Stone in Jest

15. Davāyasilāvijjhanakathāyaṃ davāsaddo hasādhippāyavācako. Paṭipubbavidha-dhātu pavaṭṭanatthoti āha “hasādhippāyena pāsāṇo na pavaṭṭetabbo”ti. Silāsaddassa pāsāṇavācakattā so eva na paṭivijjhitabboti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “na kevalañcā”tiādi. Yadi evaṃ sabbesampi atthāya na vaṭṭeyyāti āha “cetiyādīnaṃ atthāyā”tiādi. Dhovanadaṇḍakanti bhaṇḍadhovanadaṇḍaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.182-183) pana “bhaṇḍakaṃ vā dhovantāti cīvaraṃ vā dhovantā. Dhovanadaṇḍakanti cīvaradhovanadaṇḍa”nti vuttaṃ.

15. In the discourse on striking a stone in jest: the word 'davā' is expressive of the intention of laughter. The root paṭipubbavidha is in the sense of setting in motion; thus it is said: 'A stone should not be set in motion with the intention of laughter.' Since the word 'silā' is a term for stone, with reference to the objection that that alone should not be struck, it is said: 'And not only…,' etc. If so, it would not be allowable for any purpose at all; thus it is said: 'For the purpose of cetiyas, etc.' 'A washing stick' means a stick for washing requisites. But in the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.182–183) it is said: '“Washing a requisite” means washing a robe. “A washing stick” means a stick for washing robes.'

Dāyālimpanakathā

The Discourse on Setting a Backfire

16. Dāyālimpanakathāyaṃ alla…pe… pācittiyanti sukkhaṭṭhānepi aggiṃ pātetvā iminā adhippāyena ālimpentassa pācittiyameva. Dukkaṭanti sukkhaṭṭhāne vā sukkhaṃ “asukkha”nti avavatthapetvā vā aggiṃ pātentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Kīḷādhippāyepi eseva nayo, kīḷādhippāyo ca paṭapaṭāyamānasaddassādavaseneva veditabbo. Paṭipakkhabhūto aggi paṭaggi. Parittakaraṇanti ārakkhakaraṇaṃ. Sayaṃ vā uṭṭhitanti vāteritānaṃ veḷuādīnaṃ aññamaññasaṅghaṭṭanena samuṭṭhitaṃ. Nirupādānoti indhanarahito. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.190) pana “khiḍḍādhippāyenapi dukkaṭanti sukkhatiṇādīsu aggikaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Allesu pana [M 2.0327] kīḷādhippāyenapi karontassa pācittiyameva. Paṭipakkhabhūto, paṭimukhaṃ gacchanto vā aggi paṭaggi, tassa allatiṇādīsupi dānaṃ anuññātaṃ. Taṃ dentena dūratova āgacchantaṃ dāvaggiṃ disvā vihārassa samantato ekakkhaṇe akatvā ekadesato paṭṭhāya vihārassa samantato saṇikaṃ jhāpetvā yathā mahantopi aggi vihāraṃ pāpuṇituṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ vihārassa samantā [V 2.0240] abbhokāsaṃ katvā paṭaggi dātabbo. So ḍāvaggino paṭipathaṃ gantvā ekato hutvā tena saha nibbāti. Parittakaraṇanti samantā rukkhatiṇādicchedanaparikhākhaṇanādiārakkhakaraṇaṃ. Tenāha ‘tiṇakuṭikānaṃ samantā bhūmitacchana’ntiādī”ti, vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 190) pana “parittanti rakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ ‘samantā bhūmitacchana’ntiādi vutta”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ.

16. In the discourse on setting a backfire: 'Wet…' etc. '…a pācittiya': for one who sets fire even in a dry place with this intention, it is a pācittiya. 'A dukkaṭa': for one who sets fire in a dry place, or without having determined that what is dry is 'not dry,' there is a dukkaṭa. This same method applies also when there is an intention of play; and the intention of play should be understood simply by way of the pleasure in the crackling sound. A fire that is a counter-measure is a 'counter-fire' (paṭaggi). 'Making a protection' means making a safeguard. 'Or arisen by itself' means arisen from the mutual friction of bamboos and so on, blown by the wind. 'Without sustenance' means without fuel. But in the Vimativinodanī it is said: '“A dukkaṭa even with the intention of play” is said with reference to making a fire in dry grass, etc. But for one who does it in wet places even with the intention of play, it is a pācittiya. A fire that is a counter-measure, or a fire that goes to meet it, is a “counter-fire” (paṭaggi); the setting of it is permitted even in wet grass, etc. When setting it, on seeing a forest fire approaching from a distance, one should not do it all at once around the monastery, but starting from one side, one should slowly burn the area all around the monastery so that even a large fire cannot reach the monastery. Thus, having made an open space all around the monastery, the counter-fire should be set. It goes on the path against the forest fire, becomes one, and is extinguished along with it. “Making a protection” means making a safeguard by cutting down trees and grass all around, digging a trench, etc. Hence it is said: “The smoothing of the ground all around grass huts,” etc.' But in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā only this much is said: '“Protection” means a safeguard; to show this, it is said: “The smoothing of the ground all around,” etc.'

Micchādiṭṭhikulābhatakathā

Discourse on What is Received from Families with Wrong View

17. Micchādiṭṭhikulābhatakathāyaṃ natthi saddhā etesūti assaddhā, maccharino, tesu assaddhesu. Micchādiṭṭhiyā yuttāni kulāni micchādiṭṭhikulāni, majjhelopatatiyātappurisasamāso, “natthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattāya dasavatthukāya micchādiṭṭhiyā yuttakulāni, tesu. Micchādiṭṭhikulesu labhitvāti sambandho. Asakkaccakārīnaṃ tesaṃ sakkaccakaraṇena, appaṇītadāyīnaṃ tesaṃ paṇītadānena bhavitabbamettha kāraṇenāti kāraṇaṃ upaparikkhitvāva bhuñjituṃ yuttanti āha “anupaparikkhitvā neva attanā bhuñjitabbaṃ, na paresaṃ dātabba”nti. Yena kāraṇena bhavitabbaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “visamissampi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na kevalaṃ piṇḍapātamevāti āha “yampī”tiādi. Tattha kāraṇamāha “apihitavatthusmimpi hī”tiādi. Tato aññampi dasseti gandhahaliddādimakkhitotiādinā[M 2.0328]. Tatthapi kāraṇaṃ dassetumāha “sarīre rogaṭṭhānānī”tiādi.

17. In the discourse on what is received from families with wrong view: 'There is no faith in them,' thus they are faithless, stingy; in those who are faithless. Families connected with wrong view are 'families with wrong view'—a Tatiyā-tappurisa compound with elision of the middle term—that is, families connected with the ten-factored wrong view that proceeds in the manner of 'There is nothing given,' etc.; in those. The connection is: 'having received from families with wrong view.' Since it must be for a reason that those who act disrespectfully do so respectfully, and that those who give unrefined things give refined things, having examined the reason, it is proper to eat. Thus it is said: 'Without examining, it should not be eaten by oneself nor given to others.' To show the reason for which it must be, it is said: 'For even if mixed with poison…,' etc. Not only almsfood; thus it is said: 'And whatever…,' etc. Therein, it states the reason: 'For even in the case of an uncovered object…,' etc. It shows another case apart from that with: 'smeared with perfumes, turmeric, etc.' There too, to show the reason, it says: 'Places of disease in the body…,' etc.

Gopakadānakathā

The Account of the Guardian's Gift

18. Gopakadānakathāyaṃ paresaṃ santakaṃ gopeti rakkhatīti gopako, tassa dānaṃ gopakadānaṃ, uyyānapālakādīhi bhikkhūnaṃ dātabbadānaṃ. Tattha paṇṇaṃ āropetvāti “ettakeheva rukkhehi ettakameva gahetabba”nti paṇṇaṃ āropetvā, likhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nimittasaññaṃ katvāti saṅketaṃ katvā. Dārakāti tesaṃ puttanattādayo dārakā. Aññepi ye keci gopakā honti, te sabbepi vuttā. Sabbatthapi gihīnaṃ gopakadāne yattakaṃ gopakā denti, tattakaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Saṅghike pana yathāparicchedameva gahetabbanti dīpitattā “atthato eka”nti vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.156) “paṇṇaṃ āropetvāti ‘ettake rukkhe rakkhitvā [V 2.0241] tato ettakaṃ gahetabba’nti paṇṇaṃ āropetvā. Nimittasaññaṃ katvāti saṅketaṃ katvā. Dārakāti tesaṃ puttanattādayo ye keci gopenti, te sabbepi idha ‘dārakā’ti vuttā”ti, vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 156) pana “ārāmarakkhakāti vissatthavasena gahetabbaṃ. Adhippāyaṃ ñatvāti ettha yassa dānaṃ paṭiggaṇhantaṃ bhikkhuṃ, bhāgaṃ vā sāmikā na rakkhanti na daṇḍenti, tassa dānaṃ appaṭicchādetvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatīti idha sanniṭṭhānaṃ, tampi ‘na vaṭṭati saṅghike’ti vutta”nti vuttaṃ.

18. In the account of the guardian's gift, a guardian is one who guards and protects the property of others; his gift is called the guardian's gift, which is a gift to be given to bhikkhus by park keepers and the like. There, 'having inscribed a leaf' means having written, it is said, 'Only this much is to be taken from these many trees.' 'Having made a sign' means having made an agreement. 'Children' refers to their sons, grandsons, and the like. Any others who are guardians are also included. In all cases of a guardian's gift from laypeople, whatever the guardians give, that much is to be taken. But in the case of what belongs to the Sangha, only what is specifically determined is to be taken; hence it is said, 'in meaning, it is one.' In the Vimativinodanī it is also said: ''Having inscribed a leaf' means having inscribed, 'After guarding this many trees, this much is to be taken.' 'Having made a sign' means having made an agreement. 'Children' refers to their sons, grandsons, and the like—any who guard are all called 'children' here.' In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā, however, it is stated: ''Park keepers' should be understood in the sense of those who are trusted. 'Having known the intention': here, if the owners do not object to or punish a bhikkhu who receives a gift or a share from someone, it is permissible to accept that gift without concealing it; this is the conclusion here. That too, it is said, 'is not allowable in the case of what belongs to the Sangha.'

Yatthāti yasmiṃ āvāse. Aññesaṃ abhāvanti aññesaṃ āgantukabhikkhūnaṃ abhāvaṃ. Tatthāti tādise āvāse. Bhājetvā khādantīti āgantukānampi sampattānaṃ bhājetvā khādantīti adhippāyo. Catūsu paccayesu sammā upanentīti [M 2.0329] ambaphalādīni vikkiṇitvā cīvarādīsu catūsu paccayesu sammā upanenti. Cīvaratthāya niyametvā dinnāti “imesaṃ rukkhānaṃ phalāni vikkiṇitvā cīvaresuyeva upanetabbāni, na bhājetvā khāditabbānī”ti evaṃ niyametvā dinnā. Tesupi āgantukā anissarāti paccayaparibhogatthāya niyametvā dinnattā bhājetvā khādituṃ anissarā. Na tesu…pe… ṭhātabbanti ettha āgantukehi heṭṭhā vuttanayena bhājetvā khāditabbanti adhippāyo. Tesaṃ katikāya ṭhātabbanti “bhājetvā na khāditabba”nti vā “ettakesu rukkhesu phalāni gaṇhissāmā”ti vā “ettakāni phalāni gaṇhissāmā”ti vā “ettakānaṃ divasānaṃ abbhantare gaṇhissāmā”ti vā “na kiñci gaṇhissāmā”ti vā evaṃ katāya āvāsikānaṃ katikāya āgantukehi ṭhātabbaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “anissarā”ti vacanena dīpitoyeva attho mahāpaccariyaṃ “catunnaṃ paccayāna”ntiādinā vitthāretvā dassito. Paribhogavasenevāti ettha eva-saddo aṭṭhānappayutto, paribhogavasena tameva bhājetvāti yojetabbaṃ. Ettha etasmiṃ vihāre, raṭṭhevā.

'Where' means: in whatever dwelling. 'The absence of others' means: the absence of other incoming bhikkhus. 'There' means: in such a dwelling. 'Having shared, they eat': the meaning is that even when incoming bhikkhus have arrived, they share and then eat. 'They properly apply it to the four requisites': this means that after selling fruits like mangoes, they properly apply the proceeds to the four requisites such as robes. 'Given with the stipulation for robes': this means they are given with the stipulation, 'The fruits of these trees must be sold and applied only to robes; they are not to be shared and eaten.' 'Even over these, incoming bhikkhus have no authority': because they were given with the stipulation for the use of the requisites, they have no authority to share and eat. Regarding 'Not for them… one must abide': here the meaning is that incoming bhikkhus are to share and eat in accordance with the method stated below. 'One must abide by their agreement': this means incoming bhikkhus must abide by the agreement made by the residents, whether it is 'It is not to be shared and eaten,' or 'We will take fruits from this many trees,' or 'We will take this many fruits,' or 'We will take them within this many days,' or 'We will take nothing.' In the Great Commentary, the very meaning clarified by the word 'have no authority' is explained in detail in the Mahāpaccarī with 'for the four requisites,' and so on. Regarding 'by way of use alone': here the word 'eva' is used in the wrong place; it should be construed as 'by way of use, they must share that very thing.' 'Here' means in this monastery, or in the country.

Senāsanapaccayanti senāsanañca tadatthāya niyametvā ṭhapitañca. Lāmakakoṭiyāti lāmakaṃ ādiṃ katvā, lāmakasenāsanato paṭṭhāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Senāsanepi tiṇādīni lāmakakoṭiyāva vissajjetabbāni, senāsanaparikkhārāpi lāmakakoṭiyāva vissajjetabbā. Mūlavatthucchedaṃ pana katvā na upanetabbanti iminā kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu tāva idaṃ vuttaṃ “sabbāni senāsanāni na vissajjetabbānīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Lāmakakoṭiyā vissajjantehipi [V 2.0242] senāsanabhūmiyo na vissajjetabbāti ayamattho vutto hotīti no khanti. Vīmaṃsitvā yaṃ ruccati, taṃ gahetabbaṃ.

'Lodging as a requisite' means lodging and what has been designated and set aside for that purpose. 'From the inferior end' means taking the inferior as the starting point; that is to say, starting from the most inferior lodging. Even for lodgings, things like grass should be disposed of from the inferior end, and lodging accessories should also be disposed of from the inferior end. 'But having made a cutting off of the root-basis, it should not be offered': what is said by this? In all three knotty points, it is first said: 'This means that all lodgings should not be disposed of.' This meaning is stated: 'Even by those disposing from the inferior end, the lodging grounds should not be disposed of.' This is not our opinion. Having investigated, what is approved of should be accepted.

Dhammasantakena [M 2.0330] buddhapūjaṃ kātuṃ, buddhasantakena vā dhammapūjaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati na vaṭṭatīti? “Tathāgatassa kho etaṃ, vāseṭṭha, adhivacanaṃ dhammakāyo itipī”ti ca “yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.87) ca vacanato vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Keci pana “evaṃ sante ‘yo, bhikkhave, maṃ upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyyā’ti (mahāva. 365) vacanato buddhasantakena gilānassapi bhesajjaṃ kātuṃ yuttanti āpajjeyya, tasmā na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Na hi “yo, bhikkhave, maṃ upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyyā”ti (mahāva. 365) iminā attano ca gilānassa ca ekasadisatā, tadupaṭṭhānassa vā samaphalatā vuttā. Ayañhettha attho – “yo maṃ ovādānusāsanīkaraṇena upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyya, mama ovādakārakena gilāno upaṭṭhātabbo”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 365). Bhagavato ca gilānassa ca upaṭṭhānaṃ ekasadisanti evaṃ panettha attho na gahetabbo, tasmā “yo vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216) vacanato “ahañca kho panidāni ekakova ovadāmi anusāsāmi, mayi parinibbute imāni caturāsīti buddhasahassāni tumhe ovadissanti anusāsissantī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.216) vuttattā ca bahussutaṃ bhikkhuṃ pasaṃsantena ca “yo bahussuto, na so tumhākaṃ sāvako nāma, buddho nāma esa cundā”ti vuttattā dhammagarukattā ca tathāgatassa pubbanayo eva pasatthataroti amhākaṃ khanti. Vimativinodaniyampi “yatthāti yasmiṃ āvāse. Aññesanti aññesaṃ āgantukānaṃ. Tesupi āgantukā anissarāti senāsane nirantaraṃ vasantānaṃ cīvaratthāya dāyakehi, bhikkhūhi vā niyametvā dinnattā bhājetvā khādituṃ anissarā. Āgantukehipi icchantehi tasmiṃ [M 2.0331] vihāre vassānādīsu pavisitvā cīvaratthāya gahetabbaṃ. Tesaṃ katikāya ṭhātabbanti sabbāni phalāphalāni abhājetvā ‘ettakesu rukkhesu phalāni bhājetvā paribhuñjissāma, aññesu phalāphalehi senāsanāni paṭijaggissāmā’ti vā ‘piṇḍapātādipaccayaṃ sampādessāmā’ti vā ‘kiñcipi abhājetvā catupaccayatthāyeva upanemā’ti vā evaṃ sammā upanentānaṃ āvāsikānaṃ katikāya āgantukehi ṭhātabbaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘anissarā’ti vacanena dīpito eva attho, mahāpaccariyaṃ ‘catunnaṃ paccayāna’ntiādinā vitthāretvā dassito. Paribhogavasenevāti ettha eva-saddo [V 2.0243] aṭṭhānappayutto, paribhogavasena tameva bhājetvāti yojetabbaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ vihāre, raṭṭhe vā. Senāsanapaccayanti senāsanañca tadatthāya niyametvā ṭhapitañca. ‘Ekaṃ vā dve vā varasenāsanāni ṭhapetvā’ti vuttamevatthaṃ puna byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ ‘mūlavatthucchedaṃ pana katvā na upanetabba’nti vuttaṃ, senāsanasaṅkhātavatthuno mūlacchedaṃ katvā sabbāni senāsanāni na vissajjetabbānīti attho. Keci panettha ‘ekaṃ vā dve vā varasenāsanāni ṭhapetvā lāmakato paṭṭhāya vissajjantehipi senāsanabhūmiyo na vissajjetabbāti ayamattho vutto’ti vadanti, tampi yuttameva imassapi atthassa avassaṃ vattabbato, itarathā keci saha vatthunāpi vissajjetabbaṃ maññeyyu”nti.

Is it allowable or not to make an offering to the Buddha with what belongs to the Dhamma, or to make an offering to the Dhamma with what belongs to the Buddha? Some say it is allowable, based on the statements, 'For the Tathāgata, Vāseṭṭha, this is a designation: 'the Dhamma-body,'' and, 'Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.' Others, however, say: 'If this were so, then based on the statement, 'Bhikkhus, whoever would attend to me should attend to the sick,' it would follow that it is right to prepare medicine for the sick with what belongs to the Buddha. Therefore, it is not allowable.' But this is without reason. For the statement, 'Bhikkhus, whoever would attend to me should attend to the sick,' does not state an identity between himself and the sick, nor that attending to them has the same fruit. The meaning here is this: 'Whoever would attend to me by acting on my advice and instruction should attend to the sick. The sick should be attended to by one who acts on my advice.' One should not take the meaning here to be that attending to the Blessed One and attending to the sick are identical. Therefore, based on the statement, 'Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya that I have taught and laid down for you will be your teacher after I have passed away,' and because it was said, 'Now I alone advise and instruct you, but after I have attained final Nibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Buddha-teachings will advise and instruct you,' and because, when praising a learned bhikkhu, it was said, 'Cunda, one who is learned is not your disciple; he is a Buddha,' and due to the Tathāgata's reverence for the Dhamma, it is our opinion that the former line of reasoning is more commendable. In the Vimativinodanī as well: ''Where' means in which residence. 'Of others' means of other incoming bhikkhus. 'Even over these, incoming bhikkhus have no authority': because it was given by donors or by bhikkhus, having been stipulated for the purpose of robes for those dwelling continuously in the lodging, they have no authority to divide and consume. Even incoming bhikkhus, if they wish, may enter that monastery during the rains retreat, etc., and take it for the purpose of robes. 'They should abide by their agreement': incoming bhikkhus should abide by the agreement of the residents who are applying it properly, whether it is 'All the various fruits should not be shared, but we will share and consume the fruits on this many trees, and with the other various fruits we will maintain the lodgings,' or 'we will procure the requisites of almsfood, etc.,' or 'without sharing anything at all, we will apply it only for the purpose of the four requisites.' In the Great Commentary, this very meaning is clarified by the word 'have no authority'; in the Mahāpaccarī, it is shown in detail with 'for the four requisites,' and so on. Regarding 'merely by way of usage': here, the word 'eva' is used in the wrong place; it should be construed as 'by way of use, they must share that very thing.' 'Here' means in this monastery or in the country. 'Lodging as a requisite' means lodging and what has been designated and set aside for that purpose. To show again by way of contrast the very meaning stated in 'Having set aside one or two excellent lodgings,' it is said, 'But having made a cutting off of the root-basis, it should not be applied.' The meaning is that having made a root-cutting of the thing designated as a lodging, all lodgings should not be disposed of. Some here say: 'This meaning is stated: "Having set aside one or two excellent lodgings, even when disposing starting from the inferior ones, the lodging grounds should not be disposed of."' This too is indeed reasonable, because this meaning must necessarily be stated; otherwise, some might think that it should be disposed of together with the physical site.'

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pārājika 153) “ettha etasmiṃ vihāre paracakkādibhayaṃ āgataṃ. Mūlavatthucchedanti ‘sabbasenāsanānaṃ ete issarā’ti vacanato itare anissarāti dīpitaṃ hoti. Ayameva bhikkhu issaroti yattha so icchati, tattha attañātahetuṃ [M 2.0332] labhatīti kira attho, api ca ‘daharo’ti vadanti. Savatthukanti saha bhūmiyāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti.

In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā: 'Here, in this monastery, fear from an enemy army and so on has arisen. 'Cutting off the root-basis': because of the statement 'these are the masters of all lodgings,' it is shown that others are not masters. 'This very bhikkhu is the master': the meaning, it seems, is that wherever he wishes, he finds a reason for himself; moreover, they call him 'young.' 'With its site' means 'together with the land,' it is said.

Dhammikārakkhayācanakathā

The Discourse on Requesting Righteous Protection

19. Dhammikārakkhayācanakathāyaṃ “gīvāyevāti āṇattiyā abhāvato. Tesaṃ anatthakāmatāyāti ‘coro’ti vuttaṃ mama vacanaṃ sutvā keci daṇḍissanti, jīvitā voropessantīti evaṃ saññāya. Etena kevalaṃ bhayena vā parikkhāraggahaṇatthaṃ vā sahasā ‘coro’ti vutte daṇḍitepi na dosoti dasseti. Rājapurisānañhi ‘coro aya’nti uddissakathane eva gīvā. Bhikkhūnaṃ, pana ārāmikādīnaṃ vā sammukhā ‘asuko coro evamakāsī’ti kenaci vuttavacanaṃ nissāya ārāmikādīsu rājapurisānaṃ vatvā daṇḍāpentesupi bhikkhussa na gīvā rājapurisānaṃ avuttattā, yesañca vuttaṃ, tehi sayaṃ corassa adaṇḍitattāti gahetabbaṃ. ‘Tvaṃ etassa santakaṃ acchindā’ti āṇattopi hi sace aññena acchindāpeti, āṇāpakassa anāpatti visaṅketattā. Attano vacanakaranti idaṃ sāmīcivasena vuttaṃ. Vacanaṃ akarontānaṃ rājapurisānampi ‘iminā gahitaparikkhāraṃ āharāpehi, mā cassa daṇḍaṃ karohī’ti uddissa vadantassapi daṇḍe gahitepi na gīvā eva daṇḍaggahaṇassa paṭikkhittattā [V 2.0244] ‘asukabhaṇḍaṃ avaharā’ti āṇāpetvā vippaṭisāre uppanne puna paṭikkhipane (pārā. 121) viya. Dāsādīnaṃ sampaṭicchane viya tadatthāya aḍḍakaraṇe bhikkhūnampi dukkaṭanti āha ‘kappiyaaḍḍo nāma, na vaṭṭatī’ti. Kenaci pana bhikkhunā khettādiatthāya vohārikānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā aḍḍe katepi taṃ khettādisampaṭicchane viya sabbesaṃ akappiyaṃ na hoti pubbe eva saṅghasantakattā. Bhikkhusseva pana payogavasena [M 2.0333] āpattiyo honti. Dāsādīnampi pana atthāya rakkhaṃ yācituṃ vohārikena puṭṭhena saṅghassa uppannaṃ kappiyakkamaṃ vattuṃ ārāmikādīhi ca aḍḍaṃ kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati eva. Vihāravatthādikappiyaaḍḍaṃ pana bhikkhunā sayampi kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. pācittiya 2.679) āgato.

19. In the Discourse on Requesting Righteous Protection: 'It is only a capital offense'—this is due to the absence of a command. It is said 'thief' due to ill will, with the perception: 'Hearing my words, some may punish him or even take his life.' By this, it is shown that there is no offense even if he is punished when one hastily says 'thief' merely out of fear or for the sake of seizing his belongings. For the king's men, it is a capital offense only when one specifically identifies someone, saying, 'This is the thief.' But if, in the presence of monks or monastery attendants, someone says, 'So-and-so is a thief, he did such and such,' and relying on this statement, the monastery attendants report it to the king's men who then inflict punishment, the monk does not incur a capital offense because he did not directly speak to the king's men. And it should be understood that those to whom he spoke did not punish the thief themselves. Even if commanded, 'You, seize his property,' if he has another seize it, the one who gave the command incurs no offense because the instruction was ambiguous. 'One who acts on their own words' is said in the sense of proper conduct. Even if the king's men do not act on his words, if one tells them, 'Have him return the requisites seized by this one, but do not punish him,' and they still inflict punishment, the one giving the instruction does not incur a capital offense, as the infliction of punishment was prohibited, just as when, after ordering, 'Take such-and-such goods,' regret arises and one retracts the order (cf. Pārā. 121). Regarding employing a legal representative for slaves and so on, for monks to do so for that purpose is a dukkaṭa offense; it is said, 'A permissible legal representation is not allowable.' Yet, if a monk goes to the legal authorities for the sake of fields, etc., and a legal representation is made, it is not improper for everyone, as in the case of accepting a field, etc., since it was previously owned by the Sangha. However, offenses arise for the monk based on his own actions. For the sake of slaves, etc., it is permissible to request protection when asked by a legal authority, to declare the Sangha’s proper procedure, and to have monastery attendants arrange a legal representation. Moreover, a monk may himself make a permissible legal representation for monastery land and so on. This is stated in the Vimativinodanī (Vmv-ṭ 2.679).

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pācittiya 681) “gīvāti kevalaṃ gīvā eva hoti, na pārājikaṃ. Kārāpetvā dātabbāti ettha sace āvudhabhaṇḍaṃ hoti, tassa dhārā na kārāpetabbā, aññena pana ākārena saññāpetabba”nti vuttaṃ.

In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vjb-ṭ 681), it is stated: "'A capital offense' means it is simply a capital offense, not a pārājika offense. In the phrase 'having had it made, it should be given,' if it is a weapon, its edge should not be caused to be made, but it should be indicated in another way."

Uccārādichaḍḍanakathā

The Discourse on Discarding Excrement, etc.

20. Uccārādichaḍḍanakathāyaṃ aṭṭhame uccārādichaḍḍane “uccārādibhāvo, anapalokanaṃ, vaḷañjanaṭṭhānaṃ, tirokuṭṭapākāratā, chaḍḍanaṃ vā chaḍḍāpanaṃ vāti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni, navame haritūpari chaḍḍane sabbesanti bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā ca. Idha khettapālakā ārāmādigopakā ca sāmikā evā”ti ettakameva sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.830) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. pācittiya 2.830) pana “aṭṭhame vaḷañjiyamānatirokuṭṭāditā, anapaloketvā uccārādīnaṃ chaḍḍanādīti dve aṅgāni. Navame ‘matthakacchinnanāḷikerampī’ti vuttattā haritūpari chaḍḍanameva paṭikkhittaṃ. Tenāha ‘anikkhittabījesū’tiādi. Yattha ca chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭati, tattha harite vaccādiṃ kātumpi vaṭṭati eva. Sabbesanti bhikkhubhikkhunīna”nti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. pācittiya 832) pana “sāmike apaloketvāva chaḍḍetīti katthaci potthake natthi, katthaci atthi, atthibhāvova seyyo kiriyākiriyattā sikkhāpadassa. Idha khettapālakā ārāmādigopakā ca sāmikā eva. ‘Saṅghassa khette ārāme ca tattha kacavaraṃ [M 2.0334] na chaḍḍetabbanti katikā ce natthi, bhikkhussa [V 2.0245] chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭati saṅghapariyāpannattā, na bhikkhunīnaṃ. Tāsampi bhikkhunisaṅghasantake vuttanayena vaṭṭati, na tattha bhikkhussa. Evaṃ santepi sāruppavaseneva kātabbanti vutta”nti vuttaṃ.

20. In the Discourse on Discarding Excrement, etc., concerning the eighth rule on discarding excrement, etc., it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sp-ṭ 3.830): 'Herein, there are these five factors: the substance being excrement, etc.; not informing; the place not being a designated disposal site; being beyond a wall or fence; and discarding or causing to discard. Concerning the ninth rule on discarding on greenery, it applies to all—that is, to monks and nuns. Here, field guards and monastery keepers, etc., are themselves the owners.' In the Vimativinodanī (Vmv-ṭ 2.830), however, it is said: 'In the eighth rule, the two factors are: being beyond a wall, etc., that is used for disposal, and discarding excrement, etc., without informing. In the ninth rule, since it is stated, "even a coconut with its top cut off," only discarding on greenery is prohibited. Hence, it is said, "on ground where seeds have not been sown," etc. And where it is permissible to discard, it is also permissible to pass excrement, etc., on greenery. "To all" means to monks and nuns.' But in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vjb-ṭ 832), it is said: 'The phrase "one discards only after informing the owner" is not found in some manuscripts, but it is in others; its presence is preferable because the training rule is one of action and non-action. Here, field guards and monastery keepers, etc., are themselves the owners. If there is no agreement stating, "Rubbish should not be discarded in the Sangha’s fields or monasteries," it is permissible for a monk to discard it there because it belongs to the Sangha, but not for nuns. For them, too, it is permissible in what belongs to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha in the way stated, but not for a monk there. Even so, it is said that it should be done in a suitable manner.'

Bhikkhuvibhaṅge pana sekhiyavaṇṇanāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 651) “asañciccāti paṭicchannaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantassa sahasā uccāro vā passāvo vā nikkhamati, asañciccakato nāma, anāpatti. Na hariteti ettha yampi jīvarukkhassa mūlaṃ pathaviyaṃ dissamānaṃ gacchati, sākhā vā bhūmilaggā gacchati, sabbaṃ haritasaṅkhātameva, khandhe nisīditvā appaharitaṭṭhāne pātetuṃ vaṭṭati. Appaharitaṭṭhānaṃ olokentasseva sahasā nikkhamati, gilānaṭṭhāne ṭhito hoti, vaṭṭati. Appaharite katoti appaharitaṃ alabhantena tiṇaṇḍupakaṃ vā palālaṇḍupakaṃ vā ṭhapetvā katopi pacchā haritaṃ ottharati, vaṭṭatiyeva. ‘Kheḷena cettha siṅghāṇikāpi saṅgahitā’ti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Na udaketi etaṃ paribhogaudakameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vaccakuṭisamauddādiudakesu pana aparibhogesu anāpatti. Deve vassante samantato udakogho hoti, anudakaṭṭhānaṃ olokentasseva nikkhamati, vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ etādise kāle anudakaṭṭhānaṃ alabhantena kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tassaṃ vaṇṇanāyaṃ vimativinodaniyañca (vi. vi. ṭī. pācittiya 2.652) “kheḷena cettha siṅghāṇikāpi saṅgahitāti ettha udakagaṇḍusakaṃ katvā ucchukacavarādiñca mukheneva harituṃ udakesu chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabba”nti vuttaṃ.

But in the Bhikkhuvibhaṅga, in the explanation of the Sekhiya rules (Pāc-a 651), it is said: '“Unintentionally”: when one is going to a concealed place and excrement or urine is suddenly discharged; this is called “done unintentionally,” and there is no offense. “Not on greenery”: here, if one goes to where the root of a living tree is visible on the ground, or a branch is touching the ground, all this is reckoned as greenery. It is permissible to sit on the trunk and drop it in a place with little greenery. If it is suddenly discharged while one is looking for a place with little greenery, or if one is standing in a place for the sick, it is permissible. “Done in a place with little greenery”: if one cannot find a place with little greenery, one may place a clump of grass or a clump of straw and do it there; even if greenery covers it afterwards, it is still permissible. “By spittle, mucus is also included here”—this is stated in the Mahāpaccariya. “Not in water”: this is said with reference only to water for use. But in the case of water not for use, such as in latrines, the ocean, etc., there is no offense. When it is raining and there is a flood of water all around, if it is discharged while one is looking for a dry spot, it is permissible. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that at such a time, if one cannot find a dry spot, it is permissible to do it.' And in the Vimativinodanī’s explanation of that passage (Vmv-ṭ 2.652) it is said: 'Regarding the statement, “By spittle, mucus is also included here,” it should be understood that it is permissible to take a mouthful of water and carry sugarcane refuse, etc., in the mouth to discard it in water.'

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne paṇḍitehi vicāretabbaṃ atthi – “vaccakuṭisamuddādiudakesu pana aparibhogesu anāpattī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, evaṃ sante nadījātassarādīsu āpatti vā anāpatti vāti. Tattha samuddādīti ādi-saddena nadījātassarāpi saṅgahitāva, tasmā anāpattīti ce? Na cevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi hi samuddādīti ettha ādi-saddena nadījātassarāpi [M 2.0335] saṅgahitā, evaṃ sati ṭīkācariyā vadeyyuṃ, na pana vadanti, aṭṭhakathāyañca “vaccakuṭisamuddādiudakesū”ti ettakameva vadeyya, tathā pana avatvā “aparibhogesū”ti hetumantavisesanapadampi gahitaṃ. Tena ñāyati “ādisaddena aparibhogāni candanikādiudakāni eva gahitāni, na paribhogāni nadījātassarādiudakānī”ti. Tena ca vaccakuṭisamuddādiudakāni aparibhogattā anāpattikarāni honti, nadījātassarādiudakāni pana [V 2.0246] paribhogattā āpattikarānīti. Kathaṃ pana “aparibhogesū”ti imassa padassa hetumantapadabhāvo jānitabboti? Yuttito āgamato ca. Kathaṃ yuttito? “Vaccakuṭisamuddādiudakāni paribhogānipi santi, aparibhogānipī”ti abyabhicāriyabhāvato. Byabhicāre hi sambhave eva sati visesanaṃ sātthakaṃ siyā. Kathaṃ āgamato? Vuttañhetaṃ ācariyabuddhadattattherena vinayavinicchaye (vi. vi. 1954) “tesaṃ aparibhogattā”ti. Tasmā ādi-saddena aparibhogāniyeva udakāni gahitāni, na paribhogāni. Vuttañhetaṃ vinayavinicchayaṭīkāyaṃ “vaccakuṭisamuddādiudakesūti ettha ādi-saddena sabbaṃ aparibhogajalaṃ saṅgayhati, teneva tesaṃ aparibhogattameva kāraṇamāhā”ti, tasmā manussānaṃ paribhogesu nadījātassarataḷākapokkharaṇiyādiudakesu uccārapassāvādikaraṇaṃ na vaṭṭatīti jānitabbametaṃ. “Deve vassante samantato udakogho hoti, anudakaṭṭhānaṃ olokentasseva nikkhamati, vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ etādise kāle anudakaṭṭhānaṃ alabhantena kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti vutta”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatattā mahantesu nadījātassarādīsu [M 2.0336] nāvādīhi gatakāle tādise kāraṇe sati “tīraṃ upanehī”ti vatvā “upanetuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṭṭhāne udakepi kātuṃ vaṭṭati, anāpattī”ti aṭṭhakathānulomato viññāyati, upaparikkhitvā gahetabbaṃ.

In this matter, the wise should consider: It is stated in the commentary, “There is no offense in regard to water from a latrine, the ocean, etc., that is not for consumption.” This being so, in rivers, natural lakes, and the like, is there an offense or not? If it is said that by the word “etc.” in “the ocean, etc.,” rivers and natural lakes are also included, and therefore there is no offense, this should not be seen as such. For if the word “etc.” here included rivers and natural lakes, the Subcommentary teachers would have said so, but they do not. And the commentary would have said only, “in water from a latrine, the ocean, etc.”; but without saying so, it has also included the qualifying term with a reason, “that is not for consumption.” By this it is known that the word “etc.” refers only to water not for consumption, such as water from a cesspool, and not to water for consumption, like that of rivers and natural lakes. Therefore, water from a latrine, the ocean, etc., does not entail an offense because it is not for consumption, whereas water from rivers and natural lakes does entail an offense because it is for consumption. But how is the phrase “that is not for consumption” to be understood as a term containing a reason? By logic and by scripture. How by logic? Because water from a latrine, the ocean, etc., can be both for consumption and not for consumption; a qualifying phrase is meaningful only when variability is possible. How by scripture? The Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta states in the Vinayavinicchaya: “Because they are not for consumption.” Therefore, the word “etc.” refers only to water not for consumption, not to water for consumption. It is stated in the Subcommentary to the Vinayavinicchaya: “Here, in ‘in water from a latrine, the ocean, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ includes all water not for consumption. For that very reason, it states their not being for consumption as the cause.” Therefore, it should be understood that defecating or urinating in water for human consumption—such as in rivers, natural lakes, reservoirs, and ponds—is not proper. Since it is stated in the commentary: “When it is raining and there is a flood of water all around, if it is discharged while one is looking for a dry spot, it is permissible. It is stated in the Mahāpaccarī that at such a time, if one cannot find a dry spot, it is permissible to do it,” it is understood in accordance with the commentary that in large rivers, natural lakes, etc., when traveling by boat, if on such an occasion, having said, “Bring it to the shore,” one is in a place where it is not possible to do so, it is proper to relieve oneself in the water; there is no offense. This should be investigated and accepted.

Nahānerukkhādighaṃsanakathā

Discourse on Rubbing against Trees, etc., while Bathing

21. Nahāne rukkhādighaṃsananti ettha aṭṭhapadākārenāti aṭṭhapadaphalakākārena, jūtaphalakasadisanti vuttaṃ hoti. Mallakamūlakasaṇṭhānenāti kheḷamallakamūlasaṇṭhānena. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.243) pana “aṭṭhapadākārenāti jūtaphalake aṭṭhagabbharājiākārena. Mallakamūlasaṇṭhānenāti kheḷamallakamūlasaṇṭhānena. Idañca vaṭṭādhārakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kaṇṭake uṭṭhāpetvā katavaṭṭakapālassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Puthupāṇikanti muṭṭhiṃ akatvā vikasitahatthatalehi piṭṭhiparikammaṃ vuccati. Etameva sandhāya hatthaparikamma”nti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 244) pana “puthupāṇinā kattabbaṃ kammaṃ puthupāṇikamma”nti vuttaṃ.

21. Regarding 'rubbing against trees, etc., while bathing': Here, 'in the shape of an aṭṭhapada' means in the shape of an aṭṭhapada board; that is to say, similar to a game board. 'In the shape of a mallaka root' means in the shape of a kheḷamallaka root. In the Vimativinodanī it is said: “'In the shape of an aṭṭhapada' means in the shape of the eight rows of squares on a game board. 'In the shape of a mallaka root' means in the shape of a kheḷamallaka root. And this is said with reference to a round support. This is a term for a round scraper made with raised prongs. 'Puthupāṇika' means massaging the back with open palms, without making a fist. With reference to this, it is called 'hand-work.'” But in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is said: “Work to be done with an open hand is called 'puthupāṇikamma' (open-hand work).”

Evaṃ pāḷianusāreneva nahāne kattabbākattabbaṃ dassetvā idāni nahānatitthe nahāyantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [V 2.0247] nahānavidhiṃ dassento “idaṃ panettha nahānavatta”ntiādimāha. Tattha passantānaṃ appasādāvahanato, gihipurisānaṃ kammaṃ viyāti garahitabbabhāvato ca vuttaṃ “yattha vā tattha vā…pe… na otaritabba”nti. Aññesu sammukhībhūtesu anudakasāṭakena nahāyituṃ dukkarattā “sabbadisā pana oloketvā vivittabhāvaṃ ñatvā”ti vuttaṃ. Evampi khāṇugumbalatādīhi paṭicchannāpi hutvā tiṭṭheyyunti āha “khāṇu…pe… ukkāsitvā”ti. Uddhaṃmukhena cīvarāpanayanaṃ harāyitabbaṃ siyāti vuttaṃ “avakujja…pe… apanetvā”ti. Tato kāyabandhanaṭṭhapanavattamāha “kāyabandhana”ntyādinā[M 2.0337]. Tato udakasāṭikāya sati taṃ nivāsetvā otaritabbaṃ siyā, tāya asatiyā kiṃ kātabbanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “sace”tiādi. Tattha pubbe “ṭhitakeneva na otaritabba”nti ahirikākārassa paṭisiddhattā idha hirimantākāraṃ dasseti udakante ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā nivāsanaṃ mocetvāti. Uṇṇaṭṭhāne, samaṭṭhāne vā pasārite sati vā tena aññattha gaccheyyāti āha “sace ninnaṭṭhāna”ntiādi.

Having thus shown in accordance with the Pāli what should and should not be done when bathing, now, explaining the bathing procedure for bhikkhus bathing at a bathing place, he begins with, “This here is the bathing observance.” In this context, because it may cause displeasure to those who see it and because it is censurable as being like the work of laymen, it is said, “One should not enter the water just anywhere….” Because it is difficult to bathe without a bathing cloth when others are present, it is said, “But having looked in all directions and ascertained that the place is secluded….” Even so, people might be standing concealed by stumps, bushes, creepers, etc., so he says, “by a stump… having cleared the throat.” Removing the robe with face upturned would be shameful, so it is said, “bending over… having taken it away.” Next, he states the observance for placing the waistband with, “the waistband…,” and so on. Then, if one has a bathing cloth, one should enter after putting it on. Addressing the question, “If one does not have it, what should be done?” he says, “If…,” and so on. Here, since entering while standing—a shameless posture—was forbidden earlier, he now shows the conscientious posture: having sat down in the squatting position at the water's edge and removed the lower garment. If the robe is spread out in a high place or a level place, it might be blown elsewhere by the wind, so he says, “If the place is low…,” and so on.

Otarantena kiṃ kātabbanti pucchaṃ sandhāya “otarantena saṇika”ntyādi. Tattha pubbe “vegena na otaritabba”nti paṭisiddhānurūpamāha “saṇika”nti. Atigambhīraṃ gacchanto udakoghataraṅgavātādīhi paharanto calitakāyo siyā, atiuttāne nisīdanto appaṭicchannakāyo siyāti vuttaṃ “nābhippamāṇamattaṃ otaritvā”ti. Attano hatthavikārādīhi vīciṃ uṭṭhāpento, saddañca karonto uddhaṭacapalabhāvo siyāti vuttaṃ “vīciṃ anuṭṭhapentena saddaṃ akarontena nivattitvā”ti. Nivattitvā kiṃ kātabbanti āha āgatadisābhimukhena nimujjitabba”nti, abhimukhena hutvāti pāṭhaseso. Idāni tapphalaṃ dassento “eva”ntyādimāha. Tato ummujjantena kiṃ kātabbanti pucchāyamāha “ummujjantenapī”tiādi. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Cīvaraṃ pārupitvāva ṭhātabbaṃ, kasmāti ce? Na tāva kāyato udakaṃ otarati, tasmā thokaṃ kālaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ cīvaraṃ ubhohi hatthehi ante gahetvā purato katvā ṭhātabbaṃ. Tato kāyassa sukkhabhāvaṃ ñatvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā yathāruci gantabbanti.

With reference to the question, “What should be done by one entering the water?” he says, “One entering slowly…,” etc. Here, in accordance with the earlier prohibition, “One should not enter with speed,” he says “slowly.” If one goes into very deep water, one's body may become unsteady, being struck by floods, waves, wind, etc.; if one sits in very shallow water, one's body may be uncovered. Therefore, it is said, “having entered to about the depth of the navel.” By making gestures with one's hands, etc., one might stir up waves and make noise, becoming agitated and fickle. Thus, it is said, “without stirring up waves and without making noise, having turned around….” What should be done after turning around? He says, “one should submerge facing the direction from which one came.” The reading is completed with 'having faced.' Now, showing the result of that, he says “thus,” etc. Then, in answer to the question, “What should be done by one emerging?” he says, “One emerging also…,” etc. The rest is easy to understand. One should stand only after having put on the robe. If it is asked why, it is because the water has not yet run off the body. Therefore, for a short while, one should stand holding the upper robe by its edges with both hands in front of oneself. Then, having noticed that the body is dry, one should put on the robe and go as one wishes.

Valikādikathā

The Discussion on Sand, etc.

22. Valikādikathāyaṃ [M 2.0338] “muttolambakādīnanti ādi-saddena kuṇḍalādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Palambakasuttanti [V 2.0248] yaññopacitākārena olambakasutta”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.245). Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.245) pana “muttolambakādīnanti ādi-saddena kuṇḍalādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Palambakasuttanti brāhmaṇānaṃ yaññopacitasuttādiākāraṃ vuccati. Valayanti hatthapādavalaya”nti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 245) pana “kaṇṇato nikkhantamuttolambakādīnaṃ kuṇḍalādīnanti likhitaṃ. ‘Kāyūra’nti pāḷipāṭho. ‘Keyūrādīnī’ti ācariyenuddhaṭa”nti vuttaṃ.

22. In the Discussion on Sand, etc., it is said: 'In "pearl pendants, etc." (muttolambakādīni), the word "etc." (ādi) includes earrings and so on. "A hanging thread" (palambakasutta) refers to a thread hanging down in the manner of a sacrificial cord'—this is in the Sāratthadīpanī. The Vimativinodanī, however, states: 'In "pearl pendants, etc." (muttolambakādīni), the word "etc." (ādi) includes earrings and so on. "A hanging thread" (palambakasutta) refers to the form of the thread, etc., of a brahmin's sacrificial cord. "A bracelet" (valaya) means a bracelet for the hands and feet.' In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā, however, it is written: 'of pearl pendants, etc., coming from the ear, and of earrings, etc.' The Pāli reading is 'kāyūra,' and 'keyūrādīni' is what the teachers have extracted.

Dīghakesakathā

The Discussion on Long Hair

23. Dīghakesakathāyaṃ sāratthadīpaniyaṃ na kiñci vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.246) pana “dvaṅguleti upayogabahuvacanaṃ, dvaṅgulappamāṇaṃ atikkāmetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti attho. Ettha ca dumāsassa vā dvaṅgulassa vā atikkantabhāvaṃ ajānantassapi kesamassugaṇanāya acittakāpattiyo hontīti vadanti. Kocchenāti usīrahīrādīni bandhitvā samakaṃ chinditvā gahitakocchena. Cikkalenāti silesayuttatelena. Uṇhābhitattarajasirānampīti uṇhābhitattānaṃ rajokiṇṇasirānaṃ. Addahatthenāti allahatthenā”ti vuttaṃ.

23. Concerning the Discussion on Long Hair, nothing is said in the Sāratthadīpanī. In the Vimativinodanī, however, it is said: 'The word "two finger-breadths" (dvaṅguleti) is a plural of usage; the meaning is that it is not proper to exceed the measure of two finger-breadths. Here, they say that even for one who does not know that the limit of two months or two finger-breadths has been exceeded, offenses are incurred unintentionally in the reckoning of hair and beard. "With a brush" (kocchena) means with a brush made by binding vetiver root, etc., and cutting it evenly. "With a sticky substance" (cikkalena) means with a glutinous oil. "Of heads afflicted by heat and dust" (uṇhābhitattarajasirānaṃ) means of heads that are afflicted by heat and covered with dust. "With a wet hand" (addahatthena) means with a moist hand.'

Upari pana pāḷiyaṃ (cūḷava. 275) “tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū massuṃ kappāpenti. Massuṃ vaḍḍhāpenti. Golomikaṃ kārāpenti. Caturassakaṃ kārāpenti. Parimukhaṃ kārāpenti. Aḍḍhadukaṃ kārāpenti. Dāṭhikaṃ ṭhapenti. Sambādhe lomaṃ saṃharāpenti. Manussā ujjhāyanti khīyanti vipācenti ‘seyyathāpi gihī kāmabhogino’ti[M 2.0339]. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – na, bhikkhave, massu kappāpetabbaṃ. Na massu vaḍḍhāpetabbaṃ. Na golomikaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ. Na caturassakaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ. Na parimukhaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ. Na aḍḍhadukaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ. Na dāṭhikā ṭhapetabbā. Na sambādhe lomaṃ saṃharāpetabbaṃ, yo saṃharāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti āgataṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyampi (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 275) “massuṃ kappāpentīti kattariyā massuṃ chedāpenti. Massuṃ vaḍḍhāpentīti massuṃ dīghaṃ kārenti. Golomikanti hanukamhi dīghaṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ eḷakamassu vuccati. Caturassakanti catukoṇaṃ. Parimukhanti udare lomasaṃharaṇaṃ. Aḍḍhadukanti udare lomarājiṭṭhapanaṃ. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti massukappāpanādīsu sabbattha āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vuttaṃ.

Further, in the Pāli text it is stated: 'Now at that time, the group-of-six bhikkhus had their beards cut. They let their beards grow long. They had goatees made. They had square beards made. They had hair removed on the abdomen. They had a line of hair left on the abdomen. They kept sideburns. They had hair removed from their private parts. People complained, grumbled, and criticized, saying: "They are just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures!" They reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, a beard should not be cut. A beard should not be allowed to grow long. A goatee should not be made. A square beard should not be made. Hair should not be removed on the abdomen. A line of hair should not be left on the abdomen. Sideburns should not be kept. Hair should not be removed from private parts. Whoever should have it removed commits an offense of wrong-doing."' In the commentary, too, it is said: '"Had their beards cut" means they had their beards cut with scissors. "Let their beards grow long" means they made their beards long. "Goatee" (golomika) is said to be a long beard kept on the chin, called a goat’s beard. "Square" (caturassaka) means four-cornered. "Around the mouth" (parimukha) means the removal of hair on the abdomen. "Half-ducat" (aḍḍhaduka) means leaving a line of hair on the abdomen. "An offense of wrong-doing": in all cases of having the beard cut and so on, there is an offense of wrong-doing.'

Puna [V 2.0249] pāḷiyaṃ (cūḷava. 275) “tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū sakkharikāyapi madhusitthakenapi nāsikālomaṃ gāhāpenti, nāsikā dukkhā honti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, saṇḍāsanti. Tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū palitaṃ gāhāpenti. Manussā ujjhāyanti khīyanti vipācenti ‘seyyathāpi gihī kāmabhogino’ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – na, bhikkhave, palitaṃ gāhāpetabbaṃ, yo gāhāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti āgataṃ. “Sakkharādīhi nāsikālomaggāhāpane āpatti natthi, anurakkhaṇatthaṃ pana saṇḍāso anuññāto”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, palitaṃ gāhāpetabbanti ettha bhamukāya vā nalāṭe vā dāṭhikāya vā uggantvā bībhacchaṃ ṭhitaṃ, tādisaṃ lomaṃ palitaṃ vā apalitaṃ vā gāhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ca vuttaṃ.

Again, in the Pāli text (Cūḷavagga 275) it is stated: 'Now at that time, bhikkhus were having their nose hairs removed with a potsherd or with beeswax, and their noses became sore. "I allow, bhikkhus, tweezers." Now at that time, the group-of-six bhikkhus were having grey hair plucked. People complained, grumbled, and criticized, saying: "Just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures!" They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [The Blessed One said:] "Bhikkhus, grey hair should not be plucked. Whoever has it plucked commits an offense of wrong-doing."' It is said in the commentary: 'There is no offense in having nose hair plucked with a potsherd, etc., but tweezers are allowed for maintenance.' And it is also said: 'Regarding the statement "Bhikkhus, grey hair should not be plucked," here it is proper to have such hair removed—whether grey or not—that has grown on the eyebrows, forehead, or sideburns and stands out repulsively.'

Ādāsādikathā

The Discussion on Mirrors, etc.

24. Ādāsādikathāyaṃ ādāso nāma maṇḍanapakatikānaṃ manussānaṃ attano mukhacchāyādassanatthaṃ kaṃsalohādīhi [M 2.0340] kato bhaṇḍaviseso. Udakapatto nāma udakaṭṭhapanako pātisarāvādiko bhājanaviseso. Kaṃsapattādīnīti ādāsabhāvena akatāni parisuddhabhāvena ālokakarāni vatthūni. Ādi-saddena suvaṇṇarajatajātiphalikādayo saṅgaṇhāti, kañjiyādīnīti ettha ādi-saddena dravajātikāni telamadhukhīrādīni. Ābādhapaccayāti attano mukhe uppannavaṇapaccayā. Tenāha “sañchavi nu kho me vaṇo”tiādi. Āyuṃ saṅkharotīti āyusaṅkhāro. Ko so? Attabhāvo, taṃ āyusaṅkhāraṃ, taṃ olokento kenākārena olokeyyāti pucchāyamāha “jiṇṇo nu khomhi noti eva”nti. Tassattho – mama attabhāvo jiṇṇo nu kho vā, no jiṇṇo nu kho vāti evaṃ iminā manasikārena kammaṭṭhānasīsena oloketuṃ vaṭṭati. “Sobhati nu kho me attabhāvo, no vā”ti evaṃ pavattena attasinehavasena oloketuṃ na vaṭṭatīti.

24. In the Discussion on Mirrors, etc., a mirror is a special item made of bronze, metal, etc., for people fond of adornment to see the reflection of their own face. A water bowl is a special vessel, such as a dish or saucer, for holding water. Bronze bowls and so on are objects not made to be mirrors but which, being pure, are reflective. By the word 'etc.' it includes gold, silver, genuine crystal, and so on. Here, in 'rice-gruel, etc.', the word 'etc.' includes liquid substances like oil, honey, milk, etc. 'On account of illness' means on account of a sore that has arisen on one's face. Therefore he said: 'Is there a sore on my skin?' etc. Because it determines the life-span, it is called the life-formation. What is that? The personal existence (attabhāva). When asked in what way one should look at that life formation, he said: 'Thus: "Am I old or not?"' The meaning is: it is proper to look with this attention, with the meditation subject as the chief thing, thus: 'Is my personal existence old, or is it not old?' It is not proper to look out of self-love with the thought: 'Is my personal existence beautiful or not?'

Na mukhaṃ ālimpitabbanti vippasannachavivaṇṇakarehi mukhalepanehi na limpitabbaṃ. Na ummadditabbanti nānāummaddanehi na ummadditabbaṃ. Na cuṇṇetabbanti mukhacuṇṇakena na makkhetabbaṃ. Na manosilikāya mukhaṃ lañjetabbanti manosilāya tilakādilañjanāni na kātabbāni[V 2.0250]. Na kevalaṃ manosilāyameva, haritālādīhipi tāni na vaṭṭantiyeva. Aṅgarāgādayo pākaṭāyeva.

'The face should not be anointed' means it should not be smeared with facial ointments that make the skin-complexion clear and bright. 'It should not be massaged' means it should not be massaged with various unguents. 'It should not be powdered' means it should not be coated with face powder. 'The face should not be marked with red arsenic' means marks such as a tilaka should not be made with red arsenic. Not only with red arsenic, but it is also not proper to use orpiment and so on. Body paints and the like are obviously not allowed.

Naccādikathā

Explanation of Dancing, etc.

25. Naccādikathāyaṃ “sādhugītanti aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttagītaṃ. Caturassena vattenāti paripuṇṇena uccāraṇavattena. Taraṅgavattādīnaṃ uccāraṇavidhānāni naṭṭhappayogānī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.248-249) vuttaṃ, vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.248-249) “sādhugītanti aniccatādipaṭisaññuttaṃ [M 2.0341] gītaṃ. Caturassena vattenāti paripuṇṇena uccāraṇavattena. Taraṅgavattādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ ‘sabbesaṃ…pe… lakkhaṇa’nti vuttaṃ. Yattakāhi mattāhi akkharaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, tatopi adhikamattāyuttaṃ katvā kathanaṃ vikārakathanaṃ nāma, tathā akatvā kathanameva lakkhaṇanti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 248-249) pana “sādhugītaṃ nāma parinibbutaṭṭhāne gītanti likhitaṃ. Dantagītaṃ gāyitukāmānaṃ vākkaraṇīyaṃ. Dantagītassa vibhāvanatthaṃ ‘yaṃ gāyissāmā’tiādimāha. Caturassavattaṃ nāma catupādagāthāvattaṃ. ‘Taraṅgavattādīni uccāraṇavidhānāni naṭṭhappayogānī’ti likhita”nti vuttaṃ.

25. In the explanation of dancing, etc., it is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.248-249): “‘Good singing’ means singing connected with impermanence, etc. ‘With a four-square rhythm’ means with a complete rhythm of articulation. The methods of articulation such as wave-rhythm are practices that have been lost.” In the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.248-249) it also says: “‘Good singing’ means singing connected with the perception of impermanence, etc. ‘With a four-square rhythm’ means with a complete rhythm of articulation. To show the common characteristic of all, such as wave-rhythm, it is said, ‘Of all… the characteristic.’ When a syllable is complete by a certain measure, to make an utterance using a longer measure than that is called a distorted utterance; not doing so is the characteristic—this is the meaning.” In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 248-249), however, it is stated: “It is written that ‘good singing’ is singing about the state of one who is completely extinguished. Teeth-singing is the vocal preparation for those who wish to sing. To explain teeth-singing, it begins with, ‘What we shall sing….’ ‘Four-square rhythm’ means the meter of a four-pāda verse. It is written: ‘The methods of articulation such as wave-rhythm are practices that have been lost.’”

Aṅgacchedādikathā

Explanation of Mutilation, etc.

26. Aṅgacchedādikathāyaṃ “attano aṅgajātaṃ chindantasseva thullaccayaṃ, tato aññaṃ chindantassa dukkaṭaṃ, ābādhapaccayā chindantassa anāpattī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.251) pana “aṅgajātanti bījavirahitaṃ purisanimittaṃ. Bīje hi chinne opakkamikapaṇḍako nāma abhabbo hotīti vadanti. Eke pana ‘bījassapi chedanakkhaṇe dukkaṭāpatti eva, kamena purisindriyādike antarahite paṇḍako nāma abhabbo hoti, tadā liṅganāsanāya nāsetabbo’ti vadanti. Tādisaṃ vā dukkhaṃ uppādentassāti muṭṭhippahārādīhi attano dukkhaṃ uppādentassā”ti vuttaṃ.

26. In the explanation of mutilation, etc., it is stated in the commentary: “For one who cuts off his own genitals, there is a grave offense; for one who cuts off another’s, a wrongdoing; but for one who cuts them off on account of illness, there is no offense.” In the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.251), however, it is said: “‘Genitals’ means the male organ without the testicles. For they say that if the testicles are cut, one becomes an ‘acquired eunuch’ (opakkamikapaṇḍaka), who is unfit for ordination. But some say that even at the moment of cutting the testicles, there is only an offense of wrongdoing; when the male faculty, etc., gradually disappears, he becomes an unfit eunuch, and then he should be expelled for destroying the male characteristic. Or, it refers to one who inflicts such suffering on himself, that is, one who causes himself suffering by blows with the fist, etc.”

Pattakathā

Explanation of the Bowl

28. Pattakathāyaṃ [V 2.0251] “bhūmiādhāraketi valayādhārake. Dāruādhārakadaṇḍādhārakesūti ekadārunā kataādhārake, bahūhi daṇḍakehi kataādhārake vāti attho[M 2.0342]. Tīhi daṇḍehi kato pana na vaṭṭati. Bhūmiyaṃ pana nikkujjitvā ekameva ṭhapetabbanti ettha ‘dve ṭhapentena upari ṭhapitapattaṃ ekena passena bhūmiyaṃ phusāpetvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti vadanti. Ālindakamiḍḍhikādīnanti pamukhamiḍḍhikādīnaṃ. Parivattetvā tattheva patiṭṭhātīti ettha ‘parivattetvā tatiyavāre tattheva miḍḍhiyā patiṭṭhātī’ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Paribhaṇḍanteti ettha paribhaṇḍaṃ nāma gehassa bahikuṭṭapādassa thirabhāvatthaṃ katā tanukamiḍḍhikā vuccati. Tanukamiḍḍhikāyāti khuddakamiḍḍhikāya. Miḍḍhantepi ādhārake ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. ‘Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ādhāraka’nti hi vacanato miḍḍhādīsu yattha katthaci ādhārakaṃ ṭhapetvā tattha pattaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati ādhārake ṭhapanokāsassa aniyamitattāti vadanti. ‘Pattamāḷo nāma vaṭṭetvā pattānaṃ agamanatthaṃ vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā iṭṭhakādīhi parikkhipitvā kato’ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Ghaṭikanti upari yojitaṃ aggaḷaṃ. Tāvakālikaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti sakideva gahetvā tena āmisaṃ paribhuñjitvā chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo. Ghaṭikaṭāheti bhājanakapāle. Pāḷiyaṃ abhuṃ meti ettha bhavatīti bhū, vaḍḍhi. Na bhūti abhū, avaḍḍhi. Bhayavasena pana sā itthī ‘abhu’nti āha, vināso mayhanti attho. Chavasīsassa pattanti chavasīsamayaṃ pattaṃ. Pakativikārasambandhe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Abhedepi vā tadupacāravasenevāyaṃ vohāro ‘silāputtakassa sarīra’ntiādīsu viya. Cabbetvāti khāditvā. Ekaṃ udakagaṇḍusaṃ gahetvāti vāmahattheneva pattaṃ ukkhipitvā mukhena gaṇḍusaṃ gahetvā. Ucchiṭṭhahatthenāti sāmisena hatthena. Ettāvatāti ekagaṇḍusaṃ gahaṇamattena. Luñcitvāti tato maṃsaṃ uddharitvā. Etesu sabbesu paṇṇattiṃ jānātu vā, mā vā, āpattiyevā”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.253-255) vuttaṃ.

28. In the explanation of the bowl: ‘A ground-stand’ refers to a ring-stand. ‘On a wood-stand or a stick-stand’ means on a stand made from a single piece of wood or from many sticks. However, a stand made with three sticks is not allowable. On the ground, only one should be placed, overturned. Here, they say: “When placing two, it is allowable to place the upper bowl so that it touches the ground on one side.” ‘On verandas, platforms, etc.’ refers to prominent platforms, etc. Regarding ‘having turned it over, it stands right there,’ it is said in the glosses: “After turning it over, on the third occasion it stands right there on the platform.” Regarding ‘on a buttress,’ here a buttress refers to a slender platform made to stabilize the outer posts of a house. ‘On a slender platform’ means on a small platform. It is also permissible to place the bowl on a stand on a platform. Because it is said, “I allow, bhikkhus, a stand,” they say it is allowable to place a stand anywhere, on a platform, etc., and place the bowl on it, since the place for placing it on a stand is not specified.
