It is said in the glosses: “A bowl-enclosure is a circular or square enclosure made with bricks, etc., to prevent the bowls from moving.” ‘A latch’ refers to a bolt fixed above. ‘It is permissible to use it temporarily’ means that it is permissible to take it just once, consume almsfood with it, and then discard it. ‘On a potsherd’ refers to a fragment of a vessel. In the Pāli, regarding ‘abhuṃ me,’ ‘bhū’ means ‘to be,’ growth. ‘Na bhū’ is ‘abhū,’ non-growth. But out of fear, that woman said ‘abhuṃ,’ meaning ‘destruction is mine.’ ‘The bowl of a corpse’s head’ refers to a bowl made of a skull. This is a genitive of material. Or even when there is no difference, this usage is metaphorical, as in phrases like ‘the body of a stone doll.’ ‘Having chewed’ means having eaten. ‘Taking one mouthful of water’ means lifting the bowl with the left hand and taking a mouthful with the mouth. ‘With a soiled hand’ means with a hand that has food on it. ‘By this much’ refers only to taking a single mouthful. ‘Tearing off’ means removing the meat from it. ‘In all these cases, whether one knows the regulation or not, there is still an offense,’ as explained in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.253-255).

Vimativinodaniyaṃ [M 2.0343] (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.252) pana “gihivikaṭānīti gihisantakāni. Pāḷiyaṃ na acchupiyantīti na phussitāni honti. Rūpakākiṇṇāni itthirūpādiākiṇṇāni. Bhūmiādhāraketi dantādīhi kate valayādhārake. Etassa valayādhārakassa anucchavitāya ṭhapitā pattā na parivattantīti ‘tayo patte ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti vuttaṃ. Anuccatañhi sandhāya ayaṃ ‘bhūmiādhārako’ti vutto. Dāruādhārakadaṇḍādhārakesūti ekadārunā [V 2.0252] kataādhārake ca bahūhi daṇḍakehi kataādhārake ca, ete ca uccatarā honti pattehi saha patanasabhāvā, tena ‘susajjitesū’ti vuttaṃ. Bhamakoṭisadisenāti yattha dhamakaraṇādiṃ pavesetvā likhanti, tassa bhamakassa koṭiyā sadiso. Tādisassa dāruādhārakassa avitthiṇṇatāya ṭhapitopi patto patatīti ‘anokāso’ti vutto. Ālindakamiḍḍhikādīnanti pamukhamiḍḍhikādīnaṃ, uccavatthukānanti attho. Bāhirapasseti pāsādādīnaṃ bahikuṭṭe. Tanukamiḍḍhikāyāti vedikāya. Sabbattha pana hatthappamāṇato abbhantare ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, ādhārake pana tato bahipi vaṭṭati. Aññena pana bhaṇḍakenāti aññena bhārabhaṇḍena bhaṇḍakena. ‘Bandhitvā olambitu’nti ca vuttattā pattatthavikāya aṃsabaddhako yathā laggitaṭṭhānato na parigaḷati, tathā sabbathāpi bandhitvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Bandhitvāpi upari ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti ‘upari nisīdantā ottharitvā bhindantī’ti vuttaṃ. Tattha ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti nisīdanasaṅkābhāvato vuttaṃ. Bandhitvā vāti bandhitvā ṭhapitachatte vā. Yo kocīti bhattapūropi tucchapattopi. Pariharitunti divase divase piṇḍāya caraṇatthāya ṭhapetuṃ. Pattaṃ alabhantena pana ekadivasaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā bhuñjitvā chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭati. Paṇṇapuṭādīsupi eseva nayo. Chavasīsassa [M 2.0344] pattoti chavasīsamayo patto, pakativikārasambandhe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Cabbetvāti niṭṭhubhitvā. ‘Paṭiggahaṃ katvā’ti vuttattā ucchiṭṭhahatthena udakaṃ gahetvā pattaṃ paripphositvā dhovanaghaṃsanavasena hatthaṃ dhovituṃ vaṭṭati. Ettakena hi pattaṃ paṭiggahaṃ katvā hattho dhovito nāma na hoti. Ekaṃ udakagaṇḍusaṃ gahetvāti pattaṃ aphusitvā tattha udakameva ucchiṭṭhahatthena ukkhipitvā gaṇḍusaṃ katvā, vāmahattheneva vā pattaṃ ukkhipitvā mukhena gaṇḍusaṃ gahetumpi vaṭṭati. Bahi udakena vikkhāletvāti dvīsu aṅgulīsu āmisamattaṃ vikkhāletvā bahi gahetumpi vaṭṭati. Paṭikhāditukāmoti ettha sayaṃ na khāditukāmopi aññesaṃ khādanārahaṃ ṭhapetuṃ labhati. Tattheva katvāti patteyeva yathāṭhapitaṭṭhānato anuddharitvā. Luñcitvāti tato maṃsameva niravasesaṃ uppaṭṭetvā”ti vuttaṃ.

In the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.252), however, it is stated: “‘Improper things for householders’ means items belonging to householders. ‘Not touched in the Pāli’ means they are not touched. ‘Crowded with figures’ refers to being crowded with figures of women, etc. ‘A ground-stand’ means a ring-stand made of ivory, etc. Because of the suitability of this ring-stand, bowls placed on it do not turn over—hence, it is said, ‘It is allowable to place three bowls.’ This is called a ‘ground-stand’ with reference to its lowness. ‘On wood-stands and stick-stands’ refers to stands made from a single piece of wood and stands made from multiple sticks. These are higher and are liable to fall together with the bowls; therefore it is said, ‘on well-prepared ones.’ ‘Like the point of a lathe’ means like the point of that lathe where they insert a drill, etc., and carve. Because such a wooden stand is not wide, a bowl placed on it falls; hence it is called ‘unsuitable.’ ‘On verandas, platforms, etc.’ refers to prominent platforms, etc., meaning high objects. ‘On the outer side’ means on the outer wall of a monastery, etc. ‘On a slender platform’ refers to a railing. In all cases, it is allowable to place them within a hand’s breadth inside, but on a stand, it is allowable even further out than that. ‘By another item’ means by another load-bearing item. And since it is said, ‘Having tied it, one may hang it,’ just as the shoulder strap of a bowl-bag, when tied, does not slip from its fastened position, so too is it allowable to fasten it securely in every way. But it is not allowable to place it above after tying—hence, it is said, ‘Those sitting above might step on it and break it.’ Here, ‘It is allowable to place it’ is said because there is no fear of it being sat on. ‘Or having tied it’ means on a tied and placed parasol. ‘Any’ means any bowl, whether full of food or empty. ‘To use it’ means to keep it for going for alms day after day. But one who does not obtain a bowl is allowed to go for alms for a single day, eat, and then discard it. The same method applies to leaf-containers, etc. ‘A bowl of a corpse’s head’ means a bowl made of a corpse’s skull—this is a genitive of material. ‘Having chewed’ means having spat out. Since it is said, ‘Having received it,’ it is allowable to take water with a soiled hand, rinse the bowl, and wash the hand by rubbing and scrubbing. For by this much, the hand is not considered to have been washed after the bowl has been accepted. ‘Having taken one mouthful of water’ means, without touching the bowl, to lift only the water with the soiled hand and make a mouthful; or it is also allowable to lift the bowl with the left hand and take a mouthful with the mouth. ‘Having rinsed it with water outside’ means rinsing off the food residue from two fingers and taking it outside. Regarding ‘wishing to reject it,’ here, even if one does not wish to eat it oneself, one is allowed to set it aside for others to eat. ‘Having done it right there’ means without lifting it from where it was placed in the bowl. ‘Having torn it off’ means having stripped off all the meat from it without remainder.”

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 254) pana “ālindakamiḍḍhikādīnanti pamukhamiḍḍhikādīnaṃ. Parivattetvā tatthevāti ettha ‘parivattetvā tatiyavāre tattheva miḍḍhikāya patiṭṭhātī’ti likhitaṃ. Paribhaṇḍaṃ nāma gehassa bahikuṭṭapādassa thirabhāvatthaṃ katā tanukamiḍḍhikā vuccati, ettha ‘parivattetvā patto bhijjatīti adhikaraṇabhedāsaṅkāraabhāve ṭhāne ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti likhitaṃ. Pattamāḷo vattetvā pattānaṃ apatanatthaṃ vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā iṭṭhakādīhi parikkhipitvā [V 2.0253] māḷakacchannena kato. ‘Pattamaṇḍalikā pattapacchikā kālapaṇṇādīhi katā’ti ca likhitaṃ. Miḍḍhante ādhārake ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati pattasandhāraṇatthaṃ vuttattā. Mañce ādhārakepi na vaṭṭati nisīdanapaccayā vāritattā. Āsannabhūmikattā olambetuṃ vaṭṭati. ‘Aṃsakūṭe laggetvāti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 254) vacanato aggahatthe [M 2.0345] laggetvā aṅke ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatī’ti keci vadanti, na sundaraṃ. Na kevalaṃ yassa pattotiādi yadi hatthena gahitapatte bhedasaññā, pageva aññena sarīrāvayavenāti katvā vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana pacuravohāravasena vuttaṃ. Ghaṭikapālamayaṃ ghaṭikaṭāhaṃ. Chavasīsassa pattanti ‘silāputtakassa sarīraṃ, khīrassa dhārā’tiādivohāravasena vuttaṃ, mañce nisīdituṃ āgatoti attho. Pisācillikāti pisācadārakātipi vadanti. Dinnakameva paṭiggahitameva. Cabbetvāti khāditvā. Aṭṭhīni ca kaṇṭakāni ca aṭṭhikaṇṭakāni. Etesu sabbesu paṇṇattiṃ jānātu vā, mā vā, āpattiyevāti likhita”nti vuttaṃ.

In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 254), however, it is said: “Ālindakamiḍḍhikādīni means the foremost ledges, etc. Regarding ‘having turned it over on the very same,’ here it is written: ‘having turned it over, on the third occasion he stands on the very same ledge.’ Paribhaṇḍa is said to be a thin ledge made for the stability of the base of the outer wall of a house. Here it is written: ‘It is allowable to place it in a place where there is no risk of the bowl breaking when turned over, due to the absence of a basis for doubt.’ A pattamāḷa is made by enclosing a circular or square area with bricks and so on, covered by a pavilion, for the purpose of preventing bowls from falling after being placed there. And it is written: ‘A pattamaṇḍalikā or pattapacchikā is made from dark leaves, etc.’ It is allowable to place it on a support at the end of a ledge, because it is said to be for holding a bowl. It is not allowable on a support on a bed, because it is prohibited as a requisite for sitting. Because it is near the ground, it is allowable to hang it down. Some say: ‘Based on the phrase “having hung it on the shoulder” (Cūḷava. Aṭṭha. 254), it is not allowable to hang it on the tip of the hand and place it on the lap,’ but this is not sound. This was said on the grounds that if there is a perception of breaking when the bowl is held by the hand, how much more so when held by another part of the body. But in the Pāḷi, it is stated according to common parlance. Ghaṭikapālamayaṃ means a pot-sherd bowl. ‘Chavasīsassa patta’ is stated in the sense of a conventional expression, like ‘the body of a stone figure’ or ‘a stream of milk’; the meaning is that he has come to sit on the bed. Pisācillikā is also said to be pisācadārakā (a young goblin). Dinnakameva means what has been given; paṭiggahitameva means what has been accepted. Cabbetvā means having chewed. Aṭṭhīni ca kaṇṭakāni ca is aṭṭhikaṇṭakāni (bones and thorns). Regarding all these, it is written: ‘Whether one knows the regulation or not, it is an offense.’”

Sabbapaṃsukūlādikathā

The Discussion on All Dust-Heap Robes, etc.

29. Sabbapaṃsukūlādikathāyaṃ paṃsu viya kucchitabhāvena ulati pavattatīti paṃsukūlaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ etassāti sabbapaṃsukūliko, pattacīvarādikaṃ sabbaṃ samaṇaparikkhāraṃ paṃsukūlaṃyeva katvā dhāraṇasīloti attho. Samaṇaparikkhāresu katamaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ katvā dhāretuṃ vaṭṭatīti pucchaṃ sandhāyāha “ettha pana cīvarañca mañcapīṭhañca paṃsukūlaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Tattha ca cīvaraṃ vinayavasena ca dhutaṅgasamādānavasena ca vaṭṭati, mañcapīṭhaṃ vinayavaseneva. Katamaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ na vaṭṭatīti āha “ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ pana dinnameva gahetabba”nti, na adinnaṃ, tasmā paṃsukūlaṃ na vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo. Ettha ca “ajjhoharaṇīya”nti vacanena piṇḍapātagilānapaccayabhesajjapaakkhāravasena ubhopi paccaye dasseti.

29. In the Discussion on All Dust-Heap Robes, etc., paṃsukūla is so called because it arises or occurs in a repulsive state like dust. One for whom all that is, is a sabbapaṃsukūlika; the meaning is one who is of the nature of wearing all monastic requisites, such as the bowl and robe, having made them from dust-heap cloths. With reference to the question, ‘Among the monastic requisites, which is it allowable to make from dust-heap cloths and wear?’ he says: ‘Here, however, a robe and a bed and seat from dust-heap cloths are allowable.’ And there, the robe is allowable both by way of the Vinaya and by way of undertaking the ascetic practices, but the bed and seat are allowable only by way of the Vinaya. He states which dust-heap cloth is not allowable: ‘But what is to be eaten should be taken only when given,’ not when not given; therefore, the intention is that it is not allowable as a dust-heap item. And here, by the word ‘what is to be eaten,’ he shows both requisites, by way of almsfood and by way of requisites of medicine for the sick.

Parissāvanakathā

The Discussion on Water-Strainers

30. Parissāvanakathāyaṃ addhānamaggo nāma sabbantimaparicchedena aḍḍhayojanappamāṇo, tattakaṃ maggaṃ parissāvanaṃ aggahetvā [M 2.0346] gacchantopi aññena aparissāvanakena bhikkhunā yāciyamāno hutvā adentopi na vaṭṭati, āpattiyeva. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, parissāvana”nti anujānitvā “coḷakaṃ nappahoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi[V 2.0254], bhikkhave, kaṭacchuparissāvana”nti (cūḷava. 258) vuttattā pakatiparissāvanato kaṭacchuparissāvanaṃ khuddakanti viññāyati. Pakatiparissāvanassa vidhānaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na vuttaṃ, kaṭacchuparissāvanassa pana vidhānaṃ “kaṭacchuparissāvanaṃ nāma tīsu daṇḍakesu vinandhitvā kata”nti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 258) vuttaṃ. Kaṭacchuparissāvanaṃ vatvā puna “coḷakaṃ nappahoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dhamakaraṇa”nti (cūḷava. 258) vuttattā kaṭacchuparissāvanatopi dhamakaraṇo khuddakataroti viññāyati. Dhamakaraṇassa vidhānaṃ heṭṭhā parikkhārakathāyaṃ vuttameva. “Bhikkhū navakammaṃ karonti, parissāvanaṃ na sammati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, daṇḍaparissāvana”nti (cūḷava 259) vuttattā pakatiparissāvanatopi daṇḍaparissāvanaṃ mahantataranti viññāyati. “Daṇḍaparissāvanaṃ na sammati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ottharaka”nti (cūḷava. 259) vacanato daṇḍaparissāvanatopi ottharakaṃ mahantataranti viññāyati. Tesaṃ pana dvinnampi parissāvanānaṃ vidhānaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 259) āgatameva.

30. In the Discussion on Water-Strainers, a journey is a distance of half a yojana as the final limit. It is not allowable for a bhikkhu to travel that distance without taking a water-strainer; nor is it allowable for one who, being asked by another bhikkhu without a water-strainer, does not give one. This is an offense. Because it is said: ‘“I allow, bhikkhus, a water-strainer,” and after allowing it, “A piece of cloth is not enough.” They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, bhikkhus, a ladle-strainer”’ (Cūḷava. 258), it is understood that a ladle-strainer is smaller than a normal water-strainer. The method for a normal water-strainer is not stated in the commentary, but the method for a ladle-strainer is stated: ‘A ladle-strainer is one made by tying it to three small sticks’ (Cūḷava. Aṭṭha. 258). Because it is said, after speaking of the ladle-strainer: ‘“A piece of cloth is not enough.” They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, bhikkhus, a water-pot”’ (Cūḷava. 258), it is understood that a water-pot is smaller than a ladle-strainer. The method for a water-pot has already been stated below in the discussion on requisites. Because it is said: ‘“Bhikkhus are doing new construction work; the water-strainer is not sufficient.” They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, bhikkhus, a pole-strainer”’ (Cūḷava. 259), it is understood that a pole-strainer is larger than a normal water-strainer. Based on: ‘“The pole-strainer is not sufficient.” They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, bhikkhus, a straining-cloth”’ (Cūḷava. 259), it is understood that a straining-cloth is larger than a pole-strainer. But the method for both of those water-strainers has come down in the commentary (Cūḷava. Aṭṭha. 259).

Naggakathā

The Discussion on Nakedness

31. Naggakathāyaṃ na naggena naggo abhivādetabboti naggena navakatarena bhikkhunā naggo vuḍḍhataro bhikkhu na abhivādetabbo na vanditabbo. Kasmā? “Na, bhikkhave, naggena naggo abhivādetabbo, yo abhivādeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 261) bhagavatā vacanato na abhivādetabboti yojanā[M 2.0347]. Ettha pana vadi abhivādanathutīsūti dhātussa curādigaṇattā ṇe-paccayo hoti, na hetvatthattā.

31. In the Discussion on Nakedness, it is said that a naked person should not be greeted by a naked person: a naked, newly ordained monk should not greet or pay respects to an older, naked monk. Why? Because the Blessed One has said, “Monks, a naked person should not be greeted by a naked person. Whoever should greet another naked person incurs an offense of wrong-doing” (Cūḷavagga 261). Therefore, the interpretation is 'should not be greeted.' Here, however, the suffix ṇe is applied to the root vad (in the sense of 'greeting' or 'praising') because it belongs to the curādi group, not because it expresses a causative meaning.

“Akammakehi dhātūhi, bhāve kiccā bhavanti te;

Sakammakehi kammatthe, arahasakkatthadīpakā”ti. –

“With intransitive verbal roots, the participles of necessity are formed in the impersonal sense; with transitive ones, they indicate the object, fitness, and respect.”

Vacanato kammatthe tabba-paccayoti daṭṭhabbo. Na naggena abhivādetabbanti ettha tu naggena bhikkhunā na abhivādetabbanti ettakameva yojanā. Nanu ca bho –

From this statement, the tabba suffix should be understood as indicating the object. However, in the phrase 'Na naggena abhivādetabbaṃ' (There should be no greeting by a naked person), the interpretation is simply that a naked monk should not greet. But indeed, sir—

“Kiccā [V 2.0255] dhātuhyakammehi, bhāveyeva napuṃsake;

Tadantā pāyato kamme, sakammehi tiliṅgikā”ti. –

“Participles of necessity from intransitive roots are always in the impersonal sense and in the neuter gender; those ending in ta, from transitive verbs, are usually in the object sense and are three-gendered.”

Vacanato, imissā ca dhātuyā sakammattā kammaṃ ajjhāharitabbaṃ, kammānurūpañca liṅgaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ, atha kasmā ettakameva yojanā katāti? Kammavacanicchābhāvato. Vuttañhi –

From this statement, and because this root is transitive, an object should be supplied, and the gender should be established in accordance with the object. Why then is only this much interpretation given? Due to the absence of a desire to express the object. For it has been said—

“Kammassāvacanicchāyaṃ, sakammākhyātapaccayā;

Bhāvepi taṃ yathā gehe, devadattena paccate”ti.

“When there is no desire to express the object, the verbal endings from transitive verbs are also used in the impersonal sense, as in 'it is cooked by Devadatta' in the house.”

Yathā ākhyātapaccayasaṅkhātā vibhattiyo sakammakadhātuto bhavantāpi kammavacanicchāya asati kammaṃ avatvā bhāvatthameva vadanti, evaṃ kiccapaccayāpi sakammakadhātuto bhavantāpi kammavacanicchāyābhāvato kammaṃ avatvā bhāvatthameva vadanti, tasmā kammañca anajjhāharitaṃ, kammānurūpañca liṅgaṃ na ṭhapitaṃ, bhāvatthānurūpameva ṭhapitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha hi “ayaṃ nāma puggalo abhivādetabbo”ti acintetvā sāmaññato kattārameva gahetvā ṭhapitoti veditabbo.

Just as the inflections known as verbal endings, though derived from transitive roots, do not express the object when there is no desire to express it, and instead express only the impersonal sense; so too, the kicca suffixes, though derived from transitive roots, do not express the object due to the absence of a desire to express it, and instead express only the impersonal sense. Therefore, the object is not supplied, and the gender is not established in accordance with the object; it should be understood as established only in accordance with the impersonal sense. For here, indeed, one should understand that the agent is established by taking it in a general sense, without thinking, “This particular person is to be greeted.”

Na naggena naggo abhivādāpetabboti ettha pana naggena vuḍḍhatarena bhikkhunā naggo navakataro bhikkhu na abhivādāpetabbo, na vandāpetabboti yojanā. Ettha hi sakāritassa kiccapaccayassa diṭṭhattā, dhātuyā ca sakammakattā navakataro bhikkhu dhātukattā hoti, vuḍḍhataro bhikkhu dhātukammaṃ[M 2.0348], puna kāritasambandhe vuḍḍhataro bhikkhu kāritakattā hoti, navakataro bhikkhu kāritakammaṃ. Vuttañhi –

But here, in the saying 'Na naggena naggo abhivādāpetabbo' (A naked one should not be made to pay homage by a naked one), the interpretation is that a naked elder monk should not make a naked junior monk pay homage or bow down. For here, because the kicca suffix is seen with a causative, and because the root is transitive, the junior monk is the agent of the root, the elder monk is the object of the root; and in relation to the causative, the elder monk is the causative agent, and the junior monk is the causative object. For it was said—

“Hetukriyāya sambandhī-bhāvā kammanti manyate;

Hetukriyāpadhānattā, aññathānupapattito”ti.

“The state of being connected with a causative action is considered the object, because the causative action is predominant, and because it is otherwise inexplicable.”

Na naggena abhivādāpetabbanti ettha tu naggena vuḍḍhatarena bhikkhunā na abhivādāpetabbaṃ, na vandāpetabbanti yojanā, etthāpi kammavacanicchāyābhāvato vuttanayena bhāveyeva kiccapaccayo hotīti daṭṭhabbo. Nanu vandāpake sati vandāpetabbo labbhatiyeva, atha “kasmā kammavacanicchāyābhāvato”ti [V 2.0256] vuttanti? “Vatticchānupubbikā saddapaṭipattī”ti vacanato vatticchābhāvato na vuttanti. Vuttañhetaṃ pubbācariyehi –

However, in the phrase 'Na naggena abhivādāpetabbaṃ' (One should not be made to pay homage by a naked person), the interpretation is that by a naked elder monk, one should not be made to pay homage, nor be made to bow. Here too, due to the absence of a desire to express the object, the kicca suffix should be understood as being in the impersonal sense, according to the method stated. But when there is someone who makes another bow, is it not indeed possible to say 'one is made to bow'? Why then is it said, 'due to the absence of a desire to express the object'? It is not said due to the absence of the speaker's intention, because of the statement, 'The application of words follows the speaker's intention.' For this has been stated by the ancient teachers—

“Vatticchā na bhave santa-mapyasantampi sā bhave;

Taṃ yathānudarā kaññā, samuddo kuṇḍikāti cā”ti.

“The speaker's intention may not be present even when something is present, and it may be present even when something is not present; for example, 'a maiden without a belly' and 'the ocean in a pot.'”

Itaresupi suviññeyyameva. Paṭicchādenti aṅgamaṅgāni etāhīti paṭicchādiyo.

In the other cases too, it is easily understood. Because they cover the major and minor limbs, they are called 'coverings' (paṭicchādiyo).

Gandhapupphakathā

The Discussion on Perfumes and Flowers

32. Gandhapupphakathāyaṃ “gandhagandhaṃ pana gahetvā kavāṭe pañcaṅguliṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vacanato gandhe dinne paṭiggahituṃ vaṭṭati, no limpitunti siddhaṃ. Idāni pana manussā bhikkhū bhojetvā hatthadhovanāvasāne hatthavāsatthāya gandhavilepanaṃ denti, taṃ bhikkhū paṭiggahetvā ekacce hatthameva limpenti, ekacce kāyampi mukhampi ālimpenti, “sugandho vatā”tiādīni vatvā haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāraṃ karonti, taṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti? “Kavāṭe pañcaṅgulikaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vihāre kavāṭadhūpanamattasseva vuttattā kāyadhūpanassa avuttattā, “mālāgandhavilepanadhāraṇamaṇḍanavibhūsanaṭṭhānā veramaṇī”ti [M 2.0349] vacanassānulomato ca na vaṭṭatīti dissati, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. “Pupphaṃ gahetvā vihāre ekamantaṃ nikkhipitu”nti vacanato pupphe dinne gahetuṃ vaṭṭati, na piḷandhanādīni kātunti siddhaṃ. Idāni pana bhikkhūsu gandhapupphesu laddhesu “surabhigandhaṃ vatidaṃ puppha”ntiādīni vatvā pahaṭṭhākāraṃ katvā siṅghanti, taṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti? Tampi vihāreyeva ekamantaṃ ṭhapanassa vuttattā siṅghitabbādibhāvassa avuttattā, mālāgandhādipāṭhassa anulomato ca na vaṭṭatīti dissati, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. “Ekamantaṃ nikkhipitu”nti vacanassa pana sāmatthiyato cetiyapaṭimāpūjanādīni ca kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti viññāyati.

32. In the discussion on perfumes and flowers, it is established that when a fragrant perfume is given, it is permissible to receive it but not to apply it, based on the statement: “It is permissible to apply a five-finger mark of perfume to a door.” Now, however, people, after feeding monks and at the end of washing hands, offer scented ointment for hand fragrance. Some monks, having received it, apply it only to their hands, while others apply it to their bodies and faces as well, saying, “How fragrant!” and so on, and display a delighted appearance. Is this permissible or not? Since it was stated only that “it is permissible to apply a five-finger mark to a door” for the purpose of perfuming the monastery door, and not for perfuming the body, and in accordance with the statement, “abstinence from the occasion of wearing garlands, using perfumes and ointments, and from adornments and embellishments,” it appears that this is not permissible. This should be carefully considered. Regarding flowers, it is established that when flowers are given, it is permissible to receive them but not to do things such as wearing them, based on the statement: “One may take the flower and place it aside in the monastery.” Now, however, when monks receive perfumes or flowers, they sometimes sniff them, making a delighted appearance and saying, “How fragrant this flower is!” and so on. Is this permissible or not? This too, since it was stated only for placing them aside in the monastery, and not for sniffing or similar actions, and in accordance with the text on garlands and perfumes, appears not to be permissible. This should be carefully considered. However, by the capacity of the phrase “place it aside,” it is understood that it is permissible to do things such as making offerings to cetiyas and images.

Āsittakūpadhānakathā

The Discussion on the Inlaid Cushion

33. Āsittakūpadhānakathāyaṃ manussānaṃ bharaṇasīlataṃ sandhāya “tambalohena vā rajatena vā”ti [V 2.0257] vuttaṃ, vikappanatthena pana vā-saddena hiraññena vā suvaṇṇena vātiādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Paṭikkhittattā panāti bhagavatā pana āsittakūpadhānassa sāmaññavasena paṭikkhittattā. Na kevalaṃ ratanapeḷā eva na vaṭṭati, atha kho dārumayāpīti. Ettha pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, taṃ na vilīvamayatālapaṇṇamayavettamayādikaṃ sampiṇḍeti.

33. In the discussion on the inlaid cushion, with reference to people's propensity for adornment, it is said: ‘with copper or with silver.’ But by the sense of alternative, the word ‘or’ includes gold or bullion, and so on. However, because it is prohibited—that is, because the inlaid cushion has been generally prohibited by the Blessed One—not only is a jeweled casket not allowable, but also a wooden one. Here, the word ‘pi’ has the meaning of inclusion, but it does not include things made of bamboo strips, palm leaves, cane, and so on.

Maḷorikakathā

The Discussion on the Bowl-Stand

34. Maḷorikakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, maḷorika”nti gilāno bhikkhu bhuñjamāno na sakkoti hatthena pattaṃ sandhāretuṃ, tasmā anuññātaṃ. Pubbe pattasaṅgopanatthaṃ ādhārako anuññāto, idāni bhuñjanatthaṃ. Daṇḍādhārako vuccatīti daṇḍādhārako padhānato maḷorikoti vuccati. Yaṭṭhi…pe… pīṭhādīnipi ādhārakasāmaññena ettheva [M 2.0350] paviṭṭhānīti sambandho. Ādhārakaṃ nāma chiddaṃ viddhampi atthi, aviddhampi atthi, tesu katamaṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “ādhārasaṅkhepagamanato hi…pe… vaṭṭatiyevā”ti.

34. In the discussion on the bowl-stand, it is said: ‘I allow, bhikkhus, a bowl-stand.’ A sick bhikkhu, while eating, is unable to hold his bowl with his hand; therefore, it was permitted. Previously, a support was permitted for the purpose of protecting the bowl; now it is for the purpose of eating. It is called a stick-support; a stick-support is principally called a bowl-stand. A staff … and so on … even seats and the like are included here under the general term ‘support’; this is the connection. A support may be one with a hole pierced through it or one without a hole. Among these, which is allowable? It is said: ‘Because it comes under the category of a support … it is certainly allowable.’

Ekabhājanādikathā

The Discussion on Eating from a Single Vessel and So On

35. Ekabhājanādikathāyaṃ ekatobhuñjanaṃ nāma ekabhājanasmiṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva sahabhuñjanaṃ, na nānābhājane. Ekabhājanasmimpi na nānākkhaṇeti āha “sace panā”tiādi. Tasmiṃ apagate tassa apagatattā itarassa sesakaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Iminā ekakkhaṇe abhuñjanabhāvaṃ dasseti. Itarassapītiādīsu itarassapīti itarītarakathanaṃ, sesabhuñjakaitarato itarassāti attho. Tena paṭhamaṃ gahetvā gatabhikkhumevāha. Tasmiṃ khīṇe tassa khaṇattā paṭhamaṃ gahitavatthussa khīṇattā puna gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Iminā sahaabhuñjanabhāvaṃ dasseti.

35. In the discussion on eating from a single vessel and so on, ‘eating together’ means eating together from a single vessel at the very same moment, not from different vessels. Even from a single vessel, it should not be at different moments; thus it is said: ‘But if…’ and so on. When one has departed, because he has departed, it is allowable for the other to eat the remainder. This shows that they are not eating at the same moment. In the phrases ‘for the other as well,’ etc., ‘for the other as well’ refers to one after the other; the meaning is ‘to the one other than the one eating the remainder.’ By this, it refers to the bhikkhu who first took his portion and left. When that is finished, because that moment has passed and the portion first taken is finished, it is allowable to take again. This shows that they are not eating together.

Na ekamañce nipajjitabbaṃ satipi nānāattharaṇe “na ekamañce tuvaṭṭitabbaṃ, yo tuvaṭṭeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 264) vacanato. Na ekattharaṇe nipajjitabbaṃ satipi nānāmañce “na ekattharaṇā tuvaṭṭitabba”nti (cūḷava. 264) vacanato, pageva ubhinnaṃ ekatteti attho. Yadi evaṃ nānāmañcanānāattharaṇesu asantesu kathaṃ anāpatti siyāti [V 2.0258] cintāyamāha “vavatthānaṃ panā”tiādi. Ekattharaṇapāvuraṇehīti ettha pana ayaṃ ekattharaṇapāvuraṇasaddo na catthasamāso hoti, atha kho bāhiratthasamāsoti āha “ekaṃ attharaṇañceva pāvuraṇañca etesanti ekattharaṇapāvuraṇā”ti, tipadatulyādhikaraṇabāhiratthasamāsoyaṃ. Kesametamadhivacanantyāha “ekaṃ antaṃ attharitvā ekaṃ pārupitvā nipajjantānametaṃ adhivacana”nti, evaṃ nipajjantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etaṃ ekattharaṇapāvuraṇapadaṃ [M 2.0351] adhivacanaṃ hotīti adhippāyo. Kesaṃ pana antanti āha “saṃhārimāna”ntiādi.

One should not lie down on a single bed, even if there is separate bedding, in accordance with the statement: ‘One should not share a single bed; whoever should do so, commits an offense of wrong-doing’ (Cv.V.11.1). One should not lie down on a single bedding, even if there are separate beds, in accordance with the statement: ‘One should not share a single bedding’ (Cv.V.11.1); how much more so when both are one—this is the meaning. If so, when there are no separate beds and separate beddings, how could there be no offense? Reflecting on this, it says: ‘But the distinction…’ and so on. Regarding ‘with a single bedding and covering,’ here the term ‘single bedding and covering’ is not a copulative compound but an external-meaning compound. Thus it says: ‘Those for whom there is a single bedding and a single covering are called “those with a single bedding and covering.”’ This is a three-word-equivalent appositional external-meaning compound. For what is this a designation? It says: ‘This is a designation for those who lie down having spread out one end and having covered themselves with the other.’ The intention is that for bhikkhus lying down in this way, the term ‘single bedding and covering’ is a designation. But the end of what? It says: ‘Of a foldable cloth…’ and so on.

Celapaṭikakathā

The Discussion on the Piece of Cloth

36. Celapaṭikakathāyaṃ celapaṭikanti celasantharaṃ. Kiṃ pana bhagavato sikkhāpadapaññāpane kāraṇanti? “Bodhirājakumāro kira ‘sace ahaṃ puttaṃ lacchāmi, akkamissati me bhagavā celapaṭika’nti iminā ajjhāsayena santhari, abhabbo cesa puttalābhāya, tasmā bhagavā na akkami. Yadi akkameyya, pacchā puttaṃ alabhanto ‘nāyaṃ sabbaññū’ti diṭṭhiṃ gaṇheyya, idaṃ tāva bhagavato anakkamane kāraṇaṃ. Yasmā pana bhikkhūpi ye ajānantā akkameyyuṃ, te gihīnaṃ paribhūtā bhaveyyuṃ, tasmā bhikkhū paribhavato mocetuṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi, idaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpane kāraṇa”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 268) vuttaṃ.

36. In the discussion on the cloth-spread, a ‘cloth-spread’ (celapaṭika) means a cloth-covering. But what was the reason for the Blessed One’s laying down of the training rule? ‘It is said that Prince Bodhi spread it out with the intention: “If I get a son, the Blessed One will step on my cloth-spread.” But he was incapable of getting a son, so the Blessed One did not step on it. If he had stepped on it, then later, upon not getting a son, the prince might have adopted the view: “This one is not all-knowing.” This, for a start, was the reason the Blessed One did not step on it. Furthermore, since bhikkhus who did not know might step on them, they would be looked down upon by the laity. Therefore, to free the bhikkhus from being looked down upon, he laid down the training rule. This is the reason for laying down the training rule,’ so it is said in the commentary (Cv-a 268).

Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.268) pana “bhagavā tuṇhī ahosīti ‘kissa nu kho atthāya rājakumārena ayaṃ mahāsakkāro kato’ti āvajjento puttapatthanāya katabhāvaṃ aññāsi. So hi rājaputto aputtako, sutañcānena ahosi ‘buddhānaṃ kira adhikāraṃ katvā manasā icchitaṃ labhantī’ti, so ‘sacāhaṃ puttaṃ labhissāmi, sammāsambuddho imaṃ celapaṭikaṃ akkamissati. No ce labhissāmi, na akkamissatī’ti patthanaṃ katvā santharāpesi. Atha bhagavā ‘nibbattissati nu kho etassa putto’ti āvajjetvā ‘na nibbattissatī’ti addasa. Pubbe kira so ekasmiṃ dīpe vasamāno bhariyāya samānacchando anekasakuṇapotake khādi. ‘Sacassa mātugāmo puññavā bhaveyya, puttaṃ labheyya, ubhohi pana samānacchandehi hutvā pāpakammaṃ kataṃ[M 2.0352], tenassa putto na nibbattissatīti aññāsi. Dusse pana akkante ‘buddhānaṃ adhikāraṃ katvā patthitaṃ labhantīti loke anussavo, mayā ca mahāadhikāro [V 2.0259] kato, na ca puttaṃ labhāmi, tucchaṃ idaṃ vacana’nti micchāgāhaṃ gaṇheyya. Titthiyāpi ‘natthi samaṇānaṃ akattabbaṃ nāma, celapaṭikampi maddantā āhiṇḍantī’ti ujjhāyeyyuṃ, etarahi ca akkamantesu bahū bhikkhū paracittaviduno, te bhabbattaṃ jānitvā akkamissanti. Abhabbataṃ jānitvā na akkamissanti. Anāgate pana upanissayo mando bhavissati, anāgataṃ na jānissanti. Tesu akkamantesu sace patthitaṃ samijjhissati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce ijjhissati, ‘pubbe bhikkhusaṅghassa adhikāraṃ katvā icchiticchitaṃ labhanti, idāni na labhanti, teyeva maññe bhikkhū paṭipattipūrakā ahesuṃ, ime pana paṭipattiṃ pūretuṃ na sakkontī’ti manussā vippaṭisārino bhavissantīti imehi tīhi kāraṇehi bhagavā akkamituṃ anicchanto tuṇhī ahosi. Pacchimaṃ janataṃ tathāgato anukampatīti idaṃ pana thero vuttesu kāraṇesu tatiyakāraṇaṃ sandhāyāhā”ti vuttaṃ.

But in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha-ṭīkā, Cūḷavagga 3.268) it is said: ‘The Blessed One remained silent. While reflecting, “For what purpose has this great honor been done by the prince?” he understood that it was done out of a desire for a son. For that prince was childless, and he had heard: “It is said that by performing a service for the Buddhas, people obtain what they wish for in their minds.” So he had the cloth spread with the aspiration: “If I get a son, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One will step on this cloth-spread. If I do not get one, he will not step on it.” Then the Blessed One, reflecting, “Will a son be born to him?” saw that one would not be born. It seems that previously, while living on an island, he, with the same inclination as his wife, had eaten many young birds. He understood: “If his wife had been meritorious, he would have gotten a son, but since they both, having the same inclination, committed an evil deed, a son will not be born to him.” Further, if he had stepped on the cloth, the prince might have adopted a wrong view, thinking: “There is a saying in the world that by performing a service for the Buddhas one obtains what is wished for. I have performed a great service, yet I do not get a son. This saying is empty.” The sectarians, too, might have complained: “There is nothing that the ascetics will not do; they wander about trampling on cloth-spreads.” Moreover, at that time many bhikkhus were knowers of the minds of others; knowing of one’s capability, they would step; knowing of one’s incapability, they would not step. In the future, however, the supporting condition will be weak, and they will not know the future. If, when they step, the wish is fulfilled, that is good. If it is not fulfilled, people will become regretful, thinking: “Previously, by performing a service for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, people obtained whatever they wished for, but now they do not. We think those bhikkhus must have been fulfillers of the practice, but these are not able to fulfill the practice.” For these three reasons, the Blessed One, being unwilling to step on it, remained silent. The Elder said the words, “The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations,” with reference to the third of these reasons.’

Pāḷiyaṃ (cūḷava. 268) “yāciyamānena celapaṭikaṃ akkamitu”nti vacanato yāciyamānena eva akkamitabbaṃ, no ayāciyamānenāti siddhaṃ, tatthapi “maṅgalatthāyā”ti (cūḷava. 268) vacanato maṅgalatthāya yāciyamānena akkamitabbaṃ, na sirisobhaggādiatthāya yāciyamānenāti ca, tatthapi “gihīna”nti (cūḷava. 268) vacanato gihīnaṃ eva celasantharaṃ akkamitabbaṃ, na pabbajitānanti ca. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 268) “yā kāci itthī apagatagabbhā vā hotu, garugabbhā vā”ti aniyamavācakena vā-saddena vacanato na kevalaṃ imā dveyeva gahetabbā, atha kho “patiṭṭhitagabbhā vā vijātiputtā vā”tiādinā yā kāci [M 2.0353] maṅgalikāyo itthiyopi purisāpi gahetabbā. “Evarūpesu ṭhānesū”ti vuttattā na kevalaṃ yathāvuttaṭṭhānesuyeva, atha kho taṃsadisesu yesu kesuci maṅgalaṭṭhānesu yesaṃ kesañci gihīnaṃ maṅgalatthāya yāciyamānānaṃ celasantharaṃ akkamituṃ vaṭṭatīti sijjhati, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ (cūḷava. 268) “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dhotapādakaṃ akkamitu”nti sāmaññavasena vacanato, aṭṭhakathāyañca (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 268) “taṃ akkamituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti avisesena vuttattā dhotapādakaṃ ayāciyamānenapi bhikkhunā akkamitabbanti siddhaṃ, “dhotehi pādehi akkamanatthāyā”ti pana vuttattā adhotehi akkamituṃ na vaṭṭatīti ca, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

In the Pāli text (Cv.V.11.5), in accordance with the words, ‘When requested, one may step on a cloth-spread,’ it is established that one should step on it only when requested, not without being requested. There, too, in accordance with the words, ‘for an auspicious purpose,’ it should be stepped on when requested for an auspicious purpose, and not when requested for a purpose such as splendor or good fortune. There, too, in accordance with the words, ‘of householders,’ the cloth-spread of householders only should be stepped on, and not that of the ordained. In the commentary (Cv-a 268), in accordance with the word ‘or,’ which is used without restriction, in the phrase ‘any woman who has already given birth or is heavily pregnant,’ not only these two should be taken, but any auspicious women or men, such as ‘one with an established pregnancy or one who has given birth to a son,’ should also be included. Because it is said, ‘in such cases,’ it is established that it is allowable to step on the cloth-spread not only in the cases mentioned, but also in any similar auspicious cases when requested by any householders for an auspicious purpose. This should be understood after investigation. In the Pāli text (Cv.V.11.5), in accordance with the general statement, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, to step on a foot-wiper,’ and because it is stated in the commentary (Cv-a 268) without specification, ‘it is allowable to step on it,’ it is established that a bhikkhu may step on a foot-wiper even without being requested. But because it is said, ‘for the purpose of stepping on it with washed feet,’ it is not allowable to step on it with unwashed feet. This should be understood after investigation.

Pādaghaṃsanīyakathā

The Discussion on Foot-Scrapers

37. Pādaghaṃsanīyakathāyaṃ [V 2.0260] paṭhamaṃ tāva akappiyapādaghaṃsaniṃ dassetuṃ “katakaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Katakaṃ nāma kīdisanti pucchāya sati vuttaṃ “katakaṃ nāma padumakaṇṇikākāra”ntiādi. Kasmā paṭikkhittanti vuttaṃ “bāhulikānuyogattā”ti. Tato kappiyapādaghaṃsaniyo dassetumāha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tisso pādaghaṃsaniyo”tiādi. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

37. In the discussion on foot-scrapers, first, to show the unallowable foot-scraper, it is said: “A kataka is not permissible.” When asked, “What is a kataka like?” it is said: “A kataka is something shaped like a lotus calyx,” and so on. When asked why it is prohibited, it is said: “Because it leads to luxurious living.” Then, to show the allowable foot-scrapers, it is said: “I allow, bhikkhus, three foot-scrapers,” and so on. The rest is easily understood.

Bījanīkathā

The Discussion on Fans

38. Bījanīkathāyaṃ paṭhamaṃ tāva akappiyabījaniṃ dassetuṃ “camarīvālehi katabījanī na vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Tato kappiyachabījaniyo dassetuṃ “makasabījanīādi vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Tattha kappiyachabījaniyo nāma makasabījanī, vākamayabījanī, usīramayabījanī, morapiñchamayabījanī, vidhūpanaṃ, tālavaṇṭañcāti. Tāsaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ “vidhūpananti bījanī vuccatī”tiādimāha[M 2.0354]. Usīramayaṃ morapiñchamayañca suviññeyyattā na vuttaṃ. “Bījaninti caturassabījaniṃ. Tālavaṇṭanti tālapattādīhi kataṃ maṇḍalikabījani”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.269) vuttaṃ.

38. In the discussion on fans, first, to show the unallowable fan, it is said: “A fan made of yak-tail hair is not permissible.” Then, to show the six allowable fans, it is said: “A fly whisk, etc., is allowable.” Herein, the six allowable fans are: a fly whisk, a bark-fiber fan, a vetiver-root fan, a peacock-feather fan, a vidhūpana, and a palm-leaf fan. To explain their special characteristics, it is said: “A vidhūpana is called a bījanī (fan),” and so on. The vetiver-root and peacock-feather fans are not explained because they are easily understood. In the Sāratthadīpanī it is said: “A bījanī refers to a square fan. A tālavaṇṭa refers to a circular fan made from palm leaves and so on.” (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.269).

Chattakathā

The Discussion on Umbrellas

39. Chattakathāyaṃ chattaṃ nāma tīṇi chattāni setacchattaṃ, kilañjacchattaṃ, paṇṇacchattanti. Tattha setacchattanti vatthapaliguṇṭhitaṃ paṇḍaracchattaṃ. Kilañjacchattanti vilīvacchattaṃ. Paṇṇacchattanti tālapaṇṇādīhi yehi kehici kataṃ. Maṇḍalabaddhaṃ salākabaddhanti idaṃ pana tiṇṇampi chattānaṃ pañjaradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tāni hi maṇḍalabaddhāni ceva honti salākabaddhāni ca. Yampi tatthajātakadaṇḍena kataṃ ekapaṇṇacchattaṃ hoti, tampi chattameva. “Vilīvacchattanti veṇuvilīvehi kataṃ chattaṃ. Tatthajātakadaṇḍakena katanti tālapaṇṇaṃ saha daṇḍakena chinditvā tameva chattadaṇḍaṃ karonti gopālakādayo viya, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vutta”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.634) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. pācittiya 2.634) pana “vilīvacchattanti [V 2.0261] veṇupesikāhi kataṃ. Maṇḍalabaddhānīti dīghasalākāsu tiriyaṃ valayākārena salākaṃ ṭhapetvā suttehi baddhāni dīghañca tiriyañca ujukameva salākāyo ṭhapetvā daḷhabaddhāni ceva tiriyaṃ ṭhapetvā dīghadaṇḍakeheva saṅkocārahaṃ katvā sutteheva tiriyaṃ baddhāni. Tatthajātakadaṇḍakena katanti saha daṇḍakena chinnatālapaṇṇādīhi kata”nti vuttaṃ. Idha pana chattadhārakapuggalavasena vuttaṃ, tasmā agilānassa bhikkhuno chattaṃ dhāretuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

39. In the discussion on umbrellas, an umbrella refers to three types: a white umbrella, a reed umbrella, and a leaf umbrella. Herein, a white umbrella means a white umbrella covered with cloth. A reed umbrella means a bamboo-splint umbrella. A leaf umbrella means one made with palm leaves or any other leaves. The terms “circular-framed” and “rib-framed” are used to describe the frame of all three umbrellas, as they are all circular-framed and rib-framed. Even a single-leaf umbrella made with its natural stem is still considered an umbrella. In the Sāratthadīpanī it is said: “A bamboo-splint umbrella is one made with bamboo strips. ‘Made with its natural stem’ refers to cutting a palm leaf along with its stem and using that stem as the umbrella handle, as cowherds and others do—this is what is meant.” (Sārattha. Ṭī. Pācittiya 3.634). The Vimativinodanī, however, says: “A bamboo-splint umbrella is one made with bamboo slats. ‘Circular-framed’ means arranging ribs crosswise in a circular pattern along long ribs and binding them with thread, making them straight both lengthwise and crosswise, firmly bound; or placing them crosswise and making them retractable with long handles, and then binding them crosswise with thread. ‘Made with its natural stem’ refers to those made with palm leaves or similar, cut along with their stems.” (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Pācittiya 2.634). Here, however, the discussion is in terms of the person carrying the umbrella; therefore, it is not permissible for a bhikkhu who is not ill to hold an umbrella. The rest is easily understood.

Nakhakathā

The Discussion on Nails

40. Nakhakathāyaṃ dīghanakhadhāraṇapaccayā uppanne vatthusmiṃ “na, bhikkhave, dīghā nakhā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti [M 2.0355] (cūḷava. 274) vacanato dhārentassa āpatti. “Nakhenapi nakhaṃ chindanti, mukhenapi nakhaṃ chindanti, kuṭṭepi ghaṃsanti, aṅguliyo dukkhā honti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, nakhacchedana”nti (cūḷava. 274) vacanato nakhacchedanasatthakaṃ dhāretuṃ vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhā ca “nakhacchedanaṃ valitakaṃyeva karonti, tasmā taṃ vaṭṭatī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) vuttaṃ. “Valitakanti nakhacchedanakāle daḷhaggahaṇatthaṃ valīhi yuttameva karonti, tasmā taṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.85) vuttaṃ. Maṃsappamāṇenāti aṅgulaggamaṃsappamāṇena. Vīsatimaṭṭhanti vīsatipi hatthapādanakhe likhitamaṭṭhe karonti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

40. In the discussion on nails, when the occasion arose because of keeping long nails, it was said: “Bhikkhus, long nails should not be kept. Whoever would keep them commits an offense of wrongdoing.” (Cūḷavagga 274). Thus, for one who keeps them, there is an offense. It was also said: “They cut nails with nails, they bite nails with their teeth, they rub them on a wall, and their fingers become sore. They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: ‘I allow, bhikkhus, a nail-cutter.’” (Cūḷavagga 274). Based on this, it is permissible to keep a nail-cutting instrument. And below, in the Commentary, it is said: “They make the nail-cutter curved; therefore, that is allowable.” (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.85). In the Vimativinodanī it is said: “‘Curved’ means that at the time of cutting nails, for the purpose of a firm grip, they make it with curves; therefore, that is allowable.” (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.85). “To the level of the flesh” means to the level of the flesh at the fingertip. “Polished twenty” means they make the twenty nails of the hands and feet scored and polished. The rest is easily understood.

Lomakathā

The Discussion on Body Hair

Lomakathāyaṃ “sambādhelomaṃ saṃharāpenti. Manussā ujjhāyanti khīyanti vipācenti seyyathāpi gihī kāmabhogino”ti vatthusmiṃ uppanne “na, bhikkhave…pe… dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 275) vacanato saṃharāpentassa āpatti. Aññatarassa bhikkhuno sambādhe vaṇo hoti, bhesajjaṃ na tiṭṭhatīti imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ābādhapaccayā sambādhe lomaṃ saṃharāpetu”nti (cūḷava. 275) vacanato ābādhapaccayā bhesajjapatiṭṭhāpanatthāya sambādhe lomaṃ harāpentassa anāpatti. “Seyyathāpi pisācillikā”ti manussānaṃ ujjhāyanapaccayā “na, bhikkhave, dīghaṃ nāsikālomaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti [V 2.0262] (cūḷava. 275) vacanato dhāraṇapaccayā āpatti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, saṇḍāsa”nti anurakkhaṇatthāya saṇḍāso anuññāto, tasmā nāsikālomaṃ saṇḍāsena harāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Palitanti paṇḍarakesaṃ. Gāhetuṃ na vaṭṭati “mā [M 2.0356] me jarābhāvo hotū”ti manasi katattā. Bībhacchaṃ hutvāti virūpaṃ hutvā. Palitaṃ vā apalitaṃ vāti paṇḍaraṃ vā apaṇḍaraṃ vā. Gāhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati appasādāvahattāti.

In the discussion on body hair, when the occasion arose concerning those who remove hair in private parts, people complained, criticized, and spread it about, saying: “They are like laypeople who enjoy sensual pleasures.” On that occasion it was said: “Bhikkhus … an offense of wrongdoing.” (Cūḷavagga 275). Thus, for one who removes it, there is an offense. A certain bhikkhu had a sore in a private part, and medicine would not adhere to it. Because of this incident, it was said: “I allow, bhikkhus, on account of illness, to have hair removed in a private part.” (Cūḷavagga 275). Thus, on account of illness, for the purpose of applying medicine, there is no offense for one who has hair removed in a private part. Because people complained, saying, “Like a goblin!” it was said: “Bhikkhus, long nose hair should not be kept. Whoever would keep it commits an offense of wrongdoing.” (Cūḷavagga 275). Thus, on account of keeping it, there is an offense. “I allow, bhikkhus, tweezers.” Tweezers were allowed for the purpose of maintenance. Therefore, it is permissible to have nose hair removed with tweezers. “Gray hair” means white hair. It is not permissible to have it plucked out because of the thought, “May I not appear old!” “Having become repulsive” means having become ugly. “Gray or not gray” means white or not white. It is permissible to have it removed because it is uninspiring.

Kāyabandhanakathā

The Discussion on the Girdle

41. Kāyabandhanakathāyaṃ akāyabandhanenāti abandhitakāyabandhanena. Bhikkhunāti seso. Atha vā akāyabandhanenāti abandhitakāyabandhano hutvāti itthambhūtatthe karaṇavacanaṃ yathā “bhinnena sīsena paggharantena lohitena paṭivisake ujjhāpesī”ti. Tenāha “abandhitvā nikkhamantena yattha sarati, tattha bandhitabba”nti. Kāyabandhanaṃ nāma cha kāyabandhanāni kalābukaṃ, deḍḍubhakaṃ, murajaṃ, maddavīṇaṃ, paṭṭikaṃ, sūkarantakanti. Tattha kalābukaṃ nāma bahurajjukaṃ. Deḍḍubhakaṃ nāma udakasappasīsasadisaṃ. Murajaṃ nāma murajavaṭṭisaṇṭhānaṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ. Maddavīṇaṃ nāma pāmaṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ. Īdisañhi ekampi na vaṭṭati, pageva bahūni. Tasmā paṭikkhittāni akappiyakāyabandhanāni nāma cattāri honti, paṭṭikaṃ, sūkarantakanti imāni dve kāyabandhanāni bhagavatā anuññātāni kappiyakāyabandhanāni nāma, tassa pakativītā vā macchakaṇṭakavāyimā vā paṭṭikā vaṭṭati, sesā kuñjaracchikādibhedā na vaṭṭati. Sūkarantakaṃ nāma kuñcikakosakasaṇṭhānaṃ hoti, ekarajjukaṃ, pana muddikakāyabandhanañca sūkarantakaṃ anulometi. Imehi pana dvīhi saddhiṃ aṭṭha kāyabandhanāni honti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, murajaṃ maddavīṇa”nti idaṃ dasāsuyeva anuññātanti pāmaṅgadasā cettha catunnaṃ upari na vaṭṭati. Sobhakaṃ nāma veṭhetvā mukhavaṭṭisibbanaṃ. Guṇakaṃ nāma mudiṅgasaṇṭhānena sibbanaṃ. Evaṃ sibbitā hi anto thirā hontīti vuccati. Pavanantoti pāsanto vuccati. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 277-278) pana “muddikakāyabandhanaṃ nāma caturassaṃ akatvā sajjitaṃ[M 2.0357]. Pāmaṅgadasā caturassā. Mudiṅgasaṇṭhānenāti saṅghāṭiyā mudiṅgasibbanākārena varakasīsākārena. Pavanantoti pāsanto, ‘dasāmūla’nti ca likhitaṃ. Akāyabandhanena sañcicca vā asañcicca vā gāmappavesane āpatti. Saritaṭṭhānato bandhitvā pavisitabbaṃ, nivattitabbaṃ vāti likhita”nti vuttaṃ.

41. In the discussion on the girdle, 'without a girdle' means with an unfastened girdle. 'By a bhikkhu' is to be supplied. Alternatively, 'without a girdle' means 'being one who has not fastened a girdle'; here the instrumental case expresses a state, as in the example: 'with a broken head and dripping blood, he provoked his neighbor.' Therefore it is said: 'When going out without having fastened it, one should fasten it wherever one remembers.' There are six kinds of girdles: the kalābuka, the deḍḍubhaka, the muraja, the maddavīṇa, the paṭṭika, and the sūkarantaka. Among these, the kalābuka has many strings. The deḍḍubhaka resembles the head of a water snake. The muraja is made by wrapping it into the shape of a drum-rim. The maddavīṇa has the shape of a pāmaṅga drum. Not even one of these is allowable, let alone many. Therefore, the first four are rejected as improper girdles. The paṭṭika and the sūkarantaka are the two girdles permitted by the Blessed One, which are called proper girdles. Of these, a paṭṭika that is a simple braid or woven in a fishbone pattern is allowable; other types, such as the 'elephant's eye' pattern, are not allowable. The sūkarantaka has the shape of a key-sheath and is a single cord; a ring-girdle (muddikakāyabandhana) is also classified as a sūkarantaka. Together with these two, there are eight kinds of girdles. The statement, 'I allow, bhikkhus, the muraja and the maddavīṇa,' was a permission granted only to a group of ten bhikkhus. The pāmaṅgadasā is not allowable in addition to the four rejected types. The sobhaka is a stitch for the border made by wrapping. The guṇaka is a stitch in the shape of a mudiṅga drum. It is said that when stitched in this way, they are firm inside. Pavananta means a loop. In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is said: 'A ring-girdle (muddikakāyabandhana) is one prepared without being made square. The pāmaṅgadasā is square. "In the shape of a mudiṅga drum" means in the manner of stitching a patchwork robe with the appearance of a mudiṅga drum stitch, in the shape of a varaka bean head. Pavananta means a loop; it is also written as "ten-rooted" (dasāmūla). For entering a village without a girdle, whether intentionally or unintentionally, there is an offense. It is written: "One should fasten it at the place where one remembers and then enter, or one should turn back."' Thus it is said.

Nivāsanapārupanakathā

The Discussion on Wearing the Lower and Upper Robes

42. Nivāsanapārupanakathāyaṃ [V 2.0263] hatthisoṇḍādivasena gihinivatthaṃ na nivāsetabbanti ettha hatthisoṇḍakaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 280; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. parimaṇḍalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) nāma nābhimūlato hatthisoṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ olambakaṃ katvā nivatthaṃ coḷikaitthīnaṃ nivāsanaṃ viya. Macchavāḷakaṃ nāma ekato dasantaṃ ekato pāsantaṃ olambitvā nivatthaṃ. Catukaṇṇakaṃ nāma uparito dve, heṭṭhato dveti evaṃ cattāro kaṇṇe dassetvā nivatthaṃ. Tālavaṇṭakaṃ nāma tālavaṇṭākārena sāṭakaṃ olambitvā nivāsanaṃ. Satavalikaṃ nāma dīghasāṭakaṃ anekakkhattuṃ obhujitvā ovaṭṭikaṃ karontena nivatthaṃ, vāmadakkhiṇapassesu vā nirantaraṃ valiyo dassetvā nivatthaṃ. Sace pana jāṇuto paṭṭhāya ekaṃ vā dve vā valiyo paññāyanti, vaṭṭati. Saṃvelliyaṃ nivāsentīti mallakammakārādayo viya kacchaṃ bandhitvā nivāsenti, evaṃ nivāsetuṃ gilānassapi maggappaṭipannassapi na vaṭṭati. Setapaṭapārutādivasena na gihipārutaṃ pārupitabbanti ettha yaṃ kiñci setapaṭapārutaṃ paribbājakapārutaṃ ekasāṭakapārutaṃ soṇḍapārutaṃ antepurikapārutaṃ mahājeṭṭhakapārutaṃ kuṭipavesakapārutaṃ brāhmaṇapārutaṃ pāḷikārakapārutanti evamādi parimaṇḍalalakkhaṇato aññathā pārutaṃ sabbametaṃ gihipārutaṃ nāma, tasmā yathā setapaṭā aḍḍhapālakanigaṇṭhā [M 2.0358] pārupanti, yathā ca ekacce paribbājakā uraṃ vivaritvā dvīsu aṃsakūṭesu pāvuraṇaṃ ṭhapenti, yathā ca ekasāṭakā manussā nivatthasāṭakassa ekena antena piṭṭhiṃ pārupitvā ubho kaṇṇe ubhosu aṃsakūṭesu ṭhapenti, yathā ca surāsoṇḍādayo sāṭakena gīvaṃ parikkhipitvā ubho ante ure vā olambenti, piṭṭhiyaṃ vā khipenti, yathā ca antepurikāyo akkhitārakamattaṃ dassetvā oguṇṭhikaṃ pārupanti, yathā ca mahājeṭṭhā dīghasāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā tasseva ekena antena sakalasarīraṃ pārupanti, yathā ca kassakā khettakuṭiṃ pavisantā sāṭakaṃ paliveṭhetvā upakacchake pakkhipitvā tasseva ekena antena sarīraṃ pārupanti, yathā ca brāhmaṇā ubhinnaṃ upakacchakānaṃ antare sāṭakaṃ pavesetvā aṃsakūṭesu pārupanti, yathā ca pāḷikārako bhikkhu ekaṃsapārupanena pārutaṃ vāmabāhuṃ vivaritvā cīvaraṃ aṃsakūṭe āropeti. Evaṃ apārupitvā sabbepi ete aññe ca evarūpe pārupanadose vajjetvā nibbikāraṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ pārupitabbaṃ. Tathā apārupitvā ārāme vā antaraghare vā anādarena yaṃ kiñci vikāraṃ karontassa dukkaṭaṃ.

42. In the discussion on wearing the lower and upper robes, it is said that one should not wear the lower robe in the manner of laypeople, such as in the 'elephant's trunk' style. Here, the 'elephant's trunk' style refers to wearing the lower robe with a piece hanging down from the navel in the shape of an elephant's trunk, like the lower garment worn by women from the Coḷa country. The 'fish-tail' style refers to wearing it with the hem hanging down on one side and a loop hanging down on the other. The 'four-cornered' style refers to wearing it so as to display four corners: two above and two below. The 'palm-leaf fan' style refers to wearing the cloth draped in the shape of a palm-leaf fan. The 'hundred-fold' style refers to wearing a long cloth by folding it many times into a roll, or wearing it so as to display continuous folds on the left and right sides. But if one or two folds are visible from the knee downwards, it is allowable. 'Wearing it tightly wrapped' refers to tying a loincloth like wrestlers, laborers, and so on; this manner of wearing is not allowed even for the sick or those on a journey. Regarding the statement that one should not wear the upper robe in the manner of laypeople, such as the 'white-cloth' style: here, any way of wearing the upper robe otherwise than in the proper 'all-around' manner—such as the white-cloth style, the wanderer's style, the single-cloth style, the drunkard's style, the harem-dweller's style, the elder's style, the hut-entering style, the brahmin's style, or the style of a bhikkhu keeping to the line—all this is called 'the layperson's way of wearing the upper robe.' Therefore, just as the white-clothed ascetics, the aḍḍhapālakanigaṇṭhas, wear their robes; and as some wanderers leave the chest bare and place the covering on both shoulders; and as people with a single cloth cover their back with one end of the cloth they are wearing and place both corners on both shoulders; and as drunkards and others wrap a cloth around their neck and let both ends hang down on their chest or throw them over their back; and as women of the inner quarters cover themselves with a veil, showing only their pupils; and as great elders wear a long lower garment and with one end of it cover their entire body; and as farmers entering a field-hut wrap a cloth around themselves, tuck it under their armpits, and cover their body with one end of it; and as brahmins insert a cloth between both armpits and wear it over their shoulders; and as a bhikkhu keeping to the line, though wearing his robe over one shoulder, uncovers his left arm and places the robe on his shoulder-tip—one should not wear the robe in these ways. Avoiding all these and other such faults in wearing the upper robe, one should wear it properly all-around without modification. For one who does not wear it thus, but out of disrespect makes any kind of modification whether in the monastery or within a house, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

Kājakathā

The Discussion on the Carrying Pole

43. Kājakathāyaṃ [V 2.0264] muṇḍaveṭhīti yathā rañño kuhiñci gacchanto parikkhārabhaṇḍaggahaṇamanussāti adhippāyo. Ubhatokājanti ekasmiṃyeva kāje purato ca pacchato ca ubhosu bhāgesu laggetvā vahitabbabhāraṃ. Ekatokājanti ekato pacchatoyeva laggetvā vahitabbabhāraṃ. Antarākājanti majjhe laggetvā dvīhi vahitabbabhāraṃ. Sīsabhārādayo sīsādīhi vahitabbabhārādayo eva. Olambakanti hatthena olambitvā vahitabbabhāraṃ. Etesu ubhatokājameva na vaṭṭati, sesā vaṭṭanti.

43. In the Discussion on the Carrying Pole, muṇḍaveṭhī means a person who takes the requisite articles when a king goes somewhere; this is the intention. Ubhatokāja is a load to be carried on a single pole, attached at both the front and the back. Ekatokāja is a load to be carried attached at one end only, at the back. Antarākāja is a load attached in the middle to be carried by two people. Sīsabhārādayo are loads and so on to be carried on the head and so on. Olambaka is a load to be carried by suspending it with the hand. Among these, only the ubhatokāja is not allowable; the rest are allowable.

Dantakaṭṭhakathā

The Discussion on the Tooth-stick

44. Dantakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 2.0359] dantakaṭṭhassa akhādane pañca dose, khādane pañcānisaṃse ca dassetvā bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ anuññātaṃ. Tattha pañca dosā nāma acakkhussaṃ, mukhaṃ duggandhaṃ, rasaharaṇiyo na visujjhanti, pittaṃ semhaṃ bhattaṃ pariyonandhati, bhattamassa nacchādetīti. Tattha acakkhussanti cakkhūnaṃ hitaṃ na hoti, parihāniṃ janeti. Nacchādetīti na ruccati. Pañcānisaṃsā vuttapaṭipakkhato veditabbā. Tato dīghadantakaṭṭhakhādane ca atimadāhakadantakaṭṭhakhādane ca dukkaṭaṃ paññapetvā aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ caturaṅgulapacchimaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ anuññātaṃ. Tattha aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ paramaṃ etassa dantakaṭṭhassāti aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ. Caturaṅgulaṃ pacchimaṃ pamāṇaṃ etassa dantakaṭṭhassāti caturaṅgulapacchimaṃ. Atimadāhakanti atikhuddakaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ mahādantakaṭṭhaṃ nāma, caturaṅgulaṃ khuddakadantakaṭṭhaṃ nāma, pañcachasattaṅgulaṃ majjhimadantakaṭṭhaṃ nāma. Tena vuttaṃ “duvidhena udakena tividhena dantakaṭṭhenā”ti. “Aṭṭhaṅgulaparamanti manussānaṃ pamāṇaṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulaparama”nti aṭṭhakathāya (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 282) māha.

44. In the Discussion on the Tooth-stick, the Blessed One, having pointed out five dangers in not chewing a tooth-stick and five benefits in chewing one, allowed tooth-sticks for the bhikkhus. The five dangers are: it is bad for the eyes, the mouth becomes foul-smelling, the taste-bearing nerves are not cleansed, bile and phlegm envelop the food, and one has no appetite for food. Here, bad for the eyes means it is not beneficial for the eyes and causes deterioration. One has no appetite means it is not agreeable. The five benefits should be understood as the opposite of the dangers mentioned. Then, having laid down an offense of wrong-doing for chewing a tooth-stick that is too long and for chewing one that is too short, he allowed a tooth-stick with a maximum of eight finger-breadths and a minimum of four finger-breadths. Here, aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ means this tooth-stick has a maximum of eight finger-breadths. Caturaṅgulapacchimaṃ means this tooth-stick has a minimum measure of four finger-breadths. Atimadāhaka means too small. A tooth-stick of eight finger-breadths is called a large tooth-stick; one of four finger-breadths is called a small tooth-stick; and one of five, six, or seven finger-breadths is called a medium tooth-stick. Hence it was said: “with two kinds of water and three kinds of tooth-sticks.” The commentary (Cūḷav. Aṭṭha. 282) says: “Aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ means a maximum of eight finger-breadths by the standard human finger-breadth.”

Ettha ca pamāṇaṅgulenāti idaṃ pakatiaṅgulenāti gahetvā manussānaṃ pakatiaṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulato adhikappamāṇaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Tattakameva ca katvā khādanti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “manussānaṃ pamāṇaṅgulena” icceva vuttaṃ, na “pakatiaṅgulenā”ti. Tasmā yaṃ vaḍḍhakihatthato aṅgulaṃ pamāṇaṃ katvā manussā gehādīni minanti, tena manussānaṃ pamāṇaṅgulabhūtena vaḍḍhakiaṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulaparamanti attho gahetabbo. Vuttañhi sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.280-282) “pamāṇaṅgulenāti [V 2.0265] vaḍḍhakiaṅgulaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti. Vimativinodaniyañca (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.282) “pamāṇaṅgulenāti vaḍḍhakiaṅgulena, keci pana ‘pakatiaṅgulenā’ti vadanti, taṃ caturaṅgulapacchimavacanena sameti. Na hi pakatiaṅgulena [M 2.0360] caturaṅgulappamāṇaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ kaṇṭhe avilaggaṃ khādituṃ sakkā”ti.

Here, taking pamāṇaṅgulena (by the standard finger-breadth) to mean by the natural finger-breadth, some say that a tooth-stick measuring more than eight finger-breadths by a person's natural finger-breadth is not allowable, and they make it just that size and chew it. But in the commentary, it is only said “by the standard human finger-breadth,” not “by the natural finger-breadth.” Therefore, the meaning should be understood as a maximum of eight finger-breadths measured by the carpenter's finger-breadth, which people use as a standard to measure houses and so on; this has become the standard human finger-breadth. For it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 3.280–282): “Pamāṇaṅgulena is said with reference to the carpenter's finger-breadth.” And in the Vimativinodanī (Vimati. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 2.282): “Pamāṇaṅgulena means by the carpenter's finger-breadth. Some, however, say ‘by the natural finger-breadth,’ but that does not agree with the statement about the minimum of four finger-breadths. For it is not possible to chew a tooth-stick four natural finger-breadths in length without it getting stuck in the throat.”

Rukkharohanakathā

The Discussion on Climbing Trees

45. Rukkhārohanakathāyaṃ puriso pamāṇo yassa rukkhassāti poriso, uddhaṃ ukkhipitahatthena saddhiṃ manussakāyappamāṇo pañcahatthamattaucco rukkhapadeso, taṃ porisaṃ rukkhaṃ, avayave samudāyavohāro yathā “samuddo diṭṭho”ti, ābhuso padanti gacchanti pavattantīti āpadā, parissayā. Yāva attho atthi etasmiṃ rukkheti yāvadattho, rukkho, attha-saddo payojanavācako. Yāva tasmiṃ rukkhe bhikkhussa attho payojanaṃ atthi, tāva abhiruhitabboti adhippāyo. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

45. In the Discussion on Climbing Trees, poriso is a tree for which a person is the measure. It is a section of a tree about five cubits high, the measure of a person's body together with their hand raised upwards. That is a porisa tree. This is a conventional expression for a part as the whole, as when one says, “The ocean has been seen.” Āpadā means dangers, perils. Yāvadattho means a tree in which there is a need; the word attha means purpose. The intention is that one may climb as long as a bhikkhu has a need or purpose in that tree. The rest is easy to understand.

Chandāropanakathā

The Discussion on Putting into Verse

46. Chandāropanakathāyaṃ chandasoti sakkaṭabhāsāya. Na āropetabbanti vācanāmaggaṃ na āropetabbaṃ. Sakāya niruttiyāti māgadhabhāsāya. Tattha santehi katāti sakkaṭā, aṭṭhakavāmakādīhi samitapāpehi isīhi katāti attho. Atha vā sakkaritabbā pūjitabbāti sakkaṭā manussānaṃ hitasukhāvahanato, tadatthikehi manussehi pūjitabbāti attho. Bhāsīyateti bhāsā, sakkaṭā ca sā bhāsā cāti sakkaṭabhāsā. Vedattayagatā nirutti, sassa esāti sakā, bhagavato vacanantyattho. Magadhe jātā māgadhikā, ādikappakāle magadharaṭṭhe jātāti attho. Uccateti utti, nīharitvā utti nirutti, piṭakattayato nīharitvā kathīyatetyattho. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

46. In the Story of Putting into Verse, `chandaso` means in the Sanskrit language. `Na āropetabbaṃ` means it should not be rendered into that mode of speech. `Sakāya niruttiyā` means in the Māgadhī language. Therein, `sakkaṭā` means “made by the good,” that is, made by sages such as Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, and others whose evil has been pacified. Or alternatively, `sakkaṭā` means “to be honored, to be revered” because it brings welfare and happiness to humans; that is, it should be revered by humans who seek that. What is spoken is a language (`bhāsā`); and that which is both `sakkaṭā` and a language is the Sanskrit language (`sakkaṭabhāsā`). The language contained in the three Vedas. `Sakā` is from `sassa esā` (his own); the meaning is the Blessed One's own speech. `Māgadhikā` means born in Magadha, that is, born in the country of Magadha at the beginning of the aeon. What is uttered (`uccate`) is an utterance (`utti`); an utterance that is brought forth is `nirutti`, meaning what is spoken, having been extracted from the three Piṭakas. For this was said by the ancients:

“Sā [M 2.0361] māgadhī mūlabhāsā;

Narā yāyādikappikā;

Brahmāno [V 2.0266] cāssutālāpā;

Sambuddhā cāpi bhāsare”ti.

“That Māgadhī is the root language, which is spoken by people of the primal aeon, by Brahmās who have not heard another language, and also by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.”

Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

The rest is easy to understand.

Lokāyatakathā

The Discussion on Lokāyata

47. Lokāyatakathāyaṃ lokiyanti patiṭṭhahanti puññāpuññāni tabbipāko cāti loko, sattaloko. Ābhuso yatanti vīriyaṃ karonti etthāti āyataṃ, lokassa āyataṃ lokāyataṃ, sattānaṃ bhuso vīriyakaraṇaṭṭhānantyattho. Kiṃ taṃ? Titthiyasatthaṃ. Sabbaṃ ucchiṭṭhaṃ, kasmā? Sakuṇādīhi paribhuttapubbattā. Sabbaṃ anucchiṭṭhaṃ imassa avasesabhojanassa kenaci aparibhuttapubbattā. Seto kāko aṭṭhissa setattā, kāḷo bako pādassa kāḷattāti. Natthi attho etthāti niratthakaṃ, niratthakameva kāraṇaṃ niratthakakāraṇaṃ. Tena paṭisaṃyuttaṃ niratthakakāraṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ. Taranti etthāti titthaṃ, paṭṭanaṃ. Titthaṃ viyāti titthaṃ, laddhi, taṃ etesaṃ atthīti titthiyā, viparītadassanā. Sāsanti attano sāvake etthāti satthaṃ, titthiyānaṃ satthaṃ titthiyasatthaṃ. Na tiracchānavijjā pariyāpuṇitabbāti ettha tiracchānavijjā nāma yā kāci bāhirakā anatthasañhitā. Na pariyāpuṇitabbāti attanā na pariyāpuṇitabbā. Na vācetabbāti paresaṃ na vācetabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

47. In the discussion on Lokāyata: `loka` is that wherein merit and demerit and their results are established; it is the world, the world of beings. `Āyataṃ` is where they strive, make an effort, intensely; thus `lokāyataṃ` is the sphere of the world, meaning the place where beings make a great effort. What is that? The teaching of the sectarians. 'Everything is a leftover.' Why? 'Because it has been previously consumed by birds and so on.' 'Nothing is a leftover, because the remainder of this food has not been previously consumed by anyone.' 'A crow is white because its bones are white; a heron is black because its feet are black.' There is no meaning in this, thus it is meaningless. A meaningless reason is just meaningless reasoning. Connected with that is 'connected with meaningless reasoning.' `Titthaṃ` is where one crosses over, a landing place. Like a ford, so `titthaṃ` means a view. Those who have this are `titthiyā,` those of wrong view. `Satthaṃ` is where one instructs one's disciples; `titthiyasatthaṃ` is the teaching of the sectarians. Herein, 'one should not learn worldly knowledge' means any external knowledge that is unbeneficial. 'Should not be learned' means one should not learn it oneself. 'Should not be taught' means one should not teach it to others. The rest is easy to understand.

Khipitakathā

The Discussion on Sneezing

48. Khipitakathāyaṃ khipīyitthāti khipito. Khipi abyattasaddeti dhātu. Bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattā tasmiṃ khipiteti [M 2.0362] vibhatyantaṃ. “Yasmiṃ kismiñci puggale”ti lakkhaṇavantakattā ajjhāharitabbo. Jīvāti jīva pāṇadhāraṇeti dhātu, vibhattilopo. Yasmiṃ kismiñci puggale khipite bhikkhunā “jīvā”ti vacanaṃ na vattabbaṃ, bhikkhusmiṃ khipite gihinā “jīvatha bhante”ti vuccamāne sati “ciraṃ jīvā”ti bhikkhunā vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti yojanā. “Vuccamāne”ti ettha pana lakkhaṇassa kammavācakattā tena samānādhikaraṇaṃ kammabhūtaṃ “bhikkhusmi”nti lakkhaṇavantakammaṃ ajjhāharitabbaṃ yathā kiṃ “gosu duyhamānāsu puriso āgato”ti[V 2.0267]. Apare pana ācariyā īdisesu ṭhānesu “santesū”ti padaṃ ajjhāharitvā idameva lakkhaṇapadaṃ, “gosu duyhamānāsū”ti padadvayaṃ pana “santesū”ti ettha pakativikativasena kattā evāti vadanti, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

48. In the discussion on sneezing: `khipita` means one who has sneezed. The root `khipi` means 'to make an indistinct sound.' Because this is a locative absolute construction, the word takes a locative ending, as in `khipite`. The words 'in whatever person' should be supplied as the characterized agent. `Jīva` is from the root `jīv,` meaning 'to sustain life'; the inflection is elided. When any person has sneezed, a bhikkhu should not say the word 'Live!' But when a householder says to a bhikkhu who has sneezed, 'Live, venerable sir!', it is permissible for the bhikkhu to say, 'May you live long.' This is the construction. Here, with `vuccamāne` (when it is said), since the characteristic is in the passive voice, the characterized object `bhikkhusmiṃ` (to the bhikkhu), which is in agreement with it, should be supplied, as in 'when the cows were being milked, the man came.' But other teachers, in such cases, supply the word `santesu` (being), taking this as the characteristic word, and they say that the two words `gosu duyhamānāsu` are the agent in relation to `santesu` by way of original and modified state. This should be investigated and accepted.

Lasuṇakathā

The Discussion on Garlic

49. Lasuṇakathāyaṃ “lasuṇaṃ nāma māgadhaka”nti (pāci. 795) pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 795) pana “māgadhakanti magadhesu jātaṃ. Magadharaṭṭhe jātalasuṇameva hi idha lasuṇanti adhippetaṃ, tampi bhaṇḍikalasuṇameva, na ekadvitimiñjakaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana ‘jātidesaṃ avatvā ‘māgadhakaṃ nāma bhaṇḍikalasuṇa’nti vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Sace dve tayo bhaṇḍike ekatoyeva saṅkharitvā ajjhoharati, ekaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Bhinditvā ekekaṃ miñjaṃ khādantiyā pana payogagaṇanāya pācittiyāni, idaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ vasena pācittiyaṃ, bhikkhussa pana dukkaṭaṃ.

49. In the discussion on garlic, it is stated in the Pāḷi: 'Garlic is called māgadhaka' (Pācittiya 795). But in the Commentary (Pācittiya-aṭṭhakathā 795) it says: '`Māgadhaka` means grown in Magadha. For here "garlic" is intended to mean only garlic grown in the country of Magadha, and that too only bulbous garlic, not that with one, two, or three cloves.' But in the Kurundī Commentary, it is said: 'Without specifying the country of origin, it is said: "`Māgadhaka` means bulbous garlic."' If one prepares two or three bulbs together and eats them, there is one pācittiya offense. But for a bhikkhunī who breaks them apart and eats each clove separately, there are pācittiya offenses according to the number of acts. This pācittiya is for bhikkhunīs; for a bhikkhu, however, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

Palaṇḍukādīnaṃ vaṇṇena vā miñjāya vā nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vaṇṇena tāva palaṇḍuko nāma paṇḍuvaṇṇo hoti. Bhañjanako lohitavaṇṇo, haritako haritavaṇṇo, miñjāya [M 2.0363] pana palaṇḍukassa ekā miñjā hoti, bhañjanakassa dve, haritakassa tisso, cāpalasuṇo amiñjako. Aṅkuramattameva hi tassa hoti. Mahāpaccariyādīsu pana “palaṇḍukassa tīṇi miñjāni, bhañjanakassa dve, haritakassa eka”nti vuttaṃ. Ete palaṇḍukādayo sabhāveneva vaṭṭanti, sūpasampākādīsu pana māgadhakampi vaṭṭati. Tañhi paccamānesu muggasūpādīsu vā macchamaṃsavikatiyā vā telādīsu vā badarasāḷavādīsu vā ambilapākādīsu vā uttaribhaṅge vā yattha katthaci antamaso yāgupattepi pakkhipituṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. “Sabhāvenevāti sūpasampākādiṃ vināva. Badarasāḷavaṃ nāma badaraphalāni sukkhāpetvā cuṇṇetvā kattabbā khādanīyavikatī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.793-797) vuttaṃ.

The differences among `palaṇḍu` and others should be understood by their color or their cloves. First, by color: `palaṇḍu` is pale-colored. `Bhañjanaka` is red-colored; `haritaka` is green-colored. By clove, however, `palaṇḍu` has one clove, `bhañjanaka` has two, and `haritaka` has three, while `cāpalasuṇa` has no cloves; it is merely a sprout. But in the Mahāpaccari and other commentaries, it is said: '`Palaṇḍu` has three cloves, `bhañjanaka` has two, `haritaka` has one.' These—`palaṇḍu` and so on—are permissible in their natural state, but as a condiment in soups and so on, even the `māgadhaka` variety is permissible. For it is said that it is permissible to put it into anything being cooked: into mung-bean soup, etc., or preparations of fish and meat, or oils, etc., or `badarasāḷava`, etc., or sour cooked dishes, or as a garnish, or anywhere at all, even into a bowl of rice-gruel. In the Sāratthadīpanī it is said: '“In their natural state” means without being a condiment in soups, etc. “Badarasāḷava” is a kind of edible preparation to be made by drying jujube fruits and grinding them to powder.'

Naakkamitabbādikathā

The Discussion on What Should Not Be Trodden Upon, etc.

50. Naakkamitabbādikathāyaṃ “paribhaṇḍakatabhūmi nāma saṇhamattikāhi katā kāḷavaṇṇādibhūmi[V 2.0268]. Senāsanaṃ mañcapīṭhādikāyeva. Tatheva vaḷañjetuṃ vaṭṭatīti aññehi āvāsikehi bhikkhūhi paribhuttanīhārena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. ‘Nevāsikā pakatiyā anatthatāya bhūmiyā ṭhapenti ce, tesampi anāpattiyevā’ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. ‘Dvārampī’tiādinā vuttadvāravātapānādayo aparikammakatāpi na apassayitabbā. Lomesūti lomesu phusantesū”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.324) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.324) “paribhaṇḍakatabhūmi vāti kāḷavaṇṇādikatasaṇhabhūmi vā. Senāsanaṃ vāti mañcapīṭhādi vā. Tatheva vaḷañjetuṃ vaṭṭatīti iminā nevāsikehi dhotapādādīhi vaḷañjanaṭṭhāne sañcicca adhotapādādīhi vaḷañjantasseva āpatti paññattāti dasseti[M 2.0364], ‘dvārampī’tiādinā sāmaññato vuttattā dvāravātapānādayo aparikammakatāpi na apassayitabbā. Ajānitvā apassayantassapi idha lomagaṇanāya āpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 323-324) “nevāsikā pakatiyā anatthatāya bhūmiyā ṭhapenti ce, tesampi anāpattiyevāti likhitaṃ, dvāravātapānādayo aparikammakatāpi na apassayitabbāti likhita”nti vuttaṃ.

50. In the discussion on what should not be trodden upon, etc.: 'A 'paribhaṇḍakatabhūmi' is a floor made with fine clay, of black color, and so on. The lodging is simply a bed, bench, and the like. It is permissible to use it in the same way; that is, it is permissible for other resident monks to use it in the manner it has been used. 'If resident monks ordinarily place something on the ground for no specific purpose, there is no offense for them either,' as stated in the Gaṇṭhipadesa. By 'Even a door,' etc., it is meant that unadorned doors, windows, and the like should not be leaned against. 'On hairs' means touching the hairs.' This is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī. The Vimativinodanī also states: 'A 'paribhaṇḍakatabhūmi' or a fine floor made of black color, and so on. A lodging or a bed, bench, etc. By “It is permissible to use it in the same way,” it is shown that an offense is laid down only for one who deliberately uses a place—which is used by resident monks with washed feet and so on—with unwashed feet and so on. Because it is stated generally by “Even a door,” etc., unadorned doors, windows, and the like should not be leaned against. Even for one who leans unknowingly, here there is an offense according to the count of hairs.' The Vajirabuddhiṭīkā states: 'It is written, “If resident monks ordinarily place something on the ground for no specific purpose, there is no offense for them either.” It is also written, “Unadorned doors, windows, and the like should not be leaned against.”'

Avandiyavandiyakathā

The Discussion on Those Not to Be Venerated and Those to Be Venerated.

51. Avandiyavandiyakathāyaṃ idha pakaraṇācariyena senāsanakkhandhakapāḷivasena dasa avandiyā, tayo vandiyā ca vuttā, aṭṭhakathāṭīkāsu ca na kiñci vuttā, tasmā idha āgatanayeneva attho daṭṭhabbo. Parivārapāḷiyaṃ (pari. 467 ādayo) pana upālipañcake pañcapañcakavasena pañcavīsati avandiyā, pañca vandiyā ca vuttā. Kathaṃ? “Kati nu kho, bhante, avandiyāti? Pañcime, upāli, avandiyā. Katame pañca? Antaragharaṃ paviṭṭho avandiyo, racchagato avandiyo, otamasiko avandiyo, asamannāharanto avandiyo, sutto avandiyo. Ime kho, upāli, pañca avandiyā. Aparepi, upāli, pañca avandiyā. Katame pañca? Yāgupāne avandiyo, bhattagge avandiyo, ekāvatto avandiyo, aññavihito avandiyo, naggo avandiyo. Ime kho, upāli, pañca avandiyā. Aparepi, upāli, pañca avandiyā. Katame pañca? Khādanto avandiyo, bhuñjanto avandiyo, uccāraṃ karonto avandiyo, passāvaṃ karonto avandiyo, ukkhittako avandiyo. Ime kho, upāli, pañca avandiyā. Aparepi, upāli, pañca avandiyā. Katame pañca? Pureupasampannena [V 2.0269] pacchāupasampanno avandiyo, anupasampanno avandiyo[M 2.0365], nānāsaṃvāsako vuḍḍhataro adhammavādī avandiyo, mātugāmo avandiyo, paṇḍako avandiyo. Ime kho, upāli, pañca avandiyā. Aparepi, upāli, pañca avandiyā. Katame pañca? Pārivāsiko avandiyo, mūlāyapaṭikassanāraho avandiyo, mānattāraho avandiyo, mānattacāriko avandiyo, abbhānāraho avandiyo. Ime kho, upāli, pañca avandiyā”ti.

51. In the discussion on those not to be venerated and those to be venerated, here the teacher of the text mentions ten types of those not to be venerated and three types of those to be venerated according to the chapter on lodgings in the Pāli. However, nothing is said in the commentaries and sub-commentaries, so here the meaning should be understood according to the method already presented. But in the Parivāra Pāli, in the Upāli Pentads, twenty-five types of those not to be venerated and five types of those to be venerated are mentioned in sets of five. How? "Venerable sir, how many are those not to be venerated?" "Upāli, there are five of those not to be venerated. Which five?
