One who has entered a house is not to be venerated, one walking on the street is not to be venerated, one who is in darkness is not to be venerated, one who is not paying attention is not to be venerated, and one who is asleep is not to be venerated. These, Upāli, are five of those not to be venerated." "Furthermore, Upāli, there are another five of those not to be venerated. Which five? One drinking rice gruel is not to be venerated, one in the refectory is not to be venerated, one who has turned away is not to be venerated, one engaged in other business is not to be venerated, and one who is naked is not to be venerated. These, Upāli, are another five of those not to be venerated." "Furthermore, Upāli, there are another five of those not to be venerated. Which five? One who is eating hard food is not to be venerated, one who is consuming a meal is not to be venerated, one who is defecating is not to be venerated, one who is urinating is not to be venerated, and one who has been suspended is not to be venerated. These, Upāli, are another five of those not to be venerated." "Furthermore, Upāli, there are another five of those not to be venerated. Which five? One ordained later is not to be venerated by one ordained earlier, one who is not ordained is not to be venerated, an elder of a different communion who speaks contrary to the Dhamma is not to be venerated, a woman is not to be venerated, and a eunuch is not to be venerated. These, Upāli, are another five of those not to be venerated." "Furthermore, Upāli, there are another five of those not to be venerated. Which five? One undergoing parivāsa penance is not to be venerated, one deserving return to the beginning of discipline is not to be venerated, one deserving mānatta penance is not to be venerated, one practicing mānatta penance is not to be venerated, and one deserving rehabilitation is not to be venerated. These, Upāli, are another five of those not to be venerated."

“Kati nu kho, bhante, vandiyāti? Pañcime, upāli, vandiyā. Katame pañca? Pacchāupasampannena pureupasampanno vandiyo, nānāsaṃvāsako vuḍḍhataro dhammavādī vandiyo, ācariyo vandiyo, upajjhāyo vandiyo, sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vandiyo. Ime kho, upāli, pañca vandiyā”ti.

"Venerable sir, how many are to be venerated? Upāli, there are these five to be venerated. Which five? One ordained later should venerate one ordained earlier. An elder of a different communion who speaks the Dhamma should be venerated. A teacher should be venerated. A preceptor should be venerated. The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is to be venerated in this world with its devas, its Māras, and its Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. These, Upāli, are the five to be venerated."

Aṭṭhakathāyañca (pari. aṭṭha. 467) “otamasitoti andhakāragato. Tañhi vandantassa mañcapādādīsupi nalāṭaṃ paṭihaññeyya. Asamannāharantoti kiccappasutattā vandanaṃ asamannāharanto. Suttoti niddaṃ okkanto. Ekāvattoti ekato āvatto sapattapakkhe ṭhito verī visabhāgapuggalo vuccati, ayaṃ avandiyo. Ayañhi vandiyamāno pādenapi pahareyya. Aññavihitoti aññaṃ cintayamāno. Khādantoti piṭṭhakhajjakādīni khādanto. Uccārañca passāvañca karonto anokāsagatattā avandiyo. Ukkhittakoti tividhenapi ukkhepanīyakammena ukkhittako avandiyo, tajjanīyādikammakatā pana cattāro vanditabbā, uposathapavāraṇāpi tehi saddhiṃ labbhanti. Ādito paṭṭhāya ca vuttesu avandiyesu naggañca ukkhittakañca vandantasseva hoti āpatti[M 2.0366], itaresaṃ pana asāruppaṭṭhena ca antarā vuttakāraṇena ca vandanā paṭikkhittā. Ito paraṃ pacchāupasampannādayo dasapi āpattivatthubhāveneva avandiyā. Te vandantassa hi niyameneva āpatti. Iti imesu pañcasu pañcakesu terasa jane vandantassa anāpatti, dvādasannaṃ vandanāya āpatti. Ācariyo vandiyoti pabbajjācariyo upasampadācariyo nissayācariyo uddesācariyo ovādācariyoti ayaṃ pañcavidhopi ācariyo vandiyo”ti āgato.

In the commentary, it is said: "‘Otamasito’ means one who is in darkness. For if one were to bow to such a person, one’s forehead might strike the bed legs or other objects. ‘Asamannāharanto’ means one who is not paying attention to the act of bowing due to being preoccupied with other duties. ‘Sutto’ means one who has fallen asleep. ‘Ekāvatto’ means a hostile person who is turned away, standing on the side of the adversary – such a person, an enemy or incompatible individual, is said to be unworthy of bowing to. If one were to bow to such a person, they might even strike with their foot. ‘Aññavihito’ means one who is thinking of something else. ‘Khādanto’ means one who is eating cakes or other food. One who is engaged in excretion or urination is not to be bowed to, as they are in an unsuitable place. ‘Ukkhittako’ refers to one who has been suspended by any of the three types of suspension acts—such a person should not be bowed to. However, those who have been subjected to acts of censure or similar disciplinary actions (tajjanīya, etc.)—four in total—may still be bowed to, and they are also permitted to participate in Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies with them. From the beginning, among those mentioned as not to be bowed to, bowing to a naked person or one who has been suspended incurs an offense. For the others, bowing is prohibited due to unsuitability and the reasons stated earlier. Beyond these, from what follows, the ten who are later ordained, etc., are not to be bowed to solely on the basis of being grounds for an offense; bowing to them invariably incurs an offense. Thus, in these five groups of five, bowing to thirteen individuals is blameless, while bowing to twelve incurs an offense. ‘Ācariyo vandiyo’ refers to five types of teachers: the ordination teacher (pabbajjācariyo), the full ordination teacher (upasampadācariyo), the dependence teacher (nissayācariyo), the recitation teacher (uddesācariyo), and the advice teacher (ovādācariyo)—all of whom should be bowed to." Thus it is handed down.

“Antarā [V 2.0270] vuttakāraṇenāti tañhi vandantassa mañcapādādīsu nalāṭaṃ paṭihaññeyyātiādinā vuttakāraṇenā”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. parivāra 3.467) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭi. parivāra 2.467) pana “mañcapādādīsupi nalāṭaṃ paṭihaññeyyāti andhakāre cammakhaṇḍaṃ paññapetvā vandituṃ onamantassa nalāṭaṃ vā akkhi vā mañcādīsu paṭihaññati. Etena vandatopi āpattiabhāvaṃ vatvā vandanāya sabbathā paṭikkhepābhāvañca dīpeti. Evaṃ sabbattha suttantarehi appaṭikkhittesu. Naggādīsu pana vandituṃ na vaṭṭatīti. Ekato āvattoti ekasmiṃ dosāgatipakkhe parivatto, paviṭṭhoti attho. Tenāha ‘sapattapakkhe ṭhito’ti. Vandiyamānoti onamitvā vandiyamāno. Vanditabbesu uddesācariyo nissayācariyo ca yasmā navakāpi honti, tasmā ‘te vuḍḍhā eva vandiyā’ti vanditabbā”ti āgataṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. parivāra 467) “ekāvattotipi paṭhanti, tassa kuddho kodhābhibhūtoti kira attho. Ekavatthotipi keci, uttarāsaṅgaṃ apanetvā ṭhitoti kira attho. Taṃ sabbaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ uddhaṭapāḷiyā virujjhati. Ekāvattoti hi uddhaṭaṃ, tasmā na gahetabbaṃ. Antarā vuttakāraṇenāti kiccappasutattā asamannāharanto [M 2.0367] ‘nalāṭaṃ paṭihaññeyyā’tiādivuttakāraṇenā”ti āgataṃ.

"The reason stated in between is that if one were to bow, the forehead might hit the bed legs, etc., as mentioned." This is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. ṭī. Parivāra 3.467). However, the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. ṭī. Parivāra 2.467) states: "The forehead might hit the bed legs, etc.; when one bows down in the dark after spreading out a piece of leather, the forehead or eyes might strike the bed, etc. By this, it is shown that there is no offense even in bowing, and that there is no absolute prohibition on bowing. Thus this applies in all cases where there is no prohibition in the suttas. However, it is not proper to bow to a naked person, etc." "Turned to one side" means turned toward one side where faults and wrong paths arise, that is, entered into such a state. Hence, it is said, 'standing on the side of the enemy.' "Being bowed to" means being bowed to by bending down. Among those who should be bowed to, the recitation teacher and the dependence teacher are included, since even junior monks may hold these positions. Therefore, it is said, 'they are indeed to be venerated as elders.'" In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. ṭī. Parivāra 467), it is said: "Some read it as 'ekāvattoti,' whose meaning is supposedly 'angry, overcome by anger.' Some others read it as 'ekavatthotipi,' whose meaning is supposedly 'standing after removing the upper robe.' All of this contradicts the Pāli quoted in the commentary. For 'ekāvattoti' is what is quoted; therefore, this should not be accepted. "The reason stated in between is due to being absorbed in activity, not considering, 'the forehead might hit,' etc., as mentioned."

Dutiyagāthāsaṅgaṇikaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pari. aṭṭha. 477) “dasa puggalā nābhivādetabbāti senāsanakkhandhake vuttā dasa janā. Añjalisāmīcena cāti sāmīcikammena saddhiṃ añjali ca tesaṃ na kātabbo. Neva pānīyapucchanatālavaṇṭaggahaṇādi khandhakavattaṃ tesaṃ dassetabbaṃ, na añjali paggaṇhitabboti attho. Dasannaṃ dukkaṭanti tesaṃyeva dasannaṃ evaṃ karontassa dukkaṭaṃ hotī”ti āgataṃ, tasmā añjalikammamattampi nesaṃ na kattabbanti.

In the commentary on the second collection of verses (Pari. Aṭṭha. 477), it is stated: "Ten types of people should not be venerated—these are the ten individuals mentioned in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. And a respectful gesture with folded hands (añjali) should not be made to them, together with proper conduct (sāmīcikamma). Nor should one show them the duties described in the Khandhaka, such as asking about water or taking the fan. The meaning is that the añjali should not be raised to them. If one does so to these ten, it is a dukkaṭa offense." Therefore, even the mere act of performing añjalikamma should not be done toward them.

“Navakatarena, bhante, bhikkhunā vuḍḍhatarassa bhikkhuno pāde vandantena kati dhamme ajjhattaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā pādā vanditabbāti? Navakatarenupāli, bhikkhunā vuḍḍhatarassa bhikkhuno pāde vandantena pañca dhamme ajjhattaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā pādā vanditabbā. Katame pañca? Navakatarenupāli, bhikkhunā vuḍḍhatarassa bhikkhuno pāde vandantena ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ katvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā ubhohi pāṇitalehi pādāni parisambāhantena pemañca gāravañca upaṭṭhāpetvā pādā vanditabbā. Navakatarenupāli, bhikkhunā vuḍḍhatarassa bhikkhuno pāde vandantena [V 2.0271] ime pañca dhamme ajjhattaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā pādā vanditabbā”ti (pari. 469) imasmiṃ ṭhāne sammāsambuddhena āyasmato upālissa vandanānayova ācikkhito.

"Venerable sir, how many qualities should a junior monk inwardly establish when paying homage to the feet of a senior monk?" "Upāli, a junior monk paying homage to the feet of a senior monk should inwardly establish five qualities. What are the five? Upāli, a junior monk paying homage to the feet of a senior monk should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, raise his joined palms, stroke the feet with both palms, and establish affection and respect before paying homage. Upāli, a junior monk paying homage to the feet of a senior monk should inwardly establish these five qualities before paying homage." In this passage, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One explained the method of paying homage to the Venerable Upāli.

Pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvāti ettha pañcasarūpañca kathitaṃ. Kathaṃ? Vuḍḍhatarassa pāde vandantena ubho aṃse vivaritvā vanditabbā, na ca ubho aṃse pārupitvā vanditabbā, atha kho ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā vanditabbāti. Etena saṅghāṭi pana ekaṃsaṃ katāpi akatāpi natthi dosoti pakāsito [M 2.0368] hoti. “Dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ karapuṭasaṅkhātaṃ añjaliṃ paggahetvāva vanditabbā, na hatthatalapakāsanamattena vā na hatthamuṭṭhipakāsanādinā vā vanditabbā”ti ca “na ekena hatthena cīvarakaṇṇachupanādimattena vanditabbā, atha kho ubhohi pāṇitalehi pādāni parisambāhantena vanditabbā”ti ca “evaṃ vandantehi na duṭṭhacittañca anādarañca upaṭṭhāpetvā vanditabbā, atha kho pemañca gāravañca upaṭṭhāpetvā pādā vanditabbā”ti ca evaṃ vandanānayo ācikkhito hoti.

Regarding 'having venerated with the five established points'—here the nature of the five is explained. How so? When venerating a senior monk’s feet, one should not venerate with both shoulders covered; rather, one should arrange the upper robe over one shoulder and then venerate. By this, it is shown that there is no fault whether the outer robe is arranged over one shoulder or not. And, 'One should venerate by raising the hands in añjali, known as a hand-bud, radiant with the joining of the ten fingernails—not merely by showing the palms, or by showing the fists, etc.' And, 'One should not venerate by merely touching the robe’s edge with one hand, but rather by stroking the feet with both palms.' And, 'While venerating in this way, one should not do so with a corrupt mind or lack of respect; instead, one should venerate the feet having established affection and reverence.' Thus, the method of veneration is explained.

Kathaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitasarūpaṃ kathitaṃ? Idha ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvāti ekaṃ, añjaliṃ paggahetvāti ekaṃ, ubhohi pāṇitalehi pādāni parisambāhantenāti ekaṃ, pemañca upaṭṭhāpetvāti ekaṃ, gāravañca upaṭṭhāpetvāti ekaṃ, evaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitasarūpaṃ kathitaṃ hoti. Tenāha “pañca dhamme ajjhattaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā pādā vanditabbā”ti. Evaṃ sakalalokassa hitasukhakārakena dhammassāminā kāyapaṇāmamanopaṇāmavasena mahato hitasukhassa pavattanatthaṃ āyasmato upālittherassa ācikkhitena vandanānayena vandituṃ vaṭṭati.

How is the nature of the five established points described? Here: arranging the upper robe over one shoulder is one; raising the joined palms is one; stroking the feet with both palms is one; establishing affection is one; and establishing reverence is one. Thus the nature of the five established points is described. Therefore it was said: 'Having established five qualities internally, the feet should be venerated.' Thus, it is fitting to venerate according to this method of veneration—explained to the Venerable Elder Upāli by the Lord of the Dhamma, the bringer of welfare and happiness for the entire world—for the purpose of generating great welfare and happiness by way of bodily prostration and mental homage.

Idāni pana ācariyā abhinavaāgatānaṃ daharānañca sāmaṇerānañca vandanānayaṃ sikkhantā na imaṃ āhaccabhāsitaṃ pāḷiṃ gahetvā sikkhanti, atha kho paveṇīāgatanayaṃyeva gahetvā sikkhanti. Kathaṃ? Yadi ṭhatvā vandatha, dve pādatalāni samaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā dve hatthatalāni samaṃ phusāpetvā nalāṭe patiṭṭhāpetvā vanditabbābhimukhaṃ onamitvā vandathāti, ayaṃ nayo “evaṃ mahāsatto suvaṇṇakadali viya bārāṇasinagarābhimukhaṃ onamitvā mātāpitaro vanditvā”ti imaṃ jātakaṭṭhakathāvacanañca “dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā”tiādiaṭṭhakathāvacanañca [M 2.0369] anulometi. Idha pana dve pādatalāni, dve hatthatalāni, nalāṭañcāti pañcasu patiṭṭhitānīti sarūpaṃ vadanti. Yadi nisīditvā vandatha, paṭhamaṃ dve pādatalāni [V 2.0272] bhūmiyaṃ samaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā dve jāṇumaṇḍalāni samaṃ ussāpetvā dve kapparāni dvinnaṃ jāṇūnaṃ upari samaṃ ṭhapetvā dve hatthatalāni samaṃ phusitāni katvā añjalisaṅkhātaṃ karapuṭaṃ sirasaṅkhāte nalāṭe patiṭṭhāpetvā vandatha. Tato onamitvā dve jāṇumaṇḍalāni ca dve kapparāni ca bhūmiyaṃ samaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā dve hatthatalāni pasāretvā samaṃ bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā sīsaṃ ubhinnaṃ hatthapiṭṭhīnaṃ upari katvā bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā vandathāti. Ettha tu dve pādatalāni ekaṃ katvā, tathā dve jāṇumaṇḍalāni ekaṃ, dve kapparāni ekaṃ, dve hatthatalāni ekaṃ, sīsaṃ ekaṃ katvā pañcapatiṭṭhitasarūpaṃ kathenti. Esa nayo pāḷiaṭṭhakathāṭīkāsu na diṭṭho.

Now, however, when teachers instruct newly arrived and young novices in the method of veneration, they do not teach by taking up this specifically stated Pāli passage, but rather they teach by taking up the method that has come down by tradition. How so? 'If you venerate while standing, you should place both soles of the feet evenly on the ground, press both palms together evenly, place them at the forehead, and bow forward in the direction of the one to be venerated.' This method conforms with the Jātaka commentary, which states: 'Thus the Great Being, like a golden banana tree, bowed toward the city of Bārāṇasī and venerated his parents,' and with other commentary passages such as: 'having raised the añjali, radiant with the joining of the ten fingernails, and placing it on the head.' Here, they describe the nature of the five points of contact as the two soles, the two palms, and the forehead. 'If you venerate while sitting, first place both soles evenly on the ground, raise both knees evenly, place both elbows evenly on top of the two knees, press both palms together evenly, form the añjali gesture with the joined hands, place it on the forehead, and venerate. Then, bowing forward, place both knees and both elbows evenly on the ground, stretch out both palms, place them evenly on the ground, rest the head on the backs of both hands, and place the head on the ground to venerate.' Here, they describe the nature of the five-point prostration by counting the two soles as one, likewise the two knees as one, the two elbows as one, the two palms as one, and the head as one. This method is not seen in the Pāli, the commentaries, or the sub-commentaries.

Samīpaṃ gantvā pādānaṃ vandanakāle pana ekacce paṭhamaṃ attano sīsaṃ hatthena parāmasitvā tena hatthadvayena therānaṃ jāṇumaṇḍalaṃ cīvarassa upariyeva sambāhanti. Ekacce paṭhamaṃ therānaṃ jāṇumaṇḍalaṃ sacīvaraṃyeva parāmasitvā teneva hatthadvayena attano sīsaṃ parāmasanti. Ekacce chupanamattameva karonti. Esapi nayo na kismiñci diṭṭho. Rāmaññadesiyā pana bhikkhū evaṃ samīpaṃ gantvā vandanakāle therānaṃ pādaggaṃ apassantāpi pariyesitvā cīvarato nīharitvā pādaggameva punappunaṃ hatthena sambāhitvā sīsena pavaṭṭetvā cumbitvā lehitvā cirappavāsāgatapiyamanāpaupajjhāyaṃ vā ācariyaṃ vā passantā viya katvā vandanti. Taṃ kiriyaṃ parivārapāḷiyaṃ “ubhohi pāṇitalehi pādāni parisambāhantena pemañca gāravañca upaṭṭhāpetvā pādā vanditabbā”ti āgatapāḷiyā saṃsandati [M 2.0370] viya dissati. Tepi na sabbe pāḷiṃ passanti, paveṇīvaseneva karonti, tasmā sabbesaṃ hitatthaṃ pāḷinayo amhehi uddhaṭo. Paveṇīāgatanayato hi pāḷinayo balavataro, tasmā bhagavato āṇaṃ garuṃ karontehi sappurisehi pāḷinayo samāsevitabboti amhākaṃ khanti, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

When approaching to venerate the feet, some first touch their own head with their hand, then with both hands they stroke the elders' knees over the robe. Some first touch the elders' knees together with the robe, then with those same two hands they touch their own head. Some merely make a touching gesture. This method, too, is not seen anywhere. However, when the monks from the Rāmañña country approach to venerate, even if they do not see the elder's feet, they search for them, draw them out from under the robe, and repeatedly stroke the very tips of the feet with their hands. Then, placing their heads upon them, they kiss and lick them, venerating as if seeing a long-absent, dear, and beloved preceptor or teacher. This action seems to accord with the passage in the Parivāra Pāḷi: 'Having stroked the feet with both palms and established affection and respect, one should venerate the feet.' Yet not all of them see the Pāli text; they act according to tradition. Therefore, for the welfare of all, we have extracted the method from the Pāli. For the method from the Pāli is more authoritative than the method that has come down through tradition. Thus, it is our conviction that good persons, who regard the Blessed One's command as weighty, should cultivate the method from the Pāli. This should be investigated and adopted.

Āsandādikathā

The Discussion on Seats, etc.

55. Āsandādikathāyaṃ caturassapīṭhanti samacaturassaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgulapādaṃ vaṭṭatīti aṭṭhaṅgulapādakameva vaṭṭati. Pamāṇātikkantopi vaṭṭatīti samacaturassameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Āyatacaturassā pana sattaṅgapañcaṅgāpi uccapādā na vaṭṭanti. Vetteheva caturassādiākārena kataṃ bhaddapīṭhanti āha “vettamayapīṭha”nti. Dārupaṭṭikāya uparīti aṭaniākārena ṭhitadārupaṭalassa heṭṭhā. Uddhaṃ pādaṃ katvā pavesanakālañhi sandhāya “uparī”ti vuttaṃ. Eḷakassa [V 2.0273] pacchimapādadvayaṃ viya vaṅkākārena ṭhitattā panetaṃ “eḷakapādapīṭha”nti (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.297) vuttaṃ.

55. In the discussion on seats, etc., a 'square seat' means one that is equally square. 'Having legs of eight finger-breadths is allowable' means that only one with legs of eight finger-breadths is allowable. 'Even if it exceeds the standard measure, it is allowable' is said with reference only to an equally square seat. However, long rectangular ones with high legs of seven or five finger-breadths are not allowable. A `bhaddapīṭha` is a seat made of wicker in a square shape, etc.; thus he said 'a wicker seat.' 'Above the wooden plank' means below the wooden board placed in the manner of a cross-bar. The word 'above' is used with reference to the time of insertion, when one has turned the leg upwards. Because it stands with a curved shape like the two hind legs of a ram, it is called a 'ram-legged seat' (Vin-ṭī-cūḷa 2.297).

Uccāsayanamahāsayanakathā

The Discussion on High and Large Beds

56. Uccāsayanamahāsayanakathāyaṃ “vāḷarūpānīti āharimāni vāḷarūpāni, ‘akappiyarūpākulo akappiyamañco pallaṅko’ti sārasamāse vuttaṃ. Dīghalomako mahākojavoti caturaṅgulādhikalomo kāḷakojavo. ‘Caturaṅgulādhikāni kira tassa lomānī’ti vacanato caturaṅgulato heṭṭhā vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Vānacitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇoti bhitticchedādivasena vicitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇo. Ghanapupphako uṇṇāmayattharaṇoti uṇṇāmayalohitattharaṇo[M 2.0371]. Pakatitūlikāti rukkhatūlalatātūlapoṭakītūlasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ tūlānaṃ aññatarapuṇṇā tūlikā. ‘Uddalomīti ubhatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Ekantalomīti ekatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇa’nti dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sārasamāse pana ‘uddalomīti ekatouggatapupphaṃ. Ekantalomīti ubhatouggatapuppha’nti vuttaṃ. ‘Koseyyakaṭṭissamayanti koseyyakasaṭamaya’nti ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ. Suddhakoseyyanti ratanaparisibbanarahitaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ panettha ‘ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ sabbāneva gonakādīni ratanaparisibbitāni na vaṭṭantī’ti vuttaṃ. Tattha ‘ṭhapetvā tūlika’nti etena ratanaparisibbanarahitāpi tūlikā na vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. ‘Ratanaparisibbitāni na vaṭṭantī’ti iminā pana yāni ratanaparisibbitāni, tāni bhūmattharaṇavasena yathānurūpaṃ mañcādīsu ca upanetuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpitanti veditabbaṃ. Ettha ca vinayapariyāyaṃ patvā garuke ṭhātabbattā idha vuttanayenevettha vinicchayo veditabbo. Suttantikadesanāya pana gahaṭṭhānampi vasena vuttattā tesaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ ‘ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ…pe… vaṭṭatī’ti vuttanti apare.

56. In the discussion on high and large beds: 'Animal figures' means artificial animal figures. In the Sārasamāsa it is said: 'A couch or divan is improper when it is filled with improper figures.' 'A large `kojavo` with long fleece' is a black woolen blanket with fleece longer than four finger-breadths. Because it is said, 'Its fleece, it seems, is longer than four finger-breadths,' some say that what is less than four finger-breadths is allowable. 'A colorful woolen spread' is a woolen spread made variegated with patterns such as wall-carvings. 'A woolen spread thick with flowers' is a red woolen spread. 'An ordinary mattress' is a mattress filled with one of three kinds of stuffing: tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, or grass-cotton. 'With fleece on both sides' is a woolen spread with fringes on both sides. 'With fleece on one side' is a woolen spread with fringes on one side'—so it is said in the Dīghanikāya commentary. But in the Sārasamāsa it is said: ''With fleece on both sides' has flowers raised on one side. 'With fleece on one side' has flowers raised on both sides.' 'Interwoven with silk' means 'made of silk and `kasaṭa`'—so it was said by the elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. 'Pure silk' means without being stitched with gems. In the Dīghanikāya commentary it is said: 'Except for the mattress, all such things as woolen blankets, etc., if stitched with gems, are not allowable.' Herein, by 'except for the mattress,' it shows that even a mattress without being stitched with gems is not allowable. However, by the phrase 'if stitched with gems, they are not allowable,' it should be understood to indicate that those things which are stitched with gems are allowable to be used as floor coverings and on beds, etc., as is appropriate. And here, since one must stand on the weighty side when it comes to the Vinaya method, the decision should be understood in accordance with the method stated here. But others say that since the Suttanta teaching was also spoken for the sake of householders, it was said 'except for the mattress... is allowable' in order to include them.

Ajinacammehīti ajinamigacammehi. Tāni kira cammāni sukhumatarāni, tasmā dupaṭṭatipaṭṭāni katvā sibbanti. Tena vuttaṃ ‘ajinappaveṇī’ti. Uttaraṃ uparibhāgaṃ chādetīti uttaracchado, vitānaṃ, tañca lohitavitānaṃ idhādhippetanti āha ‘uparibaddhena rattavitānenā’ti, ‘rattavitānesu ca kāsāvaṃ vaṭṭati, kusumbhādirattameva na vaṭṭatī’ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Mahāupadhānanti pamāṇātikkantaṃ upadhānaṃ. Ettha ca kiñcāpi dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘alohitakāni dvepi vaṭṭantiyeva, tato uttari labhitvā aññesaṃ [M 2.0372] dātabbāni. Dātumasakkonto [V 2.0274] mañce tiriyaṃ attharitvā uparipaccattharaṇaṃ datvā nipajjitumpi labhatī’ti avisesena vuttaṃ, senāsanakkhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 297) pana ‘agilānassa sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcāti dvayameva vaṭṭati. Gilānassa bimbohanāni santharitvā upari ca paccattharaṇaṃ datvā nipajjitumpi vaṭṭatī’ti vuttattā gilānoyeva mañce tiriyaṃ attharitvā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Abhinissāya nisīditunti apassāya nisīditu”nti ettako vinicchayo sāratthadīpaniyaṃ āgato.

'By hides' means the hides of black antelope and deer. Those hides, it seems, are very fine; therefore they are sewn by making them two-layered or three-layered. For that reason it is called 'a patchwork of hides.' 'It covers the upper part' is an upper covering, a canopy; and a red canopy is intended here, thus he said 'with a red canopy attached above.' 'And for red canopies, the ochre color is allowable, but a red from safflower, etc., is not allowable'—so it is said in the glosses. 'A large pillow' means a pillow that exceeds the standard measure. And here, although in the Dīghanikāya commentary it is said without distinction, 'Two non-red ones are allowable, and if one obtains more than that, they should be given to others. If unable to give them away, one may also spread them crosswise on the bed, place a coverlet on top, and lie down,' yet in the commentary on the Senāsanakkhandhaka (Cūḷa-aṭṭha. 297) it is said: 'For one who is not ill, only two are allowable: a head pillow and a foot pillow. For one who is ill, it is also allowable to spread out cushions, place a coverlet on top, and lie down.' Therefore, it should be understood that only one who is ill is allowed to spread them crosswise on the bed and lie down. 'To sit relying on' means 'to sit leaning against.' This much of a decision has come in the Sāratthadīpanī.

Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.254) – pana vāḷarūpānīti āharimāni vāḷarūpāni. Caturaṅgulādhikānīti uddalomīekantalomīhi visesadassanaṃ. Caturaṅgulato hi ūnāni kira uddalomīādīsu pavisanti. Vānacitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇoti nānāvaṇṇehi uṇṇāmayasuttehi bhitticchedādivasena vāyitvā katacittattharaṇo. Ghanapupphakoti bahalarāgo. Pakatitūlikāti tūlapuṇṇā bhisi. Vikatikāti sīharūpādivasena vānacitrāva gayhati. “Uddalomīti ubhatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Ekantalomīti ekantadasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇa”nti dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Koseyyakaṭṭissamayanti kosiyasuttānaṃ antarā suvaṇṇamayasuttāni pavesetvā vītaṃ, suvaṇṇasuttaṃ kira kaṭṭissaṃ kasaṭanti ca vuccati. Teneva “koseyyakasaṭamaya”nti ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttanti vadanti. Ratanaparisibbitanti suvaṇṇalittaṃ. Suddhakoseyyanti ratanaparisibbanarahitaṃ.

But in the Vimativinodanī (Vin-ṭī-mahā 2.254) it is said: 'Animal figures' means artificial animal figures. 'Longer than four finger-breadths'—this shows a distinction from 'with fleece on both sides' and 'with fleece on one side.' For those less than four finger-breadths, it seems, are included under 'with fleece on both sides,' etc. 'A colorful woolen spread' is a decorated spread made by weaving with woolen threads of various colors in the manner of wall-carving patterns, etc. 'Thick with flowers' means of a deep color. 'An ordinary mattress' is a bolster filled with stuffing. 'Figured' is to be understood as colorful with animal figures such as lions, etc. In the Dīghanikāya commentary it is said: ''With fleece on both sides' is a woolen spread with fringes on both sides. 'With fleece on one side' is a woolen spread with fringes on one side.' 'Interwoven with silk' is woven by inserting golden threads between the silk threads; a golden thread, it seems, is called `kaṭṭissa` and also `kasaṭa`. For that reason, they say, it was called 'made of silk and `kasaṭa`' by the elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. 'Stitched with gems' means gilded with gold. 'Pure silk' means devoid of being gilded.

Ajinamigacammānaṃ atisukhumattā dupaṭṭatipaṭṭāni katvā sibbantīti vuttaṃ “ajinappaveṇī”ti. Rattavitānenāti sabbarattena [M 2.0373] vitānena. Yaṃ pana nānāvaṇṇaṃ vānacittaṃ vā lepacittaṃ vā, taṃ vaṭṭati. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānepi eseva nayo. Citraṃ vāti idaṃ pana sabbathā kappiyattā vuttaṃ, na pana ubhatoupadhānesu akappiyattā. Na hi lohitakasaddo citte vaṭṭati. Paṭaliggahaṇeneva cittakassapi attharaṇassa saṅgahetabbappasaṅgato. Kāsāvaṃ pana lohitaṅgavohāraṃ na gacchati, tasmā vitānepi ubhatoupadhānepi vaṭṭati. Sace pamāṇayuttantiādi aññassa pamāṇātikkantassa bimbohanassa paṭikkhittabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana uccāsayanamahāsayanabhāvadassanatthaṃ tathā avuttattā, taṃ pana upadhānaṃ uposathikānaṃ gahaṭṭhānaṃ vaṭṭati. Uccāsayanamahāsayanameva hi tadā tesaṃ na vaṭṭati. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathādīsu kiñcāpi “ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ sabbāneva gonakādīni ratanaparisibbitāni na vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ, vinayaṭṭhakathā [V 2.0275] eva pana kappiyākappiyabhāve pamāṇanti gahetabbaṃ. Abhinissāyāti apassāyāti vuttaṃ.

Because the hides of black antelope and deer are extremely fine, they are sewn by making them two-layered or three-layered; thus it is called 'a patchwork of hides.' 'With a red canopy' means with a canopy that is entirely red. But whatever is of various colors, whether woven with patterns or painted with patterns, that is allowable. This same method applies also to pillows that are red on both ends. 'Or patterned' is said because it is permissible in every way, not because pillows with two red ends are impermissible, for the word 'red' does not apply to what is patterned, and because the inclusion of 'paṭalikā' would also entail the inclusion of a patterned covering. But the ochre color does not come under the designation of 'red,' therefore it is allowable for canopies and for pillows with two red ends. 'If it is of the proper size,' etc., is said to show the rejection of other cushions that exceed the standard measure, not to show the status of high and large beds, as it was not stated in that way. But that pillow is allowable for householders observing the Uposatha. For at that time, only high and large beds are not allowable for them. Although in the Dīghanikāya commentary and others it is said, 'Except for the mattress, all such things as woolen blankets, etc., if stitched with gems, are not allowable,' yet the Vinaya commentary alone should be taken as the authority on the matter of what is allowable and unallowable. 'Relying on' means 'leaning against,' it is said.

Pāsādaparibhogakathā

The Account of Using a Palace

Pāsādaparibhogakathāyaṃ sāratthadīpaniyaṃ vajirabuddhiṭīkāyañca na kiñci vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. cūḷavagga 2.320) pana “suvaṇṇarajatādivicitrānīti saṅghikasenāsanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Puggalikaṃ pana suvaṇṇādivicitraṃ bhikkhussa sampaṭicchitumeva na vaṭṭati ‘na kenaci pariyāyena jātarūparajataṃ sāditabba’nti (mahāva. 299) vuttattā. Tenevettha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 320) ‘saṅghikavihāre vā puggalikavihāre vā’ti vuttaṃ. Gonakādiakappiyabhaṇḍavisaye eva vuttaṃ ekabhikkhussapi tesaṃ gahaṇe dosābhāvā”ti vuttaṃ.

In the Account of Using a Palace, nothing is said in the Sāratthadīpanī or the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā. However, in the Vimativinodanī it is said: ‘“Adorned with gold, silver, and so on”—this is said with reference to a dwelling belonging to the Sangha. But it is not allowable for a bhikkhu to accept an individual dwelling adorned with gold and so on, because it is said: “In no way should gold and silver be accepted” (Mahāva. 299). For that reason it is said here in the commentary (Cūḷava. Aṭṭha. 320): “in a monastery belonging to the Sangha or in an individual monastery.” This was said only in regard to the matter of unsuitable articles such as a goṇaka-rug, because there is no fault for even a single bhikkhu in accepting them.’

Upāhanakathā

The Account of Footwear

Upāhanakathāyaṃ [M 2.0374] “addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇāti abhinavāriṭṭhaphalavaṇṇā, udakena tintakākapattavaṇṇātipi vadanti. Uṇṇāhi katapādukāti uṇṇālomamayakambalehi, uṇṇālomehi eva vā katapādukā. Kāḷasīhoti kāḷamukhavānarajāti. Sesamettha pāḷito ca aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyamevā”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.246) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.246) pana “addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇāti allāriṭṭhaphalavaṇṇā, tintakākapakkhavaṇṇātipi vadanti. Rajananti uparilittanīlādivaṇṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha ‘coḷakena puñchitvā’ti. Tañhi tathā puñchite vigacchati. Yaṃ pana cammassa duggandhāpanayanatthaṃ kāḷarattādirajanehi rañjitattā kāḷarattādivaṇṇaṃ hoti, taṃ coḷādīhi apanetuṃ na sakkā cammagatikameva, tasmā taṃ vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Khallakanti sabbapaṇhipidhānacammaṃ aparigaḷanatthaṃ paṇhiyā uparibhāge apidhāya āropanabandhanamattaṃ vaṭṭati. Vicitrāti saṇṭhānato vicitrapaṭṭā adhippetā, na vaṇṇato sabbaso apanetabbesu khallakādīsu paviṭṭhattā. Biḷālasadisamukhattā mahāulūkā pakkhibiḷālāti vuccanti, tesaṃ cammaṃ nāma pakkhalomameva. Uṇṇāhi katapādukāti ettha uṇṇāmayakambalehi katapādukā saṅgayhanti. Kāḷasīhoti [V 2.0276] kāḷamukhavānarajāti. Cammaṃ na vaṭṭatīti nisīdanattharaṇaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, bhūmattharaṇādivasena paribhogo vaṭṭatevā”ti vuttaṃ.

In the Account of Footwear, it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī: ‘“Of the color of fresh soapberry” means the color of a fresh soapberry fruit; some also say it is the color of a crow's wing wet with water. “Footwear made with wool” means footwear made with blankets of wool-fleece, or just with wool-fleece. “Kāḷasīha” is a species of black-faced monkey. The rest here is to be easily understood from both the Pāli text and the commentary.’ However, in the Vimativinodanī it is said: ‘“Of the color of fresh soapberry” means the color of a wet soapberry fruit; some also say it is the color of a wet crow's wing. “Dye” refers to a color such as blue smeared on top. Therefore he said, “having wiped it with a cloth,” for when wiped thus, it goes away. But as for the black, red, or other color that results from dyeing with black, red, or other dyes to remove the bad smell of the leather, that cannot be removed by a cloth or the like as it has become inherent to the leather; therefore, it should be understood that this is allowable. “Khallaka” means a piece of leather covering the whole heel; it is allowable merely to fasten it by placing it over the upper part of the heel to prevent it from slipping off. “Variegated” is intended to mean straps variegated in shape, not in color, as it is included among the khallaka and other things that are to be completely removed. Because their faces are like a cat's, large owls are called “bird-cats”; their “leather” is just their plumage. Here, by “footwear made with wool,” footwear made with woolen blankets is included. “Kāḷasīha” is a species of black-faced monkey. “The leather is not allowable” means it is not allowable to make it into a sitting mat, but its use as a ground-covering and so on is certainly allowable.’

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 259) pana “migamātukoti tassa nāmaṃ, vātamigoti ca tassa nāmaṃ. ‘Kāḷasīho kāḷamukho kapī’ti likhitaṃ. Cammaṃ na vaṭṭatīti yena pariyāyena cammaṃ vaṭṭissati, so parato āvibhavissati. ‘Attano puggalikavasena [M 2.0375] paccāhāro paṭikkhitto’ti vuttaṃ. ‘Na, bhikkhave, kiñci cammaṃ dhāretabba’nti ettāvatā siddhe ‘na, bhikkhave, gocamma’nti idaṃ parato ‘anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbapaccantimesu janapadesu cammāni attharaṇānī’ti (mahāva. 259) ettha anumatippasaṅgabhayā vuttanti veditabba”nti vuttaṃ.

However, in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is said: ‘“Migamātuka” is its name, and “vātamiga” is also its name. It is written: “A kāḷasīha is a black-faced monkey.” As to “The hide is not allowable”—the way in which the hide will be allowable will become clear later. It is said: “Bringing it back for one's personal use is rejected.” When it has been established by the statement, “Bhikkhus, no kind of hide should be worn,” it should be understood that the words “Bhikkhus, no cowhide” were said because of the fear that permission might be wrongly inferred later in the passage, “I allow, bhikkhus, hides as coverings in all the border districts” (Mahāva. 259).’

Yānakathā

The Account of Vehicles

Yānakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, purisayuttaṃ hatthavaṭṭaka”nti (mahāva. 253) ettha anujānāmi, bhikkhave, purisayuttaṃ, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, hatthavaṭṭakanti evaṃ paccekaṃ vākyaparisamāpanaṃ adhippetanti āha “purisayuttaṃ itthisārathi vā…pe… purisā vā, vaṭṭatiyevā”ti. “Pīṭhakasivikanti pīṭhakayānaṃ. Pāṭaṅkinti andolikāyetaṃ adhivacana”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.253) vuttaṃ, “pīṭhakasivikanti phalakādinā kataṃ pīṭhakayānaṃ. Paṭapotalikaṃ andolikā. Sabbampi yānaṃ upāhanenapi gantuṃ asamatthassa gilānassa anuññāta”nti vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.253).

In the Account of Vehicles, concerning the passage ‘I allow, bhikkhus, a hand-drawn vehicle yoked with men’ (Mahāva. 253), he said the following, intending that the sentence be completed for each term separately, thus: ‘I allow, bhikkhus, that which is yoked with men,’ and ‘I allow, bhikkhus, a hand-drawn vehicle.’ ‘Yoked with men’ means with a female charioteer or … or with men; it is certainly allowable. In the Sāratthadīpanī it is said: ‘A pīṭhakasivikā is a seat-vehicle. Pāṭaṅki is a synonym for a litter.’ In the Vimativinodanī it is said: ‘A pīṭhakasivikā is a seat-vehicle made with planks and so on. A paṭapotalikā is a litter. Any vehicle is allowed for a sick person who is unable to go even with footwear.’

Cīvarakathā

The Account of Robes

57. Cīvarakathāyaṃ “ahatakappānanti ekavāradhotānaṃ. Utuddhaṭānanti ututo dīghakālato uddhaṭānaṃ hatavatthakānaṃ, pilotikānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāpaṇiketi antarāpaṇato patitapilotikacīvare. Ussāho karaṇīyoti pariyesanā kātabbā. Paricchedo panettha natthi, paṭṭasatampi vaṭṭati. Sabbamidaṃ sādiyantassa bhikkhuno vasena vuttaṃ. Aggaḷaṃ tunnanti ettha uddharitvā allīyāpanakhaṇḍaṃ aggaḷaṃ, suttena saṃsibbitaṃ tunnaṃ, vaṭṭetvā karaṇaṃ ovaṭṭikaṃ. Kaṇḍupakaṃ [V 2.0277] vuccati muddikā. Daḷīkammanti anuddharitvāva upassayaṃ katvā allīyāpanakaṃ [M 2.0376] vatthakhaṇḍa”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgataṃ. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.348) pana “acchupeyyanti patiṭṭhapeyyaṃ. Hatavatthakānanti kālātītavatthānaṃ. Uddharitvā allīyāpanakhaṇḍanti dubbalaṭṭhānaṃ apanetvā allīyāpanavatthakhaṇḍa”nti vuttaṃ. Diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭinti dupaṭṭaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ. Ekacciyanti ekapaṭṭaṃ aggapaṭṭaṃ. Aggaḷaṃ ajjhāpessanti jiṇṇaṭṭhāne pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ laggāpeyyaṃ.

57. In the Account of Robes, it is stated in the commentary: ‘“Suitable new cloths” means those washed once. “Taken out after the season” means old cloths, that is, rags, taken out after a long time from the season. “Belonging to a shop” means a robe made from a rag fallen in the marketplace. “An effort should be made” means a search should be undertaken. There is no limit here; even a hundred pieces are allowable. All this is said with respect to a bhikkhu who consents to it. Here, in “a patch and a darn,” a piece for applying that has been cut out is a “patch” (aggaḷa); sewing it together with thread is a “darn” (tunna); making it by folding it over is an “overcast stitch” (ovaṭṭika). A thimble (muddikā) is called a kaṇḍupaka. “Strengthening work” means applying a piece of cloth as a support without cutting out the old part.’ However, in the Sāratthadīpanī it is said: ‘“I would touch” means “I would establish.” “Of old cloths” means of cloths that are past their time. “A piece for applying that has been cut out” means a piece of cloth for applying after having removed the weak spot.’ ‘A double saṅghāṭī’ means a two-layered saṅghāṭī. ‘A single one’ means a single-layered one, a top-layer one. ‘I will apply a patch’ means ‘I would attach a piece of rag to the worn-out spot.’

Chinnacīvarakathā

The Discourse on Cut-up Robes

Chinnacīvarakathāyaṃ tīsu pana cīvaresu dve vā ekaṃ vā chinditvā kātabbanti ettha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, chinnakaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ chinnakaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ chinnakaṃ antaravāsaka”nti (mahāva. 345) vacanato pañcakhaṇḍasattakhaṇḍādivasena chinditvāva kātabbaṃ, na acchinditvāti attho. Sace nappahoti, āgantukapaṭṭaṃ dātabbanti ettha yadi chinditvā kate tiṇṇampi cīvarānaṃ atthāya sāṭako nappahoti, dve cīvarāni chinnakāni kātabbāni, ekaṃ cīvaraṃ acchinnakaṃ kattabbaṃ. Dvīsu cīvaresu chinditvā katesu sāṭako nappahoti, dve cīvarāni acchinnakāni, ekaṃ cīvaraṃ chinnakaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ekasmimpi cīvare chinditvā kate sāṭako nappahoti, evaṃ sati acchinditvā āgantukapaṭṭaṃ dātabbanti attho. Tamatthaṃ pāḷiyā sādhetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādimāha. Tattha anvādhikampi āropetunti evaṃ appahonte sati āgantukapaṭṭampi āropetuṃ anujānāmīti attho.

In the Discourse on Cut-up Robes, it is said that among the three robes, two or one should be made by cutting them up. Here, according to the statement, 'I allow, bhikkhus, a cut-up outer robe, a cut-up upper robe, and a cut-up inner robe' (Mahāvagga 345), it means that a robe should be made only after cutting it into five sections, seven sections, and so on, not without cutting it. If there is not enough cloth, an additional patch should be given. Here, if, after cutting and making the robes, the cloth is not sufficient for all three robes, two robes should be made as cut-up robes and one robe should be made as an uncut robe. If, when making two cut-up robes, the cloth is not sufficient, two robes should be made as uncut robes and one robe should be made as a cut-up robe. If, even when making one cut-up robe, the cloth is not sufficient, in that case, an additional patch should be given without cutting up the robe—this is the meaning. To establish this meaning with the Pāḷi, he says, 'For it has been said,' and so on. There, 'even an extra amount may be added' means: 'When it is thus insufficient, I allow even an additional patch to be added.'

Akappiyacīvarakathā

The Discourse on Unsuitable Robes

Akappiyacīvarakathāyaṃ “naggiyaṃ kusacīraṃ phalakacīraṃ kesakambalaṃ vāḷakambalaṃ ulūkapakkhikaṃ ajinakkhipa”nti imāni titthiyasamādānattā thullaccayavatthūnīti bhagavatā paṭikkhittāni[M 2.0377]. Tattha naggiyanti naggabhāvo acelakabhāvo. Kusacīranti kusena ganthetvā katacīvaraṃ. Vākacīranti tāpasānaṃ vakkalaṃ. Phalakacīranti phalakasaṇṭhānāni phalakāni sibbitvā katacīvaraṃ. Kesakambalanti kesehi tante vāyitvā katakambalaṃ. Vālakambalanti cāmarīvālehi vāyitvā katakambalaṃ. Ulūkapakkhikanti ulūkasakuṇassa pakkhehi katanivāsanaṃ[V 2.0278]. Ajinakkhipanti salomaṃ sakhuraṃ ajinamigacammaṃ. Tāni titthiyaddhajabhūtāni acīvarabhāvena pākaṭānīti ācariyena idha na vuttāni. Potthako pana apākaṭoti taṃ vatvā sabbanīlakādīni dukkaṭavatthukāni vuttāni. “Tipaṭṭacīvarassa vā majjhe dātabbānī”ti vuttattā tipaṭṭacīvaraṃ dhāretuṃ vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Tipaṭṭādīnañca bahupaṭṭacīvarānaṃ antare īdisāni asāruppavaṇṇāni paṭapilotikāni kātabbānīti dasseti. Kañcukaṃ nāma sīsato paṭimuñcitvā kāyāruḷhavatthaṃ. Tenāha “phāletvā rajitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Veṭhananti sīsaveṭhanaṃ. Tirīṭanti makuṭaṃ. Tassa visesaṃ dassetuṃ “tirīṭakaṃ panā”tiādimāha.

In the Discourse on Unsuitable Robes, the Blessed One has rejected the following, which are grounds for a grave offense because they are observances of the sectarians: 'Nakedness, a grass garment, a garment of wooden planks, a human-hair blanket, a horse-hair blanket, a garment of owl's wings, and a hide garment.' Here, 'nakedness' means the state of being naked, the state of being without clothes. 'Grass garment' means a garment made by weaving kusa grass together. 'Bark-fibre garment' means the bark-cloth of ascetics. 'Garment of wooden planks' means a garment made by sewing together planks shaped like boards. 'Human-hair blanket' means a blanket woven with human hair as thread. 'Horse-hair blanket' means a blanket woven with the hair of a chowrie's tail. 'Garment of owl's wings' means a lower garment made from the feathers of an owl. 'Hide garment' means the hide of an antelope with the fur and hooves. Since these are banners of the sectarians and are manifestly not robes, they were not mentioned here by the Teacher. But since a garment made of cloth-strips is not obviously unsuitable, having mentioned that, he states that all-blue robes and so on are grounds for a dukkaṭa offense. Because it is said, 'They should be placed in the middle of a three-layered robe,' it is established that it is allowable to wear a three-layered robe. And he shows that such patches of unsuitable colors and rags should be placed between the layers of multi-layered robes such as the three-layered one. A kañcuka is a garment that covers the body, put on over the head. Therefore he said: 'It is allowable to tear it up, dye it, and use it.' A veṭhana is a head-wrap. A tirīṭa is a diadem. To show its specific kind, he said: 'But a tirīṭaka…,' and so on.

Cīvaravicāraṇakathā

The Discourse on the Arrangement of Robes

Cīvaravicāraṇakathāyaṃ “paṇḍito, bhikkhave, ānando, mahāpañño, bhikkhave, ānando. Yatra hi nāma mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ ājānissati, kusimpi nāma karissati, aḍḍhakusimpi nāma karissati, maṇḍalampi nāma karissati, aḍḍhamaṇḍalampi nāma karissati, vivaṭṭampi nāma karissati, anuvivaṭṭampi nāma karissati, gīveyyakampi nāma karissati, jaṅgheyyakampi nāma karissati, bāhantampi nāma karissati, chinnakaṃ bhavissati, satthalūkhaṃ samaṇasāruppaṃ paccatthikānañca anabhicchita”nti (mahāva. 345) vacanato “passasi [M 2.0378] tvaṃ, ānanda, magadhakhettaṃ acchibaddhaṃ pāḷibaddhaṃ mariyādabaddhaṃ siṅghāṭakabaddha”nti bhagavato saṃkhittena vuttavacanaṃ sutvā āyasmā ānando bhagavato ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cīvaraṃ saṃvidahi. Tathā idānipi evarūpaṃ cīvaraṃ saṃvidahitabbaṃ.

In the Discourse on the Arrangement of Robes, it is said: 'Ānanda is astute, bhikkhus, Ānanda is of great wisdom, bhikkhus, in that he will understand in detail the meaning of what has been stated by me in brief. He will make a kusī, he will make a half-kusī, he will make a maṇḍala, he will make a half-maṇḍala, he will make a vivaṭṭa, he will make an anuvivaṭṭa, he will make a neck-piece, he will make a leg-piece, he will make an arm-piece. It will be a cut-up robe, roughly stitched, suitable for a recluse, and undesirable to opponents' (Mahāvagga 345). Thus, having heard the Blessed One's brief statement, 'Do you see, Ānanda, the Magadhan rice fields, laid out in squares, bounded by embankments, marked off by boundaries, and divided by cross-dikes?,' the Venerable Ānanda, in accordance with the Blessed One's intention, designed robes for many bhikkhus. So too, even now, a robe of such a kind should be designed.

Tattha “acchibaddhanti caturassakedārabaddhaṃ. Pāḷibaddhanti āyāmato ca vitthārato ca dīghamariyādabaddhaṃ. Mariyādabaddhanti antarantarā rassamariyādabaddhaṃ. Siṅghāṭakabaddhanti mariyādāya mariyādaṃ vinivijjhitvā gataṭṭhāne siṅghāṭakabaddhaṃ, catukkasaṇṭhānanti attho. Yatra hi nāmāti yo nāma. Kusimpi nāmātiādīsu kusīti āyāmato ca vitthārato ca anuvātādīnaṃ dīghapaṭṭānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Aḍḍhakusīti antarantarārassapaṭṭānaṃ nāmaṃ. Maṇḍalanti pañcakhaṇḍikassa cīvarassa ekekasmiṃ khaṇḍe mahāmaṇḍalaṃ. Aḍḍhamaṇḍalanti khuddakamaṇḍalaṃ. Vivaṭṭanti maṇḍalañca aḍḍhamaṇḍalañca ekato katvā sibbitaṃ majjhimakhaṇḍaṃ. Anuvivaṭṭanti tassa ubhosu passesu dve khaṇḍāni. Gīveyyakanti gīvāveṭhanaṭṭhāne daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ aññasuttasaṃsibbitaṃ [V 2.0279] āgantukapaṭṭaṃ. Jaṅgheyyakanti jaṅghapāpuṇanaṭṭhāne tatheva saṃsibbitaṃ paṭṭaṃ. Gīvāṭṭhāne ca jaṅghaṭṭhāne ca paṭṭānametaṃ nāmanti. Bāhantanti anuvivaṭṭānaṃ bahi ekekaṃ khaṇḍaṃ. Iti pañcakhaṇḍikacīvarenetaṃ vicāritanti. Atha vā anuvivaṭṭanti vivaṭṭassa ekapassato dvinnaṃ ekapassato dvinnanti catunnampi khaṇḍānametaṃ nāmaṃ. Bāhantanti suppamāṇaṃ cīvaraṃ pārupantena saṃharitvā bāhāya upari ṭhapitā ubho antā bahimukhā tiṭṭhanti, tesaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Ayameva hi nayo mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 345) āgato.

Here, 'acchibaddha' means laid out in square plots. 'Pāḷibaddha' means bounded by long boundaries both lengthwise and widthwise. 'Mariyādabaddha' means bounded by short boundaries in between. 'Siṅghāṭakabaddha' means bound at the place where one boundary cuts across another, forming a cross-dike; the meaning is a four-cornered shape. 'Yatra hi nāma' means 'who indeed.' In such phrases as 'kusim pi nāma,' 'kusī' is a term for the long strips, lengthwise and widthwise, such as the anuvāta. 'Aḍḍhakusī' is the name for the short strips in between. 'Maṇḍala' is the large panel in each section of a five-section robe. 'Aḍḍhamaṇḍala' is the small panel. 'Vivaṭṭa' is the central section sewn by joining a maṇḍala and an aḍḍhamaṇḍala together. 'Anuvivaṭṭa' means the two sections on both sides of that. 'Gīveyyaka' is an additional patch sewn on with other thread for strengthening at the neck-opening. 'Jaṅgheyyaka' is a patch similarly sewn on at the place that reaches the shins. This is the name for the strips at the neck-place and the shin-place. 'Bāhanta' is the single section outside the anuvivaṭṭas. Thus this is explained with reference to the five-section robe. Alternatively, 'anuvivaṭṭa' is the name for all four sections: two on one side of the vivaṭṭa and two on the other side. 'Bāhanta' means: when one wearing a robe of proper size gathers it and places it over the arm, the two ends face outwards; this is the name for them. 'This very method is stated in the Great Commentary.' This comes from the Commentary (on Mahāvagga 345).

Cīvarasibbanakathā

The Discourse on Sewing Robes

Daṇḍakathinenacīvarasibbanakathāyaṃ [M 2.0379] – tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū tattha tattha khīlaṃ nikkhanitvā sambandhitvā cīvaraṃ sibbenti, cīvaraṃ vikaṇṇaṃ hoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kathinaṃ kathinarajjuṃ, tattha tattha obandhitvā cīvaraṃ sibbetunti. Visame kathinaṃ pattharanti, kathinaṃ paribhijjati…pe… na, bhikkhave, visame kathinaṃ pattharitabbaṃ, yo patthareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassāti.

In the Discourse on Sewing Robes with a Stick-Frame, it is said: Now at that time, monks drove in pegs here and there, tied them together, and sewed robes, but the robes became uneven. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. He said: “I allow, monks, a kathina frame and a kathina cord. Having fastened it here and there, you may sew robes.” They spread the kathina frame on uneven ground, and the frame broke…. “Monks, a kathina frame should not be spread on uneven ground. Whoever does so incurs an offense of wrong-doing.”

Chamāya kathinaṃ pattharanti, kathinaṃ paṃsukitaṃ hoti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tiṇasanthārakanti. Kathinassa anto jīrati. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ āropetunti. Kathinaṃ nappahoti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, daṇḍakathinaṃ bidalakaṃ salākaṃ vinandhanarajjuṃ vinandhanasuttakaṃ vinandhitvā cīvaraṃ sibbetunti. Suttantarikāyo visamā honti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kaḷimbhakanti. Suttā vaṅkā honti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, moghasuttakanti.

They spread the kathina on the ground, and it became soiled with dust. “I allow, monks, a grass mat.” The edge of the kathina frayed. “I allow, monks, to attach a protective border.” The kathina was not sufficient. “I allow, monks, a stick-kathina, a bamboo splint, a pin, a tying rope, and a tying thread. Having bound the robe with these, you may sew it.” The spaces between the threads became uneven. “I allow, monks, a marking-strip.” The threads became crooked. “I allow, monks, a basting thread.”

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū adhotehi pādehi kathinaṃ akkamanti, kathinaṃ dussati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – na, bhikkhave, adhotehi pādehi kathinaṃ akkamitabbaṃ, yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassāti.

Now at that time, monks stepped on the kathina with unwashed feet, and it became soiled. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, the kathina should not be stepped on with unwashed feet. Whoever does so incurs an offense of wrong-doing.”

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū allehi pādehi kathinaṃ akkamanti, kathinaṃ dussati. Bhagavato [V 2.0280] etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – na, bhikkhave, allehi pādehi kathinaṃ akkamitabbaṃ, yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassāti.

Now at that time, monks stepped on the kathina with wet feet, and it became soiled. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, the kathina should not be stepped on with wet feet. Whoever does so incurs an offense of wrong-doing.”

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū saupāhanā kathinaṃ akkamanti, kathinaṃ dussati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – na, bhikkhave, saupāhanena kathinaṃ akkamitabbaṃ. Yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassāti.

Now at that time, monks wearing sandals stepped on the kathina, and it became soiled. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, the kathina should not be stepped on with sandals. Whoever does so incurs an offense of wrong-doing.”

Tena [M 2.0380] kho pana samayena bhikkhū cīvaraṃ sibbantā aṅguliyā paṭiggaṇhanti, aṅguliyo dukkhā honti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, paṭiggahanti.

Now at that time, while sewing robes, monks pushed the needle with their fingers, and their fingers became sore. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, a thimble.”

Tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū uccāvace paṭiggahe dhārenti suvaṇṇamayaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ. Manussā ujjhāyanti khīyanti vipācenti “seyyathāpi gihī kāmabhogino”ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – na, bhikkhave, uccāvacā paṭiggahā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassāti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭhimayaṃ…pe… saṅkhanābhimayanti.

Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were using various thimbles made of gold and silver. People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying: “Just like householders enjoying sensual pleasures!” They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, various kinds of thimbles should not be used. Whoever uses them incurs an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, those made of bone … horn … ivory … conch-shell.”

Tena kho pana samayena sūciyopi satthakāpi paṭiggahāpi nassanti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āvesanavitthakanti. Āvesanavitthake samākulā honti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, paṭiggahathavikanti. Aṃsabaddhako na hoti…pe… anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṃsabaddhakaṃ bandhanasuttakanti.

Now at that time, needles, small knives, and thimbles were getting lost. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, a sewing box.” The sewing boxes became cluttered. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, a sewing bag.” There was no shoulder strap…. “I allow, monks, a shoulder strap and a tying cord.”

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū abbhokāse cīvaraṃ sibbantā sītenapi uṇhenapi kilamanti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kathinasālaṃ kathinamaṇḍapanti. Kathinasālā nīcavatthukā hoti, udakena ottharīyati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, uccavatthukaṃ kātunti. Cayo paripatati. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cinituṃ tayo caye iṭṭhakacayaṃ, silācayaṃ, dārucayanti. Ārohantā vihaññanti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tayo sopāne iṭṭhakasopānaṃ, silāsopānaṃ, dārusopānanti. Ārohantā paripatanti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ālambanabāhanti. Kathinasālāya tiṇacuṇṇaṃ paripatati[V 2.0281]. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ogumphetvā [M 2.0381] ullittāvalittaṃ kātuṃ setavaṇṇaṃ kāḷavaṇṇaṃ gerukaparikammaṃ mālākammaṃ latākammaṃ makaradantakaṃ pañcapaṭikaṃ cīvararajjunti.

Now at that time, monks sewing robes in the open were afflicted by cold and heat. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, a kathina hall and a kathina pavilion.” The kathina hall had a low foundation and was inundated by water. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, to make it with a high foundation.” The foundation mound collapsed. “I allow, monks, to build three kinds of foundation mounds: of brick, of stone, and of wood.” When climbing up, they were troubled. “I allow, monks, three kinds of stairways: of brick, of stone, and of wood.” When climbing up, they fell down. “I allow, monks, a handrail.” Grass and dust fell into the kathina hall. “I allow, monks, to interweave a roof and plaster it inside and out, to apply white coloring, black coloring, red-ochre work, garland-work, creeper-work, ‘monster-teeth’ design, five-strip design, and a robe-line.”

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū cīvaraṃ sibbetvā tatheva kathinaṃ ujjhitvā pakkamanti, undūrehipi upacikāhipi khajjati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kathinaṃ saṅgharitunti. Kathinaṃ paribhijjati. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, goghaṃsikāya kathinaṃ saṅgharitunti. Kathinaṃ viniveṭhiyati. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, bandhanarajjunti.

Now at that time, after sewing robes, monks would depart, leaving the kathina just as it was. It was eaten by mice and termites. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, to store the kathina away.” When they did so, the kathina broke. “I allow, monks, to store the kathina using an ox-jaw piece.” The kathina unrolled. “I allow, monks, a tying rope.”

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū kuṭṭepi thambhepi kathinaṃ ussāpetvā pakkamanti, paripatitvā kathinaṃ bhijjati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, bhittikhīle vā nāgadante vā laggetunti. Ayaṃ khuddakavatthukhandhake āgato pāḷipāṭho.

Now at that time, monks would lean the kathina against walls and pillars and then depart. It would fall down and break. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, to hang it on a wall-peg or an ‘elephant’s tooth’ peg.” This is the Pali text that comes in the Khandhaka on Minor Matters.

“Kathinanti nisseṇimpi, tattha attharitabbakaṭasārakakilañjānaṃ aññatarampi. Kathinarajjunti yāya dupaṭṭacīvaraṃ sibbantā kathine cīvaraṃ vibandhanti. Kathinaṃ nappahotīti dīghassa bhikkhuno pamāṇena kataṃ kathinaṃ ittarassa bhikkhuno cīvaraṃ patthariyamānaṃ nappahoti, antoyeva hoti, daṇḍake na pāpuṇātīti attho. Daṇḍakathinanti tassa majjhe ittarassa bhikkhuno pamāṇena aññaṃ nisseṇiṃ bandhituṃ anujānāmīti attho. Bidalakanti daṇḍakathinappamāṇena kaṭasārakassa pariyante paṭisaṃharitvā duguṇakaraṇaṃ. Salākanti dupaṭṭacīvarassa antare pavesanasalākaṃ. Vinandhanarajjunti mahānisseṇiyā saddhiṃ khuddakanisseṇiṃ vinandhituṃ rajjuṃ. Vinandhanasuttakanti khuddakanisseṇiyā cīvaraṃ vinandhituṃ suttakaṃ. Vinandhitvā cīvaraṃ sibbitunti tena suttakena tattha cīvaraṃ vinandhitvā [M 2.0382] sibbetuṃ. Visamā hontīti kāci khuddakā honti, kāci mahantā. Kaḷimbhakanti pamāṇasaññākaraṇaṃ yaṃ kiñci tālapaṇṇādiṃ. Moghasuttakanti vaḍḍhakīnaṃ dārūsu kāḷasuttena viya haliddisuttena saññākaraṇaṃ. Aṅguliyā paṭiggaṇhantīti sūcimukhaṃ aṅguliyā paṭicchanti. Paṭiggahanti aṅgulikosakaṃ. Āvesanavitthakaṃ nāma yaṃ kiñci pāticaṅkoṭakādi. Uccavatthukanti paṃsuṃ ākiritvā uccavatthukaṃ kātuṃ anujānāmīti attho. Ogumphetvā ullittāvalittaṃ kātunti chadanaṃ odhunitvā ghanadaṇḍakaṃ katvā anto ceva bahi ca mattikāya limpitunti attho. Goghaṃsikāyāti veḷuṃ vā rukkhadaṇḍakaṃ [V 2.0282] vā anto katvā tena saddhiṃ saṃharitunti attho. Bandhanarajjunti tathā saṃharitassa bandhanarajju”nti ayaṃ aṭṭhakathāpāṭho (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 256).

“‘Kathina’ means a ladder-frame, or any of the things to be spread on it, such as a mat, a frame, or reeds. ‘Kathina-rope’ is the rope with which they bind the robe to the kathina when sewing a double-layered robe. ‘The kathina is not sufficient’ means: a kathina made to the measure of a tall monk is not sufficient when the robe of a shorter monk is spread out; it remains inside and does not reach the frame-sticks. This is the meaning. ‘Stick-kathina’ means: I allow another ladder-frame to be tied in the middle of it to the measure of a shorter monk. This is the meaning. ‘Bamboo splint’ is the doubling achieved by folding back the edges of the mat-frame to the size of the stick-kathina. ‘Pin’ is the insertion-pin for the space between the double-layered robe. ‘Tying rope’ is the rope for tying the small ladder-frame together with the large ladder-frame. ‘Tying thread’ is the thread for tying the robe to the small ladder-frame. ‘Having tied the robe, you may sew it’ means to sew the robe after having tied it there with that thread. ‘They are uneven’ means some are small, some are large. ‘Marking-strip’ is any kind of marker for measurement, such as a palm leaf. ‘Basting thread’ is for making a mark with a yellow thread, like carpenters do with a black thread on wood. ‘They receive with the finger’ means they receive the point of the needle with a finger. ‘Thimble’ means a finger-sheath. ‘Sewing box’ is any kind of small bowl or basket. ‘High foundation’ means: I allow a high foundation to be made by piling up earth. This is the meaning. ‘To interweave a roof and plaster it inside and out’ means to cover the roof, make a solid framework, and plaster it with clay inside and out. This is the meaning. ‘With an ox-jaw piece’ means to roll it up together with a bamboo or wooden stick placed inside. This is the meaning. ‘Tying rope’ is the rope for tying what has been rolled up in this way.” This is the text from the commentary (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 256).

“Anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍanti kilañjādīsu karotīti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Bidalakanti duguṇakaraṇasaṅkhātassa kiriyāvisesassa adhivacanaṃ. Kassa duguṇakaraṇaṃ? Yena kilañjādinā mahantaṃ kathinaṃ atthataṃ, tassa. Tañhi daṇḍakathinappamāṇena pariyante saṃharitvā duguṇaṃ kātabbaṃ. Paṭiggahanti aṅgulikañcukaṃ. Pāti nāma paṭiggahasaṇṭhānena kato bhājanaviseso. Na sammatīti nappahoti. Nīcavatthukaṃ cinitunti bahikuṭṭassa samantato nīcavatthukaṃ katvā cinitu”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.260-262).

“‘A protective border’: it is said in the section on knots that this is made with reed-mats and so on. ‘Bamboo splint’ is a term for the specific action known as doubling. The doubling of what? Of that large kathina that is spread out with reed-mats and so on. For that, having gathered the edges to the measure of the stick-kathina, it should be doubled. ‘Thimble’ means a finger-stall. ‘Pāti’ is a particular kind of vessel made in the shape of a bowl. ‘Na sammati’ means ‘it is not sufficient.’ ‘To build a low foundation’ means to build by making a low foundation all around the outer wall.” This is from the Sāratthadīpanī (Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Cūḷavagga 3.260–262).

“Nisseṇimpīti catūhi daṇḍehi cīvarappamāṇena āyatacaturassaṃ katvā baddhapaṭalampi. Ettha hi cīvarakoṭiyo samakaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ yathāsukhaṃ sibbanti. Tattha attharitabbanti tassā nisseṇiyā upari cīvarassa upatthambhanatthāya attharitabbaṃ. Kathinasaṅkhātāya nisseṇiyā cīvarassa bandhanakarajju kathinarajjūti [M 2.0383] majjhimapadalopī samāsoti āha “yāyā”tiādi. Tattha yasmā dvinnaṃ paṭalānaṃ ekasmiṃ adhike jāte tattha valiyo honti, tasmā dupaṭṭacīvarassa paṭaladvayampi samakaṃ katvā bandhanakarajju kathinarajjūti veditabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ (cūḷava. 256) kathinassa anto jīratīti kathine baddhassa cīvarassa pariyanto jīratī”ti vimativinodaniyaṃ vuttaṃ.

“By ‘a scaffolding’ is meant a long rectangle made with four poles to the measure of a robe, with a bound frame. Here, having bound the corners of the robe evenly, they sew the robe at their convenience. There, ‘it should be spread out’ means it should be spread out over that scaffolding for the purpose of supporting the robe. The binding cord for the robe on the scaffolding known as the kathina is the ‘kathina-cord’; he says ‘yāyā,’ etc., explaining that this is a compound with the elision of the middle term. There, because folds arise when one of the two layers becomes larger, for a double-layered robe both layers should be made even, and the binding cord should be understood as the ‘kathina-cord.’ In the Pāli (Cūḷavagga 256), it is said in the Vimativinodanī: ‘“The edge of the kathina wears out” means the border of the robe bound to the kathina wears out.’”

“Bidalakaṃ nāma diguṇakaraṇasaṅkhātassa kiriyāvisesassa adhivacanaṃ. Kassa diguṇakaraṇaṃ? Yena kilañjādinā mahantaṃ kathinaṃ atthataṃ, tassa. Tañhi daṇḍakathinappamāṇena pariyante saṃharitvā diguṇaṃ kātabbaṃ, aññathā khuddakacīvarassa anuvātaparibhaṇḍādividhānakaraṇe hatthassa okāso na hoti. Salākāya sati dvinnaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ ñatvā sibbitāsibbitaṃ sukhaṃ paññāyati. Daṇḍakathine kate na bahūhi sahāyehi payojanaṃ. ‘Asaṃkuṭitvā cīvaraṃ samaṃ hoti, koṇāpi samā hontī’ti likhitaṃ, ‘haliddisuttena saññākaraṇa’nti vuttattā ‘haliddisuttena cīvaraṃ sibbetumpi vaṭṭatī’ti siddhaṃ. Tattha hi keci akappiyasaññino. Paṭiggaho nāma aṅgulikoso. Pātīti paṭiggahasaṇṭhānaṃ. Paṭiggahathavikanti [V 2.0283] aṅgulikosathavika”nti vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. cūḷavagga 256) āgataṃ.

“By ‘bidalaka’ is meant the specific action known as doubling. The doubling of what? Of that large kathina that has been spread out with a mat, etc. For it should be gathered at the edges to the measure of the pole-kathina and made double; otherwise, there is no room for the hand when making the lining, border, etc., for a small robe. When there is a pin, one can know which of the two layers it is, and it is easy to distinguish the sewn from the unsewn. When a pole-kathina is made, there is no need for many assistants. It is written: ‘The robe becomes even without shrinking, and the corners also become even.’ Because it is said, ‘making a mark with a turmeric thread,’ it is established that ‘it is also allowable to sew the robe with a turmeric thread.’ For here some perceive it as unallowable. ‘Paṭiggaha’ means a finger-sheath. ‘Pāti’ has the form of a paṭiggaha. ‘Paṭiggahathavika’ means a finger-sheath bag.” This is found in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Cūḷavagga 256).

Gahapaticīvarādikathā

The Discussion on Robes from Householders, etc.

Gahapaticīvarādikathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gahapaticīvaraṃ, yo icchati, paṃsukūliko hotu, yo icchati, gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyatu, itarītarenapāhaṃ, bhikkhave, santuṭṭhiṃ vaṇṇemī”ti (mahāva. 337) vacanato asamādinnadhutaṅgo yo bhikkhu paṃsukūlaṃ dhāretuṃ icchati, tena paṃsukūlikena bhavitabbaṃ[M 2.0384]. Yo pana gihīhi dinnaṃ gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyituṃ icchati, tena gahapaticīvarasādiyakena bhavitabbaṃ. Samādinnadhutaṅgo pana bhikkhu “gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipāmi, paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti adhiṭṭhahanato gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyituṃ na vaṭṭati. Gahapaticīvaranti gahapatīhi dinnaṃ cīvaraṃ. Itarītarenapīti appagghenapi mahagghenapi yena kenacīti attho.

In the discussion on robes from householders, etc.: “I allow, bhikkhus, the householder’s robe. Whoever wishes may be a rag-robe wearer; whoever wishes may accept the householder’s robe. With one or the other, bhikkhus, I praise contentment.” (Mahāvagga 337) According to this, a bhikkhu who has not undertaken the ascetic practices but wishes to wear a rag-robe should be a rag-robe wearer. But one who wishes to accept a householder’s robe given by laypeople should be an accepter of a householder’s robe. However, a bhikkhu who has undertaken the ascetic practices is not allowed to accept a householder’s robe, since he has made the determination: “I reject the householder’s robe; I undertake the practice of the rag-robe wearer.” “A householder’s robe” is a robe given by householders. “With one or the other” means with anything whatsoever, whether of little value or of great value; that is the meaning.

“Itarītarenāti itarena itarena. Itara-saddo pana aniyamavacano dvikkhattuṃ vuccamāno yaṃkiñci-saddehi samānattho hotīti vuttaṃ appagghenapi mahagghenapi yena kenacī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.337), “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pāvāraṃ, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, koseyyapāvāraṃ, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kojava”nti (mahāva. 337) vacanato pāvārādīnipi sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha pāvāroti salomako kappāsādibhedo. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kojavanti ettha pakatikojavameva vaṭṭati, mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavaṃ na vaṭṭati. Kojavanti uṇṇāmayo pāvārasadiso. “Mahāpiṭṭhi kojavanti hatthipiṭṭhīsu attharitabbatāya ‘mahāpiṭṭhiya’nti laddhasamaññaṃ caturaṅgulapupphaṃ kojava”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.337) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.337) “mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavanti hatthipiṭṭhiyaṃ attharitabbatāya ‘mahāpiṭṭhiya’nti laddhasamaññaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 337) pana “mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavaṃ nāma atirekacaturaṅgulapupphaṃ kirā”ti vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kambala”nti (mahāva. 338) vacanato aḍḍhakāsiyādīni mahagghānipi kambalāni vaṭṭanti[V 2.0284]. Aḍḍhakāsiyanti ettha kāsīti sahassaṃ vuccati, taṃagghanako kāsiyo. Ayaṃ pana pañca satāni agghati, tasmā aḍḍhakāsiyoti vutto.

“‘With one or the other’ means with one and with the other. The word ‘itara,’ however, is an indefinite term, and when spoken twice, it has the same meaning as the words for ‘whatever’; thus it is said: ‘with anything whatsoever, whether of little value or of great value’” — so it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.337). Based on the passage, “I allow, bhikkhus, a cloak; I allow, bhikkhus, a silk cloak; I allow, bhikkhus, a fleecy coverlet” (Mahāvagga 337), it is allowable to accept cloaks and so on. Here, a ‘pāvāra’ is a type of cloth such as cotton with fleece attached. Regarding “I allow, bhikkhus, a fleecy coverlet,” here only an ordinary coverlet is allowable; a ‘great-back’ coverlet is not allowable. A ‘kojava’ is made of wool, similar to a cloak. It is said in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.337): “A ‘great-back kojava’ is a kojava with flowers four fingers wide that has received the designation ‘great-back’ because it is to be spread on the backs of elephants.” The Vimativinodanī (Vimativinodanīṭīkā, Mahāvagga 2.337) also states: “A ‘great-back kojava’ is a woolen spread that has received the designation ‘great-back’ because it is to be spread on an elephant’s back.” But in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajirabuddhiṭīkā, Mahāvagga 337) it is said: “A ‘great-back kojava,’ it seems, is one with flowers exceeding four fingers.” Based on the passage, “I allow, bhikkhus, a blanket” (Mahāvagga 338), even expensive blankets such as an aḍḍhakāsī are allowable. Here, regarding ‘aḍḍhakāsī’: ‘kāsī’ is said to be a thousand; a thing worth that is a ‘kāsīya.’ This one, however, is worth five hundred; therefore it is called ‘aḍḍhakāsī.’”

Chacīvarakathā

The Discussion on the Six Robes

Chacīvarakathāyaṃ [M 2.0385] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cha cīvarāni khomaṃ kappāsikaṃ koseyyaṃ kambalaṃ sāṇaṃ bhaṅga”nti (mahāva. 339) vacanato khomādīni cha cīvarāni dukūlādīni cha anulomacīvarāni ca vaṭṭanti. Tattha “khomanti khomasuttehi vāyitaṃ khomapaṭṭacīvaraṃ. Kappāsikanti kappāsato nibbattasuttehi vāyitaṃ. Koseyyanti kosakārakapāṇakehi nibbattasuttehi vāyitaṃ. Kambalanti uṇṇāmayacīvaraṃ. Sāṇanti sāṇasuttehi katacīvaraṃ. Bhaṅganti khomasuttādīni sabbāni, ekaccāni vā missetvā katacīvaraṃ. Bhaṅgampi vākamayamevāti keci. Dukūlaṃ paṭṭuṇṇaṃ somārapaṭaṃ cīnapaṭaṃ iddhijaṃ devadinnanti imāni pana cha cīvarāni etesaṃyeva anulomānīti visuṃ na vuttāni. Dukūlañhi sāṇassa anulomaṃ vākamayattā. Paṭṭuṇṇadese sañjātavatthaṃ paṭṭuṇṇaṃ. ‘Paṭṭuṇṇakoseyyaviseso’ti hi abhidhānakose vuttaṃ. Somāradese cīnadese ca jātavatthāni somāracīnapaṭāni. Paṭṭuṇṇādīni tīṇi koseyyassa anulomāni pāṇakehi katasuttamayattā. Iddhijaṃ ehibhikkhūnaṃ puññiddhiyā nibbattacīvaraṃ, taṃ khomādīnaṃ aññataraṃ hotīti tesaṃ eva anulomaṃ. Devatāhi dinnaṃ cīvaraṃ devadinnaṃ. Kapparukkhe nibbattaṃ jāliniyā devakaññāya anuruddhattherassa dinnavatthasadisaṃ, tampi khomādīnaṃyeva anulomaṃ hoti tesu aññatarabhāvato”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.462-463) vuttaṃ.

In the discussion on the six robes: “I allow, bhikkhus, six kinds of robes: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and a blend.” (Mahāvagga 339) According to this statement, the six robes—linen and so on—along with six conforming robes such as fine cloth and others, are allowable. Here, “linen” refers to a robe woven from linen threads. “Cotton” means a robe woven from threads produced from cotton. “Silk” is a robe woven from threads produced by silk-cocoon creatures. “Wool” is a robe made of wool. “Hemp” is a robe made from hemp threads. “A blend” refers to a robe made by mixing all or some of the above threads, such as linen and so on. Some say that a blend is also made of bark-fiber. The six conforming robes—fine cloth, silk-wool, Somāra cloth, Chinese cloth, cloth produced by psychic power, and cloth given by deities—are not mentioned separately as they are considered to conform to these. For instance, fine cloth conforms to hemp because it is made of bark-fiber. Silk-wool refers to cloth produced in the Paṭṭuṇṇa region. Indeed, it is stated in the Abhidhānakosa: “Silk-wool is a special type of silk.” Somāra and Chinese cloth are fabrics produced in the Somāra and Chinese regions, respectively. These three—silk-wool, Somāra, and Chinese cloth—conform to silk because they are made from threads produced by creatures. Cloth produced by psychic power is a robe produced by the meritorious power of the ‘come, bhikkhu’ monks; since it is one of the six—linen or another—it thus conforms to them. Cloth given by deities is a robe given by deities. Cloth produced from a kappa-tree, like the garment given by the celestial maiden Jālinī to the Elder Anuruddha, is similar, and it also conforms to the six robes, being one of them. This is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. 2.462-463).

Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.463) pana “khomanti khomasuttehi vāyitaṃ khomapaṭacīvaraṃ, taṃ vākamayanti vadanti. Kappāsasuttehi vāyitaṃ kappāsikaṃ. Evaṃ sesānipi. Kambalanti eḷakādīnaṃ lomamayasuttena vāyitaṃ paṭaṃ. Bhaṅganti khomasuttādīni sabbāni, ekaccāni vā missetvā vāyitaṃ cīvaraṃ, bhaṅgampi vākamayamevāti keci[M 2.0386]. Dukūlaṃ paṭṭuṇṇaṃ somārapaṭaṃ cīnapaṭaṃ iddhijaṃ devadinnanti imāni cha cīvarāni etesaññeva anulomānīti visuṃ na vuttāni. Dukūlañhi sāṇassa anulomaṃ vākamayattā. ‘Paṭṭuṇṇaṃ koseyyaviseso’ti abhidhānakose vuttaṃ. Somāradese cīnadese ca jātavatthāni somāracīnapaṭāni. Paṭṭuṇṇādīni tīṇi [V 2.0285] koseyyassa anulomāni pāṇakehi katasuttamayattā. Iddhijanti ehibhikkhūnaṃ puññiddhiyā nibbattacīvaraṃ, kapparukkhehi nibbattaṃ, devadinnañca khomādīnaṃ aññataraṃ hotīti tesaṃ sabbesaṃ anulomānī”ti vuttaṃ.

But in the Vimativinodanī it is stated: “‘Linen’ means a linen-cloth robe woven with linen threads; they call that bark-fiber. ‘Cotton’ is woven with cotton threads. And so for the rest. ‘Wool’ means a cloth woven from thread made of the wool of sheep and other animals. ‘A blend’ is a robe woven by mixing all or some threads such as linen, etc.; and some say that a blend is also made of bark-fiber. ‘Fine cloth,’ ‘silk-wool,’ ‘Somāra cloth,’ ‘Chinese cloth,’ ‘produced by psychic power,’ and ‘given by a deity’—these six robes are not mentioned separately because they conform to these same categories. For fine cloth conforms to hemp because it is made of bark-fiber. ‘Silk-wool is a variety of silk,’ it is stated in the Abhidhānakosa. ‘Somāra cloth’ and ‘Chinese cloth’ are fabrics produced in the Somāra and Cīna countries. The three—‘silk-wool,’ etc.—conform to silk because they are made of thread produced by living beings. ‘Produced by psychic power’ refers to a robe produced by the meritorious power of the ‘come, bhikkhu’ monks, or produced by kappa-trees; and ‘given by a deity’ is one of the robes beginning with linen, thus all of these conform to them.”

Rajanādikathā

The Discussion on Dyes, etc.

Rajanādikathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cha rajanāni mūlarajanaṃ khandharajanaṃ tacarajanaṃ pattarajanaṃ puppharajanaṃ phalarajana”nti vacanato imesu chasu rajanesu ekakena cīvaraṃ rajitabbaṃ, na chakaṇena vā paṇḍumattikāya vā rajitabbaṃ. Tāya rajitacīvaraṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ hoti. Charajanānaṃ sarūpaṃ heṭṭhā parikkhārakathāyaṃ vuttameva. Tattha chakaṇenāti gomayena. Paṇḍumattikāyāti tambamattikāya. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, rajanaṃ pacituṃ cullaṃ rajanakumbhi”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato sītudakāya cīvaraṃ na rajitabbaṃ. Tāya hi rajitacīvaraṃ duggandhaṃ hoti. Tattha sītudakāti apakkarajanaṃ vuccati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, uttarāḷumpaṃ bandhitu”nti vacanato uttarāḷumpaṃ bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha uttarāḷumpanti vaṭṭādhārakaṃ, rajanakumbhiyā majjhe ṭhapetvā taṃ ādhārakaṃ parikkhipitvā rajanaṃ pakkhipituṃ anujānāmīti attho. Evañhi kate rajanaṃ na uttarati. Tattha “rajanakumbhiyā majjhe ṭhapetvāti antorajanakumbhiyā majjhe ṭhapetvā. Evaṃ vaṭṭādhārake antorajanakumbhiyā pakkhitte majjhe udakaṃ tiṭṭhati, vaṭṭādhārakato bahi samantā antokumbhiyaṃ rajanacchalli. Pakkhipitunti [M 2.0387] rajanacchalliṃ pakkhipitu”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.344) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.344) pana “evañhi kateti vaṭṭādhārassa anto rajanodakaṃ, bahi challikañca katvā viyojane kate. Na uttaratīti kevalaṃ udakato pheṇuṭṭhānābhāvā na uttaratī”ti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 344) pana “gomaye āpatti natthi, virūpattā vāritaṃ. Kuṅkumapupphaṃ na vaṭṭatīti vadantī”ti vuttaṃ.

In the discussion on dyes, etc., it is said: “I allow, bhikkhus, six kinds of dyes: root dye, stem dye, bark dye, leaf dye, flower dye, and fruit dye.” A robe should be dyed with one of these six dyes, not with cow dung or red clay. A robe dyed with these becomes discolored. The nature of these six dyes has already been explained above in the discussion on requisites. Here, ‘with cow dung’ means with cow dung. ‘With red clay’ means with copper-colored clay. “I allow, bhikkhus, a small dye pot to cook dye in.” Therefore, a robe should not be dyed with cold water, for a robe dyed with that becomes foul-smelling. Here, ‘cold water’ refers to uncooked dye. “I allow, bhikkhus, to tie on a support ring.” Therefore, it is allowable to tie on a support ring. Here, ‘support ring’ means a circular support. The meaning is: “I allow placing it in the middle of the dye pot, surrounding that support, and then adding the dye.” When this is done, the dye does not overflow. Here, “placing in the middle of the dye pot means placing it inside the dye pot. When the circular support is placed inside the dye pot, water remains in the middle, while the dye-stuff is all around outside the support within the pot. ‘Adding’ means adding the dye-stuff.” This is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī. But in the Vimativinodanī it is stated: “‘When this is done’ means when a separation is made with the dye water inside the circular support and the dye-stuff outside. ‘It does not overflow’ means it does not overflow because foam does not arise from the water alone.” In the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is stated: “There is no offense in using cow dung; it is forbidden because it is unsuitable. They say that the saffron flower is not allowable.”

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, udake vā nakhapiṭṭhikāya vā thevakaṃ dātu”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato tathā katvā rajanassa pakkāpakkabhāvo jānitabbo. Tattha udake vā nakhapiṭṭhikāya vāti sace paripakkaṃ hoti, udakapātiyā dinno thevo sahasā na visarati, nakhapiṭṭhiyampi avisaranto tiṭṭhati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, rajanuḷuṅkaṃ daṇḍakathālaka”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato [V 2.0286] rajanassa olokanakāle kumbhiyā rakkhaṇatthaṃ uḷuṅkadaṇḍakathālikāni icchitabbāni.
