Tattha rajanuḷuṅkanti rajanauḷuṅkaṃ. Daṇḍakathālakanti daṇḍameva daṇḍakaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, rajanakolambaṃ rajanaghaṭa”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato tānipi icchitabbāni. Tattha rajanakolambanti rajanakuṇḍaṃ. Tattha rajanakuṇḍanti pakkarajanaṭṭhapanakaṃ mahāghaṭaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, rajanadoṇika”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato pātiyampi patte cīvare maddante cīvarassa paribhijjanato cīvararakkhaṇatthaṃ rajanadoṇikā icchitabbā. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tiṇasantharaka”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato chamāya cīvare patthariyamāne cīvarassa paṃsukitattā tato rakkhaṇatthaṃ tiṇasantharaṃ kātabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cīvaravaṃsaṃ cīvararajju”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato tiṇasanthārake upacikādīhi khajjamāne cīvaravaṃse vā cīvararajjuyā [M 2.0388] vā cīvaraṃ pattharitabbaṃ majjhena cīvare laggite rajanassa ubhato gaḷitattā.

“I allow, bhikkhus, to place a drop in water or on the back of a nail.” By doing so, one should determine whether the dye is cooked or uncooked. Here, “in water or on the back of a nail” means: if it is fully cooked, a drop placed in a water bowl does not scatter immediately, and it also remains without scattering on the back of a nail. “I allow, bhikkhus, a dye-ladle, a stick, and a small bowl.” Therefore, when examining the dye, a ladle, stick, and small bowl should be used for the protection of the pot. Here, “dye-ladle” means a dye-ladle. “A stick-and-bowl” means just a stick. “I allow, bhikkhus, a dye-vat and a dye-pot.” Therefore, these too should be used. Here, “dye-vat” means a dye-basin. Here, “dye-basin” means a large pot for storing cooked dye. “I allow, bhikkhus, a dye-trough.” Therefore, when kneading the robe in a bowl or basin, a dye-trough should be used to protect the robe from tearing. “I allow, bhikkhus, a grass mat.” Therefore, when spreading the robe on the ground, a grass mat should be made to protect it from becoming soiled. “I allow, bhikkhus, a robe-pole and a robe-rope.” Therefore, if the grass mat is being eaten by termites and so on, the robe should be spread on a robe-pole or a robe-rope, for when the robe is attached by the middle, the dye drips from both sides.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kaṇṇe bandhitu”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato kaṇṇe bandhitabbaṃ cīvarassa kaṇṇe bandhiyamāne kaṇṇassa jiṇṇattā. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kaṇṇasuttaka”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato kaṇṇasuttakena bandhitabbaṃ evaṃ bandhante rajanassa ekato gaḷitattā. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, samparivattakaṃ samparivattakaṃ rajetuṃ, na ca acchinne theve pakkamitu”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato tathā rajitabbaṃ. Yāva rajanabindu gaḷitaṃ na chijjati, tāva na aññatra gantabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, udake osāretu”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato patthinnaṃ cīvaraṃ udake osāretabbaṃ. Tattha patthinnanti atirajitattā thaddhaṃ. Udake osāretunti udake pakkhipitvā ṭhapetuṃ. Rajane pana nikkhante taṃ udakaṃ chaḍḍetvā cīvaraṃ madditabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pāṇinā ākoṭetu”nti (mahāva. 344) vacanato pharusaṃ cīvaraṃ pāṇinā ākoṭetabbaṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, acchinnakāni cīvarāni dhāretabbāni, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 344) vacanato acchinnakāni cīvarāni dantakāsāvāni na dhāretabbāni. Tattha dantakāsāvānīti ekaṃ vā dve vā vāre rajitvā dantavaṇṇāni dhārenti.

“I allow, bhikkhus, to bind at the corners.” Therefore, the corners of the robe should be bound, for when a robe is bound by its corners, the corners wear out. “I allow, bhikkhus, a corner-thread.” Therefore, it should be bound with a corner-thread; when binding in this way, the dye drips from one side. “I allow, bhikkhus, to dye the robe turning it over and over, and not to depart while the dripping is unbroken.” Therefore, it should be dyed in this manner. As long as the dripping of the dye-drop has not been cut off, one should not go elsewhere. “I allow, bhikkhus, to lower it into water.” Therefore, a stiffened robe should be lowered into water. Here, ‘stiffened’ means stiff from being over-dyed. ‘To lower into water’ means to place it in water and leave it. But when the dye has come out, that water should be discarded and the robe should be rubbed. “I allow, bhikkhus, to beat it with the hand.” Therefore, a rough robe should be beaten by hand. “Bhikkhus, uncut robes are not to be worn. Whoever should wear one commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, uncut robes—that is, ‘tooth-colored’ robes—are not to be worn. Here, ‘tooth-colored robes’ means those that are worn when they are tooth-colored after having been dyed only once or twice.

Atirekacīvarakathā

The Discussion on the Extra Robe

Atirekacīvarakathāyaṃ [V 2.0287] “na, bhikkhave, atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo dhāreyya, yathādhammo kāretabbo”ti (mahāva. 347) vacanato niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ ubbhatasmiṃ kathine dasāhato paraṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhārentassa nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretu”nti (mahāva. 347) vacanato ubbhatepi kathine dasāhabbhantare [M 2.0389] dhārentassa atthatakathinānaṃ anubbhatepi kathine pañcamāsabbhantare tato parampi dasāhabbhantare anatthatakathinānampi dasāhabbhantare atirekacīvaraṃ anāpatti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, atirekacīvaraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 347) vacanato dasāhato paraṃ vikappetvā atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretuṃ vaṭṭati. Kittakaṃ pana cīvaraṃ vikappetabbanti? “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āyāmena aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ sugataṅgulena caturaṅgulavitthataṃ pacchimaṃ cīvaraṃ vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358) vacanato sabbantimena paricchedena sugataṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulāyāmaṃ caturaṅgulavitthāraṃ cīvaraṃ vikappetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha sugataṅgulaṃ nāma majjhimapurisaṅgulasaṅkhātena vaḍḍhakīaṅgulena tivaṅgulaṃ hoti, manussānaṃ pakatiaṅgulena aḍḍhapañcakaṅgulaṃ, tasmā dīghato vaḍḍhakīhatthena ekahatthaṃ pakatihatthena diyaḍḍhahatthaṃ vitthārato vaḍḍhakīhatthena vidatthippamāṇaṃ pakatihatthena chaḷaṅgulādhikavidatthippamāṇaṃ pacchimaṃ cīvaraṃ vikappetuṃ vaṭṭati, tato ūnappamāṇaṃ na vaṭṭati, adhikappamāṇaṃ pana vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In the account of the extra robe: Because of the statement, “Monks, an extra robe is not to be kept. Whoever should keep one is to be dealt with according to the Dhamma,” (Mahāvagga 347) for one who keeps an extra robe for more than ten days after the kaṭhina privileges have been withdrawn upon the completion of the robes, it is an offense entailing forfeiture and expiation. Because of the statement, “I allow, monks, an extra robe to be kept for a maximum of ten days,” (Mahāvagga 347) for those who have received the kaṭhina privileges, there is no offense in keeping it within ten days even after the kaṭhina has been withdrawn; while the kaṭhina has not been withdrawn, there is no offense within the five-month period and for ten days thereafter; and for those who have not received the kaṭhina privileges, there is no offense for an extra robe within ten days. Because of the statement, “I allow, monks, to place an extra robe under shared ownership,” (Mahāvagga 347) it is permissible to keep an extra robe after ten days by placing it under shared ownership. But what is the size of the robe to be placed under shared ownership? Because of the statement, “I allow, monks, to place under shared ownership as the smallest robe one that is eight Buddha’s fingerbreadths in length and four fingerbreadths in width,” (Mahāvagga 358) by the very smallest measure, it is permissible to place under shared ownership a robe that is eight Buddha’s fingerbreadths in length and four Buddha’s fingerbreadths in width. Here, a Buddha’s fingerbreadth is three carpenter’s fingerbreadths, which is reckoned by the fingerbreadth of a medium-sized man; by an ordinary person’s fingerbreadth, it is four and a half fingerbreadths. Therefore, in length, it is one carpenter’s cubit or one and a half ordinary cubits; in width, it is the measure of a span by the carpenter’s measure, or by the ordinary measure, a span plus six fingerbreadths. It is permissible to place the smallest robe under shared ownership accordingly. A measure smaller than this is not permissible, but it should be understood that a larger measure is permissible.

Aṭṭhavarakathā

The Account of the Eight Allowances

Aṭṭhavarakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vassikasāṭikaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ gamikabhattaṃ gilānabhattaṃ gilānupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ gilānabhesajjaṃ dhuvayāguṃ bhikkhunisaṅghassa udakasāṭika”nti vacanato imāni aṭṭha dānāni sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha nikkhittacīvarā hutvā kāyaṃ ovassantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ naggiyaṃ asuci jegucchaṃ paṭikūlaṃ hoti, tasmā vassikasāṭikā anuññātā. Āgantuko bhikkhu na vīthikusalo hoti, na gocarakusalo, kilanto piṇḍāya carati, tasmā āgantukabhattaṃ anuññātaṃ, gamiko bhikkhu attano bhattaṃ pariyesamāno satthā vā vihāyissati[M 2.0390], yattha vā vāsaṃ gantukāmo bhavissati, tattha vikālena upagacchissati, kilanto addhānaṃ gamissati, tasmā gamikabhattaṃ. Gilānassa bhikkhuno sappāyāni bhojanāni alabhantassa ābādho vā abhivaḍḍhissati, kālakiriyā vā bhavissati, tasmā gilānabhattaṃ. Gilānupaṭṭhāko bhikkhu attano bhattaṃ pariyesamāno gilānassa ussūre bhattaṃ nīharissati, tasmā gilānupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ. Gilānassa bhikkhuno sappāyāni bhesajjāni alabhantassa [V 2.0288] ābādho vā abhivaḍḍhissati, kālakiriyā vā bhavissati, tasmā gilānabhesajjaṃ. Yasmā bhagavatā andhakavinde dasānisaṃse sampassamānena yāgu anuññātā, tasmā dhuvayāgu. Yasmā mātugāmassa naggiyaṃ asuci jegucchaṃ paṭikūlaṃ hoti, tasmā bhikkhunisaṅghassa udakasāṭikā anuññātā.

In the account of the eight allowances, it is said: “I allow, monks, a rainy-season cloth, food for a newcomer, food for one setting out, food for the sick, food for a sick-attendant, medicine for the sick, constant gruel, and a bathing cloth for the order of nuns.” Thus, it is permissible to accept these eight gifts. Here, when monks who have set aside their robes are being drenched by the rain, their nakedness is impure, loathsome, and disgusting; therefore, a rainy-season cloth is permitted. A newcomer monk is not skilled in the streets or in seeking alms; he wanders for alms even when weary; therefore, food for a newcomer is permitted. A monk setting out on a journey, while searching for his own food, might be left behind by the caravan or might arrive at the place where he wishes to stay at the wrong time; he would travel the road while exhausted; therefore, food for one setting out is permitted. If a sick monk does not obtain suitable food, his illness might worsen or he might die; therefore, food for the sick is permitted. A monk attending the sick, while searching for his own food, might bring food to the sick person late; therefore, food for a sick-attendant is permitted. If a sick monk does not obtain suitable medicine, his illness might worsen or he might die; therefore, medicine for the sick is permitted. Because gruel was permitted by the Blessed One at Andhakavinda, who saw ten benefits, constant gruel is therefore permitted. Because for a woman nakedness is impure, loathsome, and disgusting, a bathing cloth for the order of nuns is therefore permitted.

Nisīdanādikathā

The Account of the Sitting Cloth and Other Items

Nisīdanādikathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kāyaguttiyā cīvaraguttiyā senāsanaguttiyā nisīdana”nti (mahāva. 353) vacanato kāyādīnaṃ asucimuccanādito gopanatthāya nisīdanaṃ dhāretuṃ vaṭṭati. Tassa vidhānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yāvamahantaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ ākaṅkhati, tāvamahantaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ kātu”nti vacanato atikhuddakena nisīdanena senāsanassa agopanattā mahantampi paccattharaṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yassa kaṇḍu vā pīḷakā vā assāvo vā thullakacchu vā ābādho, kaṇḍupaṭicchādi”nti vacanato īdisesu ābādhesu santesu cīvarādiguttatthāya kaṇḍupaṭicchādi vaṭṭati. Tattha pamāṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave[M 2.0391], mukhapuñchanacoḷa”nti (mahāva. 355) vacanato mukhasodhanatthāya mukhapuñchanacoḷaṃ vaṭṭati. Tampi heṭṭhā vuttameva. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, parikkhāracoḷaka”nti vacanato ticīvare paripuṇṇe parissāvanathavikādīhi atthe sati parikkhāracoḷaṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ, vassikasāṭikaṃ vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ tato paraṃ vikappetuṃ, nisīdanaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ, paccattharaṇaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ, kaṇḍupaṭicchādiṃ yāva ābādhā adhiṭṭhātuṃ tato paraṃ vikappetuṃ, mukhapuñchanacoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ, parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358) vacanato vuttanayena adhiṭṭhānañca vikappanā ca kātabbā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana heṭṭhā vuttova.

In the account of the sitting cloth and other items, it is said: “I allow, monks, a sitting cloth for the protection of the body, the protection of the robe, and the protection of the lodging.” (Mahāvagga 353) Therefore, it is permissible to use a sitting cloth to protect the body and other things from the discharge of impurities. Its regulation is as stated below. “I allow, monks, to make a ground-covering as large as one desires.” Because a very small sitting cloth does not protect the lodging, it is permissible to make even a large ground-covering. “I allow, monks, for one who has an illness such as an itch, a boil, a discharge, or a bad skin disease, a cloth for covering itches.” Therefore, when such ailments are present, a cloth for covering itches is permissible for the protection of one’s robes and so on. Its measurement is as stated below. “I allow, monks, a face-wiping cloth.” (Mahāvagga 355) Therefore, a face-wiping cloth is permissible for the purpose of cleaning the face. That too is as stated below. “I allow, monks, a requisites-cloth.” Therefore, when the three robes are complete and there is need for a water-strainer, a bag, etc., a requisites-cloth is permissible. “I allow, monks, to determine the three robes but not to place them under shared ownership; to determine the rainy-season cloth for the four months of the rains but to place it under shared ownership afterward; to determine a sitting cloth but not to place it under shared ownership; to determine a ground-covering but not to place it under shared ownership; to determine a cloth for covering itches as long as the ailment persists but to place it under shared ownership afterward; to determine a face-wiping cloth but not to place it under shared ownership; to determine a requisites-cloth but not to place it under shared ownership.” (Mahāvagga 358) Therefore, determination and placing under shared ownership should be done in the manner described. This is the summary here; the details, however, are as stated below.

Adhammakammakathā

The Talk on Unlawful Acts

58. Adhammakammakathāyaṃ [V 2.0289] na, bhikkhave…pe… dukkaṭassāti idaṃ “tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū saṅghamajjhe adhammakammaṃ karonti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – na, bhikkhave, adhammakammaṃ kātabbaṃ, yo kareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 154) imaṃ uposathakkhandhake āgatapāṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Anujānāmi…pe… paṭikkositunti tatheva āgataṃ “bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, adhammakamme kayiramāne paṭikkositu”nti imaṃ. Tattha karontiyevāti paññattampi sikkhāpadaṃ madditvā adhammakammaṃ karontiyevāti attho. “Anujānāmi…pe… paṭikkositu”nti evaṃ adhammakamme kayiramāne sati “pesalehi bhikkhūhi taṃ adhammakammaṃ akataṃ, kammaṃ dukkaṭaṃ kammaṃ puna kātabba”nti evaṃ paṭikkositabbaṃ, na tuṇhībhāvena khamitabbanti [M 2.0392] attho. Iti vacanatoti idaṃ pana pubbapāṭhaṃ gahetvā iti vacanato. Adhammakammaṃ na kātabbanti aparapāṭhaṃ gahetvā iti vacanato kayiramānañca adhammakammaṃ bhikkhūhi nivāretabbanti dvidhā yojanā kātabbā.

58. In the Talk on Unlawful Acts, the passage beginning, “Monks, … an offense of wrongdoing,” was said in reference to this text that has come down in the Uposatha Khandhaka: “At that time, the monks of the group of six were performing an unlawful act in the midst of the Sangha. They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: ‘Monks, an unlawful act should not be performed. Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrongdoing.’” (Mahāvagga 154) The passage beginning, “I allow … to be protested,” has come down in the same way: “They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: ‘Monks, I allow one to protest when an unlawful act is being performed.’” Herein, “while they are performing it” means that they are performing an unlawful act even by overriding a training rule that has been laid down. The passage, “I allow … to be protested,” means that when an unlawful act is being performed, virtuous monks should protest it thus: “This unlawful act is invalid, the act is wrongly done, the act must be done again.” It should not be endured with silence; this is the meaning. From the statement 'Thus...', this is to be understood by taking the earlier passage. By taking the later passage, 'An unlawful act should not be performed,' the application should be made in two ways: the act is not to be performed, and an unlawful act being performed should be prevented by the monks.

Nivārentehi cātiādi pana “tena kho pana samayena pesalā bhikkhū chabbaggiyehi bhikkhūhi adhammakamme kayiramāne paṭikkosanti, chabbaggiyā bhikkhū labhanti āghātaṃ, labhanti appaccayaṃ, vadhena tajjenti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, diṭṭhimpi āvikātu”nti (mahāva. 154) pāṭhañca “tesaṃyeva santike diṭṭhiṃ āvikaronti, chabbaggiyā bhikkhū labhanti āghātaṃ, labhanti appaccayaṃ, vadhena tajjenti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, catūhi pañcahi paṭikkosituṃ, dvīhi tīhi diṭṭhiṃ āvikātuṃ, ekena adhiṭṭhātuṃ na metaṃ khamatī”ti ime pāṭhe sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vacanatoti idaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ tīṇi sampadānāni gahetvā tīhi kiriyāpadehi visuṃ visuṃ yojetabbaṃ. Sabbañcetaṃ anupaddavatthāya vuttaṃ, na āpattisabbhāvatoti yojanā. Kathaṃ anupaddavasambhavoti? Niggahakammaṃ kātuṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvato, aññassa upaddavassa ca nivāraṇato. Tena vuttaṃ vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 154) “tesaṃ anupaddavatthāyāti saṅgho saṅghassa kammaṃ na karoti, aññopi upaddavo bahūnaṃ hoti, tasmā vutta”nti.

The passage beginning, “And by those preventing,” was said with reference to this text: “At that time, virtuous monks protested when an unlawful act was being performed by the monks of the group of six. The monks of the group of six became resentful and displeased, and they threatened them with violence. They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: ‘Monks, I allow one to declare one’s view.’” (Mahāvagga 154) And also this text: “They declared their view in the presence of those very monks. The monks of the group of six became resentful and displeased, and they threatened them with violence. They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: ‘Monks, I allow protesting with four or five and declaring one’s view with two or three, but I do not approve of one resolving on this alone.’” This was said in reference to these passages. “By the statement”: this should be connected separately with the three verbs by taking the three datives in the Pāli. The connection is that all this was said for the sake of non-affliction, not because of the existence of an offense. How is the occurrence of non-affliction possible? Because of the inability to perform an act of censure and because of the prevention of other trouble. Thus it is said in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 154): “‘For the sake of their non-affliction’ means that the Sangha does not perform an act for the Sangha, and other trouble arises for many; therefore it was said.”

Okāsakatakathā

The Discourse on Seeking Permission

59. Okāsakatakathāyaṃ [V 2.0290] na, bhikkhave, anokāsakatotiādi “tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū anokāsakataṃ [M 2.0393] bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā codenti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ – na, bhikkhave, anokāsakato bhikkhu āpattiyā codetabbo, yo codeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, okāsaṃ kārāpetvā āpattiyā codetuṃ, karotu āyasmā okāsaṃ, ahaṃ taṃ vattukāmo”ti (mahāva. 153) idaṃ pāṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Adhippāyesu cāvanādhippāyoti, sāsanato cāvetukāmo. Akkosādhippāyoti paraṃ akkositukāmo paribhāsitukāmo. Kammādhippāyoti tajjanīyādikammaṃ kattukāmo. Vuṭṭhānādhippāyoti āpattito vuṭṭhāpetukāmo. Uposathappavāraṇaṭṭhapanādhippāyoti uposathaṃ, pavāraṇaṃ vā ṭhapetukāmo. Anuvijjanādhippāyoti upaparikkhitukāmo. Dhammakathādhippāyoti dhammaṃ desetukāmo. Iti paraṃ codentānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ adhippāyabhedo anekavidho hotīti attho. Purimesu catūsu adhippāyesūti cāvanādhippāyaakkosādhippāyakammādhippāyavuṭṭhānādhippāyesu okāsaṃ akārāpentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Kārāpetvāpi sammukhā codentassa yathānurūpaṃ saṅghādisesapācittiyadukkaṭāni, asammukhā pana dukkaṭamevāti ayamettha piṇḍattho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

59. In the Discourse on Seeking Permission, the passage beginning, “Monks, not without having been given leave,” was said in reference to this text: “At that time, the monks of the group of six accused a monk of an offense without his having been given leave. They reported this matter to the Blessed One, who said: ‘Monks, a monk who has not been given leave should not be accused of an offense. Whoever should accuse him commits an offense of wrongdoing. I allow, monks, that one may accuse a monk of an offense after having had permission made, saying: “May the venerable one grant me leave; I wish to speak to you.”’” (Mahāvagga 153) This was said in reference to this passage. Among the intentions, there is the intention to make one fall, that is, one wishes to make one fall away from the Teaching; the intention to abuse, that is, one wishes to insult or revile another; the intention for a formal act, that is, one wishes to carry out an act of censure, etc.; the intention to rehabilitate, that is, one wishes to raise one up from an offense; the intention to suspend the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, that is, one wishes to suspend the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā; the intention to investigate, that is, one wishes to scrutinize; the intention to give a Dhamma talk, that is, one wishes to teach the Dhamma. The meaning is that the intentions of monks who accuse another are of many kinds. In the first four intentions—the intention to make one fall, the intention to abuse, the intention for a formal act, and the intention to rehabilitate—for one who does not have permission made, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Even after having had permission made, for one who accuses him face-to-face, there are the Saṅghādisesa, Pācittiya, or Dukkaṭa offenses as are appropriate; but if not face-to-face, it is only an offense of wrongdoing. This is the summary meaning here. The rest is easy to understand.

“Ṭhapanakkhettaṃ pana jānitabba”nti vatvā taṃ dassento “suṇātu me”tiādimāha. Anuvijjakassa anuvijjanādhippāyena vadantassa okāsakammaṃ natthīti yojanā. Dhammakathikassa anodissa kammaṃ kathentassa okāsakammaṃ natthi. Sace pana odissa katheti, āpatti, tasmā taṃ dassetvā gantabbanti yojetabbaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Having said, “But the proper grounds for suspension should be known,” he shows this by saying, “Let the Sangha listen to me,” etc. The connection is that for an investigator speaking with the intention of investigating, there is no act of seeking permission. For a Dhamma teacher speaking about a formal act without specifying an individual, there is no act of seeking permission. But if he speaks specifying an individual, there is an offense; therefore, having pointed that out, one should proceed—this is how it should be connected. The rest is easy to understand.

Saddhādeyyavinipātanakathā

The Discourse on Dissipating a Gift of Faith

60. Saddhādeyyavinipātanakathāyaṃ [M 2.0394] “mātāpitaroti kho, bhikkhave, vadamāne kiṃ vadeyyāma. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, mātāpitūnaṃ dātuṃ, na ca, bhikkhave, saddhādeyyaṃ vinipātetabbaṃ, yo vinipāteyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 361) vacanato dāyakehi saddhāya bhikkhussa dinnaṃ vinipātetvā gihīnaṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. “Na ca, bhikkhave, saddhādeyyanti [V 2.0291] ettha sesañātīnaṃ dento vinipātetiyeva. Mātāpitaro pana sace rajje ṭhitāpi patthayanti, dātabba”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 361) vuttattā bhātubhaginīādīnaṃ ñātakānampi dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Vuttañhi ācariyadhammasirittherena khuddasikkhāyaṃ –

60. In the Discourse on Dissipating a Gift of Faith, it is said: “Monks, when speaking of mother and father, what should we say? I allow, monks, giving to mother and father; but, monks, a gift of faith should not be dissipated. Whoever dissipates it, commits an offense of wrongdoing.” (Mahāvagga 361) Based on this statement, it is not proper to dissipate what was given in faith by donors to a bhikkhu and give it to laypeople. “And, monks, regarding ‘a gift of faith,’ giving it to other relatives is indeed to dissipate it. But if parents, even if they are established in a kingdom, desire it, it should be given.” Since this is stated in the commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 361), it is also not proper to give to siblings and other relatives. For it was stated by the Elder Ācariyadhammasiri in the Khuddasikkhā:

“Na labbhaṃ vinipātetuṃ, saddhādeyyañca cīvaraṃ;

Labbhaṃ pitūnaṃ sesānaṃ, ñātīnampi na labbhatī”ti.

“It is not allowable to dissipate a robe that is a gift of faith; it is allowable for one’s parents, but not for other relatives.”

Kayavikkayasamāpattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanāyampi “mātaraṃ pana pitaraṃ vā ‘imaṃ dehī’ti vadato viññatti na hoti, ‘imaṃ gaṇhāhī’ti vadato saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ na hoti. Aññātakaṃ ‘imaṃ dehī’ti vadato viññatti hoti, ‘imaṃ gaṇhāhī’ti vadato saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ hoti. ‘Iminā imaṃ dehī’ti kayavikkayaṃ āpajjato nissaggiyaṃ hotī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.595) vuttaṃ. Tattha “sesañātakesu saddhādeyyavinipātasambhavato tadabhāvaṭṭhānampi dassetuṃ ‘mātaraṃ pana pitaraṃ vā’ti vutta”nti vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.593-595) vuttaṃ.

Also in the explanation of the training rule on engaging in buying and selling, it is stated in the Commentary: “However, when one says to one’s mother or father, ‘Give this,’ it is not an intimation; when one says, ‘Take this,’ it is not a dissipation of a gift of faith. When one says to a non-relative, ‘Give this,’ it is an intimation; when one says, ‘Take this,’ it is a dissipation of a gift of faith. When one engages in buying and selling, saying, ‘Give this for this,’ it entails forfeiture.” (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 2.595) Here, it is stated in the Vimativinodanī: “The phrase ‘to one’s mother or father’ is stated to show also the instance of its absence, since there is the possibility of dissipating a gift of faith in the case of other relatives.” (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. 1.593-595)

Santaruttarakathā

The Discourse on Wearing the Inner and Upper Robes

61. Santaruttarakathāyaṃ antara-saddo majjhavācako. Vasati sīlenāti vāsako, “antare vāsako antaravāsako”ti [M 2.0395] vattabbe “rūpabhavo rūpa”ntiādīsu viya uttarapadalopīsamāsavasena “antaro”ti vutto. Uttarasaddo uparivācako, ābhuso sajjatīti āsaṅgo, “uttare āsaṅgo uttarāsaṅgo”ti vattabbe vuttanayena “uttaro”ti vutto, antaro ca uttaro ca antaruttarā, saha antaruttarehi yo vattatīti santaruttaro, sahapubbapadabhinnādhikaraṇadvipadabahubbīhisamāso. Atha vā saha antarena ca uttarena ca yo vattatīti santaruttaro, tipadabahubbīhisamāso. Saṅghāṭiṃ ṭhapetvā antaravāsakauttarāsaṅgamattadharo hutvā gāmo na pavisitabboti attho. “Paribbājakamadakkhi tidaṇḍakenā”tiādīsu viya itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, tasmā antaravāsakaṃ timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādentena parimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā saṅghāṭiñca uttarāsaṅgañca diguṇaṃ katvā pārupitvā gāmo pavisitabbo.

61. In the Discourse on Wearing the Inner and Upper Robes, the word `antara` means ‘inner.’ It is called `vāsaka` (garment) from `vasati sīlena` (‘one dresses with it’). When one should say `antare vāsako` (‘the inner garment’), making `antaravāsako`, it is said as `antaro` by way of a compound with elision of the final member, as in `rūpabhavo` becoming `rūpa`. The word `uttara` means ‘upper.’ It is called `āsaṅgo` (robe) from `ābhuso sajjati` (‘it clings repeatedly’). When one should say `uttare āsaṅgo` (‘the upper robe’), making `uttarāsaṅgo`, it is said as `uttaro` by the same method. `Antaro` and `uttaro` become `antaruttarā`. One who goes about `saha antaruttarehi` (‘with the inner and upper robes’) is a `santaruttaro`. This is a two-membered bahubbīhi compound with `saha` as the first member, where the members are in different cases. Alternatively, one who goes about `saha antarena ca uttarena ca` (‘with the inner and with the upper’) is a `santaruttaro`; this is a three-membered bahubbīhi compound. The meaning is that one should not enter a village having laid aside the outer cloak (`saṅghāṭi`) and wearing only the lower garment (`antaravāsaka`) and the upper robe (`uttarāsaṅga`). As in such phrases as “he saw the wanderer with the triple staff,” this is an instrumental case indicating a specific state. Therefore, one should enter a village having dressed in the lower garment so that it is even all around and covers the three circles, having fastened the waistband, and having put on the upper robe and the outer cloak folded in two.

Cīvaranikkhepakathā

The Discourse on Laying Aside the Robe

62. Cīvaranikkhepakathāyaṃ [V 2.0292] saṃharīyateti saṅghāṭi, tassā saṅghāṭiyā, bhāvayoge kammatthe chaṭṭhī. Nikkhepāyāti ṭhapanāya, saṅghāṭiṃ aggahetvā vihāre ṭhapetvā gamanāya pañca kāraṇāni hontīti attho. Gilāno vā hotīti gahetvā gantuṃ asamattho gilāno vā hoti. Vassikasaṅketaṃ vā hotīti “vassikakālo aya”nti saṅketaṃ vā kataṃ hoti. Nadīpāragataṃ vā hotīti nadiyā pāraṃ gantvā bhuñjitabbaṃ hoti. Aggaḷaguttivihāro vā hotīti aggaḷaṃ datvāpi dātabbo suguttavihāro vā hoti. Atthatakathinaṃ vā hotīti tasmiṃ vihāre kathinaṃ atthataṃ vā hoti atthatakathinānaṃ asamādānacārasambhavato. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Āraññikassa pana vihāro na sugutto hotīti [M 2.0396] appabhikkhukattā corādīnaṃ gamanaṭṭhānato ca. Bhaṇḍukkhalikāyāti cīvarādiṭṭhapanabhaṇḍukkhalikāya. Sesaṃ suviññeyyaṃ.

62. In the Discourse on Laying Aside the Robe, it is called `saṅghāṭi` because it is folded up (`saṃharīyati`). For that `saṅghāṭi`, the genitive is used in the sense of the object of the action. `Nikkhepāya` means for laying aside. The meaning is that there are five reasons for going away after leaving the `saṅghāṭi` in the monastery without taking it. (1) One might be sick, that is, one is sick and unable to take it and go. (2) Or there is a marker for the rains-residence, that is, a sign has been made that “this is the time of the rains-residence.” (3) Or one has to go to the other side of a river, that is, one has to go across a river to eat. (4) Or the monastery is guarded by a bolt, that is, it is a well-guarded monastery furnished with a bolt. (5) Or the Kathina has been spread, that is, in that monastery the Kathina has been spread, because for those for whom the Kathina has been spread, it is possible to go about without having taken up the full set of robes. The rest is easy to understand. But for a forest-dweller, the monastery is not well-guarded because there are few bhikkhus and it is a place frequented by thieves and others. `Bhaṇḍukkhalikāya` means in a storage basket for placing robes and other requisites. The rest is easy to understand.

Satthakammavatthikammakathā

The Discourse on Surgical Procedures and Enema Procedures

63. Satthakammavatthikammakathāyaṃ satthakammaṃ vā vatthikammaṃ vāti ettha yena kenaci satthādinā chindanādi satthakammaṃ nāma hoti. Yena kenaci cammādinā vatthipīḷanaṃ vatthikammaṃ nāma. “Sambādhe dahanakammaṃ paṭikkhepābhāvā vaṭṭatī”ti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.279). Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.279) pana “vatthipīḷananti yathā vatthigatatelādi antosarīre ārohanti, evaṃ hatthena vatthimaddana”nti vuttaṃ.

63. In the Discourse on Surgical Procedures and Enema Procedures, regarding ‘a surgical procedure or an enema procedure,’ here, cutting and so on with any kind of knife or the like is called a surgical procedure. Squeezing the enema bag with leather or the like is called an enema procedure. In the Sāratthadīpanī it is said: “Cauterization in a constricted place is allowable as there is no prohibition.” But in the Vimativinodanī it is said: “Squeezing for an enema means pressing the abdomen with the hand in such a way that oil and so on that has entered the enema tube ascends into the inner body.”

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 279) pana “sambādheti vaccamagge, bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā ca passāvamaggepi anulomato dahanaṃ paṭikkhepābhāvā vaṭṭati. Satthavatthikammānulomato na vaṭṭatīti ce? Na, paṭikkhittapaṭikkhepā, paṭikkhipitabbassa tapparamatādīpanato. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Pubbe paṭikkhittampi satthakammaṃ sampiṇḍetvā pacchā ‘na, bhikkhave…pe… thullaccayassā’ti dvikkhattuṃ satthakammassa parikkhepo kato. Tena sambādhassa sāmantā dvaṅgulaṃ paṭikkhipitabbaṃ nāma satthavatthikammato uddhaṃ natthīti dasseti. Kiñca bhiyyo – pubbe sambādheyeva satthakammaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ, pacchā sambādhassa sāmantā dvaṅgulampi paṭikkhittaṃ[V 2.0293], tasmā tasseva paṭikkhepo, netarassāti siddhaṃ. Ettha ‘satthaṃ nāma satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyā’tiādīsu (pārā. 167) viya yena chindati, taṃ sabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ ‘kaṇṭakena vā’tiādi. Khārudānaṃ panettha bhikkhunīvibhaṅge pasākhe pamukhe anuññātanti veditabbaṃ, eke pana ‘satthakammaṃ vā’ti [M 2.0397] pāṭhaṃ vikappetvā vatthikammaṃ karonti. Vatthīti kiṃ? Agghikā vuccati, tāya chindanaṃ vatthikammaṃ nāmāti ca atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti, te ‘satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyā’ti imassa padabhājanīyaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipitabbā. Aṇḍavuddhīti vātaṇḍakā, ādānavattīti anāhavattī”ti vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

But in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is said: “In a constricted place, that is, in the passage for excrement of a bhikkhu and also in the passage for urine of a bhikkhunī, cauterization is allowable in a suitable way because there is no prohibition. If it is said: ‘Is it not allowable in conformity with surgical and enema procedures?’ No, because it is a prohibition of what was already prohibited, since it shows that as the highest limit. What is meant? Having consolidated the surgical procedures that were previously prohibited, a boundary for surgical procedures was later made twice, ending with ‘…an offense of grave transgression.’ Thereby it shows that what is to be prohibited is the two finger-breadths around the constricted place, and that there is nothing beyond the surgical and enema procedures. Furthermore, previously a surgical procedure in a constricted place itself was prohibited; later, even two finger-breadths around the constricted place was prohibited. Therefore, the prohibition is of that very thing, not of another; this is established. Here, as in such texts as ‘a knife means one might seek a knife-bearer for him,’ whatever cuts is all included. Thus it is said, ‘or with a thorn,’ etc. It should be understood that here the giving of a caustic substance is allowed in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga on a side-branch or protuberance. But some, altering the reading ‘or a surgical procedure,’ make it ‘an enema procedure.’ And they explain the meaning thus: What is a `vatthi`? It is called an `agghikā` (a small knife), and cutting with it is called `vatthikamma`. They should be refuted by showing the word-analysis of the phrase ‘one might seek a knife-bearer for him.’ `Aṇḍavuddhi` means a hydrocele. `Ādānavatti` means a suppository for retention.” The rest should be understood in the way stated in the Commentary.

Nahāpitapubbakathā

The Story of the Former Barber

64. Nahāpitapubbakathāyaṃ nahāpito pubbeti nahāpitapubbo, pubbe nahāpito hutvā idāni bhikkhubhūtoti attho. Tena nahāpitapubbena bhikkhunā. Khurabhaṇḍanti khurādinahāpitabhaṇḍaṃ, “laddhātapatto rājakumāro”tiādīsu viya upalakkhaṇanayoyaṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, pabbajitena akappiyaṃ samādapetabbaṃ, yo samādapeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Na ca, bhikkhave, nahāpitapubbena khurabhaṇḍaṃ pariharitabbaṃ, yo parihareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 303) ca dvidhā paññatti, tasmā nahāpitapubbena vā anahāpitapubbena vā pabbajitena nāma akappiyasamādapanaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Nahāpitapubbena pana bhikkhunā khurena abhilakkhitaṃ khurabhaṇḍaṃ, khurabhaṇḍakhurakosanisitapāsāṇakhurathavikādayo na pariharitabbā eva. Sesaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 300) pana “na, bhikkhave, pabbajitena akappiye samādapetabbanti vuttattā anupasampannassapi na kevalaṃ dasasu eva sikkhāpadesu, atha kho yaṃ bhikkhussa na kappati, tasmimpīti adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ.

64. In the story of the former barber, 'former barber' means one who was a barber before but is now a bhikkhu; this is the meaning. By that bhikkhu who was formerly a barber. 'Barber's tools' means the barber's equipment such as razors. This is a method of indication, as in such examples as, 'The prince has received the parasol.' 'Bhikkhus, one who has gone forth should not have what is unallowable undertaken. Whoever should have it undertaken incurs an offense of wrong-doing. And, bhikkhus, a former barber should not carry barber's tools. Whoever should carry them incurs an offense of wrong-doing' (Mahāvagga 303). The regulation is twofold. Therefore, one who has gone forth, whether a former barber or not, should not have what is unallowable undertaken. However, a bhikkhu who was formerly a barber must not carry barber's tools marked with a razor—such as the set of barber's tools, razor cases, whetstones, razor bags, and the like. The rest should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary. But in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is said: 'Since it is said, "Bhikkhus, one who has gone forth should not have what is unallowable undertaken," the intention is that this applies not only to the ten training rules for an unordained person but also to whatever is not allowable for a bhikkhu.'

Dasabhāgakathā

The Account of the Tenth Part

65. Dasabhāgakathāyaṃ saṅghikānīti saṅghasantakāni bījāni. Puggalikāyāti puggalassa santakāya bhūmiyā. Bhāgaṃ datvāti [M 2.0398] mūlabhāgasaṅkhātaṃ dasamabhāgaṃ bhūmisāmikānaṃ datvā. Paribhuñjitabbānīti tesaṃ bījānaṃ phalāni ropakehi paribhuñjitabbānīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva[V 2.0294]. Idaṃ kira jambudīpe porāṇakacārittanti ādikappakāle paṭhamakappikā manussā bodhisattaṃ mahāsammataṃ nāma rājānaṃ katvā sabbepi attano attano taṇḍulaphalasālikhettato pavattataṇḍulaphalāni dasa koṭṭhāse katvā ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ bhūmisāmikabhūtassa mahāsammatarājino datvā paribhuñjiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya jambudīpikānaṃ manussānaṃ cāritattā vuttaṃ. Teneva sāratthadīpanīnāmikāyampi vinayaṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 304) “dasabhāgaṃ datvāti dasamabhāgaṃ datvā. Tenevāha ‘dasa koṭṭhāse katvā eko koṭṭhāso bhūmisāmikānaṃ dātabbo’ti” vuttaṃ.

65. In the account of the tenth part, 'belonging to the Saṅgha' means seeds that are the property of the Saṅgha. 'On personal' means on land that is the property of an individual. 'Having given a share' means having given the tenth part, called the basic share, to the landowners. 'They are to be enjoyed' means that the fruits of those seeds are to be enjoyed by the planters; this is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand. This, it seems, was an ancient custom in Jambudīpa: in the beginning of the aeon, the people of the first cosmic cycle made the Bodhisatta king, named Mahāsammata, 'the Great Elect.' All of them, from their own paddy fields producing rice grains, divided the produced rice grains into ten portions, gave one portion to King Mahāsammata who had become the landowner, and enjoyed the rest. It is said that from that time onwards this became the custom for the people of Jambudīpa. For that reason, in the Vinaya subcommentary named Sāratthadīpanī it is said: '“Having given a tenth part” means having given the tenth part. Therefore he said: “Having made ten portions, one portion is to be given to the landowners”' (cf. Vajira. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 304).

Pātheyyakathā

The Account of Provisions

66. Pātheyyakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave”tiādi bhaddiyanagare amitaparibhogabhūtena meṇḍakaseṭṭhinā abhiyācito hutvā anuññātaṃ, idha pana paṭhamaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca gorase khīraṃ dadhiṃ takkaṃ navanītaṃ sappi”nti (mahāva. 299) pañca gorasā anuññātā. Tato paraṃ seṭṭhino abhiyācanānurūpaṃ vatvā anujānituṃ “santi, bhikkhave, maggā kantārā”tiādimāha. Sesaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tathā alabhantena aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato yācitvāpi gahetabbanti etena evarūpesu kālesu viññattipaccayā doso natthīti dasseti. “Ekadivasena gamanīye magge ekabhattatthāya pariyesitabba”nti vuttattā pana tato upari yācanaṃ na vaṭṭatīti dassitaṃ. “Dīghe addhāne”tiādinā sace māsagamanīye [M 2.0399] magge sattāhagamanīyo eva kantāro hoti, tattha sattāhayāpanīyamattameva pātheyyaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ, tato paraṃ piṇḍacārikādivasena subhikkhasulabhapiṇḍamaggattā na pariyesitabbanti.

66. In the account of provisions, the passage beginning 'I allow, bhikkhus,' was permitted in Bhaddiyanagara after a request was made by the treasurer Meṇḍaka, who was one of unlimited consumption. Here, however, first the five dairy products were allowed: 'I allow, bhikkhus, the five dairy products: milk, curds, buttermilk, fresh butter, and ghee' (Mahāvagga 299). Then, in order to grant permission, speaking in accordance with the treasurer's request, he said, 'Bhikkhus, there are roads that are wildernesses,' and so on. The rest should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary. Similarly, by the statement that one who does not obtain them may take them even by asking from a place of non-relatives where one has not been invited, it is shown that on such occasions there is no fault on account of a request. But since it is said, 'On a road that can be traveled in a single day, one should seek for the sake of a single meal,' it is shown that asking for more than that is not proper. By the passage beginning 'on a long journey,' if on a road that takes a month to travel there is a wilderness that takes only seven days to travel, provisions should be sought only for what is sufficient to sustain one for seven days. It is not to be sought for more than that, because the road has abundant and easily obtainable almsfood by means of the almsround and so on.

Mahāpadesakathā

The Account of the Great Authorities

67. Mahāpadesakathāyaṃ mahāpadesā nāma appaṭikkhittā dve, ananuññātā dveti cattāroti dassento “yaṃ bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tesu appaṭikkhittepi akappiyānulomakappiyānulomavasena dve, tathā ananuññātepīti.

67. In the account of the Great Authorities, to show that the Great Authorities are four, namely two 'unrejected' and two 'unallowed,' he said the passage beginning 'Whatever, bhikkhus....' Among these, in the 'unrejected' there are two by way of conformity with the unallowable and conformity with the allowable; likewise also in the 'unallowed'.

Tattha [V 2.0295] “parimaddantāti upaparikkhantā. Paṭṭaṇṇudese sañjātavatthaṃ paṭṭuṇṇaṃ. ‘Paṭṭuṇṇaṃ koseyyaviseso’ti hi abhidhānakose vuttaṃ. Cīnadese somāradese ca sañjātavatthāni cīnasomārapaṭāni. Paṭṭuṇṇādīni tīṇi koseyyassa anulomāni pāṇakehi katasuttamayattā. Iddhimayaṃ ehibhikkhūnaṃ puññiddhiyā nibbattacīvaraṃ, taṃ khomādīnaṃ aññataraṃ hotīti tesaṃyeva anulomaṃ. Devatāhi dinnacīvaraṃ devadattiyaṃ, taṃ kapparukkhe nibbattaṃ jāliniyā devakaññāya anuruddhattherassa dinnavatthasadisaṃ, tampi khomādīnaṃyeva anulomaṃ hoti tesu aññatarabhāvato. Dve paṭāni desanāmena vuttānīti tesaṃ sarūpadassanamattametaṃ, nāññanivattanapadaṃ paṭṭuṇṇapaṭṭassapi desanāmeneva vuttattā. Tumbāti tīṇi bhājanāni. Phalakatumbo lābuādi. Udakatumbo udakukkhipanakuṭako. Kilañjacchattanti veḷuvilīvehi vāyitvā katachatta”nti sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.305) vuttaṃ.

Here, 'they rub' means they examine. Paṭṭuṇṇa is cloth produced in the Paṭṭuṇṇa country. For in the Abhidhānakosa it is said: 'Paṭṭuṇṇa is a special kind of silk.' Cīna-cloth and Somāra-cloth are fabrics produced in the country of Cīna and the country of Somāra. The three beginning with paṭṭuṇṇa are conformable with silk because they are made from thread produced by living creatures. The 'miraculous' is the robe produced by the spiritual power of merit for the 'Come, bhikkhu' bhikkhus; since it is one of the materials beginning with linen, it is conformable with them. The 'divinely given' is a robe given by deities; it is produced from a wishing tree and is like the cloth given by the deva-maiden Jālinī to the Elder Anuruddha. This too is conformable with linen and the others, because it is one of them. The two cloths are mentioned by their country's name; this is merely an indication of their nature, not a term to exclude others, because paṭṭuṇṇa-cloth is also mentioned by its country's name. 'Gourds' means three kinds of vessels: a fruit-gourd such as a calabash; a water-gourd, which is a pot for lifting water; and a 'mat-umbrella,' which is an umbrella made by weaving bamboo strips.' So it is said in the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.305).

“Yāvakālikapakkānanti [M 2.0400] pakke sandhāya vuttaṃ. Āmāni pana anupasampannehi sītudake madditvā parissāvetvā dinnapānaṃ pacchābhattampi kappati eva. Ayañca attho mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ sarūpato avuttoti āha ‘kurundiyaṃ panā’tiādi. Ucchuraso nikasaṭoti idaṃ pātabbatāsāmaññena yāmakālikakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pana sattāhakālikamevāti gahetabbaṃ. Ime cattāro rasāti phalapattapupphaucchurasā cattāro”ti vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.300) vuttaṃ. “Dve paṭā desanāmenevāti cīnapaṭasomārapaṭāni. Tīṇīti paṭṭuṇṇena saha tīṇi. Iddhimayaṃ ehibhikkhūnaṃ nibbattaṃ. Devadattiyaṃ anuruddhattherena laddha”nti vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 305).

'Of cooked things for the limited period' is said with reference to what is ripe. But a drink made from unripe ones, crushed in cold water, strained, and given by unordained persons, is allowable even after the meal. And since this meaning is not stated in its essence in the Great Commentary, he said the passage beginning 'But in the Kurundī....' 'Sugarcane juice is astringent': this is said in the account of the watch-period allowance in the general sense of being drinkable, but it should be understood as being only a seven-day allowance. 'These four juices' means the four: fruit juice, leaf juice, flower juice, and sugarcane juice.' So it is said in the Vimativinodanī (Vi. Vi. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 2.300). '“Two cloths by country’s name” means Cīna-cloth and Somāra-cloth. “Three” means three including paṭṭuṇṇa. “The miraculous” was produced for the ‘Come, bhikkhu’ bhikkhus. “The divinely given” was obtained by the Elder Anuruddha.' So it is said in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 305).

Saṃsaṭṭhakathā

A Discussion on Mixtures

Saṃsaṭṭhakathāyaṃ tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ kāle kappatītiādi sabbaṃ sambhinnarasaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sace hi challimpi apanetvā sakaleneva nāḷikeraphalena saddhiṃ pānakaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ hoti, nāḷikeraṃ apanetvā taṃ vikālepi kappati. Upari sappipiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā sītalapāyāsaṃ denti, yaṃ pāyāsena asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ sappi, taṃ apanetvā sattāhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Baddhamadhuphāṇitādīsupi eseva nayo. Takkolajātiphalādīhi alaṅkaritvā piṇḍapātaṃ denti, tāni uddharitvā dhovitvā yāvajīvaṃ paribhuñjitabbāni, yāguyaṃ pakkhipitvā dinnasiṅgiverādīsupi, telādīsu pakkhipitvā dinnalaṭṭhimadhukādīsupi [V 2.0296] eseva nayo. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ asambhinnarasaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ ekato paṭiggahitampi yathā suddhaṃ hoti, tathā dhovitvā vā tacchetvā vā tassa tassa kālassa vasena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

In the discussion on mixtures, everything said—such as 'what is received on that day is allowable at the proper time'—was stated in reference to mixed flavors. For if a drink is received together with a whole coconut, without even removing the husk, then after removing the coconut, it is allowable even at the wrong time. If they give cool rice-porridge with a lump of ghee placed on top, the ghee that is not mixed with the rice-porridge can be removed and consumed for seven days. The same principle applies to hardened honey, molasses, and so on. When almsfood is given adorned with cubeb pepper, nutmeg, and so on, those items can be removed, washed, and consumed for life. The same applies to ginger and so on given after being put into gruel, or to licorice sticks and so on given after being put into oil. Thus, whatever has an unmixed flavor, even if received together, can be consumed according to its respective time period after being washed or scraped, just as if it were pure.

Sace [M 2.0401] pana sambhinnarasaṃ hoti saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, na vaṭṭati. Yāvakālikañhi attanā saddhiṃ sambhinnarasāni tīṇipi yāmakālikādīni attano sabhāvaṃ upaneti. Yāmakālikaṃ dvepi sattāhakālikādīni attano sabhāvaṃ upaneti. Sattāhakālikaṃ attanā saddhiṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ attano sabhāvaññeva upaneti, tasmā tena tadahupaṭiggahitena saddhiṃ tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ vā purepaṭiggahitaṃ vā yāvajīvikaṃ sattāhaṃ kappati, dvīhapaṭiggahitena chāhaṃ…pe… sattāhapaṭiggahitena tadaheva kappatīti veditabbaṃ. Tasmāyeva hi “sattāhakālikena, bhikkhave, yāvajīvikaṃ tadahupaṭiggahita”nti avatvā “paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ kappatī”ti vuttaṃ.

But if the flavor is mixed and blended, it is not allowable. For a yāvakālika item, when mixed with them, brings all three—the yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, and yāvajīvika—to its own nature. A yāmakālika brings both the sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika to its own nature. A sattāhakālika, when mixed with it, brings a yāvajīvika to its own nature. Therefore, a yāvajīvika received on that day or previously is allowable for seven days when mixed with a sattāhakālika that was received on that day. When mixed with a sattāhakālika received two days ago, it is allowable for six days… and so on… when mixed with one received seven days ago, it is allowable only for that day. This should be understood. It is for this very reason that the Blessed One did not say, 'Bhikkhus, a yāvajīvika received on that day with a sattāhakālika…,' but said, 'what has been received is allowable for seven days.'

Kālayāmasattāhātikkamesu cettha vikālabhojanasannidhibhesajjasikkhāpadānaṃ vasena āpattiyo veditabbā. Imesu ca pana catūsu kālikesu yāvakālikaṃ yāmakālikanti idameva dvayaṃ antovutthakañceva sannidhikārakañca hoti, sattāhakālikañca yāvajīvikañca akappiyakuṭiyaṃ nikkhipitumpi vaṭṭati, sannidhimpi na janetīti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthameva.

Here, when the time limits for the daytime-item, the watch-item, and the seven-day-item are transgressed, offenses should be understood in accordance with the training rules on eating at the wrong time, storing food, and medicines. Among these four time-limited items, these two—the yāvakālika and the yāmakālika—are subject to the prohibitions on keeping things overnight and on storing. The sattāhakālika and the yāvajīvika, however, may be deposited even in an unsuitable dwelling and do not constitute storing. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Pañcabhesajjakathā

A Discussion on the Five Medicines

Pañcabhesajjakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tāni pañca bhesajjāni kāle paṭiggahetvā kāle paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 261) vacanato sāradikena ābādhena phuṭṭhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāgupi pītā uggacchati, bhattampi bhuttaṃ uggacchati, te tena kisā honti lūkhā dubbaṇṇā uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātā dhamanisanthatagattā. Tesaṃ yaṃ bhesajjañceva assa bhesajjasammatañca, lokassa āhāratthañca phareyya, na ca oḷāriko āhāro [M 2.0402] paññāyeyya. Tatrimāni pañca bhesajjāni. Seyyathidaṃ – sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ madhu phāṇitaṃ, tāni bhesajjāni kāle paṭiggahetvā kāle paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha “sāradikena ābādhenāti saradakāle uppannena pittābādhena. Tasmiñhi kāle vassodakenapi tementi, kaddamampi maddanti, antarantarā [V 2.0297] ābādhopi kharo hoti, tena tesaṃ pittaṃ koṭṭhabbhantaragataṃ hoti. Āhāratthañca phareyyāti āhāratthaṃ sādheyyā”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 260) vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.260) “pittaṃ koṭṭhabbhantaragataṃ hotīti bahisarīre byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ abaddhapittaṃ koṭṭhabbhantaragataṃ hoti, tena pittaṃ kupitaṃ hotīti adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ.

In the discussion on the five medicines: According to the passage (Mahāvagga 261), 'I allow, bhikkhus, those five medicines to be received at the proper time and to be consumed at the proper time,' for bhikkhus afflicted by the autumnal illness, even the gruel they drink comes up, and even the food they eat comes up. Because of this, they become thin, haggard, discolored, pale and jaundiced, with their veins standing out on their limbs. For them, there was a need for something that would be both a medicine and be regarded as a medicine, that would serve as nourishment for people, and yet would not be considered coarse food. These are the five medicines. Namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses. It is allowable to receive these medicines at the proper time and consume them at the proper time. Here, 'by the autumnal illness' means by a bilious illness that arises in the autumn season. For at that time, they are also soaked by the monsoon water and they tread in mud, and from time to time the illness is severe; because of this, their bile enters the abdomen. 'And would serve as nourishment' means 'it would accomplish the purpose of nourishment,' so it is said in the Commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 260). In the Vimativinodanī-ṭīkā (on Mahāvagga 2.260) it is said: '“Their bile enters the abdomen” means that the unbound bile that has spread and is established in the outer body enters the abdomen; the intention is that the bile becomes agitated.'

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 260) “yaṃ bhesajjañceva assāti parato ‘tadubhayena bhiyyosomattāya kisā hontī’tiādinā virodhadassanato nidānānapekkhaṃ yathālābhavasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yathānidānaṃ kasmā na vuttanti ce? Tadaññāpekkhādhippāyato. Sabbabuddhakālepi hi sappiādīnaṃ sattāhakālikabhāvāpekkhoti. Tathā vacanena bhagavato adhippāyo. Teneva ‘āhāratthañca phareyya, na ca oḷāriko āhāro paññāyeyyā’ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi kāle paṭiggahetvā kāle paribhuñjitunti ettha ca kālaparicchedo na kato, kutoyeva pana labbhā tadaññāpekkhādhippāyo bhagavatā mūlabhesajjādīni tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvanti kālaparicchedo. Yaṃ pana ‘anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tāni bhesajjāni kāle paṭiggahetvā kāle paribhuñjitu’nti (mahāva. 260) vacanaṃ, taṃ ‘sannidhiṃ katvā aparāparasmiṃ divase kāle eva paribhuñjituṃ anujānāmī’ti adhippāyato vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Aññathā atisayattā bhagavato [M 2.0403] ‘yaṃ bhesajjañceva assā’tiādivitakkuppādo na sambhavati. Paṇītabhojanānumatiyā pasiddhattā ābādhānurūpasappāyāpekkhāya vuttānīti ce? Tañca na, ‘bhiyyosomattāyā’ti kisādibhāvāpattidassanato. Yathā ucchurasaṃ upādāya phāṇitanti vuttaṃ, tathā navanītaṃ upādāya sappīti vattabbato navanītaṃ visuṃ na vattabbanti ce? Na visesadassanādhippāyato. Yathā phāṇitaggahaṇena siddhepi parato ucchuraso visuṃ anuññāto ucchusāmaññato guḷodakaṭṭhāne ṭhapanādhippāyato, tathā navanīte visesavidhidassanādhippāyato navanītaṃ visuṃ anuññātanti veditabbaṃ. Visesavidhi panassa bhesajjasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāvasena (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.619-621) veditabbo. Vuttañhi tattha ‘pacitvā sappiṃ katvā paribhuñjitukāmena adhotampi pacituṃ vaṭṭatī’ti. Tattha sappi pakkāva hoti, nāpakkā, tathā phāṇitampi. Navanītaṃ apakkamevā”tiādi.

In the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā (on Mahāvagga 260) it is said: Regarding the phrase 'what would be both a medicine…,' because a contradiction is seen in what follows, namely, 'due to an excess of both, they become thin,' etc., it should be understood that this was said based on what is available, without regard to the specific cause of illness. If it is asked, 'Why was it not stated according to the specific cause?' it is because the intention was with regard to other things. For even in the time of all Buddhas, it is expected that ghee and so on have the nature of sattāhakālika items. Such was the Blessed One's intention in this statement. For that reason it was said, 'It would serve as nourishment, and would not appear to be coarse food.' Thus, in the phrase 'having received at the proper time, to be consumed at the proper time,' no time limit was specified. How then, when the Blessed One's intention was with regard to other things, could a time limit of 'for life' be obtained for receiving and using those root medicines? The statement, 'I allow, bhikkhus, those medicines to be received at the proper time and to be consumed at the proper time' (Mahāvagga 260), should be understood as having been said with the intention, 'I allow them to be stored and consumed on subsequent days at the proper time.' Otherwise, due to the Blessed One's excellence, the arising of a thought such as 'what would be a medicine…' would not be possible. (If it is said:) 'Were they spoken of with regard to what is suitable and appropriate for the illness, since the allowance of fine foods is well-known?' That is also not so, because of seeing the state of becoming thin, etc., from the phrase 'due to an excess.' (If it is said:) 'Just as it is said that molasses comes from sugarcane juice, so too it should be said that ghee comes from fresh butter; therefore, should fresh butter not be mentioned separately?' No, because the intention is to show a special point. Just as sugarcane juice was later permitted separately, even though it is covered by the allowance of molasses, with the intention of placing it in the category of sweetened water due to its general nature as sugarcane; so too, fresh butter was permitted separately with the intention of showing a special rule for it. This should be understood. The special rule for it should be understood from the Commentary on the training rule about medicines (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.619-621). For it is said there: 'One who wishes to consume it by cooking it into ghee may cook it even unwashed.' In that context, ghee is cooked, not uncooked, and so too is molasses. Fresh butter, however, is only uncooked.

Dutiyabhesajjakathā

The Second Discourse on Medicine

Dutiyabhesajjakathāyaṃ [V 2.0298] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tāni pañca bhesajjāni paṭiggahetvā kālepi vikālepi paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 261) vacanato “tāni pañca bhesajjāni kāle paṭiggahetvā kāle paribhuñjantānaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yānipi tāni pākatikāni lūkhāni bhojanāni, tāni nacchādenti, pageva senesitāni. Te tena ceva sāradikena ābādhena phuṭṭhā iminā ca bhattācchādakena tadubhayena bhiyyosomattāya kisā hontī”ti imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ kālepi vikālepīti anuññātattā vikālepi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha “nacchādentīti na jīranti, na vātarogaṃ paṭippassambhetuṃ sakkonti. Senesitānīti siniddhāni. Bhattācchādakenāti [M 2.0404] bhattaṃ arocikenā”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 261) vuttaṃ, ṭīkāsu (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.261; vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.261-262) pana “nacchādentīti ruciṃ na uppādentī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ, mahāvibhaṅge (pārā. 622) pana “yāni kho pana tāni gilānānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭisāyanīyāni bhesajjāni. Seyyathidaṃ – sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ madhu phāṇitaṃ, tāni paṭiggahetvā sattāhaparamaṃ sannidhikārakaṃ paribhuñjitabbāni, taṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiya”nti vacanato imesaṃ pañcabhesajjānaṃ sattāhakālikabhāvo veditabbo, idha pana aṭṭhuppattivasena vuttoti.

In the Second Discourse on Medicine: “I allow, bhikkhus, having received those five medicines, to consume them both at the proper time and at the wrong time.” Based on the statement (Mahāvagga 261): “For those bhikkhus who receive and consume those five medicines at the proper time, even the plain, coarse foods they normally eat do not agree with them, let alone rich foods. Afflicted by that autumnal illness and also by this loss of appetite, they become even more emaciated on account of both.” In this case, since it was allowed to be consumed “both at the proper time and at the wrong time,” it is allowable to consume it even at the wrong time. Here, the commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 261) says: “‘Do not agree with them’ means they do not digest, nor are they able to calm the wind-illness. ‘Rich foods’ means oily. ‘Loss of appetite’ means loss of appetite for food.” But in the subcommentaries (Sārattha-ṭīkā, Mahāvagga 3.261; Vimativinodanī-ṭīkā, Mahāvagga 2.261-262) it is just said: “‘Do not agree with them’ means they do not arouse appetite.” However, in the Mahāvibhaṅga (Pārājika 622) it is said: “Whatever medicines are to be used by sick bhikkhus, that is: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses, these may be received and consumed for up to seven days while stored. For one who exceeds that, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture.” From this, the seven-day period for these five medicines should be understood. But here it is stated on account of the origin of the matter.

Vasābhesajjakathā

The Discourse on Fat as Medicine

Vasābhesajjakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sūkaravasaṃ gadrabhavasaṃ kāle paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjituṃ. Vikāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, anāpattī”ti (mahāva. 262). Tattha “kāle paṭiggahitantiādīsu majjhanhike avītivatte paṭiggahetvā pacitvā parissāvetvā cāti attho. Telaparibhogena paribhuñjitunti [V 2.0299] sattāhakālikatelaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 262) vuttaṃ, ṭīkāsu (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.262; vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.261-262) pana “susukāti [M 2.0405] samudde bhavā ekā macchajāti, kumbhilātipi vadanti. Saṃsaṭṭhanti parissāvitaṃ. Telaparibhogenāti sattāhakālikaparibhogaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana heṭṭhā catukālikakathāyaṃ vuttoyeva.

In the Discourse on Fat as Medicine: “I allow, bhikkhus, fats as medicines—bear fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat—to be consumed with the use of oil, if it is received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time. If, bhikkhus, it is received at the wrong time, cooked at the wrong time, and mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of three wrongdoings. If, bhikkhus, it is received at the proper time but cooked at the wrong time and mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of two wrongdoings. If, bhikkhus, it is received at the proper time and cooked at the proper time but mixed at the wrong time, and one consumes it, there is an offense of one wrongdoing. If, bhikkhus, it is received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, and one consumes it, there is no offense” (Mahāvagga 262). Here, the commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 262) says: “‘Received at the proper time,’ etc., means having received it, cooked it, and strained it before midday has passed. ‘To be consumed with the use of oil’ means to be consumed with the use of oil that is allowable for seven days.” But in the subcommentaries (Sārattha-ṭīkā, Mahāvagga 3.262; Vinayavinicchaya-ṭīkā, Mahāvagga 2.261-262) it is said: “‘Susukā’ is a type of sea-fish; some also call it a crocodile. ‘Mixed’ means strained. ‘With the use of oil’ is said in reference to the seven-day use.” This is the summary here; the detailed explanation has already been given below in the Discourse on the Four Time-Periods.

Mūlabhesajjakathā

The Discourse on Root-Medicines

Mūlabhesajjakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, mūlāni bhesajjāni, haliddiṃ siṅgiveraṃ vacaṃ vacattaṃ ativisaṃ kaṭukarohiṇiṃ usīraṃ bhaddamuttakaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi mūlāni bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharanti, tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ. Asati paccaye paribhuñjantassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti. Tattha vacattanti setavacaṃ. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

In the Discourse on Root-Medicines: “I allow, bhikkhus, root medicines: turmeric, ginger, sweet flag, white sweet flag, ativisa, kaṭukarohiṇī, vetiver, and fragrant nutgrass, or whatever other root medicines there are that do not serve as a hard food for the purpose of hard food, nor as a soft food for the purpose of soft food. These may be received and kept for life, to be consumed when there is a need. For one who consumes them when there is no need, there is an offense of wrongdoing.” Here, `vacatta` means white sweet flag. The rest is as stated before.

Piṭṭhabhesajjakathā

The Discourse on Ground Medicine

Piṭṭhabhesajjakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, nisadaṃ nisadapotaka”nti (mahāva. 263) vacanato pisitehi cuṇṇakatehi mūlabhesajjehi atthe sati nisadañca nisadapotakañca pariharituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha nisadaṃ nisadapotakanti pisanasilā ca pisanapoto ca. Nisadanti pisanti cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karonti mūlabhesajjādayo etthāti nisadaṃ, pisanasilā. Nisadanti pisanti cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karonti mūlabhesajjādayo etenāti nisadaṃ, posetabboti poto, dārako. Khuddakappamāṇatāya poto viyāti poto, nisadañca taṃ poto cāti nisadapoto, taṃ nisadapotakaṃ. Nipubbasada cuṇṇakaraṇeti dhātu.

In the Discourse on Ground Medicine: “I allow, bhikkhus, a grinding slab and a small grinding stone” (Mahāvagga 263). Based on this statement, when there is a need for root medicines to be ground into powder, it is permissible to keep a grinding slab and a small grinding stone. Herein, ‘a grinding slab and a small grinding stone’ means a grinding slab (`pisanasilā`) and a small grinding stone (`pisanapota`). ‘Grinding slab’ (`nisada`): that on which they grind (`nisadanti`)—crush into fine powder—root medicines and so on. ‘Small grinding stone’ (`nisadapota`): that by which they grind (`nisadanti`) is a `nisada`. It is a `pota` (a young one) because it is small, like a child (`dārako`). A `nisada` that is a `pota` is a `nisadapota`; hence the form `nisadapotaka`. The root is `sad` with the prefix `ni-` in the sense of ‘grinding’.

Kasāvabhesajjakathā

The Discourse on Astringent Medicines

Kasāvabhesajjakathāyaṃ [M 2.0406] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kasāvāni bhesajjāni nimbakasāvaṃ kuṭajakasāvaṃ paṭolakasāvaṃ phaggavakasāvaṃ nattamālakasāvaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi kasāvāni [V 2.0300] bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharanti, tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ, asati paccaye paribhuñjantassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 263) vacanato tānipi kasāvabhesajjāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha phaggavanti latājāti. Nattamālanti karañjaṃ. “Kasāvehīti tacādīni udake tāpetvā gahitaūsarehī”ti vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.263) vuttaṃ.

In the Discourse on Astringent Medicines: "I allow, bhikkhus, astringent medicines—neem astringent, kuṭaja astringent, paṭola astringent, phaggava astringent, nattamāla astringent, or whatever other astringent medicines there are that do not serve as hard food for the purpose of hard food, nor as soft food for the purpose of soft food. Having accepted them, they may be kept for life and consumed when there is a reason. For one who consumes them when there is no reason, there is an offense of wrongdoing." According to this statement (Mahāvagga 263), it is permissible to accept those astringent medicines, keep them for life, and consume them when there is a reason. Herein, "phaggava" is a species of vine. "Nattamāla" is karañja. It is said in the Vimativinodanī (Vimativinodanī-ṭīkā, Mahāvagga 2.263): "'With astringents' means with the extracts taken after heating bark and so on in water."

Paṇṇabhesajjakathā

The Discourse on Medicinal Leaves

Paṇṇabhesajjakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, paṇṇāni bhesajjāni nimbapaṇṇaṃ kuṭajapaṇṇaṃ paṭolapaṇṇaṃ nattamālapaṇṇaṃ phaggavapaṇṇaṃ sulasipaṇṇaṃ kappāsapaṇṇaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi paṇṇāni bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharanti, tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ, asati paccaye paribhuñjantassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 263) vacanato khādanīyabhojanīyatthaṃ apharantāni tānipi paṇṇāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Acchavasantiādīsu nissaggiyavaṇṇanāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Mūlabhesajjādivinicchayopi khuddakavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttoyeva, tasmā idha yaṃ yaṃ pubbe avuttaṃ, taṃ tadeva vaṇṇayissāma.

In the Discourse on Medicinal Leaves: "I allow, bhikkhus, medicinal leaves: neem leaves, kuṭaja leaves, paṭola leaves, nattamāla leaves, phaggava leaves, tulsi leaves, cotton leaves, or whatever other medicinal leaves there are that do not serve as hard food for the purpose of hard food, nor as soft food for the purpose of soft food. Having accepted them, they may be kept for life and consumed when there is a reason. For one who consumes them when there is no reason, there is an offense of wrongdoing." According to this statement (Mahāvagga 263), it is permissible to accept those leaves that do not serve the purpose of hard or soft food, keep them for life, and consume them when there is a reason. The meaning concerning bear fat and so on should be understood in the same way as explained in the commentary on the Nissaggiya rules (Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā 2.623). The ruling on root medicines and so on has also been stated in the Khuddaka commentary. Therefore, here we will explain only what has not been previously stated.

Phalabhesajjakathā

The Discourse on Medicinal Fruits

Phalabhesajjakathāyaṃ [M 2.0407] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, phalāni bhesajjāni biḷaṅgaṃ pippaliṃ maricaṃ harītakaṃ vibhītakaṃ āmalakaṃ goṭṭhaphalaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi phalāni bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharanti, tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ, asati paccaye paribhuñjantassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 263) vacanato khādanīyabhojanīyatthaṃ apharantāni tāni phalāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjitumpi vaṭṭati.

In the Discourse on Medicinal Fruits: "I allow, bhikkhus, medicinal fruits—biḷaṅga, pippali, marica, harītaka, vibhītaka, āmalaka, goṭṭhaphala, or whatever other medicinal fruits there are that do not serve as hard food for the purpose of hard food, nor as soft food for the purpose of soft food. Having accepted them, they may be kept for life and consumed when there is a reason. For one who consumes them when there is no reason, there is an offense of wrongdoing." According to this statement (Mahāvagga 263), it is permissible to accept those fruits that do not serve the purpose of hard or soft food, keep them for life, and also to consume them when there is a reason.

Jatubhesajjakathā

The Discourse on Medicinal Resins

Jatubhesajjakathāyaṃ [V 2.0301] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, jatūni bhesajjāni hiṅguṃ hiṅgujatuṃ hiṅgusipāṭikaṃ takaṃ takapattiṃ takapaṇṇiṃ sajjulasaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi jatūni bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharanti, tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ, asati paccaye paribhuñjantassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 263) vacanato tāni jatūni bhesajjāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha hiṅguhiṅgujatuhiṅgusipāṭikā hiṅgujātiyoyeva. Takatakapattitakapaṇṇayo lākhājātiyo.

In the Discourse on Medicinal Resins: "I allow, bhikkhus, medicinal resins: asafoetida, asafoetida-resin, asafoetida-pod, taka, takapatti, takapaṇṇī, pine resin, or whatever other medicinal resins there are that do not serve as hard food for the purpose of hard food, nor as soft food for the purpose of soft food. Having accepted them, they may be kept for life and consumed when there is a reason. For one who consumes them when there is no reason, there is an offense of wrongdoing." According to this statement (Mahāvagga 263), it is permissible to accept those medicinal resins, keep them for life, and consume them when there is a reason. Herein, asafoetida, asafoetida-resin, and asafoetida-pod are of the asafoetida type. Taka, takapatti, and takapaṇṇī are of the lac type.

Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 263) pana “hiṅgujatu nāma hiṅgurukkhassa daṇḍapallavapavāḷapākanipphannā. Hiṅgusipāṭikā nāma tassa mūlasākhapākanipphannā. Takaṃ nāma tassa rukkhassa tacapākodakaṃ. Takapattīti tassa pattapākodakaṃ. Takapaṇṇīti tassa phalapākodakaṃ. Atha vā ‘takaṃ nāma lākhā. Takapattīti kittimalohasākhā[M 2.0408]. Takapaṇṇīti pakkalākhā’ti likhitaṃ. Sati paccayeti ettha satipaccayatā gilānāgilānavasena dvidhā veditabbā. Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadassa hi anāpattivāre yāmakālikādīnaṃ tiṇṇampi avisesena satipaccayatā vuttā. Imasmiṃ khandhake ‘anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa guḷaṃ agilānassa guḷodakaṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa loṇasovīrakaṃ, agilānassa udakasambhinna’nti (mahāva. 273) vuttaṃ, tasmā siddhaṃ ‘satipaccayatā gilānāgilānavasena duvidhā’ti, aññathā asati paccaye guḷodakādi āpajjati, tato ca pāḷivirodho. Āhāratthanti āhārapayojanaṃ, āhārakiccayāpananti atthoti ca. Telaparibhogenāti sattāhakālikaparibhogena. Piṭṭhehīti pisitatelehi. Koṭṭhaphalanti koṭṭharukkhassa phalaṃ, madanaphalaṃ vāti ca likhita”nti vuttaṃ.

But in the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā (Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā, Mahāvagga 263) it is said: "'Hiṅgujatu' is that produced from the prepared stems, shoots, and sprouts of the hiṅgu tree. 'Hiṅgusipāṭikā' is that produced from the prepared roots and branches of that same tree. 'Taka' is the water from the prepared bark of that tree. 'Takapatti' is the water from its prepared leaves. 'Takapaṇṇī' is the water from its prepared fruit. Alternatively, it is written: 'Taka is lac. Takapatti is a branch of the kittimaloha tree. Takapaṇṇī is cooked lac.' Herein, 'when there is a reason' should be understood in two ways: with reference to the sick and the not-sick. For in the non-offense clauses of the training rule on eating at the wrong time, 'having a reason' is stated without distinction for all three—the yāmakālika, etc. In this chapter it is said: 'I allow, bhikkhus, jaggery for the sick and jaggery-water for the not-sick. I allow, bhikkhus, salt-sour gruel for the sick and the same mixed with water for the not-sick' (Mahāvagga 273). Therefore, it is established that 'having a reason' is twofold, with reference to the sick and the not-sick; otherwise, consuming jaggery-water and so on without a reason would entail an offense, and that would contradict the Pāli text. 'For the purpose of food' means for the purpose of nutriment, or it means for sustaining the bodily function. 'By the use of oil' means by the use of a seven-day allowable. 'With ground substances' means with oils from ground substances. 'Koṭṭhaphala' is the fruit of the koṭṭha tree, or it is written that it is the madana fruit."

Loṇabhesajjakathā

The Discussion on Salt-Medicines

Loṇabhesajjakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, loṇāni bhesajjāni sāmuddikaṃ kāḷaloṇaṃ sindhavaṃ ubbhidaṃ bilaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi loṇāni bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ [V 2.0302] pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharanti, tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ, asati paccaye paribhuñjantassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 263) vacanato tāni loṇāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvaṃ pariharituṃ, sati paccaye paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha sāmuddanti samuddatīre vālukaṃ viya santiṭṭhati. Kāḷaloṇanti pakatiloṇaṃ. Sindhavanti setavaṇṇaṃ pabbate uṭṭhahati. Ubbhidanti bhūmito aṅkuraṃ viya uṭṭhahati. Bilanti dabbasambhārehi saddhiṃ pacitaṃ, taṃ rattavaṇṇaṃ. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.263) pana “ubbhidaṃ nāma ūsarapaṃsumaya”nti [M 2.0409] vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.263) pana “ubbhidanti ūsarapaṃsumayaṃ loṇaṃ. Bilanti loṇaviseso”ti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyampi tatheva vuttaṃ.

In the discussion on salt-medicines: “I allow, monks, salt-medicines: sea salt, black salt, rock salt, efflorescent salt, pit salt, or whatever other salts are medicinal—not used for the purpose of a condiment in condiments, nor for the purpose of food in foods—to be accepted and kept for life, to be used when there is a reason. For one who uses them without a reason, there is an offense of wrong-doing.” (Mahāvagga 263) Thus, it is permissible to accept those salts and keep them for life, using them when there is a reason. Herein, “sea salt” refers to what settles on the seashore like sand. “Black salt” means natural salt. “Rock salt” is white in color and arises from a mountain. “Efflorescent salt” emerges from the ground like a sprout. “Pit salt” is cooked with various substances and is reddish in color. The Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.263) states: “Efflorescent salt is made of saline earth and dust.” The Vimativinodanī (Vimati. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 2.263) says: “Efflorescent salt is salt made of saline earth and dust. Pit salt is a type of salt.” The Vajirabuddhiṭīkā also states the same.

Cuṇṇakathā

The Discussion on Powders

Cuṇṇakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yassa kaṇḍu vā pīḷakā vā assāvo vā thullakacchu vā ābādho kāyo vā duggandho cuṇṇāni bhesajjāni, agilānassa chakaṇaṃ mattikaṃ rajananippakkaṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, udukkhalaṃ musala”nti (mahāva. 264). “Kāyo vā duggandhoti kassaci assādīnaṃ viya kāyagandho hoti, tassapi sirīsakosumbādicuṇṇāni vā gandhacuṇṇāni vā sabbāni vaṭṭanti. Chakaṇanti gomayaṃ. Rajananippakkanti rajanakasaṭaṃ, pākatikacuṇṇampi koṭṭetvā udakena temetvā nhāyituṃ vaṭṭati, etampi rajananippakkasaṅkhameva gacchatī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 264) vuttaṃ. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.264) pana “chakaṇanti gomayaṃ. Pākatikacuṇṇaṃ nāma apakkakasāvacuṇṇaṃ. Tena ṭhapetvā gandhacuṇṇaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭatīti vadantī”ti vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.264-265) “chakaṇanti gomayaṃ. Pākatikacuṇṇanti apakkakasāvacuṇṇaṃ, gandhacuṇṇaṃ pana na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyampi (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 264) “chakaṇanti gomayaṃ. Pākatikacuṇṇaṃ nāma apakkakasāvacuṇṇaṃ. Tena ṭhapetvā gandhacuṇṇaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭatīti vadantī”ti vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cuṇṇacālini”nti (mahāva. 264) vacanato gilānānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cuṇṇehi bhesajjehi cālitehi atthe sati cuṇṇacālinī vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dussacālini”nti (mahāva. 264) vacanato saṇhehi cuṇṇehi atthe sati dussacālinī vaṭṭati[V 2.0303]. “Cuṇṇacālininti udukkhale koṭṭitacuṇṇaparissāvani”nti vimativinodaniyaṃ [M 2.0410] (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.264-265) vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyampi (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 264) “cālitehīti parissāvitehī”ti vuttaṃ.

In the discussion on powders: “I allow, monks, for one who has itching, boils, a discharge, thick scabies, an afflicted body, or a foul-smelling body, medicinal powders; for one who is not ill, cow dung, clay, and dye-sediment. I allow, monks, a mortar and pestle.” (Mahāvagga 264). The commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 264) says: “‘Or a foul-smelling body’: if someone has a body odor like that of assādi fruits, etc., for them powders made from sirīsa, kusumbha, or any fragrant powders are all permissible. ‘Cow dung’ means cow manure. ‘Dye-sediment’ means dye residue. It is also permissible to grind up natural powder, moisten it with water, and bathe with it; this too is included under dye-sediment.” The Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.264) states: “‘Cow dung’ means cow manure. ‘Natural powder’ means the powder of unboiled astringent substances. They say that by this, everything is permissible except for fragrant powder.” The Vimativinodanī (Vimati. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 2.264-265) states: “‘Cow dung’ means cow manure. ‘Natural powder’ means the powder of unboiled astringent substances, but fragrant powder is not permissible.” The Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 264) similarly states: “‘Cow dung’ means cow manure. ‘Natural powder’ means the powder of unboiled astringent substances. They say that by this, everything is permissible except for fragrant powder.” From the statement, “I allow, monks, a powder-sieve” (Mahāvagga 264), a powder-sieve is permissible for ill monks when there is a need for sieved medicinal powders. From the statement, “I allow, monks, a cloth-sieve” (Mahāvagga 264), a cloth-sieve is permissible when fine powders are needed. The Vimativinodanī (Vimati. Ṭī.
