Mahāvagga 2.264-265) states: “‘Powder-sieve’ means a sieve for powder ground in a mortar.” The Vajirabuddhiṭīkā (Vajira. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 264) also states: “‘Sieved’ means filtered.”

Amanussikābādhakathā

The Discussion on Sickness Caused by Non-humans

Amanussikābādhakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, amanussikābādhe āmakamaṃsaṃ āmakamaṃsalohita”nti (mahāva. 264) vacanato yassa bhikkhuno āmakamaṃsaṃ khāditassa āmakalohitaṃ pivitassa so amanussābādho paṭippassambhati, tassa anāpatti. Tattha āmakamaṃsañca khādi, āmakalohitañca pivīti na taṃ bhikkhu khādi, na pivi, amanusso khāditvā ca pivitvā ca pakkanto. Tena vuttaṃ “tassa so amanussikābādho paṭippassambhī”ti.

In the discussion on sickness caused by non-humans: “I allow, monks, in case of sickness caused by non-humans, raw meat and raw blood.” (Mahāvagga 264) Accordingly, for a monk for whom, after he has eaten raw meat and drunk raw blood, that sickness caused by non-humans subsides, there is no offense. Herein, it is not the monk who ate the raw meat and drank the raw blood; the non-human, having eaten and drunk, has departed. Therefore it is said: “For him, that sickness caused by non-humans subsides.”

Añjanakathā

The Discussion on Eye-Salves

Añjanakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, añjanaṃ kāḷañjanaṃ rasañjanaṃ sotañjanaṃ gerukaṃ kapalla”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato bhikkhūnaṃ cakkhuroge sati añjanādīni vaṭṭanti. Tattha “añjananti sabbasaṅgāhikavacanametaṃ. Kāḷañjananti ekā añjanajāti. Rasañjananti nānāsambhārehi kataṃ. Sotañjananti nadīsotādīsu uppajjanakaañjanaṃ. Geruko nāma suvaṇṇageruko. Kapallanti dīpasikhato gahitamasī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 264) vuttaṃ. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.265) “suvaṇṇagerukoti suvaṇṇatutthādī”ti vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.264-265) tatheva vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, candanaṃ tagaraṃ kāḷānusāriyaṃ tālīsaṃ bhaddamuttaka”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato añjanūpapisanehi atthe sati imāni candanādīni vaṭṭanti. Tattha “candananti lohitacandanādikaṃ yaṃ kiñci candanaṃ. Tagarādīni [M 2.0411] pākaṭāni. Aññānipi nīluppalādīni vaṭṭantiyeva. Añjanūpapisanehīti añjanehi saddhiṃ ekato pisitabbehi. Na hi kiñci añjanūpapisanaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 264) ṭīkāyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.265) pana “añjanūpapisananti añjanatthāya upapisitabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci [V 2.0304] cuṇṇajātī”ti vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.264-265) pana “pāḷiyaṃ añjanūpapisananti añjane upanetuṃ pisitabbabhesajja”nti vuttaṃ.

In the discussion on eye-salves: “I allow, monks, eye-salve: black salve, rasañjana, sotañjana, ochre, and lampblack.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, when monks have an eye disease, these eye-salves and the like are permissible. Herein, the commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 264) says: “‘Eye-salve’ is a general term. ‘Black salve’ is one type of eye-salve. ‘Rasañjana’ is made from various ingredients. ‘Sotañjana’ is an eye-salve that arises in river currents and the like. ‘Ochre’ is golden ochre. ‘Lampblack’ is the soot taken from the flame of a lamp.” The Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.265) says: “‘Golden ochre’ means golden vitriol and the like.” The Vimativinodanī (Vimati. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 2.264-265) says the same. “I allow, monks, sandalwood, tagara, black anusāriya, tālisa, and bhaddamuttaka.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, when there is a need for substances to be ground up with eye-salve, these things—sandalwood and the like—are permissible. Herein, the commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 264) says: “‘Sandalwood’ means red sandalwood or any other kind of sandalwood. ‘Tagara’ and the others are well-known. Other things like blue lotuses are also permissible. ‘For substances to be ground up with eye-salve’ means those to be ground together with the eye-salves. For indeed, any substance to be ground up with eye-salve is permissible.” But the subcommentary (Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.265) says: “‘Substance to be ground up with eye-salve’ means any kind of powder to be ground up for the purpose of eye-salve.” The Vimativinodanī (Vimati. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 2.264-265) says: “In the Pāli, ‘substance to be ground up with eye-salve’ means a medicine to be ground for applying with the eye-salve.”

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, añjani”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato añjanaṭhapanaṭṭhānaṃ vaṭṭati. “Na, bhikkhave, uccāvacā añjanī dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭhimayaṃ dantamayaṃ visāṇamayaṃ naḷamayaṃ veḷumayaṃ kaṭṭhamayaṃ jatumayaṃ lohamayaṃ saṅkhanābhimaya”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato etāni kappiyāni. Tattha aṭṭhimayanti manussaṭṭhiṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaaṭṭhimayaṃ. Dantamayanti hatthidantādisabbadantamayaṃ. Visāṇamayepi akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Naḷamayādayo ekantakappiyāyeva.

“I allow, monks, an eye-salve container.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, a container for keeping eye-salve is permissible. “Monks, elaborate eye-salve containers should not be used. Whoever should use one commits an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, those made of bone, ivory, horn, reed, bamboo, wood, lac, metal, or from a conch shell.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, these are permissible. Herein, “made of bone” means made of any bone except human bone. “Made of ivory” means made of any kind of tusk, such as an elephant’s tusk. Among those made of horn, there is nothing impermissible. Those made of reed and so on are entirely permissible.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, apidhāna”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato añjanīapidhānampi vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, suttakena bandhitvā añjaniyā bandhitu”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato apidhānaṃ suttakena bandhitvā añjaniyā bandhitabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, suttakena sibbetu”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato apatanatthāya añjanīsuttakena sibbetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, añjanisalāka”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato añjanisalākampi vaṭṭati. “Na, bhikkhave, uccāvacā añjanisalākā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭhimayaṃ…pe… saṅkhanābhimaya”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato etāyeva añjanisalākā vaṭṭanti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, salākaṭṭhāniya”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato añjanisalākaṭṭhāniyampi vaṭṭati. Tattha salākaṭṭhāniyanti yattha salākaṃ odahanti, taṃ susiradaṇḍakaṃ vā thavikaṃ vā anujānāmīti [M 2.0412] attho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, añjanitthavika”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato thavikampi vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṃsabaddhakaṃ bandhanasuttaka”nti (mahāva. 265) vacanato añjanitthavikāya aṃse lagganatthāya aṃsabaddhakampi bandhanasuttakampi vaṭṭati.

“I allow, monks, a lid.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, a lid for the eye-salve container is also permissible. “I allow, monks, tying it with a thread and binding it to the eye-salve container.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, the lid should be tied with a thread and bound to the container. “I allow, monks, to stitch it with a thread.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, it is permissible to stitch the eye-salve container with a thread to prevent it from falling. “I allow, monks, an eye-salve stick.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, an eye-salve stick is also permissible. “Monks, elaborate eye-salve sticks should not be used. Whoever should use one commits an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, those made of bone…pe… from a conch shell.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, these eye-salve sticks are permissible. “I allow, monks, a holder for the stick.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, a holder for the eye-salve stick is also permissible. Herein, ‘a holder for the stick’ means a place where one puts the stick; the meaning is, “I allow a hollow tube or a pouch.” “I allow, monks, a pouch for the eye-salve container.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, a pouch is also permissible. “I allow, monks, a shoulder-strap and a tying-thread.” (Mahāvagga 265) Accordingly, for attaching the eye-salve pouch to the shoulder, a shoulder-strap and a tying-thread are also permissible.

Natthukathā

The Account of Nasal Treatment

Natthukathāyaṃ [V 2.0305] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, muddhani telaka”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato sīsābhitāpassa bhikkhuno muddhani telaṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, natthukamma”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato nakkhamanīye sati natthukammaṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, natthukaraṇi”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato natthuyā agaḷanatthaṃ natthukaraṇī vaṭṭati. “Na, bhikkhave, uccāvacā natthukaraṇī dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭhimayaṃ…pe… saṅkhanābhimaya”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato etāyeva natthukaraṇiyo vaṭṭanti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yamakanatthukaraṇi”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato natthu visamaṃ āsiñcayanti ce, yamakanatthukaraṇiṃ dhāretabbaṃ. Tattha yamakanatthukaraṇinti samaso tāhi dvīhi panāḷikāhi ekaṃ natthukaraṇiṃ.

In the account of nasal treatment: “I allow, monks, oil on the head.” By this, oil on the head is allowable for a monk suffering from a head affliction. “I allow, monks, nasal treatment.” By this, when there is something to be expelled from the nose, nasal treatment is allowable. “I allow, monks, a nasal treatment instrument.” By this, a nasal treatment instrument is allowable so that the nasal medicine does not drip. “Monks, various kinds of nasal treatment instruments are not to be used. Whoever should use one commits an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, one made of bone …pe… of conch-shell.” By this, only these nasal treatment instruments are allowable. “I allow, monks, a double nasal treatment instrument.” By this, if the nasal medicine is administered unevenly, a double nasal treatment instrument is to be used. Herein, a “double nasal treatment instrument” means a single nasal treatment instrument with two equal tubes.

Dhūmanettakathā

The Account of the Smoke Pipe

Dhūmanettakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dhūmaṃ pātu”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato yamakanatthukaraṇiyā nakkhamanīye sati dhūmaṃ pātuṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dhūmanetta”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato tameva vaṭṭiṃ ālimbetvā pivanapaccayā kaṇṭhe dahantena dhūmanettadhūmo pivitabbo. “Na, bhikkhave, uccāvacāni dhūmanettāni dhāretabbāni, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭhimayaṃ…pe… saṅkhanābhimaya”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato etāni eva dhūmanettāni dhāretabbāni. “Anujānāmi[M 2.0413], bhikkhave, apidhāna”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato pāṇakādiappavisanatthaṃ dhūmanettatthavikampi vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yamakatthavika”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato ekato ghaṃsiyamāne sati yamakatthavikaṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṃsabaddhakaṃ bandhanasuttaka”nti (mahāva. 266) vacanato dhūmanettatthavikassa aṃsabaddhabandhanasuttaṃ vaṭṭati.

In the account of the smoke pipe: “I allow, monks, to inhale smoke.” By this, when an ailment is not expelled by a double nasal instrument, it is allowable to inhale smoke. “I allow, monks, a smoke pipe.” By this, the smoke from a smoke pipe is to be inhaled by one whose throat burns on account of inhaling directly from a smeared wick. “Monks, various kinds of smoke pipes are not to be used. Whoever should use one commits an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, those made of bone …pe… of conch-shell.” By this, only these kinds of smoke pipes are to be used. “I allow, monks, a lid.” By this, a lid is allowable to prevent small living beings and so on from entering, and a pouch for the smoke pipe is also allowable. “I allow, monks, a double bag.” By this, when they are rubbing against each other, a double bag is allowable. “I allow, monks, a shoulder strap and a tying cord.” By this, a shoulder strap and a tying cord for the smoke pipe bag are allowable.

Telapākakathā

The Account of Medicated Oil

Telapākakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, telapāka”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato vātābādhe [V 2.0306] sati telapāko vaṭṭati. Tattha anujānāmi, bhikkhave, telapākanti yaṃ kiñci bhesajjapakkhittaṃ sabbaṃ anuññātameva hoti. “Na, bhikkhave, atipakkhittamajjaṃ telaṃ pātabbaṃ, yo piveyya, yathādhammo kāretabbo. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ telapāke majjassa na vaṇṇo na gandho na raso paññāyati, evarūpaṃ majjapakkhittaṃ telaṃ pātu”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato yasmiṃ telapāke pakkhittassa majjassa vaṇṇo vā gandho vā raso vā na paññāyati, tādisaṃ telaṃ pivitabbaṃ. Tattha atipakkhittamajjānīti ativiya khittamajjāni, bahuṃ majjaṃ pakkhipitvā yojitānīti attho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, abbhañjanaṃ adhiṭṭhātu”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato atipakkhittamajjattā apivitabbe tele sati abbhañjanaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tīṇi tumbāni lohatumbaṃ kaṭṭhatumbaṃ phalatumba”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato telapakkabhājanāni imāni tīṇi tumbāni vaṭṭanti.

In the account of medicated oil: “I allow, O monks, medicated oil.” By this, when there is a wind-disease, medicated oil is allowable. Herein, by “I allow, O monks, medicated oil,” whatever has medicine mixed in is entirely allowed. “Monks, oil with an excessive mixture of intoxicants is not to be drunk. Whoever should drink it is to be dealt with according to the rule. I allow, O monks, to drink oil mixed with an intoxicant in which the color, smell, or taste of the intoxicant is not discernible.” By this, such oil should be drunk in which the color, smell, or taste of the added intoxicant is not discernible. Herein, “with an excessive mixture of intoxicants” means with intoxicants mixed in excessively; the meaning is, prepared by adding a large quantity of intoxicants. “I allow, O monks, to determine it for anointing.” By this, when oil is undrinkable on account of an excessive mixture of intoxicants, it is allowable to determine it for anointing. “I allow, O monks, three kinds of gourds: a metal gourd, a wooden gourd, and a fruit-gourd.” By this, these three kinds of gourds are allowable as vessels for medicated oil.

Sedakammakathā

The Account of Sweating

Sedakammakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sedakamma”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato aṅgavāte sati sedakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati[M 2.0414]. Tattha aṅgavātoti hatthapāde vāto. Nakkhamanīyo hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sambhāraseda”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato sedakammena nakkhamanīye sati sambhārasedaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha sambhārasedanti nānāvidhapaṇṇasambhārasedaṃ. Nakkhamanīyo hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, mahāseda”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato sambhārasedanakkhamanīye sati mahāsedaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha mahāsedanti mahantaṃ sedaṃ, porisappamāṇaṃ āvāṭaṃ aṅgārānaṃ pūretvā paṃsuvālikādīhi pidahitvā tattha nānāvidhāni vātaharaṇapaṇṇāni santharitvā telamakkhitena gattena tattha nipajjitvā samparivattantena sarīraṃ sedetuṃ anujānāmīti attho. Nakkhamanīyo hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, bhaṅgodaka”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato mahāsedena nakkhamanīye sati bhaṅgodakaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha bhaṅgodakanti nānāpaṇṇabhaṅgakuthitaṃ udakaṃ, tehi paṇṇehi ca udakena ca siñcitvā siñcitvā sedetabbo. Nakkhamanīyo hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, udakakoṭṭhaka”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato bhaṅgodakena nakkhamanīye sati udakakoṭṭhakaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha udakakoṭṭhakanti [V 2.0307] udakakoṭṭhe cāṭiṃ vā doṇiṃ vā uṇhodakassa pūretvā tattha pavisitvā sedakammakaraṇaṃ anujānāmīti attho.

In the account of sweating: “I allow, O monks, sweating.” By this, when there is wind in the limbs, it is allowable to perform sweating. Herein, “wind in the limbs” means wind in the hands and feet. If it is not expelled, “I allow, O monks, sweating with materials.” By this, when it is not expelled by sweating, it is allowable to perform sweating with materials. Herein, “sweating with materials” means sweating with materials of various kinds of leaves. If it is not expelled, “I allow, O monks, a great sweating.” By this, when it is not expelled by sweating with materials, it is allowable to perform a great sweating. Herein, “a great sweating” means a large sweating; the meaning is: I allow one to sweat the body by filling a pit the size of a person with embers, covering it with soil, sand, and so on, spreading various kinds of wind-dispelling leaves on it, and then, with the body anointed with oil, lying down there and turning over. If it is not expelled, “I allow, O monks, a decoction bath.” By this, when it is not expelled by a great sweating, it is allowable to take a decoction bath. Herein, “a decoction bath” means water boiled with broken pieces of various leaves; one should be made to sweat by repeatedly sprinkling with those leaves and that water. If it is not expelled, “I allow, O monks, a water chamber.” By this, when it is not expelled by a decoction bath, it is allowable to use a water chamber. Herein, “a water chamber” means: I allow the performance of sweating by filling a jar or a trough in a water chamber with hot water and entering it.

Lohitamocanakathā

The Discussion on Letting Blood

Lohitamocanakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, lohitaṃ mocetu”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato pabbavāte sati lohitaṃ mocetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha pabbavāto hotīti pabbe pabbe vāto vijjhati. Lohitaṃ mocetunti satthakena lohitaṃ mocetuṃ. Nakkhamanīyo hoti, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, lohitaṃ mocetvā visāṇena gāhetunti (mahāva. 267).

In the discussion on letting blood: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, the letting of blood' (Mahāvagga 267), it is permissible to let blood when there is wind in the joints. Here, 'wind in the joints' means that wind pierces each joint. 'To let blood' means to let blood with a lancet. When this is not effective, [the Blessed One said]: 'I allow, bhikkhus, having let the blood, to draw it with a horn' (Mahāvagga 267).

Pādabbhañjanakathā

The Discussion on Anointing the Feet

Pādabbhañjanakathāyaṃ [M 2.0415] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pādabbhañjana”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato pādesu phalitesu pādabbhañjanaṃ pacitabbaṃ. Nakkhamanīyo hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pajjaṃ abhisaṅkharitu”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato pādabbhañjanatelena nakkhamanīye sati pajjaṃ abhisaṅkharitabbaṃ. Tattha pajjaṃ abhisaṅkharitunti yena phalitapādā pākatikā honti, taṃ nāḷikerādīsu nānābhesajjāni pakkhipitvā pajjaṃ abhisaṅkharituṃ, pādānaṃ sappāyabhesajjaṃ pacitunti attho.

In the discussion on anointing the feet: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, the anointing of feet' (Mahāvagga 267), when the feet are cracked, a foot ointment should be prepared. When this is not effective, [the Blessed One said]: 'I allow, bhikkhus, to prepare a foot-treatment' (Mahāvagga 267). When anointing the feet with oil is not effective, a foot-treatment should be prepared. Here, 'to prepare a foot-treatment' means to prepare a beneficial medicine for the feet by putting various medicinal substances into a coconut shell or the like, by which cracked feet are restored to their natural state; this is the meaning.

Gaṇḍābādhakathā

The Discussion on the Ailment of Boils

Gaṇḍābādhakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, satthakamma”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato gaṇḍābādhe sati satthakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kasāvodaka”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato kasāvodakena atthe sati kasāvodakaṃ dātabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tilakakka”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato tilakakkena atthe sati tilakakkaṃ dātabbaṃ. Tilakakkena atthoti piṭṭhehi tilehi attho. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave kabaḷika”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato kabaḷikāya atthe sati kabaḷikā dātabbā. Tattha kabaḷikanti vaṇamukhe sattupiṇḍaṃ pakkhipituṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vaṇabandhanacoḷa”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato [V 2.0308] vaṇabandhanacoḷena atthe sati vaṇabandhanacoḷaṃ dātabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sāsapakuṭṭena phositu”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato sace vaṇo kuṇḍavatī, sāsapakuṭṭena phositabbaṃ. Tattha sāsapakuṭṭenāti sāsapapiṭṭhena.

In the discussion on the ailment of boils: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, a surgical operation' (Mahāvagga 267), a surgical operation should be performed when there is an ailment of boils. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, astringent water' (Mahāvagga 267), astringent water should be given when there is a need for it. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, sesame paste' (Mahāvagga 267), sesame paste should be given when there is a need for it. 'A need for sesame paste' means a need for ground sesame. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, a poultice' (Mahāvagga 267), a poultice should be given when there is a need for it. Here, 'a poultice' means to place a ball of groats on the opening of the wound. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, a bandage cloth' (Mahāvagga 267), a bandage cloth should be given when there is a need for it. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to sprinkle with mustard powder' (Mahāvagga 267), if the wound has maggots, it should be sprinkled with mustard powder. Here, 'with mustard powder' means with ground mustard.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dhūmaṃ kātu”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato yadi vaṇo kilijjittha, dhūmaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, loṇasakkharikāya chinditu”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato yadi vaḍḍhamaṃsaṃ vuṭṭhāti[M 2.0416], chinditabbaṃ. Tattha vaḍḍhamaṃsanti adhikamaṃsaṃ āṇī viya uṭṭhahati. Loṇasakkharikāya chinditunti khārena chindituṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vaṇatela”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato yadi vaṇo na ruhati, vaṇaruhanatelaṃ pacitabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vikāsikaṃ sabbaṃ vaṇapaṭikamma”nti (mahāva. 267) vacanato yadi telaṃ gaḷati, vikāsikaṃ dātabbaṃ, sabbaṃ vaṇapaṭikammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Tattha vikāsikanti telarundhanapilotikaṃ. Sabbaṃ vaṇapaṭikammanti yaṃ kiñci vaṇapaṭikammaṃ nāma atthi, sabbaṃ anujānāmīti attho. Mahāvikaṭakathā pubbe vuttāva.

In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to apply smoke' (Mahāvagga 267), if a wound is suppurating, it is permissible to apply smoke. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to cut with a caustic substance' (Mahāvagga 267), if proud flesh grows, it should be cut. Here, 'proud flesh' means additional flesh that rises up like a peg. 'To cut with a caustic substance' means to cut with an alkali. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, wound-oil' (Mahāvagga 267), if a wound does not heal, a wound-healing oil should be prepared. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, an oil-retaining dressing and all treatments for a wound' (Mahāvagga 267), if the oil leaks out, an oil-retaining dressing should be applied, and every treatment for a wound should be performed. Here, 'an oil-retaining dressing' means a piece of cloth for stopping the oil. 'All treatments for a wound' means: 'Whatever treatment for a wound there is, I allow it all'; this is the meaning. The discussion on the great abnormal substances has been stated previously.

Sāmaṃ gahetvāti idaṃ na kevalaṃ sappadaṭṭhasseva, aññasmimpi daṭṭhavise sati sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ, aññesu pana kāraṇesu paṭiggahitameva vaṭṭati.

'Taking it oneself': this applies not only to one bitten by a snake, but also when there is poison from another kind of bite, one may take it oneself and consume it. In other cases, however, it is proper only to use what has been received.

Visapītakathā

The Discussion on Drinking Poison

Visapītakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gūthaṃ pāyetu”nti (mahāva. 268) vacanato pītavisaṃ bhikkhuṃ gūthaṃ pāyetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ karonto paṭiggaṇhāti, sveva paṭiggaho kato, na puna paṭiggahetabbo”ti (mahāva. 268) vacanato tadeva vaṭṭati. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 268) pana na puna paṭiggahetabboti sace bhūmippatto, paṭiggahāpetabbo, appattaṃ pana gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

In the discussion on drinking poison: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to administer excrement to drink' (Mahāvagga 268), it is permissible to make a bhikkhu who has drunk poison drink excrement. In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, that when one receives something while performing an action, that itself is the act of receiving; it need not be received again' (Mahāvagga 268), that itself is proper. But in the Commentary it is said: Regarding 'it need not be received again,' if it has reached the ground, it should be formally received; but if it has not reached the ground, it is permissible to take it.

Gharadinnakābādhakathā

The Discussion on the Ailment from a House-Given Potion

Gharadinnakābādhakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sītāloḷiṃ pāyetu”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato [V 2.0309] gharadinnakābādhassa bhikkhuno sītāloḷiṃ pāyetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha gharadinnakābādhoti vasīkaraṇapāṇakasamuṭṭhitarogo. Ṭīkāyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.269) pana [M 2.0417] “gharadinnakābādho nāma vasīkaraṇatthāya gharaṇiyā dinnabhesajjasamuṭṭhito ābādho. Tenāha ‘vasīkaraṇapāṇakasamuṭṭhitarogo’ti. Ghara-saddo cettha abhedena gharaṇiyā vattamāno adhippeto”ti vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyampi (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.267-269) “gharadinnakābādho nāma gharaṇiyā dinnavasīkaraṇabhesajjasamuṭṭhito ābādho”ti vuttaṃ. Sītāloḷinti naṅgalena kasantassa phāle laggamattikaṃ udakena āloḷetvā pāyetuṃ anujānāmīti attho.

In the discussion on the ailment from a house-given potion: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to administer a cool mixture to drink' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible to make a bhikkhu afflicted by a house-given ailment drink a cool mixture. Here, 'a house-given ailment' is a disease arising from an enchantment potion. And in the Subcommentary it is said: 'An ailment from a house-given potion is an ailment arising from medicine given by a housewife for the purpose of enchantment. Hence it is said, "a disease arising from an enchantment potion." Here, the word "house" is intended to refer without distinction to the housewife.' The Vimativinodanī also states: 'An ailment from a house-given potion is an ailment arising from an enchantment medicine given by a housewife.' 'A cool mixture' means: 'I allow to administer for drinking water mixed with clay adhering to the ploughshare of one who is ploughing'; this is the meaning.

Duṭṭhagahaṇikakathā

The Discussion on Severe Dysentery

Duṭṭhagahaṇikakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āmisakhāraṃ pāyetu”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato duṭṭhagahaṇikassa bhikkhuno āmisakhāraṃ pāyetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha duṭṭhagahaṇikoti vipannagahaṇiko, kicchena uccāro nikkhamatīti attho. Āmisakhāranti sukkhodanaṃ jhāpetvā tāya chārikāya paggharitaṃ khārodakaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.267-269) pana “tāya chārikāya paggharitaṃ khārodakanti parissāvane taṃ chārikaṃ pakkhipitvā udake abhisiñcite tato chārikato heṭṭhā paggharitaṃ khārodaka”nti vuttaṃ.

In the discussion on severe dysentery: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to administer an alkaline concoction' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible to administer an alkaline concoction to a bhikkhu with severe dysentery. Here, ‘one with severe dysentery’ means one whose bowels are impaired; the meaning is that feces are passed with difficulty. ‘Alkaline concoction’ is alkali-water filtered from the ash of burnt dried rice. But in the Vimativinodanī it is said: “‘Alkali-water filtered from that ash’ means that the ash is placed in a strainer, water is sprinkled on it, and then the alkali-water that filters down from the ash.”

Paṇḍurogābādhakathā

The Discussion on the Illness of Jaundice

Paṇḍurogābādhakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, muttaharītakaṃ pāyetu”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato paṇḍurogābādhassa bhikkhuno muttaharītakaṃ pāyetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha muttaharītakanti gomuttaparibhāvitaṃ harītakaṃ.

In the discussion on the illness of jaundice: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to administer myrobalan steeped in urine' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible to administer myrobalan steeped in urine to a bhikkhu afflicted with the illness of jaundice. Here, ‘myrobalan steeped in urine’ means myrobalan steeped in cow’s urine.

Chavidosābādhakathā

The Discussion on the Illness of Skin Disease

Chavidosābādhakathāyaṃ [M 2.0418] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gandhālepaṃ kātu”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato chavidosābādhassa bhikkhuno gandhālepaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

In the discussion on the illness of skin disease: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to apply a fragrant paste' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible for a bhikkhu afflicted with a skin disease to apply a fragrant paste.

Abhisannakāyakathā

The Discussion on a Congested Body

Abhisannakāyakathāyaṃ [V 2.0310] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, virecanaṃ pātu”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato abhisannakāyassa bhikkhuno virecanaṃ pātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha abhisannakāyoti ussannadosakāyo. Acchakañjiyā attho hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, acchakañjiya”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato acchakañjiyaṃ pātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha acchakañjiyanti taṇḍulodakamaṇḍo. Akaṭayūsena attho hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, akaṭayūsa”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato akaṭayūsaṃ pātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha akaṭayūsanti asiniddho muggapacitapānīyo. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.269) pana vimativinodaniyañca (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.267-269) “akaṭayūsenāti anabhisaṅkhatena muggayūsenā”ti vuttaṃ. Kaṭākaṭena attho hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kaṭākaṭa”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato kaṭākaṭaṃ pāyetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha kaṭākaṭanti sova dhotasiniddho. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.269) vimativinodaniyañca (vi. vi. ṭī. mahāvagga 2.267-269) “kaṭākaṭenāti mugge pacitvā acāletvāva parissāvitena muggayūsenā”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭicchādanīyena attho hoti, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, paṭicchādanīya”nti (mahāva. 269) vacanato paṭicchādanīyaṃ pātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha paṭicchādanīyenāti maṃsarasena.

In the discussion on a congested body: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to drink a purgative' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible for a bhikkhu with a congested body to drink a purgative. Here, ‘a congested body’ means a body with an excess of humors. There is a need for clear gruel; in accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, clear gruel' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible to drink clear gruel. Here, ‘clear gruel’ means the scum of rice-water. There is a need for unprepared broth; in accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, unprepared broth' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible to drink unprepared broth. Here, ‘unprepared broth’ means a non-greasy drink of boiled mung beans. But in the Sāratthadīpanī and the Vimativinodanī it is said: ‘“By unprepared broth” means by uncompounded mung bean broth.’ There is a need for prepared broth; in accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, prepared broth' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible to administer prepared broth. Here, ‘prepared broth’ means that same broth, washed and made greasy. In the Sāratthadīpanī and the Vimativinodanī it is said: ‘“By prepared broth” means by mung bean broth that has been boiled and strained without stirring.’ There is a need for a covering; in accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, a covering' (Mahāvagga 269), it is permissible to drink a covering. Here, ‘a covering’ means meat broth.

Loṇasovīrakakathā

The Discussion on Salted Sour Gruel

Loṇasovīrakakathāyaṃ [M 2.0419] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa loṇasovīrakaṃ, agilānassa udakasambhinnaṃ pānaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 273) vacanato gilānena bhikkhunā loṇasovīrakaṃ pātabbaṃ, agilānena udakasambhinnaṃ katvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ, tañca “pānaparibhogenā”ti vacanato vikālepi vaṭṭati.

In the discussion on salted sour gruel: In accordance with the words, 'I allow, bhikkhus, salted sour gruel for one who is sick, and for one who is not sick, mixed with water to be consumed as a beverage' (Mahāvagga 273), salted sour gruel should be drunk by a sick bhikkhu, while one who is not sick should consume it mixed with water. And in accordance with the words ‘to be consumed as a beverage,’ it is permissible even at the wrong time.

Tattha loṇasovīrakaṃ nāma sabbarasābhisaṅkhataṃ ekaṃ bhesajjaṃ, taṃ kira karonto harītakāmalakavibhītakakasāve sabbadhaññāni sabbaaparaṇṇāni sattannampi dhaññānaṃ odanaṃ kadaliphalādīni sabbaphalāni vettaketakakhajjūrikaḷīrādayo sabbakaḷīre macchamaṃsakhaṇḍāni anekāni [V 2.0311] ca madhuphāṇitasindhavaloṇatikaṭukādīni bhesajjāni pakkhipitvā kumbhimukhaṃ limpitvā ekaṃ dve tīṇi saṃvaccharāni ṭhapenti, taṃ paripaccitvā jamburasavaṇṇaṃ hoti, vātakāsakuṭṭhapaṇḍubhagaṇḍalādīnaṃ siniddhabhojanabhuttānañca uttarapānaṃ bhattajīraṇakabhesajjaṃ tādisaṃ natthi, taṃ panetaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pacchābhattampi vaṭṭati, gilānānaṃ pākatikameva. Agilānānaṃ pana udakasambhinnaṃ pānaparibhogenāti.

Here, salted sour gruel is a medicine compounded with all essences. It is said that in making it, one puts in the astringent juices of chebulic, emblic, and belleric myrobalan; all grains; all pulses; the cooked rice of the seven kinds of grain; all fruits such as bananas; all shoots such as rattan, screwpine, date palm, and bamboo; pieces of fish and meat; and many medicines such as honey, molasses, rock salt, and the three pungent spices. Then, having sealed the mouth of the pot, they set it aside for one, two, or three years. When it has fully matured, it becomes the color of rose-apple juice. For those who have eaten rich food and for those with ailments such as wind-disease, cough, leprosy, jaundice, and fistula, there is no such post-meal drink and medicine for digesting food. This is permissible for bhikkhus even after the meal; for the sick, it is taken as it is. But for the healthy, it is mixed with water and consumed as a beverage.

Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 2.191-192) pana “pānaparibhogenāti vuttattā loṇasovīrakaṃ yāmakālika”nti vuttaṃ. Vimativinodaniyaṃ (vi. vi. ṭī. 1.192) pana “pānaparibhogena vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Evaṃ pana vuttattā loṇasovīrakaṃ yāmakālikanti keci vadanti, keci pana ‘gilānānaṃ pākatikameva, agilānānaṃ pana udakasambhinna’nti vuttattā guḷaṃ viya sattāhakālika”nti vuttaṃ. Vajirabuddhiṭīkāyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. mahāvagga 263) pana “avisesena satipaccayatā vuttā[M 2.0420]. Imasmiṃ khandhake ‘anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa guḷaṃ, agilānassa guḷodakaṃ, gilānassa loṇasovīrakaṃ, agilānassa udakasambhinna’nti (mahāva. 284) vuttaṃ, tasmā siddhaṃ ‘satipaccayatā gilānāgilānavasena duvidhā’ti” vuttaṃ.

But in the Sāratthadīpanī it is said: “Because it is stated ‘to be consumed as a beverage,’ salted sour gruel is a limited-period permissible.” In the Vimativinodanī, however, it is said: “The connection is that it is permissible to be consumed as a beverage. But because it is stated thus, some say that salted sour gruel is a limited-period permissible, while others, based on the statement ‘for the sick, it is taken as it is, but for the healthy, it is mixed with water,’ say that like molasses, it is a seven-day permissible.” And in the Vajirabuddhiṭīkā it is said: “An allowance on occasion is stated without distinction. In this chapter it is said: ‘I allow, bhikkhus, molasses for the sick and molasses-water for the healthy; salted sour gruel for the sick and for the healthy mixed with water’ (Mahāvagga 284). Therefore it is established that ‘the allowance on occasion is twofold, according to whether one is sick or not sick.’”

Antovutthādikathā

The Discussion on Storing Inside, etc.

Antovutthādikathāyaṃ “tena kho pana samayena bhagavato udaravātābādho hoti, atha kho āyasmā ānando ‘pubbepi bhagavato udaravātābādho tekaṭulayāguyā phāsu hotī’ti sāmaṃ tilampi taṇḍulampi muggampi viññāpetvā anto vāsetvā anto sāmaṃ pacitvā bhagavato upanāmesi ‘pivatu bhagavā tekaṭulayāgu’nti. Jānantāpi tathāgatā pucchanti, jānantāpi na pucchanti, kālaṃ viditvā pucchanti, kālaṃ viditvā na pucchanti, atthasañhitaṃ tathāgatā pucchanti, no anatthasañhitaṃ, anatthasañhite setughāto tathāgatānaṃ. Dvīhi ākārehi buddhā bhagavanto bhikkhū paṭipucchanti ‘dhammaṃ vā desessāma, sāvakānaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmā’ti.

In the discussion on storing inside, etc., it is said: “Now at that time the Blessed One was afflicted with a disorder of wind in the stomach. Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: ‘On a previous occasion when the Blessed One was afflicted with a disorder of wind in the stomach, he found relief with a three-ingredient gruel.’ So he himself, having requested sesame, rice, and mung beans, stored them inside, cooked them himself inside, and offered it to the Blessed One, saying, ‘May the Blessed One drink the three-ingredient gruel.’ Though knowing, the Tathāgatas ask; though knowing, they do not ask. Knowing the right time, they ask; knowing the right time, they do not ask. The Tathāgatas ask what is connected with the goal, not what is unconnected with the goal; for the Tathāgatas, there is a barrier against what is unconnected with the goal. The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, question the bhikkhus on two grounds: ‘We will either teach the Dhamma or we will lay down a training rule for our disciples.’”

Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi ‘kutāyaṃ, ānanda, yāgū’ti. Atha kho [V 2.0312] āyasmā ānando bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Vigarahi buddho bhagavā ananucchavikaṃ, ānanda, ananulomikaṃ appatirūpaṃ assamaṇakaṃ akappiyaṃ akaraṇīyaṃ, kathañhi nāma tvaṃ, ānanda, evarūpāya bāhullāya cetessasi, yadapi, ānanda, anto vutthaṃ, tadapi akappiyaṃ. Yadapi anto pakkaṃ, tadapi akappiyaṃ. Yadapi sāmaṃ pakkaṃ, tadapi akappiyaṃ. Netaṃ, ānanda, appasannānaṃ vā pasādāya…pe… vigarahitvā dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā bhikkhū āmantesi – na, bhikkhave, anto vutthaṃ anto [M 2.0421] pakkaṃ sāmaṃ pakkaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ, yo paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anto ce, bhikkhave, vutthaṃ anto pakkaṃ sāmaṃ pakkaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Anto ce, bhikkhave, vutthaṃ anto pakkaṃ aññehi pakkaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Anto ce, bhikkhave, vutthaṃ bahi pakkaṃ sāmaṃ pakkaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Bahi ce, bhikkhave, vutthaṃ anto pakkaṃ sāmaṃ pakkaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Anto ce, bhikkhave, vutthaṃ bahi pakkaṃ aññehi pakkaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Bahi ce, bhikkhave, vutthaṃ anto pakkaṃ aññehi pakkaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Bahi ce, bhikkhave, vutthaṃ bahi pakkaṃ sāmaṃ pakkaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Bahi ce, bhikkhave, vutthaṃ bahi pakkaṃ aññehi pakkaṃ, tañce paribhuñjeyya, anāpattī”ti (mahāva. 274) vacanato sahaseyyappahonake ṭhāne vutthatā, tattha pakkatā, upasampannena sāmaṃ pakkatāti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ aṅgānaṃ sambhave sati tisso āpattiyo, dvinnaṃ sambhave dve āpattiyo, ekassa aṅgassa sambhave ekā āpattīti veditabbaṃ.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: ‘Ānanda, where is this gruel from?’ Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Blessed One of this matter. The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him: ‘Ānanda, this is unsuitable, uncongenial, inappropriate, not befitting a recluse, unallowable, not to be done. How could you, Ānanda, strive for such abundance? Ānanda, that it was stored inside is unallowable. That it was cooked inside is unallowable. That it was cooked by oneself is unallowable. This, Ānanda, is not for the confidence of the unconfident… and so on… Having rebuked him and given a talk on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus: ‘Bhikkhus, what is stored inside, cooked inside, and cooked by oneself should not be consumed. Whoever should consume it commits an offense of wrong-doing. If, bhikkhus, it was stored inside, cooked inside, and cooked by oneself, and one consumes it, one commits three offenses of wrong-doing. If, bhikkhus, it was stored inside and cooked inside but cooked by others, and one consumes it, one commits two offenses of wrong-doing. If, bhikkhus, it was stored inside and cooked outside but cooked by oneself, and one consumes it, one commits two offenses of wrong-doing. If, bhikkhus, it was stored outside and cooked inside and cooked by oneself, and one consumes it, one commits two offenses of wrong-doing. If, bhikkhus, it was stored inside and cooked outside but cooked by others, and one consumes it, one commits an offense of wrong-doing. If, bhikkhus, it was stored outside and cooked inside but cooked by others, and one consumes it, one commits an offense of wrong-doing. If, bhikkhus, it was stored outside and cooked outside but cooked by oneself, and one consumes it, one commits an offense of wrong-doing. If, bhikkhus, it was stored outside and cooked outside and cooked by others, and one consumes it, there is no offense.’ From this statement (Mahāvagga 274), it should be understood that when these three factors are present—its having been stored in a place suitable for sleeping together, its having been cooked there, and its having been cooked by an ordained person himself—there are three offenses; when two are present, there are two offenses; when one factor is present, there is one offense.

Anto vutthanti akappiyakuṭiyaṃ vutthaṃ. Sāmaṃ pakkanti ettha yaṃ kiñci āmisaṃ bhikkhuno pacituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sacepissa uṇhayāguyā sulasipaṇṇāni vā siṅgiveraṃ vā loṇaṃ vā pakkhipanti, tampi cāletuṃ na vaṭṭati. “Yāguṃ nibbāpemī”ti pana cāletuṃ vaṭṭati. Uttaṇḍubhattaṃ labhitvāpi pidahituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana manussā pidahitvāva denti, vaṭṭati. “Bhattaṃ vā mā nibbāyatū”ti pidahituṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, puna pākaṃ pacitu”nti (mahāva. 274) vacanato pubbe anupasampannehi pakkaṃ puna pacituṃ vaṭṭati. Vuttañhi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 274) “khīratakkādīsu [M 2.0422] pana sakiṃ kuthitesu aggiṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati punapākassa anuññātattā”ti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anto vāsetu”nti (mahāva. 274) vacanato [V 2.0313] dubbhikkhasamaye taṇḍulādīni anto vāsetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anto pacitu”nti (mahāva. 274) vacanato dubbhikkhasamaye anto pacituṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sāmaṃ pacitu”nti (mahāva. 274) vacanato dubbhikkhasamaye sāmampi pacituṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anto vutthaṃ anto pakkaṃ sāmaṃ pakka”nti (mahāva. 274) vacanato dubbhikkhasamaye tīṇipi vaṭṭanti.

‘Stored inside’ means stored in an unallowable dwelling. ‘Cooked by oneself’: here it is not allowable for a bhikkhu to cook any kind of food himself. If they add basil leaves, ginger, or salt to his hot gruel, it is not allowable for him even to stir it. But it is allowable to stir it thinking, ‘I will cool the gruel.’ Even having received partially cooked rice, it is not allowable to cover it. But if people give it already covered, it is allowable. It is allowable to cover it thinking, ‘Lest the rice cool down.’ From the statement, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, to recook’ (Mahāvagga 274), it is allowable to recook what was previously cooked by unordained persons. For it was said in the commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 274): ‘But in the case of milk, curds, and the like, once they have boiled, it is allowable to apply heat, since recooking has been allowed.’ From the statement, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, to store inside’ (Mahāvagga 274), during a time of famine it is allowable to store rice and the like inside. From the statement, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, to cook inside’ (Mahāvagga 274), during a time of famine it is allowable to cook inside. From the statement, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, to cook by oneself’ (Mahāvagga 274), during a time of famine it is allowable even to cook by oneself. From the statement, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, what was stored inside, cooked inside, and cooked by oneself’ (Mahāvagga 274), during a time of famine, all three are allowable.

Uggahitapaṭiggahitakathā

The Discussion on Taking Up and Receiving

Uggahitapaṭiggahitakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yattha phalakhādanīyaṃ passati, kappiyakārako ca na hoti, sāmaṃ gahetvā haritvā kappiyakārake passitvā bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipitvā paṭiggahāpetvā paribhuñjituṃ, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, uggahitaṃ paṭiggahitu”nti (mahāva. 275) vacanato tathā katvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, āpatti na hotīti.

In the Discussion on Taking Up and Receiving: "Bhikkhus, I allow that where one sees edible fruit and there is no one to make it allowable, one may take it oneself, carry it away, and upon seeing a person who can make it allowable, place it on the ground, have it received, and then consume it. Bhikkhus, I allow one to receive what has been taken up." (Mahāvagga 275) In accordance with this, it is permissible to consume it after having done so, and there is no offense.

Tatonīhaṭakathā

The Discussion on What Is Brought Out from There

Tato nīhaṭakathāyaṃ “paṭiggaṇhatha, bhikkhave, paribhuñjatha. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tato nīhaṭaṃ bhuttāvinā pavāritena anatirittaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 276) vacanato yasmiṃ dāne nimantitā hutvā bhikkhū bhuñjanti, tato dānato nīhaṭaṃ bhojanaṃ pavāritena bhikkhunā bhuñjitabbaṃ, na pavāritasikkhāpadena āpatti hoti. Vuttañhi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 276) “tato nīhaṭanti yattha nimantitā bhuñjanti, tato nīhaṭa”nti.

In the Discussion on What Is Brought Out from There: "Accept, bhikkhus, and partake. Bhikkhus, I allow one who has eaten and indicated satisfaction to partake of what is brought out from there, if it has not been made a leftover." (Mahāvagga 276) In accordance with this, when bhikkhus eat after having been invited to a meal, food brought out from that meal may be eaten by a bhikkhu who has indicated satisfaction; there is no offense under the training rule concerning having indicated satisfaction. For it is said in the Commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 276): "'What is brought out from there' means brought out from where they were invited and ate."

Purebhattapaṭiggahitakathā

The Discussion on What Is Received Before the Meal

Purebhattapaṭiggahitakathāyaṃ [M 2.0423] “paṭiggaṇhatha, bhikkhave, paribhuñjatha, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ bhuttāvinā pavāritena anatirittaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 277) vacanato purebhattaṃ paṭiggahetvā nikkhipitaṃ pavāritena bhikkhunā atirittaṃ akatvā bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, pavāritasikkhāpadena āpatti na hoti.

In the Discussion on What Is Received Before the Meal: "Accept, bhikkhus, and partake. Bhikkhus, I allow one who has eaten and indicated satisfaction to partake of what was received before the meal, if it has not been made a leftover." (Mahāvagga 277) In accordance with this, it is permissible for a bhikkhu who has indicated satisfaction to eat what was received before the meal and set aside, without making it a leftover; there is no offense under the training rule concerning having indicated satisfaction.

Vanaṭṭhapokkharaṭṭhakathā

The Discussion on What Is in the Forest and in a Lotus Pond

Vanaṭṭhapokkharaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 2.0314] “tena kho pana samayena āyasmato sāriputtassa kāyaḍāhābādho hoti. Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca ‘pubbe te, āvuso sāriputta, kāyaḍāhābādho kena phāsu hotī’ti. Bhisehi ca me, āvuso, muḷālikāhi cāti…pe… atha kho āyasmato sāriputtassa bhise ca muḷālikāyo ca paribhuttassa kāyaḍāhābādho paṭippassambhi…pe… paṭiggaṇhatha, bhikkhave, paribhuñjatha. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vanaṭṭhaṃ pokkharaṭṭhaṃ bhuttāvinā pavāritena anatirittaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 278) vacanato vanaṭṭhaṃ pokkharaṭṭhaṃ pavāritena bhikkhunā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, pavāritasikkhāpadena āpatti na hoti. Tattha vanaṭṭhaṃ pokkharaṭṭhanti vane ceva paduminigacche ca jātaṃ.

In the Talk on What Is in the Forest and in a Lotus Pond: "Now at that time the Venerable Sāriputta was afflicted with a burning sensation in the body. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna went to the Venerable Sāriputta and said to him: 'Friend Sāriputta, what has previously brought you relief from this burning sensation in the body?' 'Friend, by lotus roots and lotus stalks.' … Then, after the Venerable Sāriputta had consumed the lotus roots and lotus stalks, his burning sensation in the body subsided. … 'Accept, monks, and partake. Monks, I allow one who has eaten and indicated satisfaction to partake of what is in the forest and in a lotus pond, if it has not been made a leftover.' (Mahāvagga 278) In accordance with this, it is permissible for a monk who has indicated satisfaction to consume what is in the forest and in a lotus pond; there is no offense under the training rule concerning having indicated satisfaction. Herein, 'what is in the forest and in a lotus pond' means what has grown in the forest and in a clump of lotuses.

Akatakappakathā

The Talk on What Has Not Been Made Allowable

Akatakappakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, abījaṃ nibbaṭṭabījaṃ akatakappaṃ phalaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 278) vacanato abījañca nibbaṭṭabījañca [M 2.0424] phalaṃ aggisatthanakhehi samaṇakappaṃ akatvāpi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha abījanti taruṇaphalaṃ, yassa bījaṃ aṅkuraṃ na janeti. Nibbaṭṭabījanti bījaṃ nibbaṭṭetvā apanetvā paribhuñjitabbakaṃ ambapanasādi, tāni phalāni kappiyakārake asati kappaṃ akatvāpi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

In the Talk on What Has Not Been Made Allowable: "Monks, I allow the consumption of fruit that is seedless or has had its seed removed, without it having been made allowable." (Mahāvagga 278) In accordance with this, it is permissible to consume fruit that is seedless or has had its seed removed even without making it suitable for a recluse by means of fire, a knife, or fingernails. Herein, 'seedless' means a young fruit whose seed does not generate a sprout. 'With its seed removed' means mango, jackfruit, and the like, which are to be consumed after the seed has been taken out and removed. It is permissible to consume these fruits without making them allowable in the absence of a person to make them allowable.

Yāgukathā

The Talk on Gruel

Yāgukathāyaṃ “dasayime, brāhmaṇa, ānisaṃsā yāguyā. Katame dasa, yāguṃ dento āyuṃ deti, vaṇṇaṃ deti, sukhaṃ deti, balaṃ deti, paṭibhānaṃ deti, yāgupītā khudaṃ paṭihanati, pipāsaṃ vineti, vātaṃ anulometi, vatthiṃ sodheti, āmāvasesaṃ pāceti. Ime kho, brāhmaṇa, dasānisaṃsā yāguyāti.

In the Talk on Gruel: "Brahmin, there are these ten benefits of gruel. What ten? One who gives gruel gives life, gives complexion, gives happiness, gives strength, gives ready wit. Having drunk gruel, one wards off hunger, dispels thirst, regulates the bodily winds, cleanses the bladder, and digests undigested food-remains. These, brahmin, are the ten benefits of gruel."

‘Yo [V 2.0315] saññatānaṃ paradattabhojinaṃ;

Kālena sakkacca dadāti yāguṃ;

Dasassa ṭhānāni anuppavecchati;

Āyuñca vaṇṇañca sukhaṃ balañca.

"One who in due season respectfully gives gruel to the restrained who eat what is given by others, provides ten things for them: life and complexion, happiness and strength.

‘Paṭibhānamassa upajāyate tato;

Khuddaṃ pipāsañca byapaneti vātaṃ;

Sodheti vatthiṃ pariṇāmeti bhattaṃ;

Bhesajjametaṃ sugatena vaṇṇitaṃ.

Ready wit arises in him from it; it dispels hunger, thirst, and bodily winds; it cleanses the bladder and digests food. This medicine is praised by the Well-Gone One.

‘Tasmā hi yāguṃ alameva dātuṃ;

Niccaṃ manussena sukhatthikena;

Dibbāni vā patthayatā sukhāni;

Mānussasobhagyatamicchatā vā’ti.

Therefore a person who is seeking happiness, whether aspiring to divine felicity or wishing for human good fortune, should always and properly give gruel."

Atha kho bhagavā taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ imāhi gāthāhi anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Atha kho bhagavā etasmiṃ nidāne etasmiṃ pakaraṇe dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā bhikkhū āmantesi – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yāguñca madhugoḷakañcā”ti [M 2.0425] (mahāva. 282) vacanato yāguñca madhugoḷakañca sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Anumodanāgāthāya “patthayataṃ icchata”nti padānaṃ “alameva dātu”nti iminā sambandho. Sace pana “patthayatā icchatā”ti pāṭho atthi, soyeva gahetabbo. “Na, bhikkhave, aññatra nimantitena aññassa bhojjayāgu paribhuñjitabbā, yo paribhuñjeyya, yathādhammo kāretabbo”ti (mahāva. 283) vacanato tathā bhuñjantassa paramparabhojanasikkhāpadena āpatti hoti. Bhojjayāgūti yā pavāraṇaṃ janeti. Yathādhammo kāretabboti paramparabhojanena kāretabbo.

Then the Blessed One, having expressed his appreciation to that brahmin with these verses, rose from his seat and departed. Then the Blessed One, on that occasion, in that connection, after giving a talk on the Dhamma, addressed the monks: "Monks, I allow gruel and honey-lumps." (Mahāvagga 282) In accordance with this, it is permissible to accept gruel and honey-lumps. In the verse of appreciation, the words "patthayataṃ icchataṃ" are connected with "alameva dātuṃ." But if the reading is "patthayatā icchatā," that very one should be taken. "Monks, one should not partake of another's food-gruel unless one has been invited; whoever should partake is to be dealt with in accordance with the rule." (Mahāvagga 283) In accordance with this, for one who eats thus, there is an offense under the training rule on consecutive meals. "Food-gruel" is that which requires an indication of satisfaction. "Is to be dealt with in accordance with the rule" means he is to be dealt with for the offense of consecutive meals.

Guḷakathā

The Talk on Sugar

Guḷakathāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa guḷaṃ, agilānassa guḷodaka”nti (mahāva. 284) vacanato [V 2.0316] gilāno bhikkhu guḷapiṇḍaṃ vikālepi khādituṃ vaṭṭati. Agilāno pana udakasambhinnaṃ katvā guḷodakaparibhogena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. “Gilānassa guḷanti tathārūpena byādhinā gilānassa pacchābhattaṃ guḷaṃ anujānāmīti attho”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 284) vuttaṃ. “Tathārūpena byādhinā”ti vuttattā yathārūpena byādhinā gilānassa guḷo paribhuñjitabbo hoti, tathārūpena eva byādhinā gilānassāti vuttaṃ viya dissati, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

In the Talk on Sugar: "I allow, monks, sugar for the sick and sugar-water for the non-sick." (Mahāvagga 284) In accordance with this, a sick monk is permitted to eat a lump of sugar even at the wrong time. A non-sick one, however, may consume it by mixing it with water in the form of sugar-water. "'Sugar for the sick' means 'I allow sugar after the meal for one who is sick with such a condition'; this is the meaning stated in the commentary (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 284). Because it is stated, 'sick with such a condition,' it seems to imply that sugar should be consumed by one who is sick with that specific kind of condition. This should be investigated and understood carefully.

Ettakāsu kathāsu yā yā saṃvaṇṇetabbappakaraṇe na dissati, sā sā amhehi pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kosallatthaṃ pāḷito ca aṭṭhakathāto ca gahetvā ṭīkācariyānaṃ vacanehi alaṅkaritvā ṭhapitā, tasmā nikkaṅkhā hutvā paṇḍitā upadhārentu.

In these talks, whatever is not found in the section to be commented upon, that we have set down—having taken it from the Pāli and the commentaries and adorned it with the words of the subcommentary teachers—for the proficiency of the virtuous monks. Therefore, let the wise examine it without doubt.

Catumahāpadesakathā

The Discourse on the Four Great Authorities

67. Yaṃ [M 2.0426] bhikkhavetiādi mahāpadesakathā nāma. Tattha mahante atthe upadissati etehīti mahāpadesā, mahantā vā atthā padissanti paññāyanti etthāti mahāpadesā, mahantānaṃ vā atthānaṃ padeso pavattidesoti mahāpadesā. Ke te? Imeyeva cattāro pāṭhā, atthā vā. Tena vuttaṃ “ime cattāro mahāpadese”tiādi. Tattha dhammasaṅgāhakattherāti mahākassapādayo. Suttaṃ gahetvāti “ṭhapetvā dhaññaphalarasa”ntiādikaṃ suttaṃ gahetvā upadhārento. Satta dhaññānīti –

67. This is called the Discourse on the Great Authorities, beginning with "O monks." Herein, great meanings are indicated by these; thus, they are called great authorities (mahāpadesā); or great meanings are seen and understood in these; thus, they are called great authorities; or they are the grounds and sources of great meanings; thus, they are called great authorities. What are they? These very four texts, or meanings. Therefore, it is said, "These four great authorities," and so on. Herein, the elders who compiled the Dhamma refers to Mahākassapa and others. Taking up a sutta means taking up a sutta like "setting aside grains, fruits, and juices," and so on, and then considering it. The seven grains are—

“Sāli vīhi ca kudrūso, godhumo varako yavo;

Kaṅgūti satta dhaññāni, nīvārādī tu tabbhidā”ti –.

"Sāli-rice and vīhi-rice, kodo millet, wheat, varaka, barley, and foxtail millet are the seven grains; wild rice and others are varieties of these."

Vuttāni satta dhaññāni. Sabbaṃ aparaṇṇanti muggamāsādayo. Aṭṭha pānānīti ambapānaṃ jambupānaṃ cocapānaṃ mocapānaṃ sālukapānaṃ muddikapānaṃ madhukapānaṃ phārusakapānañca.

The seven kinds of grain have been stated. All other grains means mung beans, other beans, and so on. The eight kinds of drinks are: mango drink, rose-apple drink, coconut drink, banana drink, lotus-root drink, grape drink, mahua drink, and phārusaka drink.

Iminā nayenāti suttānulomanayena. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “suttānulomaṃ nāma cattāro mahāpadesā”ti. Pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca anapekkhitvāti pāḷiyaṃ nītatthato āgatameva aggahetvā[V 2.0317]. Aññānipīti tato aññānipi. Etena mahāpadesā nāma na kevalaṃ yathāvuttā eva, atha kho anekāni nānappakārāni vinayadharassa ñāṇānubhāvappakāsitānīti dasseti.

By this method, that is, by conformity with the Suttas. For it is said in the commentary, "Conformity with the Suttas is called the four great authorities." 'Without being limited to the Pāli and the commentary' means not accepting only what is derived from the explicit meaning in the Pāli. 'And other things too' means other things besides those. By this, it is shown that the great authorities are not only as stated, but are also the many diverse kinds manifested through the power of knowledge of a Vinaya expert.

Ānisaṃsakathā

The Discourse on Advantages

68. Ānisaṃsakathāyaṃ vinayaṃ dhāretīti vinayadharo, sikkhanavācanamanasikāravinicchayanatadanulomakaraṇādinā vinayapariyattikusalo [M 2.0427] bhikkhu. Vinayapariyattimūlaṃ etesanti vinayapariyattimūlakā. Ke te? Pañcānisaṃsā. Vinayapariyattiyeva mūlaṃ kāraṇaṃ katvā labhitabbaānisaṃsā, na aññapariyattiṃ vā paṭipattiādayo vā mūlaṃ katvāti attho. Atha vā pariyāpuṇanaṃ pariyatti, vinayassa pariyatti vinayapariyatti, sā mūlaṃ etesanti vinayapariyattimūlakā, vinayapariyāpuṇanahetubhavā ānisaṃsāti attho. “Katame”tiādinā tesaṃ pañcānisaṃsādīnaṃ sarūpaṃ pucchitvā “attano”tiādinā vissajjetvā taṃ vacanaṃ pāḷiyā samatthetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādimāha.

68. In this discourse on benefits, a 'Vinayadhara' is one who upholds the discipline, a monk skilled in the learning of the Vinaya through study, recitation, reflection, investigation, acting in accordance with it, and so on. These have the learning of the Vinaya as their root, thus they are `vinayapariyattimūlakā`. What are they? The five benefits. The meaning is: the benefits are to be obtained by making the learning of the Vinaya itself the root, not by making other kinds of learning or practice the root. Alternatively, `pariyatti` means learning, and `vinayapariyatti` means the learning of the Vinaya; these have that as their root; thus, `vinayapariyattimūlakā` means benefits having the learning of the Vinaya as their cause. Having asked about the nature of those five benefits, beginning with 'Which are they?' and having answered, beginning with 'for oneself,' etc., in order to support that statement with the Pāli, he said, 'For it has been stated,' etc.

Evaṃ pañcānisaṃsānaṃ sarūpaṃ dassetvā idāni teyeva vitthārato dassetuṃ “kathamassā”tiādinā pucchitvā “idhekacco”tiādinā vissajjeti. Tattha attano sīlakkhandhasuguttabhāvo nāma āpattianāpajjanabhāveneva hoti, no aññathāti āpattiāpajjanakāraṇaṃ dassetvā tadabhāvena anāpajjanaṃ dassetuṃ “āpattiṃ āpajjanto chahākārehi āpajjatī”tiādimāha. Tattha –

Having thus shown the nature of the five benefits, now to explain them in detail, it is asked, 'How is it?' and answered with, 'Here, a certain one...' Herein, the state of one's own aggregate of virtue being well-guarded is precisely the state of not incurring an offense, not otherwise. Therefore, after showing the cause of incurring an offense, to show the state of not incurring one by its absence, it is said, 'One who incurs an offense does so in six ways.' Herein –

“Sañcicca āpattiṃ āpajjati;

Āpattiṃ parigūhati;

Agatigamanañca gacchati;

Ediso vuccati alajjipuggalo”ti. (pari. 359) –

"He intentionally commits an offense; he conceals the offense; and he goes a wrong going; such a person is called shameless."

Vuttena alajjīlakkhaṇena na lajjati na hirīyatīti alajjī, tassa bhāvo alajjitā. Natthi ñāṇaṃ etassāti aññāṇaṃ, tassa bhāvo aññāṇatā. Kukatassa bhāvo kukkuccaṃ, tena pakato kukkuccapakato, tassa bhāvo kukkuccapakatatā. Kappatīti kappiyaṃ, na kappiyaṃ akappiyaṃ[V 2.0318], tasmiṃ akappiye[M 2.0428], kappiyaṃ iti saññā yassa so kappiyasaññī, tassa bhāvo kappiyasaññitā. Itaraṃ tappaṭipakkhato kātabbaṃ, imesu pañcasu padesu yakāralopo, tasmā “alajjitāya āpattiṃ āpajjatī”tiādinā yojetabbāni. Hetvatthe cetaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ. Saratīti sati, samussanaṃ sammoso. Satiyā sammoso satisammoso, tasmā satisammosā. Hetvatthe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Idāni tāni kāraṇāni vitthārato dassetuṃ “katha”ntyādimāha. Taṃ nayānuyogena viññeyyameva.

By the stated characteristic of shamelessness, one who is not ashamed and has no moral dread is shameless (`alajjī`); their state is shamelessness (`alajjitā`). There is no knowledge in this, thus it is ignorance (`aññāṇaṃ`); its state is ignorance (`aññāṇatā`). The state of wrongdoing is remorse (`kukkuccaṃ`); one affected by it is remorseful (`kukkuccapakato`); their state is being remorseful (`kukkuccapakatatā`). What is allowable is `kappiyaṃ`; what is not allowable is `akappiyaṃ`. Regarding the unallowable, one who has the perception that it is allowable is `kappiyasaññī`; their state is `kappiyasaññitā`. The other should be understood from its opposite. In these five instances, the letter 'ya' is elided, so they should be construed as follows: 'They commit an offense due to shamelessness (`alajjitāya`),' and so on. This is an ablative expression in the sense of cause. Remembering is mindfulness (`sati`); forgetting is `sammoso`. The forgetting of mindfulness is `satisammoso`; hence, 'due to forgetfulness' (`satisammosā`). This is an instrumental expression in the sense of a cause. Now, to explain those causes in detail, it begins with 'how,' and so on. That should be understood by applying the method.

Ariṭṭho iti bhikkhu ariṭṭhabhikkhu, kaṇṭako iti sāmaṇero kaṇṭakasāmaṇero, vesāliyā jātā vesālikā, vajjīnaṃ puttā vajjiputtā, vesālikā ca te vajjiputtā cāti vesālikavajjiputtā, ariṭṭhabhikkhu ca kaṇṭakasāmaṇero ca vesālikavajjiputtā ca ariṭṭhabhikkhukaṇṭakasāmaṇeravesālikavajjiputtakā. Parūpahāro ca aññāṇañca kaṅkhāvitaraṇañca parūpahāraaññāṇakaṅkhāvitaraṇā. Ke te? Vādā. Te ādi yesaṃ teti parūpahāraaññāṇakaṅkhāvitaraṇādayo. Vadanti etehīti vādā, parūpahāraaññāṇakaṅkhāvitaraṇādayo vādā etesanti parū…pe… vādā. Ke te? Micchāvādino. Ariṭṭha…pe… puttā ca parūpahāra…pe… vādā ca mahāsaṅghikādayo ca sāsanapaccatthikā nāmāti samuccayadvandavasena yojanā kātabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Ariṭṭha the monk is `ariṭṭhabhikkhu`; Kaṇṭaka the novice is `kaṇṭakasāmaṇero`; those born in Vesālī are Vesālians (`vesālikā`); the sons of the Vajjis are Vajjiputtas; they are both Vesālians and Vajjiputtas, thus `vesālikavajjiputtā`; Ariṭṭha the monk, Kaṇṭaka the novice, and the Vesālikan Vajjiputtas are `ariṭṭhabhikkhukaṇṭakasāmaṇeravesālikavajjiputtakā`. 'Harming others,' 'ignorance,' and 'overcoming doubt' are `parūpahāraaññāṇakaṅkhāvitaraṇā`. What are they? Doctrines (`vādā`). Those of which these are the beginning are `parūpahāraaññāṇakaṅkhāvitaraṇādayo`. 'They speak by means of these,' thus they are `vādā` (doctrines). Those who hold these doctrines—harming others, ignorance, overcoming doubt, and so on—are `parū…vādā`. Who are they? Holders of wrong views. Ariṭṭha...puttas, and the holders of the doctrines of harming others..., and the Mahāsaṅghikas and so on, are called 'opponents of the Dispensation.' The construal should be made by way of a copulative compound. The rest is easily understood.

Ānisaṃsakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on benefits is concluded.

Iti vinayasaṅgahasaṃvaṇṇanābhūte vinayālaṅkāre

Thus, in the Vinayālaṅkāra, which is a commentary on the Vinayasaṅgaha,

Pakiṇṇakavinicchayakathālaṅkāro nāma

The Ornament of the Discourse on Miscellaneous Decisions

Catuttiṃsatimo paricchedo.

The Thirty-Fourth Chapter.

Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Concluding Discourse

Nigamagāthāsu [M 2.0429] paṭhamagāthāyaṃ saddhammaṭṭhitikāmena sāsanujjotakārinā parakkamabāhunā narindena ajjhesito so ahaṃ vinayasaṅgahaṃ akāsinti yojanā.

In the first of the concluding verses, the construction is: 'Having been requested by King Parakkamabāhu, who desired the stability of the true Dhamma and was an illuminator of the Dispensation, I composed this Compendium of the Vinaya.'

Dutiyatatiyagāthāyaṃ [V 2.0319] teneva parakkamabāhunarindeneva kārite ramme ramaṇīye pāsādasatamaṇḍite pāsādānaṃ satena paṭimaṇḍite nānādumagaṇākiṇṇe bhāvanābhiratālaye bhāvanāya abhiratānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ālayabhūte sītalūdakasampanne jetavane jetavananāmake vihāre vasaṃ vasanto hutvā, atha vā vasaṃ vasanto sohaṃ so ahaṃ yogīnaṃ hitaṃ hitabhūtaṃ sāraṃ sāravantaṃ imaṃ īdisaṃ vinayasaṅgahaṃ akāsinti yojanā.

In the second and third verses, the construction is: 'While residing in the delightful Jetavana monastery—which was built by that same King Parakkamabāhu, adorned with a hundred mansions (that is, ornamented with a hundred mansions), teeming with various kinds of trees, a home for those who delight in meditation (that is, a dwelling place for bhikkhus who delight in meditation), and endowed with cool water—I, that same person, composed this Compendium of the Vinaya, which is for the welfare of and is the essence for yogis.'

Sesagāthāsu iminā ganthakaraṇena yaṃ puññaṃ mayhaṃ siddhaṃ, aññaṃ ito ganthakaraṇato aññabhūtaṃ yaṃ puññaṃ mayā pasutaṃ hoti, etena puññakammena dutiye attasambhave tāvatiṃse pamodento sīlācāraguṇe rato pañcakāmesu alaggo devaputto hutvā paṭhamaṃ paṭhamabhūtaṃ phalaṃ sotāpattiphalaṃ patvāna antime attabhāvamhi lokaggapuggalaṃ nāthaṃ nāthabhūtaṃ sabbasattahite rataṃ metteyyaṃ metteyyanāmakaṃ munipuṅgavaṃ muniseṭṭhaṃ disvāna tassa dhīrassa saddhammadesanaṃ sutvā aggaṃ phalaṃ arahattaphalaṃ adhigantvā labhitvā jinasāsanaṃ sobheyyaṃ sobhāpeyyanti ayaṃ pākaṭayojanā.

In the remaining verses, the evident construction is as follows: 'By the merit I have acquired through composing this book, and by whatever other merit I have generated, by this meritorious deed may I, in my next existence, become a devaputta in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Rejoicing there, delighting in the virtue of good conduct and unattached to the five cords of sensual pleasure, may I first attain the primary fruit, the fruit of stream-entry. Then, in my final existence, having seen the Protector Metteyya—the supreme person in the world, a refuge who delights in the welfare of all beings, the bull among sages (that is, the chief of sages)—and having heard the teaching of the true Dhamma from that wise one, may I attain the supreme fruit, the fruit of arahantship, and thereby illuminate the Dispensation of the Victor.' This is the evident construction.

Etissāya pana yojanāya sati ācariyavarassa vacanaṃ na sampaṭicchanti paṇḍitā. Kathaṃ? Ettha hi ito dutiyabhave tāvatiṃsabhavane devaputto hutvā sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā antimabhave metteyyassa bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā arahattaphalaṃ labheyyanti ācariyassa patthanā, sā ayuttarūpā [M 2.0430] hoti. Sotāpannassa hi sattabhavato uddhaṃ paṭisandhi natthi, tāvatiṃsānañca devānaṃ bhavasatenapi bhavasahassenapi bhavasatasahassenapi metteyyassa bhagavato uppajjanakālo appattabbo hoti. Athāpi vadeyya “antarā brahmaloke nibbattitvā metteyyassa bhagavato kāle manusso bhaveyyā”ti, evampi na yujjati. Na hi brahmalokagatānaṃ ariyānaṃ puna kāmabhavūpapatti atthi. Vuttañhi abhidhamme yamakappakaraṇe (yama. 2.anusayayamaka. 312) “rūpadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa satteva anusayā anusentī”ti. Athāpi vadeyya “brahmalokeyeva ṭhatvā aggaphalaṃ labheyyā”ti, tathā ca ācariyassa vacane na dissati, “sobheyyaṃ jinasāsana”nti vuttattā bhikkhubhūtattameva dissati. Na hi bhikkhubhūto sāsanaṃ sobhāpetuṃ sakkoti. Abhidhammatthavibhāvaniyañca –

However, with this construction, the wise do not accept the venerable teacher's statement. How so? Here, the teacher's aspiration is that in his next life he would be reborn as a devaputta in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, attain the fruit of stream-entry, and then in his final existence, after hearing the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed Metteyya, he would attain the fruit of arahantship. This aspiration is unsuitable. For a stream-enterer has no relinking beyond seven existences, and for the Tāvatiṃsa devas, even after a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand existences, the time of the Blessed Metteyya's arising would not be reached. And if one were to say, 'Having been reborn in a Brahmā world in the interim, he would become a human at the time of the Blessed Metteyya,' this too is not tenable. For noble ones who have gone to a Brahmā world do not take rebirth again in the sense-sphere existence. For it is stated in the Abhidhamma, in the Yamakappakaraṇa: 'For one who has passed away from the form realm and is reborn in the sense-sphere realm, seven latent tendencies indeed lie dormant.' And if one were to say, 'He could attain the supreme fruit while remaining in the Brahmā world itself,' that is not seen in the teacher's statement; for since it is said, 'may I illuminate the Dispensation of the Victor,' it is seen that he must become a bhikkhu. For one who has not become a bhikkhu is not able to illuminate the Dispensation. And in the Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī:

“Jotayantaṃ [V 2.0320] tadā tassa, sāsanaṃ suddhamānasaṃ;

Passeyyaṃ sakkareyyañca, garuṃ me sārisambhava”nti. –

"Then may I see my teacher, a scion of Sāriputta, with a pure mind, illuminating his Dispensation, and may I pay him homage."

Bhikkhubhūtameva vuttaṃ. Athāpi vadeyya “antarā dīghāyuko bhummadevo hutvā tadā manusso bhaveyyā”ti, evampi ekassa buddhassa sāvakabhūto ariyapuggalo puna aññassa buddhassa sāvako na bhaveyyāti, ācariyo pana sabbapariyattidharo anekaganthakārako anekesaṃ ganthakārakānaṃ therānaṃ ācariyapācariyabhūto, tena na kevalaṃ idheva imā gāthāyo ṭhapitā, atha kho sāratthadīpanīnāmikāya vinayaṭīkāya avasāne ca ṭhapitā, tasmā bhavitabbamettha kāraṇenāti vīmaṃsitabbametaṃ.

It is indeed stated that he becomes a bhikkhu. Even if one were to say, 'In the interim, having become a long-lived earth-deity, he might then become a human,' even so, a noble person who has become a disciple of one Buddha would not again become a disciple of another Buddha. However, the teacher was a master of all the scriptural learning, the author of many books, and the teacher and grand-teacher of many elder authors. Therefore, he placed these verses not only here but also at the end of the Vinaya subcommentary named Sāratthadīpanī. For that reason, it must be that there is some reason for this, and this matter should be investigated.

Atha vā iminā…pe… devaputto hutvā paṭhamaṃ tāva phalaṃ yathāvuttaṃ tāvatiṃse pamodanasīlācāraguṇe rataṃ [M 2.0431] pañcakāmesu alaggabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ patvāna antime attabhāvamhi…pe… sobheyyanti yojanā. Atha vā iminā…pe… pañcakāmesu alaggo hutvā antime attabhāvamhi…pe… saddhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā tato paraṃ aggaphalaṃ arahattaphalaṃ adhigantvā jinasāsanaṃ sobheyyanti yojanā. Yathā amhākaṃ bhagavato dhammacakkappavattanasuttantadhammadesanaṃ sutvā aññātakoṇḍaññatthero sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā pacchā arahattaphalaṃ adhigantvā jinasāsanaṃ sobhesi, evanti attho. Ito aññānipi nayāni yathā therassa vacanānukūlāni, tāni paṇḍitehi cintetabbāni.

Alternatively, the construction is: 'By this… having become a devaputta, first attaining the fruit—that is, the benefit described as delighting in the virtue of good conduct and joy in Tāvatiṃsa and being unattached to the five cords of sensual pleasure—then in the final existence… may he adorn the Dispensation.' Or, the construction is: 'By this… being unattached to the five cords of sensual pleasure, in the final existence… having heard the teaching of the true Dhamma, may he first attain the primary fruit, the fruit of stream-entry, and thereafter attain the supreme fruit, the fruit of arahantship, and thus adorn the Dispensation of the Victor.' The meaning is that this is just as when our Blessed One delivered the discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the Elder Aññāta Koṇḍañña, having heard the teaching, attained the fruit of stream-entry and later, having attained the fruit of arahantship, adorned the Dispensation of the Victor. Other interpretations that are in accordance with the Elder's words should also be considered by the wise.

Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Concluding Verses is finished.

Nigamanakathā

The Concluding Verses

1.

1.

Jambudīpatale [M 2.0432] ramme, marammavisaye sute;

Tambadīparaṭṭhe ṭhitaṃ, puraṃ ratananāmakaṃ.

In the delightful land of Jambudīpa, in the renowned Maramma region, in the country of Tambadīpa, there was a city named Ratana.

2.

2.

Jinasāsanapajjotaṃ[V 2.0321], anekaratanākaraṃ;

Sādhujjanānamāvāsaṃ, soṇṇapāsādalaṅkataṃ.

It was a lamp for the Victor's Dispensation, a mine of various gems, an abode for good people, and adorned with golden mansions.

3.

3.

Tasmiṃ ratanapuramhi, rājānekaraṭṭhissaro;

Sirīsudhammarājāti, mahāadhipatīti ca.

In that city of Ratana, there was a king, a lord of many realms, named Sirīsudhammarājā, and also a great sovereign.

4.

4.

Evaṃnāmo mahātejo, rajjaṃ kāresi dhammato;

Kārāpesi rājā maṇi-cūḷaṃ mahantacetiyaṃ.

Thus named, of great majesty, he ruled the kingdom righteously. The king had a jeweled pinnacle made for the great cetiya.

5.

5.

Tassa kāle brahāraññe, tiriyo nāma pabbato;

Pubbakāraññavāsīnaṃ, nivāso bhāvanāraho.

In his time, in the great forest, there was a mountain named Tiriyo, a dwelling suitable for meditation for the residents of the Pubbakārañña forest.

6.

6.

Aṭṭhārasahi dosehi, mutto pañcaṅgupāgato;

Araññalakkhaṇaṃ patto, baddhasīmāyalaṅkato.

It was free from the eighteen faults, possessed the five factors, had attained the characteristics of a forest dwelling, and was adorned with a fixed boundary.

7.

7.

Tasmiṃ pabbate vasanto, mahāthero supākaṭo;

Tipeṭakālaṅkāroti, dvikkhattuṃ laddhalañchano.

Dwelling on that mountain was a very famous great elder named Tipeṭakālaṅkāra, who had twice received marks of honor.

8.

8.

Tebhātukanarindānaṃ, garubhūto supesalo;

Kusalo pariyattimhi, paṭipattimhi kārako.

He was a teacher to the three brother kings, very amiable, skilled in the scriptural learning, and an accomplisher in the practice.

9.

9.

Sohaṃ lajjīpesalehi, bhikkhūhi abhiyācito;

Sāsanassopakārāya, akāsiṃ sīlavaḍḍhanaṃ.

Requested by conscientious and amiable monks, for the benefit of the Dispensation, I composed this Sīlavaḍḍhana.

10.

10.

Vinayālaṅkāraṃ nāma, lajjīnaṃ upakārakaṃ;

Suṭṭhu vinayasaṅgaha-vaṇṇanaṃ sādhusevitaṃ.

Named the Vinayālaṅkāra, it is a help to the conscientious, a good explanation of the compendium of the Vinaya, frequented by the good.

11.

11.

Rūpachiddanāsakaṇṇe[M 2.0433][V 2.0322], sampatte jinasāsane;

Chiddasuññasuññarūpe, kaliyugamhi āgate.

When the year 2091 of the Victor's Dispensation had arrived, and the year 1009 of the Kaliyuga had come.

12.

12.

Niṭṭhāpitā ayaṃ ṭīkā, mayā sāsanakāraṇā;

Dvīsu soṇṇavihāresu, dvikkhattuṃ laddhaketunā.

This subcommentary was completed by me for the sake of the Dispensation—by me who has twice received the banner of honor in the two Golden Monasteries.

13.

13.

Iminā puññakammena, aññena kusalena ca;

Ito cutāhaṃ dutiye, attabhāvamhi āgate.

By this meritorious deed and by other wholesome actions, when I have passed away from here and arrived in a second existence,

14.

14.

Himavantapadesamhi, pabbate gandhamādane;

Āsanne maṇiguhāya, mañjūsakadumassa ca.

in the Himalayan region, on Mount Gandhamādana, near the Jewel Cave and the Mañjūsaka tree,

15.

15.

Tasmiṃ hessaṃ bhummadevo, atidīghāyuko varo;

Paññāvīriyasampanno, buddhasāsanamāmako.

may I be a terrestrial deity there, very long-lived and excellent, endowed with wisdom and energy, and devoted to the Buddha's Dispensation.

16.

16.

Yāva tiṭṭhati sāsanaṃ, tāva cetiyavandanaṃ;

Bodhipūjaṃ saṅghapūjaṃ, kareyyaṃ tuṭṭhamānaso.

For as long as the Dispensation lasts, may I with a delighted mind perform the veneration of cetiyas, the worship of the Bodhi tree, and the worship of the Sangha.

17.

17.

Bhikkhūnaṃ paṭipannānaṃ, veyyāvaccaṃ kareyyahaṃ;

Pariyattābhiyuttānaṃ, kaṅkhāvinodayeyyahaṃ.

May I perform services for the monks who are engaged in the practice; may I dispel the doubts of those devoted to the scriptural learning.

18.

18.

Sāsanaṃ paggaṇhantānaṃ, rājūnaṃ sahāyo assaṃ;

Sāsanaṃ niggaṇhantānaṃ, vāretuṃ samattho assaṃ.

May I be an ally to kings who support the Dispensation; may I be capable of restraining those who suppress the Dispensation.

19.

19.

Sāsanantaradhāne tu, mañjūsaṃ rukkhamuttamaṃ;

Nandamūlañca pabbhāraṃ, niccaṃ pūjaṃ kareyyahaṃ.

But at the disappearance of the Dispensation, may I constantly worship the reliquary, the excellent tree, and the Nandamūla cave.

20.

20.

Yadā [V 2.0323] tu paccekabuddhā, uppajjanti mahāyasā;

Tadā tesaṃ niccakappaṃ, upaṭṭhānaṃ kareyyahaṃ.

And when Paccekabuddhas of great fame arise, then may I constantly attend upon them.

21.

21.

Teneva attabhāvena, yāva buddhuppādā ahaṃ;

Tiṭṭhanto buddhuppādamhi, manussesu bhavāmahaṃ.

Remaining in that very same existence until the arising of a Buddha, at the time of a Buddha's arising may I be born among human beings.

22.

22.

Metteyyassa [M 2.0434] bhagavato, pabbajitvāna sāsane;

Tosayitvāna jinaṃ taṃ, labhe byākaraṇuttamaṃ.

Having gone forth in the Dispensation of the Blessed One Metteyya and having satisfied that Victor, may I receive the supreme prediction.

23.

23.

Byākaraṇaṃ labhitvāna, pūretvā sabbapāramī;

Anāgatamhi addhāne, buddho hessaṃ sadevaketi.

Having received the prediction and fulfilled all the perfections, in a future time I will become a Buddha for the world with its devas.

Vinayālaṅkāraṭīkā samattā.

The Subcommentary on the Vinayālaṅkāra is complete.
